## Social Network Diffusion, Influence, and Online Collective Behavior

This community centers on how information, opinions, products, and epidemics spread through social and temporal networks. Major themes include influence maximization and seed selection; cascade, meme, rumor, and misinformation dynamics; popularity and engagement prediction; diffusion-network inference; opinion formation, polarization, and collective intelligence; and community, topical, geographic, and multiplex structure.

Typical methods combine graph algorithms with probabilistic and dynamical models. Submodular optimization, adaptive and sequential seeding, sampling, centrality, random walks, percolation, and network design support influence and resource-allocation problems. Continuous-time diffusion is modeled using Hawkes and Poisson processes, survival analysis, epidemic and Bass models, stochastic differential equations, and point processes. Researchers also use Bayesian inference, sparse recovery, causal analysis, optimal control, and experiments to reconstruct networks and estimate social effects. Machine-learning approaches include recurrent and attention-based deep models, graph neural networks, representation learning, and multimodal prediction using textual, visual, temporal, and behavioral signals.

Recent work emphasizes dynamic, nonstationary, and competing diffusion; adaptive decisions with partial or myopic feedback; scalable real-time algorithms; neural microscopic cascade prediction; fairness, privacy, and polarization; and applications to misinformation prevention, cyberbullying, social good, marketing, community health, and online platform governance.

### Scientometrics, Research Evaluation, and Science Mapping

This community centers on measuring, mapping, and explaining scientific research and technological development. Major themes include citation-based impact assessment; alternatives and extensions to the h-index, journal impact factor, SNIP, I3, percentiles, PageRank, and other multidimensional indicators; field and fractional normalization; institutional, national, and individual performance comparisons; and the validity, fairness, and unintended consequences of rankings and research-assessment exercises. Gender, ethnicity, nationality, mobility, collaboration, funding, and internationalization are examined as determinants of scientific participation and impact.

Typical methods include bibliometric and scientometric network analysis of coauthorship, cocitation, citation, patent, editorial-board, and affiliation networks; community detection, clustering, overlay maps, and centrality measures; reference publication year spectroscopy and algorithmic historiography; statistical models for skewed citation distributions, productivity, and rankings; machine learning, embeddings, text mining, and neural networks for author disambiguation, topic identification, prediction, and trend detection. Comparisons among Web of Science, Scopus, Microsoft Academic, Google Scholar, and Dimensions are frequent.

Recent directions emphasize open and large-scale data, improved author and institution identification, contextual and weighted citations, interdisciplinarity, breakthrough and emerging-field detection, prediction of citations and research trends, and more equitable, transparent evaluation aligned with peer review.

### Semantic Retrieval, Clustering, and Structured Data Management

This community focuses on improving information organization and retrieval across text, mathematics, XML, and graphs. Major themes include probabilistic and user-guided text clustering, semantic text classification and search, mathematical information retrieval, XML summarization and query processing, and similarity computation in uncertain graphs.

Typical methods combine statistical models with structured knowledge. Multinomial mixture models produce soft document–cluster associations, while interactive clustering learns user-intended dimensions from minimal feedback. Text classification and retrieval exploit association-rule pruning, dependency syntax, hyperonymization, named entities, WordNet relations, and ontological features such as classes and identifiers. Mathematical retrieval combines formula and keyword queries through query expansion, result merging, and evaluation with metrics such as Bpref. XML systems use declarative XPath-based summaries, adaptive indexing, and distributed fragment placement to accelerate workloads. Graph research extends SimRank to uncertain networks using possible-world and random-walk formulations.

Recent trends emphasize semantic enrichment beyond keywords, integrating entities, lexical relations, formulas, and structural metadata. There is also movement toward interactive and adaptive systems: users guide clustering, XML summaries are refined declaratively, content placement adapts to workloads, and digital mathematical repositories support web-based publication and reuse.

abstracts x20|eb03e19d24b7a764c5447251fd.text:
## Information Diffusion and Dynamics in Social Networks

This community studies how information, behaviors, and influence propagate through evolving online and social networks. Core themes include source identification from incomplete cascades, rumor and meme diffusion, cascade structure and semantics, product adoption, collective intelligence, and social-network-assisted recruitment. Researchers also examine attention, affect, virality, video engagement, popularity growth, and latent interactions such as remixing.

Typical methods combine diffusion and threshold models, continuous-time networks with tie decay, strategic games, influence maximization, and adaptive greedy algorithms with approximation guarantees. Empirical work uses large-scale Twitter, YouTube, scholarly, and cross-platform datasets, applying cascade analysis, topic modeling, community detection, centrality and clustering, statistical measurement, and scalable visual-meme detection. Studies also develop frameworks for limited data collection and partially observed cascades.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and adaptive settings: networks change as ties form or decay, users provide only myopic feedback, and observations are incomplete. Attention is shifting beyond simple views or network topology toward watch-time engagement, content-agnostic popularity factors, affect, semantics, and multimodal video signals. Applications increasingly target intervention and decision support, including malicious-source tracing, hot-topic discovery, political segmentation, marketing, and mobile crowd sensing.

abstracts x20|9149694b802d8a0651bbc55036.text:
## Scientometrics, Research Evaluation, and Scholarly Networks

This community studies how scientific knowledge, performance, and collaboration can be measured and mapped. Major themes include citation and impact indicators, field normalization, institutional and national comparisons, technology and research-front mapping, author recognition, and cognitive similarity. Several studies address equity and structure in academia, examining gendered collaboration, nepotism, and the North–South divide in Italian higher education.

Typical methods combine bibliometric databases (Web of Science, Scopus, Microsoft Academic, and Dimensions) with citation, co-citation, co-authorship, and bipartite-network analysis. Researchers develop centrality indices, fractional and source-normalized citation measures, stochastic performance models, similarity-adapted publication vectors, and network-based author-name disambiguation. Mapping studies use journal profiles, subject categories, publication-level indicators, expert validation, and precision/recall assessment.

Recent trends emphasize more reliable and field-sensitive evaluation: testing database concordance, statistical significance, and the universality of metrics; exploiting fine-grained textual and citation proximity; and delineating emerging interdisciplinary fields such as nanotechnology. Other work highlights changing scholarly communication in the digital age, where article-level visibility weakens the link between journal impact factors and paper citations, while newer platforms such as Dimensions expand the data infrastructure for impact assessment.

abstracts x10|9149694b802d8a0651bbc55036.text:
**Scientometrics, Research Evaluation, and Academic Networks**

This community studies how scientific and technological knowledge, researchers, and institutions can be mapped and evaluated. Major themes include technology-field relatedness and forecasting, citation-based assessment, research-front evolution, collaboration, and inequalities associated with gender, geography, and academic family ties. Studies examine Italy’s north–south divide, nepotism and career advancement, and gender differences in collaboration among top scientists.

Typical methods are large-scale bibliometric analysis using Web of Science, Scopus, patents, and publication records. Researchers construct citation, co-citation, author–paper bipartite, and collaboration networks; identify highly interconnected research fronts; and compare performance across matched groups, disciplines, ranks, and regions. Statistical comparisons, textual and reference similarity measures, percentile indicators, fractional citation counting, and models of citation dynamics are also prominent.

Recent directions emphasize more refined and interpretable metrics: the K-index for recognition, source-normalized and fractional impact measures, and analyses of how evaluation outcomes depend on journal choice. Co-citation research moves toward finer textual levels—from journals and articles to paragraphs and sentences—while dynamic studies link recent citation activity to future bursts. Overall, the community increasingly combines network structure, normalization, and temporal analysis to improve evaluation and understand the development of science and technology.

abstracts x10|eb03e19d24b7a764c5447251fd.text:
### Social Information Diffusion, Cascades, and Network Dynamics

This community studies how information, rumors, products, memes, and scholarly topics spread through evolving social and information networks. Major themes include source identification from partially observed cascades; comparing rumor-propagation mechanisms beyond a fixed Twitter graph; influence computation under limited data-access resources; and links between cascade structure, content, user profiles, affect, and virality. Other work examines strategic product adoption, collective intelligence in adaptive networks, latent interactions in video remixing, and the growth of meme popularity.

Typical methods combine diffusion, threshold, game-theoretic, and biological-inspired dynamical models with large-scale empirical analysis. Researchers use cascade traces, social-network and text data, multimodal signals such as visual memes, and scholarly metadata. Techniques include two-stage inference for reconstructing diffusion histories, scalable detection and topic modeling, approximate network maintenance, comparative cascade-size analysis, and optimization or complexity analysis of influence and equilibrium problems.

Recent trends emphasize moving beyond static, fully observed networks: incorporating mass media, absent or spontaneous participants, changing ties, limited probing, and latent content interactions. Studies increasingly connect structural complexity with semantics and spreading behavior, use very large datasets, and seek predictive explanations of popularity, hot topics, and collective decision quality.
