## Community Report: Semantic Search, Mathematical Information, and Graph Analytics

This community centers on intelligent retrieval and organization of heterogeneous information. A major theme is mathematical information retrieval: formula repositories, notation and identifier namespaces, math-aware indexing, formula rendering and embeddings, equation-aware question answering, and plagiarism detection using mathematical content and citations. Closely related work studies semantic text search through ontologies, named entities, WordNet, latent concepts, spreading activation, query expansion, and structured query reformulation.

Text classification is another strong focus, including authorship attribution, opinion-spam and sentiment detection, hierarchical and short-text categorization, document-type classification, and subject indexing. Methods include multinomial mixtures, naïve Bayes, vector-space and term-relevance models, k-nearest neighbors, k-medoids, association rules, genetic optimization, feature selection, and semantic relations.

A substantial graph-oriented stream develops SimRank and related similarity search, link analysis, role and tie-strength discovery, heterogeneous-network ranking, neighborhood-pattern mining, and attributed-graph associations. XML and semi-structured data receive attention through path summaries, tree edit distance, keyword search, adaptive redistribution, and multimodel management.

Recent directions emphasize scalable, dynamic, and top-*k* graph computation; formula embeddings and contextual mathematical representations; integrated scientific-document crawling; ontology-enhanced retrieval; personalized and diversified search; and applications combining machine learning with social, agricultural, and digital-library data.

abstracts x20|ec7c4d1352b38c5e727f4fdc5e.text:
### Semantic Retrieval, Scalable Graph Analytics, and Structured Scholarly Data

This community centers on organizing and searching complex digital information. Major themes include probabilistic and interactive text clustering, supervised text categorization, association-rule feature engineering, and semantic retrieval using named entities, WordNet, ontologies, and query expansion. Mathematical information retrieval receives particular attention through combined text–formula queries, repositories of formulae, identifier-definition extraction, and analysis of mathematical notation.

A second theme is XML data management at Web and peer-to-peer scale. DescribeX, LiquidXML, and ViP2P use declarative structural summaries, adaptive fragment redistribution, distributed hash tables, and materialized XML views to support efficient XPath and collection queries.

Graph analytics focuses strongly on similarity and pattern mining. Several works address SimRank through random walks, sampling, indexing, push-based processing, and possible-world models for uncertain graphs. Other methods propagate scores over website–image bipartite graphs or mine neighborhood patterns in single large labeled graphs.

Typical methods combine probabilistic modeling, vector-space retrieval, machine learning, clustering, graph propagation, random walks, sampling, indexing, and distributed storage. Recent directions emphasize semantic and multimodal retrieval, interactive user-guided clustering, uncertainty-aware and real-time graph similarity, provable scalability, and exploiting mathematical structure as searchable data.

abstracts x10|3e1b7b82094c051109804d31b6.text:
## Community and Temporal Network Analysis

This community centers on extracting structure, behavior, and predictive signals from complex, social, and temporal networks. A major theme is community discovery: work examines how to classify detection methods, evaluate partitions using multiple criteria, and improve scalability and stability through LabelRank’s controlled label propagation.

A second theme is modeling network evolution. Studies address online social-network assembly and the effects of growth, adoption, and user heterogeneity; dynamic visualization seeks to preserve the mental map across successive layouts; and the temporal event graph provides a static, lossless representation based on inter-event times and temporal motifs.

Typical methods include graph-based centrality and pair-dependency measures for ranking criminal intermediaries, survival models and generalized linear models for peer effects in subscriber churn, and supervised or unsupervised techniques for detecting static and dynamic, labelled and unlabelled social-network anomalies. Link prediction is extended to weighted networks through reliable-route similarity indices capable of predicting both links and weights.

Recent directions emphasize multi-criteria evaluation, robust and reproducible community algorithms, temporal representations, dynamic visualization, heterogeneous network growth, and practical detection or prediction in large real-world networks.

titles<=300|3e1b7b82094c051109804d31b6be.text:
## Community Detection and Analysis in Complex Networks

This community spans community discovery, network structure, and scalable graph mining across social, temporal, multiplex, signed, attributed, and biological networks. Major themes include identifying disjoint, overlapping, fuzzy, hierarchical, role-based, and core–periphery communities; evaluating partition quality and stability; understanding detectability, modularity, polarization, and structural diversity; and applying communities to anomaly detection, fraud, recommendations, influence, vulnerability, and social behavior.

Typical methods include modularity optimization and its multilayer extensions, stochastic block models and degree-corrected variants, label propagation, spectral and nonlinear optimization, belief propagation, random walks, personalized PageRank, heat kernels, conductance-based seed expansion, density and k-truss methods, and manifold or kernel clustering. Researchers also use graph sampling, motif and triangle counting, graph signal processing, matrix completion, graph grammars, and generative models to analyze or reconstruct large networks.

Recent trends emphasize dynamic and streaming networks, temporal community tracking, multilayer and multiplex structure, attributed and signed graphs, local and distributed algorithms, and scalable computation for massive graphs. Work increasingly addresses uncertainty, sampling bias, missing edges, adversarial attacks, robustness, privacy, and principled model selection, while linking community structure to centrality, diffusion, link prediction, and real-world social and information processes.

abstracts x20|3e1b7b82094c051109804d31b6.text:
## Community-Centric Analysis of Complex and Social Networks

This community focuses on detecting, evaluating, and interpreting structure in complex, social, and temporal networks. Major themes include community discovery and quality assessment, including multi-criteria evaluation, classifications of detection methods, fuzzy and overlapping modularity metrics, stabilized label propagation (LabelRank), multilayer probabilistic modeling, and inclusive approaches that reduce bias against low-degree nodes. Distributed dynamics, such as two-choices majority processes, are also studied for recovering communities through metastable internal consensus.

A second theme is node importance and relational influence. Methods include reliance-based intermediary ranking, evolving-teleportation PageRank, core–periphery analysis of peer influence, survival and generalized panel-data models for churn, and studies of smartphone adoption. Network prediction and inference are addressed through reliable-route weighted link prediction and analyses of sampling bias.

Additional work examines temporal structure and visualization, using temporal event graphs, regularized dynamic layouts, and diffusion-based signal distances. Security-oriented research covers static and dynamic anomaly detection and fraud de-anonymization using behavioral traits and graph cuts.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic, multilayer, weighted, and heterogeneous networks; probabilistic and variational inference; distributed algorithms; robustness and debiasing; and applications to online fraud, telecommunications, and evolving social systems.

abstracts x20|6c41f2f8cb4e737c4349f13fc4.text:
## Multilayer Social Networks, Identity, and Dynamic Prediction

This community centers on computational analysis of complex social and information networks, especially multiplex and multilayer structures. Major themes include measuring multilayer centrality, modeling interacting spreading processes, detecting evolving groups, studying homophily across online/offline ties, and analyzing coevolving relationships.

A second focus is prediction and recommendation: papers develop link-prediction indices using common neighbors, triangles, clustering coefficients, structural similarity, homophily, and cross-layer dependencies. Social recommendation systems use weighted direct, semantic, and object-based relations. Related work addresses sampling heterogeneous networks, generating massive synthetic graphs with specified degree distributions, and characterizing random-key networks through triangle counts, clustering, and small-world properties.

Identity and cross-platform analysis are prominent. Research introduces datasets for cross-platform personas and methods for unsupervised user identity linkage, factoid embedding, and cross-device matching using feature engineering, negative sampling, and model selection. Privacy, deanonymization, and fragmented digital identities provide important motivations.

Typical methods combine graph-theoretic measures, community and evolution algorithms, probabilistic network models, topic modeling, sentiment analysis, embedding, optimization, and empirical evaluation on social-media, email, browsing, and mobile-sensing data. Recent trends emphasize dynamic multiplex networks, sparse-observation disease tracking, misinformation assistance through related fact checks, and integrated analysis of heterogeneous data sources.

titles<=300|6c41f2f8cb4e737c4349f13fc46f.text:
## Multilayer Social Networks, Diffusion, and Identity

This community centers on modeling and mining social networks as multiplex, multilayer, dynamic, and heterogeneous systems. Major themes include community and group evolution, link prediction, centrality and influence, information and epidemic diffusion, social contagion, and network robustness. A parallel line studies online identity across platforms, profile matching, re-identification, de-anonymization, privacy, and the relationship between online and offline ties.

Typical methods combine structural measures—clustering coefficients, similarity, mutual information, graphlets, centrality, shortest paths, and network geometry—with probabilistic, optimization, and learning approaches. Community research uses Louvain, Infomap, GED, temporal clustering, and evolutionary models. Diffusion studies employ branching processes, epidemic and competing-spreading models, game theory, graph-coupled HMMs, sampling, and influence-aware estimation. Identity linkage relies on record linkage, embeddings, stylometry, graph matching, active alignment, tensor decomposition, and graph neural networks. Social-media analysis also uses language models, sentiment classification, association rules, anomaly detection, and data fusion.

Recent directions emphasize coevolving and interdependent layers, layer similarity and entanglement, robust attacks and privacy, large-scale synthetic and real-world datasets, and multimodal behavioral signals from phones, mobility, and proximity. Applications increasingly target misinformation, spam, health surveillance, mental health, recommendations, organizational knowledge diffusion, and cross-platform user behavior.

titles<=300|facb6e0ef3714962c5c2f5d7665a.text:
## Social Media Intelligence, Misinformation, and Political Manipulation

This community centers on analyzing social-media behavior, information diffusion, and online political communication. Major themes include fake news, rumors, clickbait, propaganda, trolls, social bots, extremist content, polarization, echo chambers, hate speech, and election manipulation. Additional work studies event detection, collective attention and emotion, popularity and trend prediction, user profiling, recommendation, privacy, censorship, and online abuse.

Typical methods combine network analysis with machine learning and natural-language processing. Researchers use community detection, matrix and tensor factorization, sentiment and linguistic analysis, embeddings, graph neural networks, deep neural networks, time-series and diffusion models, causal inference, weak and semi-supervised learning, and multimodal analysis of text, images, and video. Crowdsourcing, social signals, propagation structure, and platform metadata support detection and verification. Case studies frequently examine Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, Reddit, Gab, and political elections.

Recent trends emphasize early and real-time detection, generalizable and interpretable misinformation models, causal and adversarial approaches, coordinated-behavior detection, and cross-platform analysis. Increasing attention is given to state-sponsored influence operations, manipulated engagement, demographic and algorithmic bias, fairness in feeds and summarization, and geometric or graph-based deep learning. Researchers also develop datasets, monitoring platforms, and intervention strategies such as fact-checking, bot-mediated action, and misinformation mitigation.

abstracts x10|6c41f2f8cb4e737c4349f13fc4.text:
### Multilayer Social Networks and Social Data Mining

This community studies the structure, dynamics, and interpretation of social and multiplex networks. Major themes include multilayer centrality, online/offline tie strength, homophily, identity across platforms, privacy and deanonymization, community and group evolution, and interacting spreading processes. Other work addresses foundational network structure, including link prediction, triangles, clustering, small-world behavior, and random key graphs relevant to wireless sensor networks and recommender systems.

Typical methods combine graph-theoretic measures and local structural indices with empirical analysis of social-media and communication data. Examples include multilayer degree centrality, clustering-coefficient-based similarity for missing-link prediction, triangle-counting and zero–one-law analysis, and GED for detecting group evolution. Data-mining approaches include Apriori association-rule mining, quantitative and generalized itemset variants, topic modeling, and sentiment analysis. Dataset construction is itself a contribution, particularly for cross-platform user profiles.

Recent trends emphasize multiplex and cross-platform perspectives: jointly modeling online and offline relationships, studying identity and information leakage across services, and analyzing several spreading processes across network layers. There is also increasing interest in automated discovery of topics, sentiments, communities, and evolving groups from large social-media datasets.

abstracts x10|facb6e0ef3714962c5c2f5d766.text:
## Social Media, Political Networks, and Trustworthy Web Systems

This community studies how online platforms shape political discourse, public opinion, information quality, and network security. Major themes include multimodal event detection on Twitter; political community discovery and voter-preference inference; search-result and data-source bias; fringe-platform dynamics such as Gab; fake-news detection and containment; and privacy, application security, and vulnerability in complex networks.

Typical methods combine large-scale platform data with machine learning and network analysis. Examples include TF-IDF and text–image fusion for event mining, endorsement-filtered graphs and nonnegative matrix factorization for political communities, sparse learning and classifiers for preference prediction, and frameworks separating input-data bias from ranking-system bias. Other work aggregates crowd flags to prioritize fact-checking and limit misinformation spread, analyzes Facebook application installations temporally, and uses fractal dimension to improve network-vulnerability indices.

Recent directions emphasize selective digital traces rather than massive datasets, integrating online behavior with surveys, and examining how misinformation and political content move across mainstream and fringe communities. The portfolio also extends beyond centralized social media toward decentralized search, privacy-preserving content distribution, and more resilient web infrastructure.

abstracts x10|e38a6a43e09514d308dc4636aa.text:
### Social and Spatial Computing from Digital Traces

This community studies how online and mobile data reveal human experiences, behavior, and urban dynamics. Major themes include urban perception and sensory mapping—smell, sound, beauty, quietness, and happiness—as well as mobility, event coordination, commercial activity, and food culture. Other work examines large-scale information networks through multilingual, longitudinal Wikipedia link graphs.

Typical methods combine crowdsourcing, geotagged social-media content, mobile applications, and platform datasets with computational analysis. Researchers construct dictionaries of sensory terms, classify and aggregate user-generated descriptions, infer business ratings from review text, and translate perceptual votes into route recommendations. Graph construction and temporal snapshots support analysis of Wikipedia’s evolution, while mobility studies use distributed subtrajectory clustering. Streaming spatial algorithms detect bursty regions continuously, and econometric and diffusion analyses assess daily-deal purchases, social influence, and reputational effects.

Recent directions emphasize scalable analysis of massive, dynamic, and heterogeneous data: multi-year, multilingual graph datasets; real-time detection over spatial streams; distributed trajectory mining; and city-scale sensing from social-media imagery. The work also increasingly moves beyond conventional shortest-path or noise-focused urban services toward emotionally pleasant routes and richer representations of everyday sensory environments.

abstracts x20|facb6e0ef3714962c5c2f5d766.text:
## Social Media Graphs, Public Opinion, and Online Safety

This community studies social media as both a sensing infrastructure and a source of societal risk. Major themes include political communities, polarization, voter preference, search bias, misinformation, fringe platforms, and the relationship between network structure and belief. Other applications address event detection, public-health interventions, hydroinformatics, popularity forecasting, and crowdsourced mapping.

Typical methods combine network analysis with machine learning and matrix factorization. Researchers use retweet, endorsement, followership, and content networks; PCA and assortativity quantify political separation; sparse learning and classifiers infer voting behavior from digital traces. NMF and structured factorization identify communities, agreement, and overlapping beliefs. Other systems use TF-IDF and multimodal text-image mining, semi-supervised real-time detectors, crowd flags for fact checking, temporal analysis, and predictive learning. Graph algorithms also support distance queries and vulnerability assessment.

Recent work emphasizes early intervention and robustness: detecting fake news and spam, modeling how segregation and fact checking affect misinformation, deploying targeted social bots for health, and exposing Sybil and privacy threats. It also examines emerging or decentralized platforms such as Gab and the Decentralized Web, while increasingly distinguishing data-driven bias from ranking-system bias.

titles<=300|e38a6a43e09514d308dc4636aa69.text:
### Graphs, Cities, and Social Knowledge

This community centers on computational analysis of web, social, and spatial systems. A major theme is Wikipedia and Wikidata: multilingual link networks, cultural and geopolitical relations, biographies, gender and historical bias, article ranking, vandalism detection, completeness, navigation, and collective memory. Search and recommendation research addresses retrieval effectiveness, snippets, query expansion, library catalogs, food and recipe recommendation, route planning, event participation, and business or retail placement.

Urban and mobility studies use geolocated social media, check-ins, taxi and trajectory data, phone records, and crowdsourced narratives to study smells, sounds, walkability, deprivation, cultural interaction, venues, disasters, and unusual crowd events. Social-platform research examines influence, diffusion, political communication, online movements, extreme-right communities, collaboration, gender, and user behavior.

Typical methods include PageRank and reduced Google matrices, spectral and network analysis, temporal and multilayer graphs, Bayesian hypothesis testing, Markov and finite-state models, density-based spatial-textual clustering, trajectory compression and mining, learning-to-rank, topic modeling, graph and hypergraph neural networks, and ensemble classification.

Recent work trends toward scalable distributed algorithms, deep and self-attentive models, higher-order and heterogeneous networks, multimodal and cross-platform data, fairness and bias measurement, knowledge-base quality assessment, and real-time monitoring of social and urban phenomena.

abstracts x20|e38a6a43e09514d308dc4636aa.text:
## Graphs and Social Data for Spatial Intelligence

This community studies how large-scale digital traces can explain places, people, and information. Major themes include urban experience mapping (smell, sound, beauty, quietness, happiness), mobility and event behavior, spatial search, and detection of bursty regions. Other work analyzes online communities and markets, including Yelp ratings, daily-deal diffusion, Twitter-list curation, food imagery, and group scheduling. Wikipedia is treated as a multilingual knowledge graph for studying geopolitical ties, university influence, trends, and language differences.

Typical methods combine user-generated content, geotagged images, reviews, page views, hyperlinks, mobility traces, and crowdsourced judgments. Researchers apply graph algorithms such as PageRank, CheiRank, reduced Google matrices, and graph-based feature extraction; machine learning and learning-to-rank support rating prediction, recommendations, topic selection, and retrieval evaluation. Spatial clustering, probabilistic geospatial representation, dictionary construction, and distributed stream processing address geographic and temporal structure.

Recent directions emphasize scalable and continuous analysis, including distributed subtrajectory clustering and streaming burst detection; cross-language, longitudinal Wikipedia datasets; and richer multimodal, qualitative geographic data. Overall, the work increasingly connects computational models with subjective human perceptions and exploratory information needs.

titles<=300|d0fc387b501c0675f0400c1d78d3.text:
## Neural, Personalized, and Entity-Centric Information Retrieval

This community centers on improving search relevance across web, enterprise, academic, e-commerce, mobile, multimedia, and conversational settings. Major themes include learning-to-rank, ad hoc and passage retrieval, query understanding and expansion, question answering, entity-oriented and table search, personalization, recommendation, and unbiased online evaluation. Dataset search, web-content quality, spam detection, clustering, hashing, indexing, and event detection extend retrieval toward large-scale and dynamic collections.

Typical methods combine neural matching and ranking architectures—including BERT, Duet, PACRR, MatchPyramid, attention networks, recurrent and convolutional models—with traditional lexical models, relevance feedback, embeddings, graph and knowledge-base representations, and kernel pooling. Listwise, pairwise, groupwise, reinforcement-learning, bandit, and counterfactual approaches address ranking and exploration. Weak supervision, multi-task learning, adversarial adaptation, and representation learning are frequent strategies.

Recent work emphasizes deep contextual re-ranking, conversational and non-factoid question answering, entity and knowledge-graph semantics, semantic hashing and scalable nearest-neighbor search, and structured data such as web tables and data lakes. There is also growing attention to interpretability, robustness, privacy-preserving model sharing, efficient production systems, and correcting position and click bias through intervention, propensity estimation, and counterfactual learning.

abstracts x10|d0fc387b501c0675f0400c1d78.text:
### Information Retrieval: Ranking, Representations, and Search Systems

This community focuses on improving information retrieval across documents, queries, experts, mobile applications, datasets, and web content. Core themes include relevance ranking, expert finding in heterogeneous bibliographic networks, query understanding and clustering, dataset discovery, and unified search across apps. Several works seek to model relevance more explicitly: DeepRank decomposes ranking into detecting relevant locations, estimating local relevance, and aggregating signals. Other research combines textual evidence with authority ranking or uses language inference and question entailment to filter and rerank answers.

Typical methods are neural representation learning, including word2vec/query2vec, locally trained embeddings, semantic hashing, dimensionality reduction, and pretrained language models such as BERT and MT-DNN. These are paired with scalable clustering, multi-task learning, query expansion guided by concept hierarchies, and heterogeneous-network analysis. Traditional retrieval foundations remain important, including inverted files, file signatures, probabilistic ranking, and theoretical ranking principles.

Recent trends emphasize deep learning, pretrained models, semantic representations, conversational and intelligent-assistant search, and retrieval over dynamic multi-stage interactions. The scope is also expanding toward specialized resources such as datasets and mobile apps, while addressing practical constraints including limited training data, large documents, heterogeneous sources, and user signals.

titles<=300|9d9a000426ec8a5a2d692593bdb5.text:
## Semantic and Linked Digital Mathematics

This community focuses on transforming mathematical knowledge from static documents into structured, reusable, and interconnected digital resources. Major themes include semantic wikis (SWiM and wiki.openmath.org), digital mathematics libraries, linked-data publication of lecture notes, and long-term archival preservation, exemplified by Math-Net.Ru.

A central concern is **formalization**: the “dimensions of formality” in mathematical knowledge management and the editing of large corpora with Semantic LaTeX (sTeX) examine how mathematical content can be represented at different levels of machine interpretability. OpenMath content dictionaries provide a foundation for expressing mathematical concepts as linked data.

Typical methods include ontology engineering, semantic markup, knowledge graphs, digital-library infrastructure, community-based editing, and conversion of scholarly materials into interoperable linked-data formats. The Planetary system extends these ideas toward executable science, connecting mathematical and STEM papers with computational functionality.

Overall, the papers indicate a trend from digitizing and archiving mathematical literature toward building open, participatory ecosystems in which formalized mathematics can be searched, linked, analyzed, collaboratively maintained, and potentially executed.

abstracts x20|9d9a000426ec8a5a2d692593bd.text:
## Semantic and Linked Mathematical Knowledge Infrastructures

This community focuses on transforming mathematical and scientific literature into machine-readable, interconnected knowledge. A central theme is Mathematical Knowledge Management (MKM): formalizing symbols, concepts, document structure, classifications, and relationships so that collections can support search, browsing, reasoning, recommendation, and proof formalization.

Typical methods include semantic markup of LaTeX and mathematical documents using OMDoc, sTeX, XHTML, MathML, and RDFa; ontology engineering, including ontologies of document structure and mathematical concepts; and semantic wikis such as SWiM for collaborative editing of OpenMath content dictionaries. Linked Data principles are used to expose content dictionaries, lecture notes, and annotations as decentralized, interoperable web resources. Case studies address software-engineering corpora, educational lecture notes, and large mathematical archives such as Math-Net.Ru.

A parallel infrastructure theme is the Digital Mathematics Library: distributed institutional repositories and comprehensive digitization of historical and contemporary publications. More recent directions emphasize digital ecosystems combining repositories, text analysis, recommender systems, and analytics. Executable papers extend semantic publishing with interactive services that let readers inspect, manipulate, and explore scientific results. Overall, the work trends from digitization and metadata toward collaborative, ontology-driven, interactive, and executable mathematical knowledge.

abstracts x10|9d9a000426ec8a5a2d692593bd.text:
### Semantic and Linked Mathematical Knowledge Ecosystems

This community focuses on making mathematical knowledge machine-readable, interconnected, and usable beyond traditional document reading. Major themes include Mathematical Knowledge Management (MKM), semantic wikis, digital mathematics libraries and archives, formalization of mathematical documents, and Linked Data for OpenMath content dictionaries.

Typical methods combine domain-specific markup such as OMDoc, semantic LaTeX/STEX, XHTML+MathML+RDFa, and RDFa-based metadata with ontologies describing mathematical concepts, document structure, and multidimensional relationships. Semantic annotations support interactive browsing, querying, reusable content dictionaries, recommender systems, text analysis, and links between distributed repositories. Wiki interfaces enable collaborative authoring and maintenance, while executable-paper systems connect annotated publications to machine-comprehensible findings and interactive services.

The papers also emphasize large-scale infrastructure: reference digital library networks, comprehensive national archives such as Math-Net.Ru, and ecosystems such as OntoMath. Recent trends move from digitizing and archiving mathematical literature toward enriching it with formal semantics, exposing it as Linked Data, and enabling lightweight reasoning, interoperability, and exploration. Collaborative semantic editing and executable, interactive publications further position mathematical documents as active knowledge resources rather than static texts.

titles<=300|bb97977ff6fa8254d9371b37ce45.text:
## Semantic Infrastructures for Web Archives and Scholarly Knowledge

This community studies how digital information can be preserved, modeled, connected, and rediscovered over time. Major themes include web archiving and temporal access; repository and digital-object architectures; semantic layers for archives; scholarly communication; and persistent annotation, provenance, and versioning.

Typical methods combine focused and social-media-seeded crawling, archive profiling, temporal search, Memento and ResourceSync protocols, caching and routing evaluations, URI canonicalization, and techniques for recovering missing pages. Researchers also use knowledge graphs, ontologies, nanopublications, micropublications, Open Annotation, SharedCanvas, and linked-data integration to represent claims, evidence, entities, events, and evolving resources. Machine learning supports domain classification, entity relatedness, timeline summarization, prosopography, schema matching, and ranking. Large-scale experiments analyze web archives, social-media collections, scientific software, newspapers, and biomedical images.

Recent work emphasizes semantic and event-centric exploration of archives, cross-lingual timelines, human-assisted curation, persistent references to changing linked data, and integration across public and private repositories. There is growing attention to archival coverage, accessibility, temporal coherence, reproducibility, decentralized dissemination, preservation of software and obsolete formats, and infrastructure for open research knowledge graphs.

abstracts x10|bb97977ff6fa8254d9371b37ce.text:
### Durable Digital Objects and Web Archive Intelligence

This community studies how digital information can be modeled, preserved, discovered, and reused over time. A central theme is representing scientific and library materials as interconnected life-cycle components rather than isolated files, with persistent identifiers, aggregation, heterogeneous content, disseminations, and rights metadata. Fedora exemplifies extensible repository architecture, while VXA addresses format obsolescence by preserving executable decoders with compressed content.

A second major focus is web archiving: estimating resource creation dates, acquiring and parsing archived pages, identifying when collection seeds become off-topic, and understanding how users discover and access the Internet Archive. Research also examines Archive-It collections and the role of social bookmarking data in improving temporal search.

Typical methods include architectural system design, metadata and object modeling, virtual-machine-based preservation, evidence aggregation from multiple web services, large-scale HTTP acquisition and text extraction, archive-log analysis, and empirical study of collection and access patterns. Recent directions emphasize user-centered archive search, longitudinal and temporal retrieval, curator support, and integrating contextual or editorial information with aggregated digital-library content.

abstracts x20|d0fc387b501c0675f0400c1d78.text:
## Information Retrieval: Neural Ranking and Specialized Search

This community centers on improving information retrieval through richer representations, ranking models, and search applications. Major themes include document and answer ranking, query understanding and clustering, expert and dataset discovery, mobile and email search, web quality and spam detection, and similarity search over large-scale data.

Typical methods combine learning-to-rank with neural language models, embeddings, and structured signals. DeepRank models relevance through local evidence detection, local scoring, and aggregation, while monoBERT and duoBERT apply pointwise and pairwise BERT ranking in multi-stage systems. Other work uses permutation-invariant set models, multi-task learning, query expansion with locally trained embeddings and concept hierarchies, and context-based query vectors. Traditional and hybrid approaches include probabilistic ranking, bipartite ranking ensembles, kernel methods, twin support vector machines, clustering, signatures, and k-nearest-neighbor graphs. Dynamic retrieval is framed through utility functions incorporating user signals, multiple stages, and overall intent.

Recent trends emphasize pretrained transformers, passage-level retrieval for non-factoid question answering, conversational and unified mobile search, agent-oriented retrieval, and scalable approximate indexing. The community also increasingly addresses practical constraints—latency, private or sparse training data, massive collections—and demands interpretability for learned ranking decisions.

abstracts x20|bb97977ff6fa8254d9371b37ce.text:
### Digital Preservation, Web Archives, and Semantic Knowledge

This community focuses on preserving, organizing, and discovering heterogeneous digital information over time. Core themes include lifecycle-based modeling of scientific artifacts, flexible digital repositories, durable compression, and preservation of evolving Linked Open Data. A major strand addresses web archiving: estimating resource dates, acquiring and extracting content from mementos, managing collection scope, understanding archive usage, and supporting temporal search. Related work examines missing pages, changing titles, disappearing links, orphaned annotations, and the social and archival context of web resources.

Typical methods combine semantic and object-oriented modeling, persistent identifiers, aggregation frameworks, executable decoders and virtual machines, repository architectures, and query languages for multiversion data. Empirical studies analyze large web-archive collections, access logs, tweets, social-bookmarking data, annotations, and cross-collection evaluations. Search and crawling approaches use tags, popularity signals, lexical or title-based evidence, and social-media integration.

Recent trends emphasize fresher and more thematically coherent collection through focused crawling and social signals; richer temporal retrieval and preservation of evolving data; and stronger semantic representation of scientific claims, mechanisms, cultural objects, and research lifecycles. The work increasingly treats archives as interconnected, dynamic ecosystems rather than static stores.

titles<=300|388cdd1ebb963ca5482496724b59.text:
### Scalable Data Management for Graphs, Analytics, and Distributed Systems

This community focuses on the design, theory, and implementation of modern data-management systems. Major themes include RDF, SPARQL, property graphs, linked data, federated querying, graph traversal, reachability, path and pattern queries, and knowledge-graph reasoning. A second strong theme is scalable analytical processing: relational and array-based computation, machine learning over databases, data cubes, time series, stream processing, and Internet-of-Things analytics.

Typical methods combine formal complexity analysis with practical optimization. Researchers develop worst-case-optimal, multiway, geometric, and matrix-based joins; cost-based, heuristic, learned, and mixed-integer query planning; adaptive indexing, summaries, sketches, compression, and materialized-view maintenance. Parallel and distributed execution—using multicore systems, GPUs, MapReduce, in-memory databases, LSM storage, and specialized graph engines—is central, as are benchmarking and workload generation.

The papers also address correctness, provenance, incomplete and uncertain information, privacy, recovery, isolation, and coordination. Recent directions emphasize high-velocity ingestion and streaming graphs, temporal and continuous queries, declarative end-to-end machine-learning workflows, unified relational/linear-algebra abstractions, graph–relational interoperability, and blockchain-based storage, transactions, and cross-chain commitment.

abstracts x10|388cdd1ebb963ca5482496724b.text:
## Scalable Query Processing and Graph Data Management

This community focuses on efficient querying, optimization, and analysis of large, heterogeneous data. A major theme is RDF and SPARQL processing, including optimization of OPTIONAL (left-outer-join) patterns, federated and SPARQL-LD queries, and heuristic query reordering. Relational query optimization is addressed through mixed-integer linear programming for join-order selection, while worst-case-optimal parallel algorithms study communication costs for conjunctive queries.

Other work explores flexible representations and retrieval: fuzzy relational summaries support imprecise data and flexible queries, and size-constrained object summaries make relational keyword-search results more concise. Graph analytics is investigated both through relational platforms such as Vertica and specialized systems including Accumulo and D4M. These systems target high-throughput graph and network updates, reporting benchmarks of up to 100 million inserts per second and one billion updates per second.

The community also includes theoretical network dynamics, such as minimum-weight initializations for multilevel opinion spreading. Recent trends emphasize scalable distributed and in-memory processing, practical exploitation of mature database infrastructure, formal optimization techniques, and handling increasingly heterogeneous, federated, streaming, and uncertain data.

titles<=300|95a9b95b79bc50927dca68899001.text:
## Data Quality, Uncertainty, and Explainable Data Management

This community focuses on making heterogeneous, incomplete, uncertain, and inconsistent data usable. Major themes include entity resolution and consolidation; data fusion, truth discovery, and conflict resolution; integrity constraints, repairs, and consistent query answering; probabilistic databases and approximate inference; provenance, causality, responsibility, and query explanations; and ontology-mediated querying, schema mapping, and knowledge-graph integration.

Typical methods combine relational and logical techniques—Datalog, the chase, dependency theory, knowledge compilation, SAT/model counting, abductive diagnosis, and complexity analysis—with probabilistic models, Bayesian inference, Markov logic, generative models, and graph matching. Scalable implementations use blocking, locality-sensitive hashing, indexes, MapReduce, GPUs, distributed databases, and approximate query processing. Crowdsourcing is frequently integrated with machine learning through active labeling, human–machine cooperation, truth discovery, and adaptive task assignment.

Recent work emphasizes deep and transfer learning for entity matching and error detection, holistic and probabilistic data-cleaning pipelines, semantic table and schema understanding, and large-scale similarity search. Other emerging directions include causal data management and algorithmic fairness, interactive and human-centric explanations, source dependence and reliability, contextual data quality, and reproducible crowd-powered data processing.

abstracts x10|95a9b95b79bc50927dca688990.text:
### Uncertain, Integrated, and Trustworthy Data Management

This community investigates how databases can support reliable decision-making over heterogeneous, uncertain, and distributed information. Major themes include uncertain frequent-itemset mining and its integrity verification, data fusion in the presence of noisy or copied sources, declarative data-quality predicates, and probabilistic query inference. Other work addresses semantic consistency and trust in peer-to-peer data exchange, as well as query-answer causality, abductive diagnosis, and view updates.

Typical methods combine formal semantics, complexity analysis, database query processing, and declarative SQL formulations. Approximate inference is performed through relational query plans and bounds rather than sampling, while data integration uses source-correlation reasoning instead of simple majority voting. Knowledge-graph studies frame fact checking and triple scoring as link prediction, using discriminative predicate paths, connectivity, type information, predicate interactions, textual evidence, knowledge bases, ensembles, and trigger-word detection. Formal pricing frameworks likewise seek arbitrage-free query valuation.

Recent directions emphasize trustworthy outsourcing and data markets, scalable approximate reasoning within standard database systems, automated fact checking, and the fusion of text, structured knowledge, and heterogeneous Web sources. These efforts reflect a broader shift toward managing uncertainty, provenance, quality, and trust as first-class database concerns.

abstracts x20|388cdd1ebb963ca5482496724b.text:
## Scalable Graph and Semantic Data Management

This community focuses on efficient querying, representation, and analysis of graph-structured and relational data. A major theme is SPARQL and RDF: optimizing OPTIONAL and federated queries, expressing qualitative preferences, mapping relational schemas to RDF/OWL, and supporting incomplete or fuzzy information. Query optimization is also studied more broadly through MILP-based join ordering, heuristic reordering, and worst-case-optimal parallel conjunctive-query algorithms.

Typical methods combine formal semantics and complexity analysis with systems experimentation. Researchers use relational joins and SQL for graph analytics, multiway joins and distribution policies for distributed execution, and indexing techniques such as hop-doubling labels for graph distance queries. Practical evaluations emphasize column stores, Accumulo, D4M associative arrays, large clusters, and specialized hardware, reporting extremely high insertion and update rates. Other work addresses concise object summaries, provenance-graph segmentation, replication staleness, and blockchain atomicity.

Recent directions emphasize scaling data-intensive workloads: single-round and communication-efficient query processing, hardware acceleration for graph pattern matching, high-throughput streaming and in-memory databases, and integrated machine learning over relational data using sparse tensors and functional dependencies. Semantic flexibility—preferences, uncertainty, fuzzy summaries, and web-scale federated sources—also remains central.

abstracts x20|95a9b95b79bc50927dca688990.text:
### Data Integration, Uncertainty, and Trustworthy Data Management

This community centers on making heterogeneous, noisy, uncertain data usable and trustworthy. Major themes include entity resolution and consolidation—from matching scholarly records to producing canonical “golden records”—as well as declarative data cleaning, syntactic-pattern discovery, approximate similarity predicates, and quality control. A related strand studies information fusion, conflicting sources, copying correlations, and knowledge-graph fact checking.

Uncertainty is addressed through probabilistic databases, uncertain frequent-itemset mining, aggregate query evaluation, and approximate lifted inference. Typical methods include relational algebra and SQL-based evaluation, semirings/semimodules and knowledge compilation, query-plan upper bounds, schema-aware optimization, statistical confidence intervals, and integrity verification for outsourced computation. Provenance, causality, responsibility, abductive diagnosis, repairs, and view updates provide formal explanations for query answers and non-answers. Peer-to-peer exchange work additionally incorporates semantic constraints and trust.

Recent trends emphasize scalable, automated, and accountable integration: deep representations reduce manual effort in entity resolution; human–machine cooperation enforces precision and recall guarantees; crowdsourcing supports spatial task assignment and worker assessment; and ensemble models combine text and knowledge bases for scoring. Knowledge-graph connectivity and predicate interactions increasingly support automated fact checking, while data marketplaces motivate formal, arbitrage-free query pricing.

titles<=300|33e295482b7d4c6dc13bff5e7321.text:
## Community Report: Data Warehousing, XML Analytics, and Large-Scale Evaluation

This community centers on engineering and optimizing data warehouses for complex, heterogeneous data. XML warehousing is especially prominent, including XML databases, structural query preferences, tree patterns, XML fragmentation, join indexes, OLAP operators, summarizability, and query-performance optimization. Related work addresses warehousing complex web, archaeological, biomedical, and personalized-medical data, as well as metadata and knowledge integration.

A second major theme is physical design and administration. Papers study joint and separate selection of indexes and materialized views, bitmap and join indexes, view replacement, query clustering, frequent-itemset mining, attribute dependencies, and cloud cost models. Clustering—particularly k-means, affinity methods, and workload-based clustering—is repeatedly used for fragmentation and view selection.

Benchmarking and performance evaluation form another strong pillar, with generic tools and benchmarks for data warehouses, XML warehouses, object-oriented databases, text processing, top-k retrieval, and CRUD operations in replicated document stores. Discrete-event simulation and application-behavior evaluation support these analyses.

Additional strands cover social-media event detection, Twitter keyword/document ranking, temporal online communities, and scalable or weakly supervised text classification. Recent directions emphasize real-time social streams, document-oriented architectures, cloud-shared optimizations, complex hierarchies, top-k inference, and neural classification.

abstracts x10|33e295482b7d4c6dc13bff5e73.text:
### Adaptive Data Management and Real-Time Information Extraction

This community spans data management, semi-structured data querying, analytical warehousing, object-oriented databases, and large-scale text and social-media analysis. A central theme is making complex or rapidly changing data usable and efficient: XML tree-pattern queries support structural and preference-based search, while data warehouses and Web warehouses enable OLAP and decision support, including lightweight solutions for small and medium-sized enterprises.

Typical methods are algorithmic and system-oriented. They include tree-pattern matching and query evaluation, incremental frequent-itemset mining for workload-driven index selection, and simulation or implementation-based comparisons of object-clustering policies. Several works emphasize adaptive physical organization, using usage statistics, reference graphs, and reclustering. For text and social streams, approaches include document-oriented architectures with preprocessing pipelines, mention-anomaly statistics, and clustering of trending entities over time.

Recent directions favor dynamic, scalable, and real-time processing. Event detection increasingly exploits social structure rather than text alone and targets streams containing millions of entities per minute. Data systems likewise adapt indexes and object layouts as workloads evolve. Across the community, there is also a movement toward simpler implementations, modular architectures, and affordable analytical infrastructure while retaining support for heterogeneous, web-scale data.

abstracts x20|33e295482b7d4c6dc13bff5e73.text:
### Adaptive Data Management, Warehousing, and Stream Analytics

This community centers on performance-oriented management and analysis of complex, heterogeneous data. A major theme is XML data warehousing and OLAP: papers address XML tree-pattern querying, structural preferences, summarizability, fragmentation, materialized-view selection, benchmarking, and unified architectures for complex, multimodal, and multisource data. More general data-warehouse research covers dynamic index selection, query-driven optimization, Web warehousing, and lightweight business intelligence for small and medium-sized enterprises.

Typical methods are workload-aware and data-mining-based. They include incremental frequent-itemset mining for index selection, query clustering for materialized views, affinity-based fragmentation, simulation for evaluating object-clustering policies, and configurable frameworks for changing database access patterns. XML research relies on query models, annotated dataguides, tree-pattern matching, and XQuery workloads.

A second strand addresses large-scale unstructured data: document-based architectures support preprocessing and scalable text analysis, while LSHTC benchmarks classification across hundreds of thousands of classes. Recent work emphasizes real-time social-stream analytics, modeling events through clusters of trending entities and detecting anomalies in Twitter mention links. Overall, the trend is toward adaptive, automated, scalable optimization and unified infrastructure for increasingly complex and dynamic data.

titles<=300|0e87154bac4da0c0b3e5bcea264d.text:
## Categorical and Algebraic Foundations for Data Integration

This community develops a categorical and algebraic account of databases, data integration, and data migration. Central themes include functorial data migration, database mappings, theory of sketches, monads, coinduction, and denotational semantics for view-based mappings. Several works establish relational and equational foundations, emphasizing formal rather than informal data transformation.

Typical methods include category-theoretic modeling of database schemas and instances, functors and adjoint-style migration constructions, Kleisli database instances, monadic and coinductive techniques, and algebraic treatments of mappings and integration. Other papers extend the framework to simplicial databases, table manipulation, algebraic property graphs, and operadic wiring diagrams for graphical database languages, recursion, and plug-and-play circuits. Matching, merging, and structural properties of the database category provide complementary tools for integration.

Recent trends move from foundational theory toward broader representational and practical settings. These include connecting functorial migration “from theory to practice,” applying categorical data integration to computational science, and incorporating graph, simplicial, and operadic structures. Overall, the papers seek compositional, formally specified, and reusable mechanisms for transforming, integrating, and interpreting heterogeneous data.

abstracts x10|d19edcd8b18b66e41ac60f9b56.text:
### Scholarly Information Retrieval, Semantics, and Open Research

This community examines how scholarly and information environments can be made more discoverable, assessable, reproducible, and responsibly managed. Main themes include task-sensitive web search, guided retrieval through knowledge maps, and discipline-specific query expansion. Studies analyze search-session behavior across task types and topics, evaluate search-term recommendations, and investigate the reliability of human relevance judgments using Fleiss’ Kappa and Krippendorff’s Alpha.

A second major theme is semantic scholarly communication. Work explores extracting structured author-contribution statements from biomedical papers, publishing scholarly information as Linked Open Data, and using queries and citation networks to assess publication quality. Citation analysis is extended beyond articles through DataRank, a network-flow approach for assigning credit to scientific datasets.

Other papers address the identity of information objects across changing carriers and encodings, as well as stewardship of university data amid open-access mandates, privacy, academic freedom, and intellectual-property concerns. Jupyter notebooks represent a practical method for sharing code, computation, and documentation.

Recent trends emphasize richer semantic metadata, credit for non-publication research outputs, computational reproducibility, and governance of increasingly open and data-intensive scholarly practices.

titles<=300|d19edcd8b18b66e41ac60f9b5666.text:
## Scholarly Information Retrieval and Knowledge Infrastructures

This community studies how scholarly information can be organized, discovered, linked, and evaluated. Major themes include bibliometric-enhanced information retrieval; query and term recommendation; classification and knowledge organization systems (KOS), including SKOS and linked data; scholarly recommender systems; and interactive, visual, and exploratory search in digital libraries.

A substantial strand addresses research data: dataset discovery and citation, metadata enrichment, data archives, reproducibility, stewardship, and data search as a sociotechnical practice. Other work develops scholarly knowledge graphs, author-contribution extraction, citation matching, reference parsing, semantic publishing, and metadata extraction from scientific literature.

Typical methods combine thesaurus and classification-based query expansion, terminology mapping, citation and co-author networks, linked-data modeling, information extraction and OCR, machine learning, embeddings, meta-learning, and scalable processing with Hadoop. Evaluation commonly uses test collections, click and log analysis, interactive retrieval sessions, user studies, relevance judgments, visualization assessment, and living labs.

Recent directions emphasize open science and research-data infrastructures, large-scale citation and metadata integration, neural and embedding-based retrieval or recommendation, richer semantic interlinking, and more realistic evaluation of personalization, usefulness, bias, position effects, temporal change, and exploratory search behavior.

abstracts x20|d19edcd8b18b66e41ac60f9b56.text:
## Scholarly Information Retrieval, Linking, and Stewardship

This community studies how researchers discover, evaluate, organize, and reuse scholarly information and data. Major themes include interactive and task-sensitive information retrieval; academic digital libraries and recommender systems; bibliometrics and citation-based credit; semantic publishing and Linked Open Data; knowledge organization systems; and responsible stewardship of research data and infrastructures.

Typical methods combine controlled retrieval experiments, user studies, search-session analysis, and behavioral signals such as queries and mouse fixations. Evaluation uses retrieval effectiveness, relevance judgments, inter-assessor agreement statistics, bibliometric measures, and controlled comparisons of query expansion, Bradfordizing, and recommendation approaches. Other work develops practical systems and services, including discipline-specific term recommendation, linked-metadata enrichment, integrated social-science search, and recommender-system-as-a-service. Extraction and neural sequence-to-sequence methods are applied to author contributions and simplified scientific titles. Qualitative interviews, ethnography, and document analysis examine infrastructure durability, while ontological analysis addresses information-object identity.

Recent trends emphasize richer, interconnected scholarly graphs: semantic annotations, citation networks, dataset attribution, and KOS integration with the Semantic Web. Open science is increasingly supported through Jupyter notebooks and linked research data, alongside growing attention to privacy, intellectual property, reproducibility, and long-term infrastructure maintenance. Visualization, social collaboration, and more adaptive, topic-aware discovery systems are also recurring directions.

abstracts x10|0e87154bac4da0c0b3e5bcea26.text:
### Categorical and Algebraic Foundations for Data Integration

This community develops formal, compositional semantics for databases, schemas, mappings, and data transformation. A central theme is **functorial data migration**, where schemas are categories and instances are set-valued functors; schema morphisms induce canonical migration operations corresponding to projections, unions, and joins. Related work gives an equational formalism and graphical IDE for specifying these transformations.

A second theme is **algebraic data integration**. Schemas and instances are represented as multisorted equational theories and initial algebras, with adjoint migration functors supporting substitution and structured translation. Other papers model view-based mappings—such as LAV, GAV, and GLAV—in a dedicated database category whose morphisms are query computations rather than ordinary functions. Sketches, separation, federation, and matching/merging are used to analyze this category’s expressive and structural properties.

Typical methods combine category theory, monads, algebraic semantics, functional programming, and database theory. Monadic and Kleisli constructions support generalized values, nulls, lists, sets, and exceptions, while simplicial databases represent tables geometrically and enable tile-based construction and querying.

Emerging trends emphasize executable tooling, geometric database representations, richer computational effects, and formally preserving data integrity throughout migration and integration rather than repairing data afterward.

abstracts x20|0e87154bac4da0c0b3e5bcea26.text:
## Categorical and Algebraic Foundations for Data Integration

This community develops formal, structure-preserving approaches to database transformation, migration, and integration. A central theme is **functorial data migration**, representing schemas as categories (often finitely presented graphs with path equations) and instances as set-valued functors. Schema functors induce adjoint migration operations—supporting projections, unions, joins, and related queries—and are implemented through the Equational/Functorial Query Language (FQL).

A second theme generalizes database semantics beyond ordinary functions. The database category **DB** models instances as relational tables and mappings as complex query computations, providing denotational semantics for LAV, GAV, and GLAV view-based mappings. Sketches, monads, and Kleisli constructions support schema mapping, non-atomic values, lists, sets, nulls, and exceptions. Simplicial databases and operads offer geometric or compositional representations for table manipulation, recursion, wiring diagrams, and plug-and-play circuits.

Recent work emphasizes practical interoperability: algebraic property graphs connect graph, relational, streaming, and microservice data; open-source tools demonstrate manufacturing and computational-science scenarios. Across the papers, formal guarantees that transformations preserve data integrity are increasingly positioned as an alternative to informal, post-hoc cleaning.

titles<=300|9c567f58410a7f0f52d122074516.text:
### Distributed and Scalable Clustering for Data Mining

This community focuses on clustering large, distributed datasets, especially spatial data. A central theme is adapting density-based clustering to distributed environments, alongside broader distributed clustering algorithms and scalable techniques.

The papers explore several methodological families: grid-based approaches, variance-based clustering, hierarchical aggregation of spatial datasets, and data-partitioning strategies for large-scale clustering. Density-based methods receive particular attention, with work addressing both distributed approaches and scalable implementations. These methods collectively emphasize dividing data or computation across distributed settings and aggregating results efficiently.

The community also includes an applied information-retrieval/search system for an anti-money-laundering application using a multinational bank’s dataset, demonstrating a practical data-mining use case beyond algorithm design.

Overall, the apparent trend is toward improving efficiency, scalability, and applicability. Recent work emphasizes large-scale processing and scalable density-based clustering, while hierarchical aggregation and partitioning provide complementary strategies for managing distributed spatial and general data-mining workloads.

abstracts x10|9c567f58410a7f0f52d1220745.text:
**Distributed Clustering and Data Mining at Scale**

This community focuses primarily on distributed clustering for very large, heterogeneous, and spatial datasets that cannot be centrally collected. A recurring concern is the aggregation of local clustering results: naive global-model construction can be complex, communication-intensive, and produce ambiguous or inaccurate clusters. Several papers propose improved aggregation strategies, including hierarchical aggregation, compact local-cluster representations, variance-based merging, and data-partitioning approaches.

Density-based clustering is a prominent theme, with methods designed to preserve clustering quality while reducing communication overhead. One scalable approach explicitly offers a user-controlled trade-off between the number of transmitted objects and clustering quality. The work also addresses distributed frequent-itemset generation and evaluates clustering in grid environments using Condor and DAGMan, emphasizing monitoring, configuration, and performance.

Typical methods follow a two-phase architecture: independent local processing at data sites, followed by global merging or aggregation. Evaluation emphasizes scalability, communication cost, compactness, accuracy, and suitability for loosely coupled or grid infrastructures.

A related application develops an efficient search tool for an international bank’s anti-money-laundering dataset, supporting customer identification and monitoring of transaction-related behavior. Overall, the trend is toward scalable, communication-aware, density-based, and infrastructure-adapted distributed mining rather than centralized analysis.

abstracts x20|9c567f58410a7f0f52d1220745.text:
## Distributed Clustering for Large, Spatial, and Heterogeneous Data

This community focuses primarily on distributed data mining, especially clustering of very large spatial datasets distributed across independent, heterogeneous sites. The central challenge is producing accurate global knowledge without centralizing data or incurring excessive communication and aggregation costs.

Typical methods use a two-phase architecture: independent local processing followed by global model construction. Proposed approaches include density-based clustering, variance-based clustering, hierarchical aggregation, and data-partitioning techniques. Several methods emphasize compact representations of local clusters to make aggregation more efficient and to reduce ambiguity in the resulting global clusters. Density-based methods also support explicit trade-offs between clustering quality and the number of transmitted objects.

The work extends beyond clustering to distributed frequent-itemset generation and grid-based execution. Experiments use grid infrastructures, including Condor and DAGMan, with monitoring and configuration tools for performance evaluation. One application develops an efficient search tool for customer and transaction data in multinational-bank anti-money-laundering analysis.

Recent trends emphasize scalability, communication reduction, robust global aggregation, and adaptation to heterogeneous, high-volume data. Overall, the community moves from simple aggregation of local results toward more structured aggregation strategies and controllable quality–overhead trade-offs.

abstracts x10|6ccc1ebb4686fd8cc117cdcbd5.text:
**Research Evaluation Through Peer Review and Bibliometrics**

This community examines how universities can evaluate research quality consistently across policy levels, disciplines, and publication cultures. A central theme is the relationship between expert peer review and quantitative indicators, especially citation-based measures and publication categories. The papers address the limited database coverage of social sciences and humanities and question whether indicators developed for international journals retain the same meaning when applied to local or newly indexed media.

Typical methods combine institutional peer-review exercises with bibliometric analysis of teams, authors, publications, and citations. Comparative analyses investigate agreement and reliability among evaluators, relate peer-review outcomes to citation results, and distinguish international from non-international publication channels. Discipline-level evaluations also use structured reflection, expert advice, and cross-assessment comparisons to inform university management.

Recent trends include integrating peer review with common core indicators, improving rating reliability through uniform reference levels and diagnostic checks, and developing quality-related publication categories for underrepresented fields. Overall, the work favors coordinated, context-sensitive evaluation systems rather than reliance on a single metric.

titles<=300|6ccc1ebb4686fd8cc117cdcbd58e.text:
### Research Evaluation and the Reliability of Peer Review

This community examines how scientific quality is assessed through peer review and publication-based indicators. Its main themes include the reliability and comparability of peer-review outcomes, disciplinary differences in evaluation, distinctions between international and non-international publication media, and quality categories in the social sciences and humanities.

Typical methods combine quantitative analysis of curriculum-vitae-based indicators with validation against peer-review judgments. Other studies use team- and author-level publication data to compare publication media, while discipline-specific peer-review procedures are examined through their outcomes. University peer-review assessments provide the basis for classifying quality-related publication categories, particularly in the social sciences and humanities.

Recent trends emphasize linking quantitative indicators to expert assessment rather than treating either approach in isolation. The papers also point toward more context-sensitive evaluation: accounting for disciplinary cultures, publication languages and venues, author or team characteristics, and differences between international and non-international outlets. Overall, the research seeks evaluation systems that are both empirically grounded and more reliable across fields.

abstracts x20|6ccc1ebb4686fd8cc117cdcbd5.text:
### Integrating Bibliometrics and Peer Review in Research Evaluation

This community studies how universities can evaluate research quality coherently across faculties, disciplines, and policy contexts. Its central themes are the validity, reliability, and comparability of peer review; the use of quantitative citation- and publication-based indicators; and the particular challenges of assessing social sciences and humanities (SSH).

Typical methods combine expert assessment with bibliometric analysis. Studies compare peer ratings of research teams with citation outcomes, examine how reviewers assign scores, and develop core indicators validated against peer-review judgments. Other work analyzes publication and author/team data across international and local journals, assessing whether standard indicators retain their meaning when database coverage expands. Discipline-level ex-post reviews are also used to generate feedback, management recommendations, and quality-related publication categories, especially where conventional databases provide limited coverage.

A recent trend is toward integrated evaluation systems rather than reliance on a single metric or review process. Expanded Web of Science and Scopus coverage of local SSH media creates opportunities for broader comparison, while also raising concerns about indicator comparability. The papers emphasize standardized reference levels, explicit reliability checks, and complementary evidence to support funding, personnel, and institutional policy decisions.

titles<=300|cedb268af045e486408e95e045b3.text:
## Privacy-Preserving Data Management and Analytics

This community centers on privacy-preserving data publishing, querying, and mining, with differential privacy as the dominant framework. Major themes include accurate release of histograms, datacubes, contingency tables, sparse data, trajectories, spatial regions, search logs, and graph patterns; private linear, range, and summation queries; and privacy-preserving classification, regression, frequent-itemset mining, and recommendation.

Typical methods include hierarchical decompositions (PrivTree), multidimensional partitioning (DPCube), wavelet and low-rank mechanisms, matrix mechanisms, convex optimization, workload- and data-adaptive query answering, consistency corrections, and composition analysis. Local differential privacy is applied to marginals, range queries, smart-device data, and location recommendations. Utility–privacy tradeoffs are studied through epsilon selection, policy-aware mechanisms, semantic guarantees, and benchmark-based evaluation.

A second strand addresses anonymization and inference threats, including k-anonymity, l-diversity, slicing, microdata and unstructured-data anonymization, linkage attacks, auxiliary information, adversarial fusion, and reconstruction. Applications cover mobility, social media, trajectories, provenance, federated databases, encrypted querying, secure hardware, and entity resolution.

Current directions emphasize high-dimensional and continuous releases, temporal correlations, personalized and group-aware privacy, spatiotemporal event protection, federated/private data exploration, and integrating fairness, preferences, and practical efficiency with formal privacy guarantees.

abstracts x10|cedb268af045e486408e95e045.text:
## Privacy-Preserving Data, Graphs, and Analytics

This community studies how to release, query, and analyze data while limiting privacy leakage and preserving utility. Major themes include differential privacy for sparse data publication, hierarchical histograms and group-size estimation, clustering, classification, and location-based recommendation. Related work examines provenance privacy in repeated public/private workflows, privacy risks in group-based anonymization, and secure querying over outsourced datasets containing both sensitive and nonsensitive attributes.

Typical methods include calibrated noise and differential-privacy mechanisms, hierarchical decomposition, wavelet-based clustering, synthetic data generation, and local differential privacy for user-generated mobility data. Other approaches use query binning to exploit safely releasable plaintext data, provenance views to conceal module outputs, and surrogate nodes or edges to support informative path queries without exposing sensitive graph elements. Several papers emphasize formal privacy definitions, error metrics, and the tradeoff between protection and analytical accuracy.

Recent directions extend privacy guarantees to increasingly complex analytics and structures: hierarchical geographic estimation, arbitrary-shape clustering, successive point-of-interest recommendation using movement transitions, and graph/provenance queries. The collection also shows growing attention to privacy attacks against anonymized releases and to exploiting partial data sensitivity rather than encrypting entire outsourced datasets.

abstracts x20|cedb268af045e486408e95e045.text:
## Privacy-Preserving Data Management and Analysis

The community focuses on protecting sensitive data while retaining utility for querying, mining, statistics, recommendations, and decision-making. Differential privacy is the dominant framework, applied to sparse-data publication, hierarchical histograms and group-size estimation, range and high-dimensional queries, clustering, wavelet transforms, decision trees, and location-based recommendation. A recurring concern is balancing privacy, accuracy, scalability, and protection against reconstruction or inference attacks; work also examines limitations of anonymization, sparse-vector variants, and the distinction between micro- and aggregate reconstruction.

Typical methods include calibrated noise, hierarchical decomposition, wavelet transforms, private partitioning, workload- and data-aware mechanisms, local differential privacy, perturbation, and synthetic or surrogate data. Systems-oriented approaches include query binning for mixed sensitive/non-sensitive outsourced data, secure multiparty computation for federated databases, provenance views, and surrogate graph nodes and edges.

Emerging directions connect formal privacy with application goals: privacy-preserving POI recommendation that retains movement transitions, private clustering and classification, and analysis of fairness in resource allocation. The papers also indicate a shift toward adaptive mechanisms tailored to data structure and query workloads, scalable high-dimensional analysis, and stronger scrutiny of whether privacy guarantees and anonymized outputs truly prevent meaningful individual disclosure.
