### Symbolic Time-Series Representation, Matching, and Recognition

This community focuses on transforming temporal data into symbolic representations and using them for comparison, classification, and pattern recognition. A central theme is discretization of temporal data, addressed both through a survey and through work on Symbolic Aggregate Approximation (SAA), including efforts to improve its efficiency.

Several papers develop distance-based methods for time-series analysis. The extended edit distance metric and time warp edit distance adapt edit-style comparisons to temporal sequences, while stiffness adjustment introduces additional flexibility for controlling time warping during matching. These methods target similarity assessment between series that may differ in timing or structure.

Another theme is recognizing or labeling patterns in streams of temporal data, suggesting applications requiring continuous analysis rather than one-time comparison. The satellite-image case study demonstrates the use of symbolic time series for analyzing an Algerian geographic zone, connecting symbolic methods with remote-sensing data.

Overall, the papers show a progression from foundational representation and discretization issues toward faster symbolic approximation, refined temporal distance measures, stream-oriented recognition, and applied satellite-image analysis.

abstracts x10|d2e96680452e5fe622ad2869be.text:
### Symbolic and Edit-Based Methods for Temporal Data

This community focuses on making high-dimensional temporal and time-series data searchable, interpretable, and evaluable. A central theme is dimensionality reduction through symbolic representations, particularly for efficient similarity search and for leveraging text-retrieval techniques. Work on faster Symbolic Aggregate Approximation (SAX) and extended edit distance seeks improved scalability and matching effectiveness.

A second major theme is edit-based similarity for temporal sequences. Time Warp Edit Distance (TWED) models time-series comparison as a minimum-cost sequence of edits, using dynamic programming and linear-segment operations. Its stiffness parameter controls the flexibility of temporal alignment, making the method suitable for event data and irregular sampling. Related work applies edit-distance alignment to labeled temporal segments, producing label-level confusion matrices for assessing recognition and labeling systems.

The papers also address discretization of temporal data, surveying methods that form time-sensitive intervals for downstream data mining. Applications include satellite image time series, where symbolic representations support dimensionality reduction and land-occupation analysis.

Overall, the research trends from representation and discretization toward specialized, parameterized edit distances, faster search, and practical evaluation of temporal pattern recognition.

abstracts x20|d2e96680452e5fe622ad2869be.text:
### Symbolic and Edit-Based Methods for Temporal Data

This community focuses on making high-dimensional temporal and time-series data searchable, interpretable, and evaluable. A central theme is dimensionality reduction through symbolic representations, enabling indexing and the use of text-retrieval techniques for similarity search. Work on faster Symbolic Aggregate Approximation (SAX) and extended edit distances seeks efficient and effective matching in large databases.

A second major theme is edit-based time-series comparison. Time Warp Edit Distance (TWED) models similarity as the minimum-cost sequence of editing operations, using dynamic programming and a stiffness parameter to regulate elastic matching. Its formulation supports timestamped data and irregular sampling, with accompanying work studying distance properties.

Methods also address temporal structure beyond raw similarity. A survey examines discretization techniques that form time-sensitive, concise intervals for mining scientific, financial, sensor, and network data. For labeled temporal streams, editing distances align predicted and ground-truth segments, enabling label-level confusion matrices and standard performance assessment.

Applications include symbolic analysis of satellite image time series for land-occupation monitoring. Overall, the research trends toward scalable symbolic indexing, flexible alignment of irregular temporal data, and more informative evaluation of temporal pattern recognition.

abstracts x10|9b9758cd7ef65a162ca60f0dd7.text:
## Scalable Data Quality and Approximate Stream Processing

This community focuses on assessing, representing, and improving data quality in large, heterogeneous, and continuously evolving datasets. Major themes include Linked Data curation and provenance, approximate quality measurement, streaming deduplication (“intelligent compression”), multidimensional membership search, and quality-aware analysis of spatial, categorical, and textual data.

Typical methods trade exactness for scalability. Reservoir sampling, Bloom filters, Stable Bloom Filters, clustering-coefficient estimation, and probabilistic approximation support efficient processing of massive datasets and streams. BLOOFI extends Bloom filters to multidimensional and distributed searches. Linked Data work combines collaborative patching with frameworks such as LUZZU, while the Dataset Quality Ontology (daQ) represents benchmark results as multidimensional statistical observations. Other studies use association-rule mining with genetic algorithms for categorical quality measurement, sampling for spatial databases, and relation extraction plus context discovery for text categorization.

Recent trends emphasize real-time, resource-efficient processing; approximate yet sufficiently accurate metrics; interoperable quality metadata; and practical support for heterogeneous Web, spatial, and streaming data. Overall, the papers move from isolated quality measures toward reusable frameworks and probabilistic infrastructures for scalable data management.

abstracts x20|9b9758cd7ef65a162ca60f0dd7.text:
## Approximate Data Quality and Intelligent Data Management

This community focuses on making large, heterogeneous, and evolving datasets usable through scalable quality assessment, metadata, deduplication, and classification. A major theme is Linked Data quality: identifying errors, measuring dataset fitness, tracking provenance, and enabling collaborative correction. The Luzzu framework supports extensible quality metrics, while LQML provides a domain-specific language for defining them. The Dataset Quality Ontology (daQ) represents benchmark results as multidimensional statistical observations.

Scalability is typically addressed through probabilistic and approximate methods, including reservoir sampling, Bloom filters, clustering-coefficient estimation, and sampling-based spatial quality assessment. Bloom-filter research also targets multidimensional search and streaming deduplication, including biased and stable variants for approximate duplicate detection in unbounded streams.

Other work studies data quality in spatial databases and warehouses, emphasizing metadata for integration, lineage, and transformed data. Categorical quality measurement uses association rules optimized with genetic algorithms. Text analysis explores context discovery, relation extraction, and fuzzy similarity for improved document categorization.

Recent trends emphasize moving from exact, costly evaluation toward efficient approximation; formalizing quality metadata and metric definitions; supporting domain-specific extensibility; and addressing continuously arriving, distributed, and noisy data.

### Data Quality, Approximation, and Intelligent Information Management

This community focuses on assessing, improving, and representing data quality across linked, spatial, categorical, and streaming datasets. A major theme is linked-data quality: Luzzu provides a quality-assessment framework, while its metric language offers a domain-specific way to define quality measures. Related work addresses probabilistic quality approximation, collaborative patching of linked data, and multidimensional metadata views.

A second theme is efficient approximate processing of streams. Bloom-filter research includes multidimensional Bloom filters, biased reservoir-sampling Bloom filters for intelligent compression, and Bloom-filter algorithms for approximate stream deduplication. These methods emphasize compact representations, probabilistic membership testing, and scalable processing.

The papers also investigate quality and similarity in structured and unstructured data. Spatial-database quality is assessed through sampling, including mobile-trajectory nearest-neighbor applications; categorical-data quality uses genetic algorithms. Text categorization methods learn contextual information and apply fuzzy-similarity models.

Overall, the work trends toward configurable quality metrics, multidimensional quality metadata, approximate and sampling-based computation, and lightweight probabilistic structures that enable scalable assessment and deduplication without exhaustive data processing.

abstracts x10|2e1004a30e0ba1a942b5240c21.text:
## Educational Data Mining for Student Success

This community focuses on applying educational data mining (EDM) and learning analytics to improve higher education, particularly in India. The central themes are predicting student performance, distinguishing high and low performers, identifying students at risk of dropout, and supporting institutional decision-making. Related studies examine enrollment, attendance, classroom teaching language, examination irregularities, abnormal result values, and the broader use of educational databases to improve quality.

Typical methods involve knowledge discovery and supervised classification. Predictive models are developed from student records, sometimes using experimentally generated databases, to produce early assessments of incoming or enrolled students. Naive Bayes classification is used to identify consistent performers and underperformers, while decision trees provide interpretable, divide-and-conquer analyses. Comparative data-mining studies evaluate such approaches for performance prediction.

The papers also emphasize that educational institutions hold substantial but underused data, and that information and communication technologies enable low-cost collection and analysis. A recent trend is the growing convergence of EDM and learning analytics: survey work describes integrated frameworks and models designed not only to predict outcomes but also to inform interventions, improve learning processes, reduce dropout, and enhance institutional performance.

titles<=300|2e1004a30e0ba1a942b5240c2187.text:
## Educational Data Mining for Student Success

This community focuses on applying data mining and learning analytics to education, especially the analysis and prediction of student outcomes. A central theme is improving student performance by identifying performers and underperformers and by predicting achievement. Dropout reduction is another important goal, suggesting the use of predictive insights for early intervention. The papers also consider broader educational contexts, including classroom teaching language and the role of data mining in the education sector.

Classification is the dominant method across the collection. It is used to categorize students by performance level, predict academic outcomes, and identify students at risk of dropping out. Several papers frame data mining as a practical tool for performance improvement, while a comparative study emphasizes evaluating alternative prediction approaches. The learning-analytics survey provides a broader synthesis of the field.

Overall, the apparent direction is toward increasingly predictive and decision-oriented educational analytics: moving beyond describing student performance to forecasting outcomes and supporting targeted improvement. At the same time, the community retains a broad perspective, linking technical prediction tasks with classroom practice and the wider adoption of data mining in education.

## Educational Data Mining for Student Success

This community focuses on applying data mining and learning analytics to improve higher education, particularly in India. Central themes include predicting student performance, distinguishing high and low performers, identifying students at risk of dropout, and supporting institutional decision-making. Other applications examine enrollment, attendance, classroom teaching language, examination irregularities, abnormal result values, and the shift from traditional classroom models.

Typical methods involve knowledge discovery from educational databases and supervised classification. Bayesian (“Byes”) classification and decision-tree classifiers are highlighted for predicting performance, identifying consistent performers or underperformers, and generating dropout-management lists for incoming students. Several studies use experimental databases or institutional records to build predictive models, while comparative work surveys data-mining tools and approaches.

The recent trend is the growing convergence of educational data mining and learning analytics. Rather than merely storing educational data, institutions are encouraged to extract actionable information to improve teaching quality, student outcomes, and retention. Survey work emphasizes emerging learning-analytics frameworks, integrated models, and the use of diverse data-mining techniques for early risk identification and performance prediction.

abstracts x10|840343932e841efdd6e719af3c.text:
### Cross-Modal Hashing and Interpretable Multimedia Retrieval

The community primarily studies efficient cross-modal and multimodal retrieval using compact binary representations. Major themes include learning discriminative, unified, and decorrelated hash codes across image, text, audio, video, and other heterogeneous modalities; exploiting complementary information from multiple views; and improving search beyond inaccurate or exhaustive Hamming-distance ranking.

Typical methods combine deep feature learning with hashing objectives, including triplet-based networks, discrete latent-factor models, joint embedding, unary and cluster losses, and unified optimization of hash functions and codes. Several works specifically address scalability by reducing pairwise or triplet training complexity and introducing probability-based indexing for faster, more accurate retrieval.

A secondary theme concerns semantic and temporal alignment between modalities, particularly for cross-modal structures. The community also extends multimodal learning to music analysis: hierarchical attention networks classify genres from lyrics, while self-attention over lyric and acoustic features supports transparent music recommendation by exposing interpretable content characteristics.

Recent trends favor end-to-end deep hashing, adaptive multi-view fusion, discrete or decorrelated code learning, and retrieval systems that jointly optimize representation quality, indexing efficiency, and interpretability.

titles<=300|840343932e841efdd6e719af3c6f.text:
### Cross-Modal Hashing and Semantic Multimedia Retrieval

This community centers on efficient cross-modal retrieval, especially hashing methods for visual, textual, audio, lyric, and event data. A major theme is learning shared semantic representations or unified hash codes across modalities, with goals of preserving cross-modal correlations, discriminative meaning, and retrieval efficiency.

Typical approaches include deep neural hashing, joint embedding, supervised matrix and latent-factor models, correlation alignment, and quantization. Several works improve code quality through triplet objectives, cluster-unary losses, decorrelation, fusion supervision, and jointly learned hashing functions. Efficiency is also addressed through query-adaptive code ranking and indexing strategies for large-scale datasets. Graph convolutional networks and attention mechanisms extend representation learning to text and music, while CycleGAN supports unsupervised hashing.

Music retrieval and recommendation form a distinct strand, combining lyrics, audio, genre classification, self-attention, hierarchical attention, and EEG-based regularization to model music semantics and improve transparency. Event retrieval similarly emphasizes shared semantic spaces and correlation alignment.

Overall, the apparent trend is from factorization and manually structured hashing toward deep, jointly optimized, and more flexible multimodal representations, alongside growing interest in unsupervised learning, efficient indexing, semantic interpretability, and richer cross-modal signals.

titles<=300|8eac289c4ee4adbcfa06c7527abe.text:
**Artifact-Centric Verification and Data-Aware Process Modeling**

This community studies formal modeling and verification of processes whose behavior is tightly coupled to relational data. A central theme is the artifact system: papers address its modeling, enactment, practical verification, UML representation, and hierarchical extension. Related work develops data-aware processes and examines verification of query completeness over such processes.

The research combines database and formal-methods perspectives. Relational databases provide the foundation for representing and managing process data, while colored Petri nets offer a modeling framework linking database state and process behavior. UML artifact-centric models support structured specification, and verification tools—including SPIN-based and practical artifact-system verifiers—enable automated analysis. The work also considers systems interacting with external services.

Recent directions emphasize broader system expressiveness and applicability: extending relational and process models, handling external services and hierarchical artifact systems, and moving from abstract formalisms toward practical verification. Query-completeness analysis indicates growing attention not only to behavioral correctness but also to whether process executions provide sufficient answers to data queries.

abstracts x20|840343932e841efdd6e719af3c.text:
### Cross-Modal Retrieval, Hashing, and Multimodal Semantic Learning

This community centers on efficient cross-modal and multimodal retrieval, especially image–text, audio–lyrics, and general heterogeneous media search. A dominant theme is learning shared or unified semantic representations that reduce the modality gap while preserving similarity, correlation, and discriminative information.

Typical methods include shallow matrix factorization, latent-factor models, semantic projections, correlation alignment, and canonical correlation learning. Deep approaches jointly learn modality-specific features and binary codes through paired networks, fusion supervision, triplet objectives, unary or cluster losses, and adversarial CycleGAN architectures. Several works address code quality by decorrelating hash bits, learning discrete representations, preserving relative similarity, or using composite correlation quantization. Efficient deployment is also emphasized through probability-based indexing, query-adaptive ranking, and improved Hamming-distance search.

A secondary theme applies multimodal learning to music: hierarchical or self-attentive lyric genre classification, audio–lyrics temporal correlation modeling, interpretable content features, and EEG-regularized music semantics. These studies extend retrieval toward perceptual and explainable representations.

Recent trends move from handcrafted features and separate code optimization toward end-to-end deep hashing, unified code learning, unsupervised correlation discovery, temporal alignment across modalities, and models that combine semantic accuracy with scalable indexing and interpretability.

abstracts x10|8eac289c4ee4adbcfa06c7527a.text:
### Data-Centric Processes and Artifact Verification

This community studies the integration of relational data with dynamic business processes and workflows. Central models include data-centric dynamic systems, db-nets (combining colored Petri nets with relational databases), quality-aware processes, and hierarchical artifact systems inspired by IBM Business Artifacts and Guard-Stage-Milestone models. These approaches aim to represent process dynamics and master data uniformly, while supporting existing relational databases.

Verification is a dominant theme. The work addresses first-order μ-calculus and LTL-FO properties, query completeness, and decidability in systems with evolving databases, task hierarchy, concurrency, richer artifact data, and external services that introduce fresh data. Typical methods combine formal process models with relational database semantics, theoretical decidability and complexity analyses, and translations between modeling formalisms.

A practical trend is the transfer of foundational results into usable tools and methodologies. SpinArt provides Spin-based verification for artifact systems, while VERIFAS implements efficient checking for LTL-FO properties. Other work connects formal verification with UML artifact-centric modeling and with process modeling and enactment. Overall, the research is moving from abstract foundations toward richer, realistic workflows and deployable verification support.

abstracts x20|8eac289c4ee4adbcfa06c7527a.text:
### Data-Centric Processes and Artifact Verification

This community studies the integration of relational data with dynamic business processes and workflows. Its central theme is **artifact-centric, data-aware process modeling**, in which structural data and process dynamics are treated jointly rather than through ad-hoc abstractions. Proposed foundations include **db-nets**, combining colored Petri nets with relational databases, and related models for enriching existing databases with process dynamics and supporting process enactment.

A major research direction is **formal verification** of these systems. The papers investigate temporal and first-order μ-calculus properties, LTL-FO specifications, and verification of hierarchical artifact systems. Models increasingly incorporate realistic features such as task hierarchy, concurrency, richer artifact data, and external services that generate fresh data, yielding infinite-state systems. Theoretical work establishes decidability and complexity results for important classes of workflows.

The community also emphasizes practical validation and transfer to modeling environments. **VERIFAS** and **SPINART** implement artifact verification using efficient, tool-supported analysis, while UML-based artifact-centric models connect formal verification results with concrete business-process methodologies. A further theme is **data quality**, particularly automatically checking query completeness over process-generated data. Overall, the trend moves from foundational models toward richer, executable, and practically verifiable data-aware workflows.

titles<=300|7f356385c9451ff3d020fb839db6.text:
### Provenance and Traceability for Scientific Big Data

This community focuses on making complex data, analyses, and evolving systems understandable and auditable through provenance and traceability. A central theme is the design of traceability into big-data infrastructures, particularly medical systems involving clinical variables and neuroimages. The Neugrid4You (N4U) project illustrates this application through the development of a large-scale neuroimaging and clinical-data atlas.

Typical methods include explicit provenance capture and analysis-traceability models, with applications spanning medical big data, high-energy-physics (HEP) analyses, and industrial settings. CRISTAL-ISE represents a practical provenance technology applied in industry, while “pattern reification” provides a more conceptual basis for description-driven systems, suggesting that recurring structures can be represented explicitly to support system description and evolution.

Overall, the work trends toward integrating provenance as a built-in property of data-intensive systems rather than treating it as an afterthought. The applications broaden from domain-specific scientific analyses and healthcare data to industrial platforms and general big-data architectures, while maintaining a shared concern with reproducibility, accountability, and lifecycle understanding.

abstracts x20|7f356385c9451ff3d020fb839d.text:
### Description-Driven Provenance for Big-Data Science

This community focuses on making large-scale scientific and clinical data accessible, traceable, and adaptable. A central theme is provenance management: recording the history of data, processes, analyses, and versions so researchers can reproduce and understand results. Applications include neuroimaging and Alzheimer’s biomarker studies, industrial systems, and potential transfer to high-energy physics (HEP).

Typical methods use description-driven architectures, in which runtime metadata and descriptive models enable systems to evolve without being tied to a single application. Pattern-based, object-oriented designs extend UML’s multilayer metamodel to represent both static and dynamic behavior. CRISTAL provides a mature implementation: items are dynamically described, stored, versioned, and managed. In the neuGRID/N4U infrastructure, pipeline services index distributed clinical datasets, while query mechanisms support user-driven analysis and linked access through a data atlas. Provenance-aware tools capture analysis histories and can map them to the interoperable PROV model.

Recent trends emphasize cloud-scale and enterprise-wide big-data environments, integrated access to heterogeneous datasets, systematic traceability by design, and cross-domain provenance interoperability. The work increasingly treats provenance as core infrastructure for flexible, reproducible, and reusable scientific analysis.

abstracts x20|4df1f349ebddb7d6a82de701ad.text:
## Representation Learning for Multilingual and Morphologically Complex Retrieval

This community focuses on improving information retrieval when queries and documents involve language gaps, translation uncertainty, or rich morphology. Two papers address dictionary-based cross-language information retrieval (CLIR), especially for agglutinative languages, where ambiguity, missing translations, out-of-vocabulary terms, and unreliable stemming reduce effectiveness. Proposed solutions include probabilistic translation modeling and query-dependent projection of low-dimensional word representations learned from pseudo-relevant documents.

A second major theme is formation matching in highly inflected texts. The work on statistical stemming and unsupervised formation matching extends beyond conventional prefix- and suffix-based similarity to identify affixes appearing at arbitrary positions, including infixes relevant to languages such as Persian, Arabic, and Malay.

Typical methods combine pseudo-relevance feedback, distributional word vectors, learned or query-specific transformation matrices, divergence minimization, and statistical analysis of word forms. Overall, the papers show a trend from surface-level lexical normalization and dictionary lookup toward adaptive, probabilistic, and low-dimensional representations. Retrieval models increasingly exploit feedback documents and learned geometric transformations to address translation and morphology jointly.

titles<=300|4df1f349ebddb7d6a82de701ad88.text:
### Cross-Lingual Retrieval for Morphologically Complex Languages

This community focuses on improving information retrieval across languages, especially agglutinative and highly inflected ones. A central theme is representing queries and documents in comparable spaces despite vocabulary mismatch and morphological variation.

Typical methods include probabilistic, dictionary-based translation; query projection across language dimensions; and feedback-driven modeling. Several works use pseudo-relevant documents or divergence minimization to refine query representations and improve ad hoc retrieval. Morphological processing is addressed through a statistical stemmer designed for complex texts and through unsupervised formation matching, which seeks correspondences among inflected word forms without relying entirely on manually constructed resources.

The emerging direction is toward combining lightweight linguistic normalization with data-driven, unsupervised or feedback-based techniques. Rather than depending solely on bilingual dictionaries or exact word matching, these approaches exploit distributional evidence, projected representations, and document feedback to handle inflection and cross-language mismatch.

abstracts x10|4df1f349ebddb7d6a82de701ad.text:
### Language-Aware Retrieval and Query Representation

This community focuses on improving information retrieval for multilingual and morphologically complex languages. A major theme is dictionary-based cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR), especially under translation ambiguity, missing dictionary entries, out-of-vocabulary terms, and the complex lexical formations of agglutinative languages.

Typical methods exploit pseudo-relevance feedback: top-ranked documents supply pseudo-relevant collections for query expansion, translation, and representation learning. Several works move beyond direct lexical matching by learning low-dimensional word vectors and estimating query-dependent projection or transformation matrices. These projections are used to map source-language representations into target-language spaces or to update ad hoc queries through rotation and scaling, with divergence minimization guiding the process. Probabilistic translation models address ambiguity and incomplete bilingual dictionaries.

A parallel line develops unsupervised or statistical formation matching. Rather than relying only on prefix and suffix similarity, the proposed stemmers identify affixes in arbitrary positions, including infixes, which are important for Persian, Arabic, Malay, and other highly inflected texts.

Overall, the research trends from surface string heuristics toward flexible affix discovery, probabilistic translation, feedback-driven modeling, and low-dimensional, query-specific representations.

titles<=300|ab7e42a6705b1d4d985292a4de52.text:
## Graph Representation and Personalized Recommendation

This community centers on recommender systems and graph representation learning. Major themes include collaborative, content-aware, social, knowledge-graph, cross-domain, multimedia, and session-based recommendation; sequential next-item, playlist, news, product, travel, and point-of-interest prediction; and link prediction, network alignment, community detection, fraud detection, and dynamic-network analysis.

Typical methods combine matrix factorization, Bayesian and pairwise ranking, factorization machines, autoencoders, variational models, tensor factorization, and hybrid content/user models. Deep learning is prominent, particularly recurrent and Transformer architectures, graph convolutional and graph attention networks, random-walk embeddings, meta-path methods, heterogeneous-network models, and knowledge-graph propagation. Reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, adversarial training, and metric learning address online optimization, exploration, robustness, and ranking. Research also emphasizes cold-start handling, explainability, diversity, fairness, and evaluation bias.

Recent trends move toward temporal and dynamic graph embeddings, multimodal and cross-domain learning, long-term sequential behavior modeling, and scalable industrial recommendation. Emerging concerns include adversarial and poisoning attacks, misinformation and fraud, reproducibility, causal and calibrated explanations, and learning policies or reward functions directly from user interactions.

abstracts x10|ab7e42a6705b1d4d985292a4de.text:
## Recommendation and Dynamic Network Representation Learning

This community centers on recommender systems and representation learning for complex, evolving information networks. Core themes include combining long-term preferences with short-term sequential behavior, collaborative filtering, personalized ranking, social and semantic recommendation, and prediction in heterogeneous temporal graphs. It also addresses practical reliability concerns, including shilling attacks, sparse interactions, online updates, and cold-start users or items.

Typical methods range from matrix factorization, item-transition Markov chains, nearest-neighbor and slope-one predictors to neural networks and variational autoencoders. Hybrid approaches integrate user–item and item–item relations, nonlinear latent-factor transformations, Bayesian or generative modeling, and multimodal text/image information. Network representation learning is used to embed large social, citation, biological, and other information networks, while temporal graph reconstruction and continuous-time modeling support future relationship prediction.

Recent directions emphasize neural and generative collaborative filtering, explicit modeling of both users and items, temporal robustness rather than static embeddings, heterogeneous continuous-time prediction, and multimodal recommendation under missing or corrupted data. The papers also show increasing attention to real-world evaluation: measuring which users are harmed by fraudulent reviews and developing efficient methods that support dynamic updates and online queries.

abstracts x20|ab7e42a6705b1d4d985292a4de.text:
## Dynamic, Graph-Based Recommendation and Representation Learning

This community centers on recommender systems, especially methods that model sequential behavior, sessions, and sparse user–item interactions. Major themes include combining long-term preferences with short-term dynamics (matrix factorization, similarity models, Markov chains), playlist and event continuation, cold-start and long-tail recommendation, and robustness to fraudulent reviews.

Typical methods range from slope-one predictors, collaborative filtering, latent semantic analysis, and probabilistic latent-variable models to neural architectures such as variational autoencoders, nonlinear user–item models, and graph neural networks. Multimodal recommendation addresses missing text or image information through modality dropout and sequential modeling. Surveys and empirical analyses compare network representation learning and session-based recommendation approaches.

A strong parallel theme is learning representations of evolving, heterogeneous networks. Work investigates temporal graph reconstruction, continuous-time relationship prediction, social-network fusion, metapath-guided cross-modal embeddings, and semantic network construction. These methods target future-link prediction, urban dynamics, and knowledge extraction from text, including entity normalization.

Recent trends emphasize neural and graph-based models, dynamic rather than static representations, anonymous-session modeling, multimodal and hybrid recommendation, and practical concerns such as missing data, sparse or long-tail items, cold start, and real-world attack impact.

titles<=300|ebb4611158ab0c44311c39ce2069.text:
## Schemas, Validation, and Semantic Data Integration

This community focuses on representing, learning, validating, and querying structured and semi-structured data. A major theme is XML schema inference, especially deterministic, single-occurrence, restricted, and unordered regular expressions with interleaving. Work combines learning algorithms, heuristics, practical evaluations on large XML and schema collections, and schema-based optimization for streams and Twig/XPath queries.

A second theme is semantic validation and annotation. Papers study RDF shape expressions, SHACL-based customization of schema.org, domain-specific validation, verification of semantic annotations, and tools such as Empusa and Semantify It for generating, publishing, and distributing machine-readable data. Schema.org is applied to dynamic content, tourism services, and machine-readable Web APIs, including action annotations and automatic processing.

Query processing and formal analysis form another strand, covering XPath containment and rewriting, tree-pattern queries, regular path queries, DAG pattern matching, document projection, and provenance workflows. Additional work addresses schemas for tabular Web data and dependencies in workflow views.

Recent directions emphasize practical semantic ecosystems—particularly tourism knowledge graphs—alongside scalable data management, graph databases, streaming, and richer integration between schemas, annotations, and query systems.

titles<=300|34f244278c854da2135f5dae4c48.text:
### Interestingness, Surprise, and Discovery in Information Systems

This community studies how computational systems can identify, rank, and present information that users find interesting, surprising, or useful. Applications span social-network friend recommendation, web search for new linearized medical-drug leads, automatic extraction of trivia facts from Wikipedia, and an “interestingness” tool for web search.

A central research theme is the modeling of interestingness as a basis for information retrieval and recommendation. The work includes reduced-variable approaches for social recommendations and automated extraction pipelines for structured factual content. The community also develops conceptual foundations: *Interestingness: A Unifying Paradigm* frames interestingness through bipolar function composition, suggesting a general mechanism for combining opposing or complementary factors.

Human-centered evaluation is another important method. The user study on human perception of surprise examines how people experience and assess unexpected information, providing a basis for aligning computational scores with human judgments.

Overall, the research trends from task-specific discovery and extraction tools toward unified interestingness models, while increasingly incorporating human perception to evaluate and refine automated notions of surprise and relevance.

abstracts x10|ebb4611158ab0c44311c39ce20.text:
## Schema Inference and Semantic Validation for Structured Web Data

This community studies how to define, learn, validate, and publish structured data schemas. A major theme is XML schema inference, particularly deterministic regular expressions and unordered XML models. Work examines restricted regular expressions with interleaving, disjunctive and disjunction-free multiplicity schemas, and unordered regular expressions, balancing expressive power with tractability. Methods include formal language analysis, complexity characterizations, polynomial inference algorithms, heuristics, and experiments on real XML corpora. Several studies identify intractable problems such as membership, containment, or minimal-schema discovery, motivating practically restricted formalisms.

A second theme is semantic validation and interoperability on the Web. Shape Expressions (ShEx) use regular bag expressions to validate RDF graph neighborhoods, with alternative typing semantics and detailed complexity analysis. Schema.org research addresses domain-specific annotation validation, publication heuristics for dynamic data, tourism providers, and machine-readable Web API actions. These studies combine schema design, semantic annotation, deployment, and empirical evaluation.

Recent trends emphasize unordered or interleaved content models, concise schemas learned from positive examples, scalable validation and publication, and extending static Web annotations toward actionable, automated service consumption.

abstracts x10|34f244278c854da2135f5dae4c.text:
### Interestingness-Driven Discovery and Recommendation

This community studies how to make information discovery more engaging, useful, and surprising. Its central theme is **interestingness**, formalized as a bipolar composition of **relevance** and **unexpectedness**. This framework supports flexible functions, including Match–Mismatch and TF-IDF, and motivates a practical Web-search tool.

Applications span several domains. Social-network friend recommendation combines conventional friend-of-a-friend methods with randomization and direct measures of interestingness, including time-dependent behavior. Web search is adapted to biomedical discovery by representing molecular fragments as linearized inputs, yielding manageable and potentially novel drug-lead results. Wikipedia is mined for “trivia-worthy” facts to enrich named-entity search results and increase engagement.

Typical methods include function composition, information-retrieval scoring, algorithmic mining, randomized recommendation, representation of structured knowledge as linear strings, and empirical case studies. A crowdsourcing study with 106 participants compares human judgments of surprise with computational rankings and finds that algorithmic surprise can be used to induce surprise in people.

Overall, the work trends from conceptualizing interestingness toward robust tools, domain-specific applications, and human-centered validation of surprise and engagement.

abstracts x20|34f244278c854da2135f5dae4c.text:
### Interestingness-Driven Search and Recommendation

This community studies how **interestingness, surprise, and unexpectedness** can improve information discovery and user engagement. A central conceptual theme defines interestingness as a bipolar composition of **relevance and unexpectedness**, while an implemented search tool operationalizes this paradigm using functions such as Match–Mismatch and TF–IDF across multiple domains.

Applications span diverse retrieval and recommendation tasks. Social-network friend recommendation combines conventional friend-of-a-friend methods with randomization and direct use of interestingness to reproduce time-dependent recommendation behavior. Web search is extended to nonstandard inputs, including linearized molecular-structure fragments for discovering medical drug leads. Wikipedia-based systems automatically extract “trivia-worthy” facts about named entities, aiming to augment search results and increase engagement.

Typical methods include function composition, heuristic and algorithmic ranking, text-based similarity measures, structure linearization, automated fact mining, and empirical case studies. A crowdsourcing study with 106 participants compares human judgments of surprise with computational models and finds that algorithmically ranked surprise can be induced in users.

Recent trends emphasize moving from abstract definitions toward robust tools, practical search applications, automated content curation, and human-centered validation of computational surprise.

### Data Mining for Prediction and Graph-Structured Analysis

This community examines data mining as a framework for diagnosis, prognosis, prediction, and exploratory analysis. Applications include cancer disease diagnosis and prognosis, prediction of workers in the public-relations departments of Orissa blocks and panchayats, and a broader survey of data-mining applications and feature scope.

The papers describe both application-oriented and structural methods. Predictive mining is applied to organizational and medical problems, while multi-relational data-mining approaches address data involving multiple kinds of relationships. A complementary line of work uses quantitative Gaifman graphs as data-analysis tools. Their decomposition supports the study of co-occurrence patterns through modular and clan decompositions, emphasizing structure within relational data.

Overall, the research moves from general surveys and domain-specific prediction toward richer relational and graph-based analysis. Recent work particularly highlights decompositional techniques for uncovering co-occurrence structure, alongside continued interest in practical predictive systems and feature-oriented data-mining applications.

abstracts x20|ebb4611158ab0c44311c39ce20.text:
## Schema Inference and Semantic Validation for Structured Web Data

This community centers on learning, validating, and exploiting schemas for XML and RDF-based web data. A major theme is XML schema inference from positive—and sometimes negative—examples, especially deterministic regular expressions, single-occurrence expressions, and expressions with interleaving. Because unordered XML better reflects many practical datasets, studies propose disjunctive multiplicity schemas, multiplicity schemas, and unordered regular expressions, analyzing membership, containment, satisfiability, and inference complexity.

Typical methods combine formal-language analysis with polynomial learning algorithms, heuristic or minimal-schema discovery, empirical evaluation on large XML corpora, and complexity characterizations. Schema information is also used operationally: DTD constraints guide event scheduling and buffer minimization for streaming XQuery, while learned queries and XPath rewritings improve structured-data access.

A second theme is semantic validation of RDF and Schema.org annotations. Shape Expressions (ShEx), regular bag expressions, domain-specific validation, and ontology-aware tools check graph topology and intended resource content. Recent work increasingly targets deployment: publishing dynamic data selectively, annotating Web APIs and actions for automated processing, and constructing tourism knowledge graphs. Schema.org applications emphasize domain profiles, complete annotations, scalable publication, and machine-readable services, linking theoretical schema techniques with search, personal assistants, and regional data ecosystems.

### Research Data Integration, Archiving, and Accessibility

This community focuses on improving the discovery, management, and long-term availability of research data. A central theme is integrating research data management with geographical information systems and connecting web-based mapping services to scientific data repositories. Geospatial interfaces support collaborative curation and retrieval of simulation data, suggesting an emphasis on making data discoverable and usable through interactive research tools.

A second major theme is data preservation. Studies examine the long-term availability of raw experimental data, including in experimental fracture mechanics, and assess how access changes as publications age. The papers also highlight policy interventions: mandated data archiving is associated with substantially improved access to research data.

Typical methods include developing or linking repository and mapping infrastructures, using geospatial interfaces for data organization and retrieval, evaluating archival availability over time, and comparing access under different policy conditions. Recent trends move toward formal archiving mandates and integrated, web-based discovery systems, while evidence of rapid decline in data availability with article age underscores the need for sustained preservation practices.

abstracts x10|6e6cabde55700cc4dcc5283fd5.text:
## Data Mining for Prediction and Structured Data Exploration

This community centers on data mining as a means of extracting actionable knowledge from large, distributed, and relational datasets. Applied studies address breast-cancer diagnosis and prognosis—distinguishing benign from malignant cases and predicting recurrence—as well as workforce-demand prediction in the Orissa Panchayat Raj Department. A broader survey emphasizes data warehouses, organizational decision-making, and the expanding scope of data-mining applications.

A major methodological theme is multi-relational data mining (MRDM), which analyzes patterns directly across multiple database tables rather than reducing them to a single propositionalized table. Complementing these predictive approaches, the graph-oriented work uses Gaifman graphs to represent relationships in first-order and multirelational data. Modular decompositions, generalized quantitative Gaifman graphs, and 2-structure-based methods support exploratory analysis and reveal structural patterns.

Recent developments emphasize hierarchical and visual interpretation of co-occurrence data through clan decompositions. The introduction of clan implications frames these decompositions as closure spaces and supports algorithmic implementations for exploratory software. Overall, the community trends from conventional application surveys and domain-specific prediction toward structured, multirelational, graph-based, and more interpretable data analysis.

abstracts x10|8e5cb07858a3ee837179b42147.text:
## Research Data Reproducibility, Preservation, and Geospatial Access

This community examines how scientific data can remain accessible, discoverable, and reusable across the research lifecycle. A major theme is integrating research data management with computational workflows: ocean modelling studies use GIS to create high-fidelity meshes while preserving the associated inputs needed to recompute simulations. Complementary work connects web-based mapping services with repositories such as Figshare and Zenodo, enabling collaborative, geospatial cataloguing and retrieval of simulation data.

Several papers empirically assess the durability of data sharing. Studies of population-genetics papers compare absent, recommended, and mandatory archiving policies, finding that mandated deposition substantially improves access. Research in experimental fracture mechanics investigates the long-term availability of raw data through direct correspondence with authors, while another study requests datasets across publication ages to measure decline in availability over time.

Typical methods include software and interface design, repository integration, geospatial visualization, policy comparison, author surveys or email requests, and longitudinal or publication-age analyses. Recent trends emphasize moving from voluntary or author-dependent sharing toward mandated archival policies, persistent repositories, and workflow-integrated metadata and provenance. Together, the papers frame reproducibility as both a technical infrastructure problem and a governance problem.

abstracts x10|7f356385c9451ff3d020fb839d.text:
## Description-Driven Provenance for Data-Intensive Science

This community focuses on making large-scale data and analysis processes accessible, adaptable, and traceable. Key applications include neuroimaging and clinical research in neuGRID/N4U, industrial systems, cloud-based big-data platforms, and potential reuse in high-energy physics (HEP).

A central theme is the **description-driven approach**, in which data and process elements (“Items”) are enriched with metadata and descriptions, modeled at runtime, and managed independently of particular applications. The proposed pattern-reification and object-oriented architectures extend multilayer UML models to represent both static and dynamic behavior. CRISTAL provides a mature implementation: Items are versioned and provenance-aware, supporting flexible system evolution.

Typical methods include pipeline services for indexing datasets, linked clinical-data atlases, dynamic user-driven querying, provenance capture and management, and traceability across analysis workflows. The N4U analysis tools demonstrate these methods for Alzheimer’s biomarker studies.

Recent work emphasizes applying provenance beyond individual domains, designing traceability into enterprise and cloud systems from the outset, and improving interoperability through mappings to the PROV model. The overall trend is from domain-specific infrastructures toward generic, reusable, and cross-disciplinary provenance frameworks.

abstracts x20|6e6cabde55700cc4dcc5283fd5.text:
## Data Mining for Prediction, Relational Analysis, and Graph-Based Exploration

This community examines data mining as a tool for decision-making, prediction, and discovery in complex datasets. Application-oriented studies address breast cancer diagnosis and prognosis, worker-demand prediction in public administration, and organizational analysis using large distributed data sources and data warehouses. Typical methods include classification and prognosis techniques, forecasting approaches, feature-oriented analysis, and general data-mining workflows.

A major theme is mining structured and multi-relational data. Multi-Relational Data Mining (MRDM) operates directly across multiple database tables, contrasting with propositionalisation into a single table and addressing challenges caused by distributed relational information.

Another prominent direction uses Gaifman graphs to analyze relational and co-occurrence data. Modular decompositions expose structural patterns, while generalized and quantitative Gaifman graphs extend the analytical scope through 2-structures. Clan decompositions provide hierarchical visualizations, and newly introduced clan implications connect these decompositions to closure spaces.

Recent work emphasizes exploratory graph-based analysis, formalizing visual patterns and developing algorithmic support for software implementations. Overall, the community is moving from conventional application-specific prediction toward scalable, structurally informed analysis of relational and multirelational data.

**Research Data Stewardship, Reproducibility, and Geospatial Access**

This community examines how research data can remain discoverable, accessible, and reusable throughout the scientific lifecycle. One theme is integrating research data management with computational workflows: ocean-modelling studies connect GIS-based mesh generation with the documentation and preservation of all inputs needed to recompute simulations. A related direction uses web-based mapping interfaces to visually catalogue, curate, and retrieve geoscientific simulation datasets from repositories such as Figshare and Zenodo, supporting collaboration across overlapping study regions.

Other papers assess the practical durability of data sharing. Studies in population genetics and experimental fracture mechanics evaluate whether raw or underlying data can be obtained from published research, while a broader longitudinal analysis investigates how availability changes with article age. Typical methods include repository and policy comparisons, direct requests to authors, analysis of contact outcomes, and tool design and evaluation.

Recent trends favor mandatory deposition policies over recommendations, integration of data management into research software and GIS, and user-oriented geospatial discovery. Collectively, the papers show that informal or author-dependent access is fragile: data become harder to retrieve over time, strengthening the case for enforced archiving and durable repositories.
