This community studies how social-network structure shapes behavior, information, and collective outcomes. Core themes include homophily and demographic prediction; network paradoxes, rich-club and dyadic effects; community structure and deviant behavior; and the evolution of online-game and social-media networks. A second major focus is information diffusion, including emergency communication, disaster damage assessment, contagious outbreaks, emotional interactions with bots, information overload, and social contagions.

Typical methods combine large-scale platform datasets with statistical network analysis, power-law and heavy-tailed distribution models, graph-based prediction, embeddings, and supervised learning. Researchers also use agent-based simulations (including the Hashkat platform), analytical models of polling and network externalities, and empirical studies of privacy controls. Applications include detecting fake accounts and money laundering groups, predicting demographics from transaction data, identifying suicide ideation, and improving disaster response.

The papers increasingly emphasize moving beyond individual-level analysis toward relational and group-level inference: exploiting friends as sensors, modeling latent agents, detecting collaborating criminal groups, and studying hierarchical influence. They also pursue practical interventions—adaptive polling, audience-control design, targeted monitoring, and information-management strategies—while highlighting privacy, exposure, and the behavioral consequences of platform-mediated social interaction.

abstracts x10|6899dbc06fb4c2f858f900f5c6.text:
## Learning- and Approximation-Driven Data Analytics

This community focuses on making complex, large-scale data querying faster, more interactive, and more accessible. A central theme is query optimization: learned cardinality estimation (MSCN) models correlated joins and sparse predicates, while Neo uses deep neural networks to generate execution plans. Complementary work develops memory-aware cost models for hash-based multi-join processing in main-memory databases.

Approximate query processing is another major direction. Deep generative models and EntropyDB learn probabilistic or distributional summaries to answer aggregate queries efficiently, trading exactness for interactive exploration. MacroBase similarly supports rapid analysis of high-volume streams through reservoir sampling, heavy-hitters sketches, explanation, and classification.

Several papers address expensive queries over rich or unstructured data. Physical-representation-aware predicates reduce CNN-based image and video extraction costs, while video monitoring uses approximate filters for object and spatial-relation queries. XML keyword search is diversified by modeling distinct data contexts, improving results for ambiguous queries. SkyServer illustrates a public, web-accessible scientific database and a platform for database performance research.

Overall, the papers show a shift toward learned components, probabilistic summaries, sampling, sketches, approximate filters, and hardware-aware execution—particularly for interactive analytics, streaming data, and multimodal content.

titles<=300|6899dbc06fb4c2f858f900f5c62c.text:
## Learned and Approximate Systems for Interactive Analytics

This community focuses on making database analytics fast, adaptive, and accessible at scale. Major themes include cardinality and selectivity estimation, cost and runtime prediction, join-order and partitioning optimization, workload management, and automatic database administration. Approximate query processing is central, using sampling, sketches, probabilistic summaries, compressed representations, and deterministic or bounded-error guarantees.

A defining direction is the integration of machine learning into database internals: deep likelihood models, neural representations, learned indexes, query embeddings, and reinforcement learning for optimization, view materialization, re-optimization, and resource allocation. Systems also target interactive exploration through progressive evaluation, visualizations, drill-down, insight recommendation, diversification, provenance, and explanations.

Application-oriented work emphasizes large-scale video, sensor, geospatial, time-series, graph, astronomical, and social-media data, often supporting low-latency exploratory queries and neural-network analytics. Natural-language interfaces and SQL generation aim to make structured data easier for nonexperts to query.

Recent trends include autonomous and self-tuning databases, shared and multi-query execution, cloud/serverless and in-browser analytics, edge and autonomous-camera processing, and tighter integration of data cleaning, feature generation, model validation, and inference. Overall, the papers combine statistical guarantees with learned, adaptive execution to trade accuracy, cost, and latency interactively.

abstracts x20|6899dbc06fb4c2f858f900f5c6.text:
## Learning-Enhanced Interactive Data Systems

This community focuses on making data management, querying, and exploration faster, more adaptive, and more accessible. Core themes include learned query optimization and cardinality estimation, approximate query processing, workload and resource management, and analytics over visual, video, spatial, and heterogeneous data. Several works target interactive exploration: probabilistic or generative summaries provide fast aggregate answers, while MacroBase prioritizes unusual behavior in high-volume streams and Foresight recommends statistically meaningful visual insights.

Typical methods combine database algorithms with machine learning. Deep neural networks model correlated joins, generate execution plans, and learn data distributions; vector representations capture SQL workload structure. Other approaches use sampling algebras, maximum-entropy summaries, sketches, reservoir sampling, and cost models for memory-resident or cloud computation. Domain-specific systems employ CNN-based visual predicates, approximate video filters, trajectory alignment, provenance, and context-aware XML search.

Recent trends emphasize learned and declarative systems that automate traditionally hand-tuned decisions, including optimization, model selection, resource allocation, and workload analysis. The papers also increasingly address interactive and exploratory use cases, where approximate answers and insight discovery trade small inaccuracies for substantial speedups. A parallel direction is broadening database access across silos and modalities through common representations, visual analytics, and spatiotemporal relationship discovery.

abstracts x20|38b6712c561bef574981e59eda.text:
## Scalable Data Management and High-Performance Query Processing

This community investigates efficient representation, indexing, querying, and execution for large-scale scientific, spatial, transactional, and information-retrieval workloads. Core themes include set and bitmap operations, multidimensional and spatial indexing, column-store predicate optimization, and low-overhead database indexes. Compression is central: work improves Variable-Byte, Huffman, SIMD-based integer, and word-aligned bitmap compression, while histogram-aware sorting reduces bitmap size and accelerates logical operations.

Typical methods combine theoretical analysis with engineered systems and empirical evaluation. Examples include worst-case bounds for set intersection, pairwise-independence analysis for recursive hashing, pruning based on geometric properties, query batching to increase data reuse, and dataflow-based distributed mining. Implementations exploit SIMD instructions, multicore CPUs, GPUs, in-memory execution, specialized bitmap libraries, and synchronization strategies such as flat combining.

The papers also address database support for finite-element analysis, petabyte-scale scientific archives, distributed data management, and high-throughput OLTP. Recent trends emphasize scaling beyond single machines, integrating databases with scientific and web-oriented applications, exploiting heterogeneous hardware, reducing storage and index-maintenance costs, and co-optimizing data layout, compression, and execution for modern SSD, NVM, GPU, and distributed environments.

titles<=300|38b6712c561bef574981e59eda34.text:
## High-Performance Analytics and Compression for Scientific Data

This community focuses on making large-scale analytical data systems faster, smaller, and more scalable. A central theme is compressed indexing: bitmap indexes, inverted indexes, multidimensional indexes, repetitive document collections, and integer sequences. Roaring bitmaps, word-aligned compression, variable-byte and Huffman coding, and quasi-succinct structures are optimized for rapid intersections, unions, decoding, and search.

A second theme is hardware-conscious execution. SIMD vectorization, CPU–GPU hybrids, in-memory processing, flat combining, and parallel dataflow accelerate compression, transaction execution, SQL analytics, graph queries, and pathology-image comparison. Column stores and relational systems are improved through predicate optimization, column and row reordering, caching, histogram-aware sorting, and analytical cost or view-size estimation.

The papers also address spatial and scientific workloads, including multidimensional databases, geospatial joins and indexing, astronomical cross-matching, finite-element data, metadata, and massive scientific archives. Related work applies OLAP and relational algebra to text, social networks, graphs, and entity relationships.

Recent directions emphasize petabyte- and exascale data management, distributed in-memory processing, database–science integration, scalable probabilistic joins, and practical libraries such as Roaring. Overall, the trend is toward modular, compressed, vectorized, and interactive systems capable of processing billions or trillions of values.

titles<=300|b52a9e6e18a32841bbcf3ae3d321.text:
### Recommendation Systems and Predictive Graph Modeling

This community focuses on improving recommender systems through collaborative, content-based, spectral, and mobile-oriented techniques. A central theme is **multi-level collaborative filtering**, including dynamic approaches designed to improve recommendation quality. Other work explores **content-based recommendation in social tagging systems**, with explicit attention to user privacy, and uses **spectral-domain features** to make collaborative filtering more efficient. Mobile recommender systems are examined by identifying their major concepts, suggesting an interest in adapting recommendation methods to mobile contexts and constraints.

The methods represented include collaborative-filtering models operating at multiple levels, dynamic adaptation, content analysis of tags, privacy-aware recommendation, and spectral feature extraction. The community also extends recommendation ideas toward security analytics: one paper moves from product recommendation to **cyberattack prediction**, generating attack graphs and forecasting future attacks.

Overall, the recent direction appears to broaden recommendation research beyond product personalization toward efficiency, privacy, mobile deployment, and predictive graph-based applications such as anticipating cyberattacks.

abstracts x10|38b6712c561bef574981e59eda.text:
### Scalable Data Management and Query Processing

This community focuses on efficient management, indexing, and analysis of large, complex datasets. Core themes include set and bitmap operations, multidimensional and spatial databases, column-store query optimization, scientific data exploration, and database-backed engineering applications. Several works target extreme scale, from terabyte- and petabyte-scale astronomy archives to massive pathology-image collections and data-intensive scientific queries.

Typical methods combine specialized data structures and execution strategies with modern hardware. Examples include linear-space set representations, bitmap logic for threshold and symmetric queries, multidimensional and spatial indexing, predicate reordering for disjunctive column-store queries, and hybrid CPU–GPU parallelism. Work on LifeRaft improves throughput by batching queries with overlapping data requirements and ordering execution to maximize data reuse. GeoPrune uses geometric properties to reduce candidate vehicles before ride-sharing selection. Other papers investigate relational databases as backends for finite-element analysis and articulate principles for distributed, heterogeneous, autonomous data sources.

Recent directions emphasize hardware-conscious acceleration, cache and I/O efficiency, scalable scientific data mining, and integration beyond traditional file-based systems. Overall, the research seeks predictable performance and practical throughput as data volume, dimensionality, and application integration continue to grow.

abstracts x10|b52a9e6e18a32841bbcf3ae3d3.text:
### Recommendation, Privacy, and Predictive Graph Methods

This community focuses primarily on improving recommender-system quality, especially collaborative filtering (CF), across e-commerce, social tagging, mobile applications, and other online environments. A recurring concern is the limited accuracy of conventional CF methods. Proposed solutions include multi-level approaches that divide Pearson Correlation Similarity into stages, and dynamic multi-level adjustment using positive and negative evidence. Evaluation includes comparisons with alternative methods on five real datasets.

Another methodological direction combines machine learning and signal processing: self-organizing maps and k-means identify similar-user clusters, after which ratings are transformed with the Discrete Fourier Transform. Power spectra and coherence-based similarity are then used for recommendation.

The papers also broaden the scope beyond accuracy. Content-based recommendation and social tagging are examined alongside user privacy risks arising from exposed profiles and activity. A survey-oriented study identifies major factors affecting mobile recommender systems, highlighting the importance of application context in addition to algorithm design.

A notable recent trend is applying recommendation and graph techniques to cybersecurity: attack graphs represent exploitable intrusion paths in maritime supply-chain infrastructure, while prediction is used to anticipate future attacks.

abstracts x20|b52a9e6e18a32841bbcf3ae3d3.text:
### Recommendation Systems: Adaptive, Privacy-Aware, and Predictive Methods

This community focuses on improving recommender systems, especially collaborative filtering (CF), while examining their broader applications and risks. Core themes include recommendation accuracy, personalization, user experience, privacy in social tagging, mobile recommender-system factors, and prediction beyond products—such as future cyber-attacks.

Typical methods enhance similarity estimation and user/item grouping. Multi-level and dynamic CF approaches divide Pearson correlation similarity into levels or apply positive and negative adjustments to improve recommendation quality, with evaluation on real datasets and comparisons against alternatives. Another method combines self-organizing maps and k-means to identify similar users, then transforms clustered ratings into the frequency domain using the Discrete Fourier Transform and derives similarity from power spectra and coherence. Content-based recommendation is considered through user annotations and ratings, alongside privacy threats arising from exposed profiles in social tagging systems.

Recent trends show movement from basic CF toward adaptive, multi-stage, and signal-processing-based techniques, with increasing attention to deployment contexts such as mobile systems and information overload. The community also extends recommendation-style prediction to cybersecurity by constructing attack graphs from maritime infrastructure data and predicting likely future attacks.

titles<=300|39a6d61753837d2030df0cf41ce2.text:
### Scientific Discovery Through Text Similarity and Recommendation

This community focuses on improving discovery, retrieval, and impact assessment across scientific and patent literature. A central theme is text-based similarity: textual spatial cosine similarity, full-text search for patent prior art, and similarity-based knowledge discovery in astronomy. These works emphasize content-driven retrieval as an alternative or complement to conventional search.

A second theme is recommendation and exploration. *Science Concierge* presents a fast content-based recommendation system, while *Real World Evaluation of Approaches to Research Paper Recommendation* examines recommendation methods in practice. *PubVis* extends discovery through interactive exploration and visualization of scientific publications.

The community also studies how unexpectedness shapes science. *Science and Technology Advance Through Surprise* links surprise with scientific and technological progress, while *The Effect of Novelty on the Future Impact of Scientific Grants* investigates whether novelty predicts later influence.

Typical methods include full-text similarity search, cosine-based textual comparison, content-based recommendation, interactive visual interfaces, and empirical evaluation in real-world settings. Overall, the apparent trend is from information retrieval toward integrated discovery systems: faster similarity computation, domain-specific retrieval (including patents and astronomy), interactive exploration, and greater attention to novelty, surprise, and the eventual impact of research.

abstracts x10|39a6d61753837d2030df0cf41c.text:
## Intelligent Discovery and the Dynamics of Scientific Novelty

This community focuses on computational systems for discovering, recommending, and evaluating scientific and technical knowledge. A major theme is information retrieval: paper and patent search, astronomy-literature exploration, prior-art identification, and document recommendation address the challenge of rapidly expanding scholarly and patent collections.

Typical methods include full-text and content-based similarity, cosine-based measures enhanced with word-placement information, machine-learning recommendation, interactive visualization, and large-scale literature reviews of retrieval approaches. Systems emphasize practical usability, including near-real-time recommendations, open-source implementations, and evaluation with user click data. PubVis combines machine learning with visual exploration to move beyond keyword search.

A second theme concerns how novelty shapes scientific progress. Large-scale analyses of NSF- and NIH-funded publications quantify grant novelty and relate it to citation trajectories. Related work models surprising combinations of concepts, contexts, and disciplines using embeddings and stochastic block models, finding that unexpected combinations can predict outsized citation impact.

Recent trends favor full-text and semantic processing over manually constructed keyword queries; scalable machine learning over massive publication, patent, and researcher datasets; interactive interfaces; and empirical, real-world evaluation. The community is increasingly linking discovery tools with broader questions about novelty, impact, and knowledge advancement.

abstracts x20|39a6d61753837d2030df0cf41c.text:
### Scientific Discovery, Retrieval, and Recommendation

This community focuses on computationally assisted discovery across scientific literature and patents. Major themes include content-based paper recommendation, interactive exploration and visualization, document and patent retrieval, semantic similarity, and the relationship between novelty and research impact. Several works address information overload in rapidly expanding literatures, including astronomy.

Typical methods include machine-learning models, text-based and full-text similarity search, cosine-based measures incorporating word placement, embeddings, and high-dimensional stochastic block models. Recommendation systems emphasize near-real-time, adaptive, open-source content analysis, while evaluations use literature surveys, implemented baselines, and user-click data. Patent studies target automated prior-art searches and review information-retrieval techniques. Large-scale analyses connect grant novelty and unexpected combinations of scientific content or contexts with subsequent citation impact.

Recent trends move beyond keyword search toward semantic and interactive discovery, scalable processing of millions of papers, patents, and researchers, and practical real-world evaluation. Surprise and novelty are increasingly modeled quantitatively: improbable combinations can predict breakthrough impact, while grant novelty is assessed against later citation dynamics. Overall, the community combines retrieval, recommendation, visualization, and science-of-science analytics to improve both access to knowledge and understanding of how new ideas emerge.

titles<=300|8523b94ee09b64d5b99000465249.text:
## Fashion Recommendation and Demand-Aware Personalization

This community focuses on intelligent fashion recommendation, combining customer behavior, product attributes, sales signals, and fit information. Key themes include session-based complementary-item recommendation, modeling how fashionability influences style sales, and constructing a “fashion DNA” that connects content and commercial data for recommendation and article mapping. Personalization is also addressed through dynamic customer modeling, particularly with LSTM-based approaches that capture evolving preferences over time. A related application targets footwear size recommendation, emphasizing fit-aware assistance alongside style discovery.

Typical methods include sequential deep learning for session and customer modeling, content–sales data integration, article-level representation and mapping, and predictive analysis of fashionability and sales. The papers suggest a movement from static product or user profiles toward dynamic, context-sensitive systems that jointly consider complementary products, changing tastes, commercial performance, and physical fit. Overall, the research trends toward richer multimodal and behavioral representations, with recommendation extending beyond “what to buy” to “what goes together,” “what is likely to sell,” and “what size will fit.”

abstracts x10|8523b94ee09b64d5b990004652.text:
## Data-Driven Personalization for Online Fashion

This community focuses on improving online fashion commerce through personalized recommendations, demand modeling, and product understanding. Key themes include complementary-item discovery, evolving customer preferences, fashionability assessment, product-to-customer matching, and footwear size prediction, including support for new customers.

Typical methods combine deep learning with behavioral, sales, and content data. ZSF-c develops session-based complementary recommendations and uses specialized sampling when interaction data are noisy. Fashion DNA employs a neural network that integrates article tags and images to predict customer purchases, producing product and customer-style vector spaces. Dynamic recommendation models use neural networks to represent changing customer and store environments amid seasonality, inventory turnover, and irregular shopping. Other work derives a style quotient from demand data to separate stylistic appeal from price and promotions, supporting assortment planning and backtesting. A production-oriented footwear system addresses fit guidance and cold-start users.

Recent trends emphasize multimodal product representations, dynamic and session-aware personalization, and commercially deployable systems. The research increasingly connects recommendation with broader retail decisions—such as assortment breadth and depth—while addressing practical constraints including sparse or poor-quality interactions, rapidly changing catalogs, stock limitations, returns, and limited customer history.

abstracts x20|8523b94ee09b64d5b990004652.text:
### Fashion Recommendation and Demand Intelligence

This community studies personalized fashion commerce, spanning complementary-item discovery, style-driven demand, dynamic customer preferences, and footwear fit. A central theme is combining behavioral or sales data with product content to improve recommendations across large, rapidly changing assortments.

Typical methods include neural recommendation models, session-based personalization, and specialized training-data sampling when interaction data are noisy. Fashion DNA uses deep networks that integrate article tags and images with sales histories, producing product and customer-style spaces for purchase-likelihood prediction and article mapping. Dynamic customer modeling uses LSTM-based neural architectures and backtesting on large-scale shopper data to address seasonality, inventory turnover, and evolving preferences. Other work derives a style quotient from demand data, separating fashionability from commercial effects such as price and promotions, and evaluates it through prediction-error analysis and backtesting. A production-oriented footwear system targets size recommendation, including users with no prior purchases.

Recent trends emphasize multimodal product representations, temporal and session-aware modeling, assortment planning informed by customer-perceived style, and practical cold-start solutions. Overall, the research moves beyond generic recommendation toward fashion-specific compatibility, style interpretation, operational constraints, and fit-aware shopping support.

titles<=300|ca40bda1e73510f871487bc4644f.text:
### Recommender Systems: Context, Geography, and Scalable Ranking

This community focuses on recommender systems, especially personalized point-of-interest (POI) and venue recommendation. Core themes include collaborative filtering beyond standard matrix factorization, top-*N* recommendation with graded relevance, and personalized or context-aware ranking. POI research increasingly integrates geographical, temporal, and social signals, including local-geographical logistic matrix factorization, joint geographical–temporal factorization, multiple location-based similarities, category-aware location embeddings, and social-centric venue scores.

Typical methods are matrix and metric factorization, logistic models, collaborative ranking, regularization, embeddings, and two-phase time-sensitive optimization. The papers also address broader system concerns: parallel and distributed collaborative filtering, GPU-based *k*-nearest-neighbor computation, and recommendation subgraphs for web discovery. Privacy is considered through a selective, poker-styled privacy-preserving framework.

Overall, the research trends from generic collaborative filtering toward richer, personalized recommendations that combine contextual, spatial, temporal, categorical, and social information. At the same time, work emphasizes scalable computation, improved top-*N* ranking quality, and privacy-aware recommendation. Surveys provide broad coverage of recommender systems and parallel or distributed collaborative filtering.

abstracts x10|ca40bda1e73510f871487bc464.text:
### Recommender Systems: Context, Ranking, and Scalable Personalization

This community centers on improving recommender-system accuracy, expressiveness, scalability, and privacy. A major theme is collaborative filtering and its extensions, including matrix/metric factorization, collaborative ranking, and direct optimization of top-\(N\) recommendations for graded relevance. Metric factorization replaces the dot product with Euclidean distance, while GAPFM targets ranked lists without reducing graded judgments to binary relevance.

Another strong focus is location-based recommendation. POI and venue models incorporate geographical similarity, user mobility, temporal activity, popularity variation, contextual appropriateness, and user-annotated tags to address sparsity and changing preferences. Typical methods include probabilistic topic or mapping models, dimensionality reduction, regularized two-phase ranking, and joint geographical-temporal matrix factorization.

The community also emphasizes systems concerns. Survey work examines parallel and distributed collaborative filtering, while GPU-based \(k\)-nearest-neighbor algorithms accelerate vector search through \(N\)-body computation and partial sorting. Privacy is addressed through selective, user-controlled disclosure in collaborative filtering.

Recent trends move beyond conventional rating prediction toward metric representations, learning-to-rank objectives, context- and time-aware personalization, heterogeneous location signals, hardware acceleration, and privacy-conscious recommendation.

abstracts x20|ca40bda1e73510f871487bc464.text:
## Recommender Systems: Context, Ranking, and Scalable Personalization

This community focuses on improving personalized recommendation, especially collaborative filtering (CF) and point-of-interest (POI)/venue suggestion in location-based social networks. Core themes include overcoming sparsity, modeling user–item similarity, producing accurate ranked lists, and scaling recommendation infrastructure.

Typical methods include matrix and metric factorization, logistic matrix factorization, collaborative ranking, and scoring-function user models. Several POI approaches incorporate geographical proximity, temporal activity, popularity variation, contextual appropriateness, venue content, reviews, social signals, and categorical information. Research also addresses direct top-*N* optimization for graded relevance rather than predicting ratings, as well as recommendation subgraphs for website navigation.

Systems-oriented work surveys parallel and distributed CF and develops GPU-based *k*-nearest-neighbor search using *N*-body computation and partial sorting. Privacy is addressed through selective, poker-style preference sharing. Neural representation learning appears in category-aware POI embeddings that combine sequential and categorical signals.

Recent trends emphasize richer contextual modeling—particularly joint geographic-temporal effects—alongside neural embeddings and auxiliary location information to mitigate sparse check-in data. The field is also moving toward ranking-native objectives, scalable hardware-aware implementations, and privacy-conscious personalization.

abstracts x10|8066cb1133f01eb9c0b490d304.text:
### Mobile Big Data for Labor Markets, Economic Activity, and Public Safety

This community examines how passively generated mobile and online data can provide timely, fine-grained measures of socioeconomic conditions. A central theme is employment: studies infer unemployment and individual employment status from mobile-phone usage, network logs, financial, social, and mobility patterns, while others track mass layoffs and estimate their effects on individuals and aggregate unemployment. Related work develops indices of employment and economic activity in China, extending economic measurement beyond traditional censuses and surveys.

Typical methods include feature extraction from call-detail records and other mobile traces, machine-learning prediction validated against household surveys, Bayesian classification, structural-break models for detecting shocks, and multiscale analysis of population behavior. The labor-market perspective also emphasizes complex interactions among institutions, employment, welfare, and economic growth.

A second theme is public-safety monitoring: Baidu Maps query data are analyzed to identify abnormal increases in collective activity and provide early warning of dangerous crowds, motivated by the Shanghai Stampede.

Overall, the research trends from static socioeconomic estimation toward dynamic, near-real-time monitoring of employment shocks, economic change, and emergent crowd risks at individual, local, and national scales.

abstracts x10|ab805da86cf06501a4193263ce.text:
### Explainable and Efficient Machine Learning for Legal Review

This community centers on predictive coding—also called Technology Assisted Review—for reducing the cost and effort of identifying relevant or privileged documents in litigation and regulatory investigations. Research themes include classifier effectiveness, explainability and lawyer trust, training-data and preprocessing choices, and efficient human-in-the-loop review.

Typical methods are empirical comparisons on real legal-review datasets. Studies evaluate Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, Convolutional Neural Networks, and deep-learning approaches, often across documents of varied lengths. Active-learning experiments examine seed-set selection and strategies for iteratively selecting documents for annotation. Other work tests how preprocessing parameters affect model performance and develops explainable classification frameworks and case studies to make predictions more interpretable to attorneys.

Recent trends move beyond fixed workflows and single algorithms toward deep learning, systematic optimization of preprocessing and training, and continuous active learning designed to reduce review burden. Explainability is increasingly treated as essential for operational and legal acceptance, not merely predictive accuracy. A related direction applies web-traffic data from Google Analytics to cybersecurity forensics, illustrating expansion of data-driven classification and monitoring beyond document review.

titles<=300|ab805da86cf06501a4193263ce1f.text:
## Machine Learning and Explainability in Legal Document Review

This community focuses primarily on predictive coding and automated text classification for legal document review. Research themes include comparing machine-learning and keyword-based approaches, assessing deep learning and convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and understanding how preprocessing choices affect classification effectiveness.

A major methodological emphasis is empirical evaluation. Studies compare learning algorithms, measure the impact of preprocessing parameters, and investigate active-learning strategies for reducing review effort. Related work examines how seed-set selection influences predictive-coding performance. Explainability is another central theme, with frameworks and case studies addressing how classification decisions can be made interpretable in legal settings.

The community’s recent direction appears to move beyond accuracy comparisons toward practical deployment concerns: selecting informative initial examples, optimizing iterative active-learning processes, and providing explanations for automated decisions. Deep learning and CNNs are evaluated alongside other algorithms rather than treated in isolation. One paper extends the broader computational-forensics perspective by applying Google Analytics to support cybersecurity investigations, but most contributions remain centered on empirical, explainable, and workflow-aware automation of legal document review.

abstracts x20|ab805da86cf06501a4193263ce.text:
### Machine Learning for Legal Review and Cybersecurity Forensics

This community centers on applying machine learning and text classification to legal document review, especially predictive coding/TAR for identifying relevant or privileged material in large electronically stored information collections. A major theme is reducing review cost and effort while preserving classification effectiveness.

Studies empirically compare Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, convolutional neural networks, and deep-learning approaches, often using data from real legal reviews and documents of varying lengths. Other work examines keyword-based methods, preprocessing parameters, training-data construction, and the selection of exemplar or seed documents.

Active learning is a recurring focus. Research evaluates alternative seed-set selection methods and active-learning strategies intended to reduce the amount of human review needed to train effective classifiers. Explainability is another important theme, addressing lawyers’ concerns about “black box” systems through frameworks and case studies of explainable predictive coding.

Recent trends include moving beyond fixed preprocessing and single-algorithm workflows, systematically comparing deep learning with established classifiers, and emphasizing transparent, defensible decision support. One related study extends data-driven analysis beyond legal review by using Google Analytics web-traffic data—including visitor, timing, page, and keyword information—to support cybersecurity monitoring and forensics.

abstracts x20|8066cb1133f01eb9c0b490d304.text:
### Mobile Big Data for Labor Markets and Collective Dynamics

This community examines how mobile and location-based data can measure socioeconomic conditions, especially employment, unemployment, economic activity, and responses to labor-market shocks. A central theme is replacing infrequent, costly surveys and censuses with temporally and spatially granular behavioral indicators.

Typical inputs include mobile phone network logs, call-detail records, Baidu Maps queries, and other geolocated digital traces. Researchers derive features capturing communication, mobility, financial, and social patterns, then apply machine-learning models to predict individual employment status and aggregate unemployment. Economic activity is summarized through indices of employment and consumption-related behavior. For abrupt disruptions, structural-break models detect mass layoffs, while Bayesian classification identifies affected individuals from changes in calling patterns. Query data are also analyzed for early warning of dangerous crowd formations.

The papers increasingly connect computational social science and complex-systems perspectives with practical monitoring. Recent trends include moving from static socioeconomic mapping toward continuous, multi-scale observation; identifying both individual vulnerability and population-level shocks; and extending mobile sensing from labor-market measurement to public-safety forecasting. Validation against household surveys and real-world events supports the use of these data for policy design and evaluation.

titles<=300|8066cb1133f01eb9c0b490d304b4.text:
### Mobile and Query Data for Socioeconomic Monitoring

This community applies computational social science and complex-systems perspectives to labor markets and population activity. Its central themes are measuring economic activity, identifying unemployment and individual employment status, and tracking employment shocks through passively generated digital traces. China is a major empirical setting, including nationwide mobile big-data analysis and a Shanghai crowd-disaster case.

Typical methods involve extracting behavioral “signatures” from mobile-phone network data, aggregating mobility patterns to estimate economic indicators, and using individual- or population-level signals to infer employment conditions. Query data—particularly from Baidu Maps—are analyzed for early warning of human crowds, illustrating a complementary use of digital search and location information.

The collection suggests a trend toward timely, scalable monitoring that moves beyond conventional surveys: from describing mobile signatures and aggregate economic activity to estimating individuals’ employment status, detecting labor-market shocks, and developing early-warning systems. Overall, the papers emphasize heterogeneous, real-time behavioral data as instruments for understanding complex labor-market and urban dynamics.

abstracts x20|8f9aa1c8bd386efd3b572786c4.text:
## Network Diffusion, Influence, and Epidemic Control

This community studies how information, influence, infections, and failures propagate through complex, social, temporal, and interdependent networks. A major theme is **inference from incomplete observations**: identifying one or multiple diffusion sources, recovering hidden network structures, and estimating edge-infection probabilities from cascades or aggregate data. Related work develops diffusion- and superposition-based distances for comparing network signals.

A second theme is **optimizing and controlling spread**. Influence maximization includes adaptive seeding under myopic feedback, community-aware heuristics, resource-constrained social-network sampling, and recruitment through social propagation. Network design formulates cascade enhancement as mixed-integer stochastic optimization. Epidemic studies address containment-resource allocation, external spreading agents, economic and social costs, and self-healing in interdependent cyber-physical systems.

Typical methods include probabilistic cascade and epidemic models, random matrix theory, message passing and factor graphs, optimization and mixed-integer programming, particle-swarm heuristics, Jordan-cover algorithms, soft-thresholding, approximation guarantees, and simulation on synthetic and real-world networks.

Recent directions emphasize adaptive and time-varying networks, non-submodular and complex contagion, arbitrary inter-switching-time models, partial or collective observations, and resilient control of cascading failures.

abstracts x10|8f9aa1c8bd386efd3b572786c4.text:
### Network Diffusion, Epidemics, and Influence

This community studies how information, disease, failures, and tasks propagate through complex and social networks, and how such diffusion can be inferred, optimized, or controlled. A major theme is **inference from incomplete observations**: papers recover hidden diffusion-network structures from cascades and identify sources and initiation times from partially observed traces. Other work quantifies epidemic consequences, including economic and social costs, spreading time, and cascading failures in interdependent cyber-physical systems.

A second theme is **influence optimization and network intervention**. Research selects seeds for adaptive influence maximization and mobile-crowd-sensing recruitment, designs networks by adding nodes or edges to increase cascade spread, and uses external agents to accelerate epidemics. Resource limitations and realistic feedback are explicitly modeled.

Typical methods include random matrix theory, stochastic epidemic and cascade models, graph diffusion and heat-kernel distances, message passing and factor graphs, soft-thresholding with recovery guarantees, mixed-integer programming, and adaptive-submodular greedy algorithms with approximation bounds. Simulations on random and real-world networks complement theoretical analysis.

Overall, the work trends toward dynamic, partially observed, resource-constrained settings and toward actionable, resilient interventions rather than diffusion modeling alone.

titles<=300|f604d0ee56412c8b8d9648d067b6.text:
**Community Report: Dynamic Topics, Social Sensing, and Event Intelligence**

This community focuses on extracting evolving topics, events, entities, and social signals from large-scale text and social-media streams. A major theme is temporal topic modeling, including dynamic, continuous-time, hierarchical, correlated, author-topic, embedding-space, and feature-conditioned models. These methods are applied to scientific literature, news, reviews, microblogs, and knowledge bases to track trends, topic evolution, communities, and timelines.

A second theme is event detection and forecasting, particularly for geographically localized or streaming data. Approaches include burst and power-law analysis, density-based spatiotextual clustering, incremental machine learning, semantic filtering, multi-instance learning, and adaptive representations. Applications include sports, disasters, protests, civil unrest, infectious diseases, and breaking news.

Other recurring topics are social sensing and prediction: sentiment, opinion influence, diffusion, user interests, engagement, trajectories, ratings, and crowd behavior. The community also develops summarization, entity summarization, hypothesis generation, biomedical surveillance, and optimal spatial-routing systems.

Typical methods combine probabilistic graphical models, Bayesian nonparametrics, matrix/tensor factorization, neural embeddings, deep learning, graph and citation analysis, submodular optimization, and scalable MapReduce or distributed inference. Recent trends emphasize real-time processing, multimodal and cross-lingual analysis, knowledge-graph timelines, scalable inference, embedding-based representations, and integrating social signals with epidemiological or other predictive models.

titles<=300|8f9aa1c8bd386efd3b572786c4a9.text:
## Network Diffusion, Influence, and Epidemic Control

This community studies how information, opinions, rumors, products, and infections propagate through social, temporal, multilayer, and cyber-physical networks. A central theme is influence maximization: selecting seeds, allocating advertisements or coupons, and designing networks to maximize spread, revenue, welfare, diversity, or positive opinion under budgets and constraints. Closely related work addresses competitive cascades, misinformation and rumor blocking, epidemic containment, vaccination, curing, and protection.

Another major direction is diffusion inference: locating one or multiple sources, reconstructing cascades and propagation paths, estimating infection times and edge probabilities, and learning network structure or diffusion parameters from incomplete, noisy, or partial-timestamp observations. Studies also examine epidemic thresholds, stability, transient dynamics, and adaptive susceptibility.

Typical methods include monotone and adaptive submodular optimization, greedy and approximation algorithms, reverse and coordinated sampling, random walks, percolation, spectral and moment analysis, message passing, Bayesian inference, sparse recovery, graph centrality, stochastic control, and simulation. Online learning, bandits, reinforcement learning, and representation learning support model-free or adaptive decisions.

Recent trends emphasize dynamic and nonstationary networks, continuous-time and non-progressive diffusion, heterogeneous and competing cascades, limited feedback, robustness, fairness, privacy, and scalability to billion-edge graphs, alongside practical misinformation prevention and epidemic response.

abstracts x10|f604d0ee56412c8b8d9648d067.text:
### Dynamic Modeling and Real-Time Mining of Social, Spatial, and Textual Data

This community focuses on extracting evolving interests, events, and patterns from large-scale, user-generated, and spatial data. Major themes include topic discovery in documents and hypertext, temporal evolution of topics, personalized recommendation, social-media popularity, real-time event detection, and spatial hotspot or cluster retrieval.

Typical methods are probabilistic generative models, including latent topic models, dynamic and hierarchical Dirichlet processes, and clustered LDA. Neural networks—particularly CNN-based sequential recommenders—are evaluated alongside classical recommendation methods. Other work develops streaming algorithms for continuous bursty-region detection, density-based top-*k* spatial-textual retrieval, and efficient Twitter data collection and event recognition. Sentiment sensing is combined with mathematical prediction models for rare environmental events.

Recent trends emphasize scalability, temporal dynamics, and real-time response. Research increasingly addresses continuously generated streams, parallelizable topic modeling, evolving popularity and revisitation behavior, and geographically localized phenomena. Social platforms are treated as human sensors, with systems demonstrated for sports-event recognition and environmental early warning, while recommendation research exploits sequential behavior and individualized content models.

abstracts x10|815b3a353199233faa10368fa9.text:
### Scientometric Mapping, Indicators, and Citation Dynamics

This community focuses on quantitative analysis of science and technology through bibliometric networks and publication data. Major themes include mapping technology fields and academic institutions, identifying research fronts, measuring cognitive and intellectual relatedness, evaluating scientific recognition, and assessing citation-based performance.

Typical methods involve citation, co-citation, author–paper bipartite, and institutional publication-profile networks; similarity and relatedness measures; centrality indices such as the proposed *K*-index; and multidimensional publication vectors for estimating cognitive distance. Studies also use hierarchical co-citation levels, percentile indicators, field- and source-normalized impact measures, fractional citation counting, and empirical comparisons of bibliographic databases.

Recent trends emphasize greater methodological precision and validation: comparing alternative relatedness measures for technology forecasting, correcting normalization and scale-invariance problems, examining increasingly fine-grained co-citation contexts, and testing the reliability of citation data across Microsoft Academic and Web of Science. Dynamic analyses increasingly address how recency predicts bursts in author citations and how research fronts emerge and evolve, while evaluation studies highlight the sensitivity of percentile outcomes to journal choice and the need for statistically interpretable normalization.

titles<=300|815b3a353199233faa10368fa910.text:
## Scientometrics, Research Evaluation, and Maps of Science

This community studies how scientific knowledge, impact, and innovation can be measured and visualized. Major themes include citation-based evaluation of researchers, journals, institutions, countries, and research programs; critiques and alternatives to the journal impact factor and h-index; percentile, field-, time-, and fractional-normalized indicators; and relationships between bibliometric metrics and peer review. Considerable attention is given to interdisciplinarity, novelty, collaboration, globalization, gender, language, and policy effects in research performance.

Typical methods construct and analyze citation, co-citation, bibliographic-coupling, co-authorship, patent, journal-relation, and text-based networks. Community detection, centrality, clustering, overlay maps, reference publication year spectroscopy, regression, bootstrap and effect-size analysis, propensity matching, and probabilistic or distributional models are common. Studies also compare Web of Science, Scopus, Microsoft Academic, Dimensions, and related data sources, while addressing author disambiguation and database coverage.

Recent work emphasizes fairer and more context-sensitive evaluation, including multidimensional impact, citation context, research quality, uncertainty, and practical significance. Emerging directions include machine learning for citation prediction and recommendation, automated historiography and survey generation, full-text and semantic metrics, interactive visualization, open citation data, and improved mapping of emerging fields, technological domains, and science–technology links.

abstracts x20|f604d0ee56412c8b8d9648d067.text:
## Dynamic Mining of Text, Events, and Entities

This community studies how to extract structure, meaning, and actionable signals from large, evolving information streams. A major theme is topic modeling: probabilistic models extend latent topics to hypertext links and temporal streams, while dynamic and clustered LDA approaches address topic birth, death, popularity, and scalable parallel processing.

A second focus is social-media analytics. Research detects real-world events, social actions, sentiments, and bursty geographic regions from Twitter and other platforms, often in real time. Related work summarizes scheduled events, tracks popularity and revisits, supports tourism decisions, and recommends posts or songs using content models, sequential patterns, and neural networks.

Other themes include spatial-text retrieval, semantic question answering, entity and knowledge-base timeline summarization, and extracting disease information from Wikipedia. Scientific literature mining appears in hypothesis-generation systems, with emphasis on topic-driven candidate ranking and large-scale validation rather than anecdotal expert assessment.

Typical methods combine probabilistic generative models, statistical and machine-learning pipelines, CNNs, density-based spatial algorithms, ontology similarity, fuzzy logic, ranking, and representative-item selection. Recent trends emphasize streaming and near-real-time operation, massive geo-tagged and multimodal data, scalable architectures, practical sensing and early warning, and more systematic evaluation of automated discovery and summarization systems.

abstracts x10|a697d623fb50f9bbcdf9ecb826.text:
## Social Network Structure, Information Diffusion, and Online Anomalies

This community studies how social and information networks form, evolve, and transmit content, with applications to crime analysis, misinformation, disasters, and scholarly discovery. Key themes include identifying influential intermediaries through pair-dependency and centrality; detecting static or dynamic, labelled or unlabelled anomalies such as spammers, predators, and fraudsters; and understanding network assembly through growth, user heterogeneity, and adoption.

Information diffusion is examined through rumor-propagation models, including effects from mass media and absent nodes, as well as the structural complexity, dynamics, semantics, and user characteristics of large-scale cascades. Other work investigates how affect influences Twitter virality, how crowd flags can prioritize fake-news fact checking, and how multimodal Twitter data support disaster response.

Typical methods combine graph centrality and dependency measures, comparative propagation modeling, large-scale cascade and social-media analysis, statistical latent-topic models, scalable visual-meme detection, multimodal datasets, and aggregation of crowd signals. Recent directions emphasize scale and multimodality: incorporating images and video remixing, modeling information sources beyond explicit network links, connecting cascade structure with meaning and emotion, and using computational signals for timely intervention against harmful content.

titles<=300|a697d623fb50f9bbcdf9ecb826c2.text:
### Online Social Networks, Diffusion, and Collective Attention

This community studies how online social networks form, evolve, and shape collective behavior. Major themes include information, meme, news, and emotional diffusion; popularity, virality, and engagement prediction; community structure, influence, homophily, weak ties, and multiplex connectivity; and network applications in crises, politics, health, crime, science, and marketing. Several works address misinformation, fake accounts, malicious URLs, polarization, privacy, cyberbullying, and information overload.

Typical methods combine graph theory and network statistics with community detection, centrality and influence measures, diffusion and epidemic models, opinion dynamics, optimal control, and stochastic processes. Hawkes and other point-process models, survival analysis, Poisson processes, agent-based simulations, and random-graph models are used to represent temporal cascades and tie dynamics. Machine-learning approaches include latent-variable models, time-series methods, deep neural networks, attention mechanisms, graph neural networks, and multimodal content analysis. Datasets frequently come from Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Reddit, Instagram, mobile phones, citation networks, and disaster events.

Recent trends emphasize continuous-time and multiplex networks, microscopic and early cascade prediction, causal evaluation of recommendations and interventions, multimodal signals, socially informed forecasting, and applications for crisis response, social good, and scientific impact.

abstracts x20|815b3a353199233faa10368fa9.text:
## Scientometrics, Citation Networks, and Research Evaluation

This community focuses on measuring, mapping, and evaluating scientific and technological activity. Major themes include technology-field relatedness, journal and institution mapping, research-front evolution, field delineation, cognitive distance, and comparisons of scholarly databases such as Web of Science, Scopus, Microsoft Academic, and Dimensions.

Typical methods are citation, co-citation, co-authorship, and bipartite-network analysis; network maps and overlays; similarity and relatedness measures; bibliographic matching; and macro-level indicators of growth, collaboration, diversity, and inequality. Studies also develop or assess indicators including the \(K\)-index, SNIP, I3, percentile ranks, field-normalized metrics, and measures of journal internationality. Validation commonly uses correlations, precision and recall, expert judgments, convergent validity, and comparisons across databases.

A central concern is the strong disciplinary and distributional bias of raw citation counts and impact factors. Recent work therefore emphasizes percentile-based and field-normalized evaluation, meaningful assessment of individual researchers, and tests of whether metrics are genuinely universal. Other emerging directions include author-level citation bursts, increasingly granular co-citation analysis, improved delineation of interdisciplinary fields, and the weakening link between journal impact factors and article-level impact in the digital age.

abstracts x20|a697d623fb50f9bbcdf9ecb826.text:
## Social Networks, Information Diffusion, and Online Behavior

This community studies how social-network structure shapes influence, information spread, anomalies, and collective behavior. Major themes include identifying important intermediaries and vulnerable network components; detecting anomalous, malicious, or fraudulent activity; understanding network assembly, community structure, homophily, and structural paradoxes; and modeling diffusion of rumors, memes, news, products, and user-generated content.

Typical methods combine graph-theoretic analysis—betweenness, pair-dependency, fractal dimension, community detection, threshold games, and temporal tie-strength models—with statistical learning and large-scale data mining. Researchers analyze cascades, social ties, user attributes, textual and visual content, crowd flags, and popularity histories. Predictive applications include fake-news intervention, disaster response, sports forecasting, scholarly hot-topic detection, gender inference, recommendation systems, and early popularity-trend prediction.

Recent directions emphasize multimodal and latent interactions, including visual video memes and crisis imagery; dynamic and continuous-time diffusion; and richer cascade analyses linking structural complexity with spreading behavior and semantics. Work increasingly models influences beyond the observed network, such as mass media and absent nodes, while addressing heterogeneity across users and platforms. There is also growing attention to the limits and unintended effects of popularity-based recommendations, misinformation propagation, and scalable early-warning or intervention systems.

titles<=300|a1d4baba0a2f0756f2a4665b4f4a.text:
## Text, Mathematics, and Scalable Data Analytics

This community combines three closely related themes. First, it develops scalable data systems: Accumulo/D4M, Graphulo, BigDAWG, Rheem, SciDB, Vertica, and Supercloud support high-throughput ingest, sparse graph and matrix analytics, polystore execution, cloud/serverless processing, provenance, and large-scale pipelines. Query optimization is a major focus, including cardinality and cost estimation, shared and cache-based execution, adaptive processing, workload management, and utility- or regret-based operator ordering.

Second, many papers address text mining and information retrieval. Methods include multinomial and topic models, association rules, naïve Bayes, k-nearest-neighbor and k-medoids hybrids, semantic and similarity-based classification, feature selection, clustering, relevance feedback, sentiment and opinion-holder extraction, authorship attribution, and web-page segmentation.

Third, mathematical information retrieval is prominent. The work builds formula repositories and search engines, uses LaTeX and contextual representations, studies formula-query merging and similarity, and explores mathematical question answering, notation namespaces, rendering, and knowledge management.

Recent trends emphasize integrated representations—associative arrays, relational lattices, tensors, and algebraic semantics—alongside cross-platform and polystore optimization. Systems increasingly target elastic cloud execution, shared-query cost reduction, provenance, and interactive discovery, while learning-based methods improve classification, workload control, and retrieval quality.

abstracts x20|a1d4baba0a2f0756f2a4665b4f.text:
### Scalable Data Management, Retrieval, and Graph Analytics

This community focuses on scalable processing and intelligent analysis of large, heterogeneous data collections. Major themes include text clustering and classification, high-recall and math information retrieval, database query optimization, polystore architectures, graph analytics, and provenance management.

Typical methods combine probabilistic mixture models, association-rule mining, dependency-based pruning, hypernym expansion, relevance feedback, active learning, graph-based score propagation, and evaluation through retrieval metrics or simulation. Database research develops memory-aware and cost-sensitive query optimizers, predicate-ordering strategies for column stores, relational-lattice formalisms, and resource/cost estimation for cloud computation. Systems work emphasizes heterogeneous engines, external-memory processing, and high-throughput storage using Accumulo, D4M, associative arrays, SSDs, Graphulo, and GraphBLAS-style kernels.

Recent trends emphasize extreme scale and streaming workloads: reported systems reach hundreds of millions to a billion updates or inserts per second, while external graph systems address datasets exceeding memory capacity. Other emerging directions include autonomous continuous active learning, sentence-level feedback for efficient review, user-directed clustering with minimal annotation, and integrated text–formula retrieval. Across the community, research increasingly connects formal models and adaptive algorithms with practical, benchmarked infrastructure for massive, dynamic data.

abstracts x10|a1d4baba0a2f0756f2a4665b4f.text:
## Scalable Text, Graph, and Mathematical Information Systems

This community spans two complementary areas: intelligent analysis of text and mathematical content, and high-performance infrastructure for large, heterogeneous data. Text research focuses on probabilistic multinomial mixture models, user-guided clustering with minimal feedback, and association-rule classification enhanced through dependency pruning and hyperonymization. Information retrieval work combines textual and mathematical-formula queries, evaluates query expansion and result-merging strategies, and supports interactive repositories of mathematical formulae.

Typical methods include soft document–cluster associations, learned similarity metrics, association-rule mining, syntactic and semantic feature engineering, retrieval evaluation metrics such as Bpref, and merging results from specialized subqueries. Infrastructure research emphasizes graph and streaming workloads, associative arrays, distributed and hierarchical in-memory databases, and benchmarking with Graph500 data. It also develops memory-aware cost models for multi-join queries and polystore architectures integrating PostgreSQL, Accumulo, and SciDB.

Recent trends favor extreme scalability—up to reported rates of 100 million inserts and one billion updates per second—alongside flexible data integration. Other emerging directions include tailoring clustering to user-desired dimensions, exploiting power-law structure to filter large datasets, and combining domain-specific mathematical resources with general search technology.

titles<=300|b001d33cbc3504f8e57cf3e69900.text:
## Community Detection in Complex, Dynamic, and Multilayer Networks

This community centers on detecting, evaluating, and interpreting mesoscale structure in complex networks. Major themes include disjoint, overlapping, fuzzy, hierarchical, bipartite, signed, attributed, directed, multiplex, and temporal communities, alongside core–periphery structures, link communities, trusses, and dense subgraphs. Applications span social media, scholarly networks, web services, mobility, cybersecurity, epidemics, recommendation, and team formation.

Typical methods combine modularity and modularity-density optimization, stochastic block models and latent-space models, spectral and graph-signal techniques, matrix factorization, belief propagation, label propagation, random walks, PageRank and heat kernels, conductance-based local expansion, k-core/k-truss analysis, and density-based or evolutionary optimization. Distributed, streaming, parallel, and scalable algorithms address very large and evolving graphs. Semi-supervised learning, pairwise constraints, graph embeddings, neural models, and ensemble methods increasingly integrate attributes and background information.

A strong methodological emphasis is placed on detectability, phase transitions, model selection, null models, robustness, and quality metrics, including overlapping-community evaluation. Recent work focuses on multilayer and temporal dynamics, local and decentralized detection, adversarial vulnerability and debiasing, automated resolution selection, dynamic tracking, higher-order and simplicial structure, and combining community discovery with visualization, graph inference, and downstream prediction.

abstracts x20|b001d33cbc3504f8e57cf3e699.text:
## Community Detection in Evolving, Heterogeneous Networks

This community centers on defining, detecting, and evaluating communities in complex networks. A major theme is the lack of a universally accepted community definition, motivating taxonomies of detection methods and multi-criteria quality evaluation. Modularity remains influential, including multislice and overlapping/fuzzy extensions, while work also examines detectability limits through graph spectra and stochastic block models.

Typical methods include label propagation (LabelRank), density-based clustering combined with manifold learning, modularity optimization, random-matrix analysis, and probabilistic generative modeling. Variational Bayes is used to infer shared and layer-specific communities in heterogeneous multilayer networks. Theoretical work studies metastable majority dynamics for distributed detection, while practical studies address bias against low-degree nodes.

The network perspective is also applied to temporal visualization and ranking: regularized layouts preserve the mental map across evolving snapshots, and evolving teleportation or damping schemes adapt PageRank to changing external interests. Empirical applications include wireless subscriber churn, smartphone adoption, bibliometric networks, Web-service interactions, social networks, and image segmentation.

Recent directions emphasize multilayer, attributed, overlapping, dynamic, and inclusive community models, alongside more stable algorithms and systematic evaluation rather than reliance on a single quality metric.

abstracts x10|b001d33cbc3504f8e57cf3e699.text:
### Community Detection, Evaluation, and Network Influence

This community focuses on discovering, evaluating, and interpreting structure in complex and evolving networks. Major themes include the lack of a universal definition of community quality, comparison of detection methods, overlapping and fuzzy memberships, multilayer heterogeneity, and inclusive assignment of low-degree nodes. Several works address social and behavioral consequences of network structure, examining peer influence in wireless-service churn and smartphone adoption, including asymmetric effects and core–periphery position.

Typical methods span multi-criteria evaluation, systematic comparisons of modularity-based quality metrics, and taxonomies of community-discovery algorithms. Scalable algorithmic approaches include stabilized label propagation, while probabilistic modeling and variational Bayes infer shared and layer-specific communities in heterogeneous multilayer networks. Distributed majority dynamics and metastability provide theoretical tools for community formation. Survival models and generalized models are applied to longitudinal subscriber data.

Recent trends emphasize robustness, reproducibility, and realism: stabilizing nondeterministic algorithms, correcting bias against sparsely connected users, modeling overlapping, fuzzy, multilayer, and dynamic structures, and preserving temporal coherence in network visualization. The research also increasingly links meso-level communities to individual outcomes and peer effects rather than treating communities solely as static partitions.

abstracts x20|3719a4721df9108102bbdef7de.text:
## Mapping Scholarly Impact in a Digital Research Ecosystem

This community studies how scholarly impact, use, and communication can be measured beyond conventional citation counts. Major themes include the validity and interpretation of altmetrics, relationships between online attention and peer-assessed quality, and the use of downloads, readership, tweets, reviews, and library loans as complementary indicators. Several studies address research evaluation for books, monographs, publishers, and humanities and social-science outputs, including publisher rankings and indicators based on output, impact, and profile.

Typical methods are large-scale data integration across Web of Science, Scopus, Book Citation Index, Altmetric, F1000Prime, Mendeley, Twitter, library systems, and digital-library logs. Statistical approaches include correlation, regression, principal-component and factor analysis, distribution modeling, and comparisons with expert assessments or research evaluations. Other work develops technical systems for noisy-reference resolution, venue recommendation, referee assignment, and knowledge-domain visualization.

Recent trends emphasize heterogeneous and rapidly generated web data, while highlighting problems of data quality, dependencies, disciplinary differences, and uncertain validity. The literature also reflects growing interest in early indicators of later citations, open-access and preprint effects, online academic profiles, content-level book-review mining, and the evolution of repositories such as arXiv.

titles<=300|3719a4721df9108102bbdef7de89.text:
## Scholarly Impact, Open Science, and Research Analytics

This community studies how scholarly impact is produced, measured, and communicated across journals, books, repositories, social media, and policy documents. A dominant theme is altmetrics: their validity, coverage, disciplinary variation, data quality, societal relevance, and relationship to citations, readership, and research quality. Twitter, Mendeley, Facebook, Wikipedia, blogs, policy documents, and downloads are examined as traces of attention and engagement, while automated accounts, private activity, and heterogeneous data complicate interpretation.

Open access and preprints are another major focus, including citation and usage advantages, self-archiving, arXiv’s role in physics, mathematics, and astronomy, repository–journal relationships, and the effects of article availability and linking. Bibliometric work addresses books, chapters, publishers, datasets, data citations, and usage-based indicators.

Typical methods include large-scale citation and readership analysis; network, co-occurrence, and co-readership mapping; surveys and case studies; web scraping and API-based data collection; text mining, OCR, sentiment analysis, classification, and knowledge graphs; and statistical modeling for normalization, prediction, and correlation analysis. Recommender systems and reviewer-assignment algorithms are also prominent.

Recent directions emphasize multidimensional and continuous evaluation, institutional and societal impact, policy-citation prediction, open citation infrastructures, author identifiers, real-time trend detection, and socially aware scholarly search and recommendation.

abstracts x10|3719a4721df9108102bbdef7de.text:
## Measuring and Mapping Scholarly Impact

This community examines how scholarly communication and research impact can be measured, represented, and improved across traditional and emerging data sources. Major themes include the validity and interpretation of altmetrics, relationships between online attention and peer-assessed quality, and the use of social-media, readership, library-loan, citation, and publisher data as indicators of influence. Several studies focus on scholarly infrastructure, including venue recommendation based on changing researcher interests, visualization of knowledge domains through Mendeley co-readership, and automated matching of noisy OCR references to bibliographic records. Peer-review processes are also analyzed, particularly referee competence and manuscript–referee assignment through bidding behavior.

Typical methods are large-scale dataset integration, correlation and factor/PCA analyses, exploratory comparisons, case studies, expert interviews, and algorithmic information-retrieval or recommendation systems. Data come from Altmetric, F1000Prime, Web of Science, academic social networks, Twitter, Mendeley, library loan systems, and publisher records.

Recent trends emphasize broadening evaluation beyond citations toward societal engagement and online activity, while recognizing substantial heterogeneity, quality problems, and source dependencies. Work also increasingly develops computational tools and alternative indicators for books, monographs, publishers, and dynamic scholarly discovery.

abstracts x10|5dc4f80d186bfa248b9d4d705a.text:
### Italian Scientometrics, Research Evaluation, and Academic Networks

This community studies the performance, organization, and governance of science, with a strong empirical focus on Italy. Major themes include university and individual research evaluation, regional inequalities between northern and southern institutions, nepotism and career advancement, gender differences in collaboration, and the influence of editorial-board membership. Several papers examine the visibility, citability, and international beneficiaries of national research.

Typical methods combine bibliometric indicators and Web of Science or DBLP data with statistical modeling. These include multivariate stochastic models, deterministic performance comparisons, quantile regression, Granger causality tests, citation and co-authorship analysis, and simulations of research-assessment rankings. Complex-network topology is used both to study collaboration and to disambiguate author identities, while triangulation against labeled datasets evaluates database quality.

Recent trends emphasize methodological scrutiny of national assessment exercises, especially distortions caused by product selection and ranking procedures; more probabilistic and causal approaches to performance measurement; improved author-name disambiguation; and analysis of science as a system of knowledge flows across countries and fields. Overall, the work connects quantitative science studies with policy recommendations for fairness, regional development, research governance, and international collaboration.

abstracts x20|5dc4f80d186bfa248b9d4d705a.text:
### Bibliometric Evaluation and Academic Networks in Italy

This community studies research performance, collaboration, careers, and evaluation within the Italian higher-education system. Major themes include regional inequality between northern and southern universities, gender differences in recruitment, authorship, and collaboration, nepotism and academic advancement, age and seniority effects, and the persistence of “star” scientists. Several studies examine how collaboration—especially international collaboration and larger author teams—relates to visibility, citations, and scientific impact. Other work traces the international beneficiaries and knowledge flows of Italian research.

Typical methods are large-scale bibliometric analyses of national professor populations and Web of Science or DBLP records. Studies use citation and productivity indicators, co-authorship and complex-network analysis, regression and quantile regression, Granger causality tests, stochastic performance models, distributional and fractal analyses, and longitudinal comparisons. Funnel plots address uncertainty in institutional rankings, while multiple labeled datasets and topological features evaluate author-name disambiguation.

Recent directions emphasize methodological reliability and fairness: assessing uncertainty and distortions in national rankings, comparing deterministic and probabilistic evaluation, improving identity resolution, and examining how institutional, geographic, gender, and career factors shape measured performance.

titles<=300|5dc4f80d186bfa248b9d4d705a1c.text:
## Scientometrics, Research Evaluation, and Academic Collaboration

This community centers on measuring and explaining research performance, especially in the Italian university and national research systems. Major themes include bibliometric indicators, university and researcher rankings, national research assessment exercises (VQR), peer review, productivity, efficiency, funding allocation, academic recruitment, and career advancement. Many studies examine how gender, age, seniority, academic rank, internationalization, geography, institutional size, and disciplinary specialization shape scientific output and impact.

A second strong theme is collaboration: coauthorship networks, team size, interdisciplinary and university–industry partnerships, knowledge diffusion, migration, and the behavior of highly cited or “star” scientists. Gender differences and inequality in authorship, collaboration, recruitment, and productivity receive sustained attention.

Typical methods include citation and publication analysis; field and fractional counting; stochastic and statistical models; data-envelopment analysis and other efficiency measures; sensitivity analysis; rankings, benchmarking, funnel plots, and uncertainty analysis; network and spatial analysis; and comparisons of peer review with bibliometrics. Machine-learning and semi-supervised methods are applied to author-name disambiguation, including deep neural networks and citation-network approaches.

Recent directions emphasize open data and infrastructures, improved author identification, early prediction of long-term impact, interdisciplinarity, territorial specialization, reproducible evaluation, and warnings about gaming, unstable rankings, inappropriate indicators, and performance-based funding.

titles<=300|20d3d8bcf19ddd362d237109801c.text:
## Multilayer Social Networks: Communities, Diffusion, and Identity

This community centers on modeling and analyzing social systems as multilayer, multiplex, temporal, and heterogeneous networks.
