Major themes include community and group evolution, multilayer centrality and similarity, link prediction, influential-user and seed selection, network sampling, and robustness under attacks. A second strong theme is information diffusion: epidemics, innovations, opinions, viral campaigns, competing cascades, immunization, and diffusion-aware sampling. Cross-platform identity matching, profile alignment, online–offline ties, endorsements, and social closeness form another substantial focus.

Typical methods include modularity maximization, stochastic block models, Louvain and Infomap clustering, tensor decomposition, probabilistic and agent-based models, branching processes, entropy and mutual-information measures, association-rule mining, convex optimization, and language-model-based ranking. Studies also use smartphone, telecommunications, Bluetooth, social-media, blog, review, and virtual-world data, alongside synthetic and generative network models.

The collection increasingly emphasizes dynamic and interdependent layers, layer similarity and entanglement, temporal centrality, missing data, and large-scale parallel processing. Applied directions include misinformation and fact checking, sentiment and topic analysis, spam and deception detection, social recommendation, human mobility, mental health, organizational knowledge diffusion, and cross-network behavioral analysis.

abstracts x10|20d3d8bcf19ddd362d23710980.text:
### Social Networks: Structure, Dynamics, and Computational Insight

This community studies social networks as multilayered, evolving systems spanning online and offline interactions. Major themes include centrality and structural analysis, community extraction and group evolution, homophily and tie strength, identity construction, privacy, and cross-platform deanonymization. Several works also address social-media content, including topic and sentiment discovery and computational responses to misinformation.

Typical methods combine graph-theoretic modeling with empirical datasets. Multilayer and multiplex networks are used to compare communication activities or online/offline ties, while centrality measures characterize node importance. GED and related algorithms identify and compare evolving groups over time. Association-rule mining builds on Apriori, with support-confidence pruning and extensions for quantitative attributes and item generalization. Topic modeling, sentiment analysis, and related-content retrieval support Twitter exploration and fact-checking. Formal analyses of random key graphs examine triangles, clustering, and small-world behavior through zero-one laws.

Recent directions emphasize richer representations of identity and relationships: multiplex ties, cross-platform profiles, and socially constructed personas. The research also increasingly moves from describing network structure toward actionable applications, including group management, privacy-risk assessment, social-media understanding, and tools for evaluating questionable news.

titles<=300|fba344e55e792fe76ac17dd06c86.text:
## Social Media Misinformation, Manipulation, and Polarization

This community focuses on the dynamics, detection, and mitigation of harmful information and behavior in online social networks. Major themes include fake news, rumors, clickbait, propaganda, state-sponsored influence campaigns, political manipulation, echo chambers, polarization, extremism, hate speech, cyberbullying, spam, fraud, and social bots. Elections—especially the 2016 U.S. election, Brexit, European elections, and U.S. midterms—are recurring case studies, alongside health misinformation and online harassment.

Typical methods combine large-scale social-media data analysis with network science, natural-language processing, and machine learning. Researchers use community detection, graph clustering, centrality, motif and cascade analysis, stance and sentiment detection, linguistic profiling, temporal modeling, causal inference, and influence estimation. Supervised, semi-supervised, multitask, transfer-learning, neural, geometric deep-learning, and interpretable approaches are applied to classify bots, trolls, fake news, abuse, clickbait, and unreliable sources. Surveys, platforms such as Hoaxy and Botometer, honeypots, crowdsourcing, and social sensing support measurement and intervention.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes multimodal and multilingual deception detection, social context beyond article content, early-warning and real-time systems, adversarially robust bot detection, fairness and bias in feeds and rankings, and intervention strategies that reduce misinformation, polarization, and exposure inequalities.

abstracts x20|20d3d8bcf19ddd362d23710980.text:
### Multiplex Social Networks, Communities, and Network Intelligence

This community centers on modeling and analyzing complex social networks, especially multiplex and multilayer structures linking people, platforms, activities, and online/offline relationships. Key themes include multilayer degree centrality, identity across social-media platforms, homophily and tie strength, influential actors, social recommendation, privacy and deanonymization, and misinformation detection.

A major research line studies community structure and temporal change. Methods include GED and SGCI for extracting and matching groups across time, community-evolution prediction, modularity maximization, stochastic block models, and analyses of reciprocity, cycles, triplets, and layer similarity. Other work examines multiplex layer entanglement and develops tunable random-key and synthetic-network models to reproduce structural properties.

Typical approaches combine graph-theoretic measures, statistical modeling, topic and sentiment modeling, association-rule mining, sampling estimators, and language models. Applications use real Web 2.0, email, Twitter, student, blogging, and cross-platform profile datasets, alongside synthetic networks.

Recent trends emphasize unified representations of interconnected identities and heterogeneous relations, scalable generation and sampling of realistic networks, automated interpretation of social content, prediction of group evolution, personalized recommendations, and computational support for fact-checking and privacy research.

abstracts x10|fba344e55e792fe76ac17dd06c.text:
## Social Web Communities, Bias, and Trust

This community studies how online platforms shape social organization, information exposure, and user security. Major themes include political polarization and search bias, fringe-network evolution (especially Gab), and community detection in Twitter using content and interaction structure. Other work addresses platform abuse—spam, malicious Facebook applications, and Sybil attacks against crowdsourced mapping—alongside socially oriented applications such as tobacco-cessation bots and suicidality analysis.

Typical methods combine network science, machine learning, and computational modeling. Structural balance and Twitter triad patterns support endorsement-filtered graphs, which are analyzed with nonnegative matrix factorization. Bias is decomposed into effects from input data versus ranking algorithms. Temporal datasets, graph clustering, centrality, and visualization characterize user and topic dynamics. Security systems use lightweight semi-supervised detectors, blacklist and near-duplicate features, while intervention bots classify users and select individualized messages. Probabilistic contagion and immunity are modeled with delay differential equations, and experiments demonstrate scalable Sybil attacks.

Recent directions emphasize monitoring alternative or fringe communities, distinguishing algorithmic from data-driven influence, deploying targeted social-media interventions, and improving resilience through decentralized search and stronger defenses against manipulation.

abstracts x10|c6ec0ecaba755de9caaa7f9ea1.text:
## Recommender Systems: Personalization, Robustness, and Inclusion

This community focuses on collaborative and sequential recommendation across products, media, and local events. A central theme is combining long-term preferences with short-term behavioral dynamics, using matrix factorization, item-transition models, and Markov chains. Other work improves rating prediction through efficient Slope One predictors and models nonlinear user–item interactions with neural networks and latent factors.

Methods increasingly incorporate richer information beyond interaction matrices: social and semantic networks, text and tags via Latent Semantic Analysis, and multimodal user/item content. Handling sparse data, cold-start users, obscure artists, and missing or corrupted modalities is a recurring concern.

The community also examines recommendation quality and societal or system-level risks. Studies address popularity bias through personalized diversification and reranking, while analyzing the effects of fraudulent review (shilling) attacks on algorithms and different user groups.

Recent directions emphasize neural and generative collaborative filtering, multimodal robustness, and sequential playlist or behavior continuation at large scale. Benchmark-driven experimentation, including the ACM RecSys Challenge 2018, complements practical methods designed for dynamic updates, online querying, and real-world deployment.

abstracts x20|fba344e55e792fe76ac17dd06c.text:
### Social-Graph Analysis, Misinformation, and Online Safety

This community centers on analyzing online social networks as systems for political communication, information diffusion, public intervention, and security. Major themes include community formation and polarization; search and platform bias; fringe communities and political influence; misinformation, conspiracy narratives, fake news, and fact-checking; and disinformation during elections and conflicts. Additional work addresses privacy and organizational reconnaissance, malicious applications, spam, Sybil attacks, and social-media-based public-health and disaster applications.

Typical methods combine large-scale Twitter, Facebook, and platform-specific data collection with network construction, clustering, centrality, subgraph analysis, and temporal or content-based modeling. Nonnegative matrix factorization integrates connectivity and user content, while supervised and semi-supervised classifiers detect stance, spam, political alignment, and tobacco-related behavior. Researchers also use simulations—including contagion and misinformation models incorporating segregation, memory, attention, and fact-checking—and deploy bots or browser tools for intervention and measurement. Graph algorithms support decentralized search and shortest-distance queries.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes platform ecosystems and societal consequences: Gab and other fringe communities, election disinformation, ISIS support, narrative trends, and bias in ranked search results. The direction is toward distinguishing data-driven from algorithmic bias, evaluating robustness of benchmarks, and combining network structure with semantic content for monitoring, curation, and targeted responses.

titles<=300|c6ec0ecaba755de9caaa7f9ea1c4.text:
## Recommender Systems: From Collaborative Filtering to Fair, Explainable Sequential Personalization

This community centers on personalized recommendation across products, music, news, images, travel, jobs, education, and research papers. Core themes include collaborative filtering and ranking, session- and sequence-aware recommendation, cold-start and missing-modality settings, social and trust-aware recommendation, cross-domain transfer, and content-rich multimedia recommendation. Popularity bias, fairness, diversity, privacy, robustness to fraud, and explainability are recurring concerns.

Typical methods range from matrix factorization, Bayesian personalized ranking, neighborhood and graph diffusion models, Markov chains, tensor factorization, factorization machines, and probabilistic latent-variable models to neural collaborative filtering, autoencoders, recurrent and convolutional networks, attention, memory networks, graph neural networks, transformers, and knowledge-graph embeddings. Reinforcement learning and contextual or multi-armed bandits address online advertising, exploration, feedback, and whole-chain recommendation. Re-ranking, determinantal point processes, metric learning, and listwise optimization target diversity and ranking quality.

Recent trends emphasize deep sequential and session modeling, multimodal representations, heterogeneous relations, cross-domain and transfer learning, explainable reasoning, causal and influence modeling, scalable retrieval, and evaluation in streaming or real-world environments. The papers also show growing attention to reproducibility, calibration, business value, and fairness-aware updating rather than accuracy alone.

abstracts x20|c6ec0ecaba755de9caaa7f9ea1.text:
### Recommender Systems: Sequential, Neural, and Responsible Personalization

This community focuses on improving personalized recommendation across collaborative, content-based, and hybrid settings. Core themes include combining long-term preferences with short-term sequential behavior; session-based recommendation for anonymous users; playlist, news, music-event, and product recommendation; and addressing cold-start, sparse data, and long-tail discovery. Several studies examine system reliability, including shilling attacks, noisy ratings, user reputation, and popularity bias.

Typical methods range from classical matrix factorization, slope-one predictors, nearest-neighbor techniques, Markov chains, co-clustering, and latent semantic analysis to neural and probabilistic models. These include variational autoencoders, nonlinear latent-factor networks, latent session-state models, context trees, multimodal learning with modality dropout, and graph neural networks for modeling complex item transitions. Signed bipartite networks support neighbor-based collaborative ranking, while mixture-of-tastes models represent users with multiple interests. Personalized reranking improves exposure for niche items while preserving accuracy.

Recent trends emphasize deep sequence and session modeling, graph-based representations, multimodal and missing-modality robustness, richer modeling of diverse user tastes, and practical concerns such as interpretability, scalability, dynamic updates, and fairness in exposure. Evaluation also increasingly considers real-world attacks, anonymous behavior, and creative or long-tail recommendation objectives.

titles<=300|fb4e550cfbc9792b5f07c6a26f82.text:
## Geosocial Analytics, Mobility, and Political Behavior

This community studies how social-media and other digital traces reveal human behavior across space, time, and networks. Major themes include Twitter-based election forecasting and political ideology, campaign dynamics, polarization, influence, fake news, and collective identity; user geolocation, home-location estimation, geotagging, and privacy; urban mobility, commuting, migration, place attractiveness, public-space use, and neighborhood structure; and business, event, venue, and recommendation analytics.

Typical methods combine natural-language processing, sentiment and topic modeling, image and hashtag analysis, supervised and deep learning, probabilistic inference, and time-series analysis. Network approaches include community detection, centrality, link prediction, diffusion and influence modeling, signed and multilayer graphs, structural balance, and tensor factorization. Spatial and trajectory research uses geocoding, spatial interaction models, clustering, trajectory compression, uncertain-path inference, check-ins, mobile-phone records, Flickr, Facebook, Yelp, Instagram, and Reddit data. Several works emphasize scalable distributed mining, RDF knowledge bases, and visualization.

Recent trends move toward high-resolution and multimodal geolocation, dynamic and individual-level mobility timelines, cross-platform and heterogeneous-data fusion, real-time social sensing, and deep models for location, privacy, misinformation, and behavior prediction. Researchers also increasingly assess sampling bias, representativeness, noise, uncertainty, and validation against polls or other population data.

abstracts x10|fb4e550cfbc9792b5f07c6a26f.text:
### Social Data Mining for Political, Urban, and Behavioral Intelligence

This community studies how user-generated and platform data can reveal preferences, behaviors, reputations, and characteristics of people, places, and organizations. Political applications infer voter preferences and voting intention from Twitter activity, Facebook likes, and candidate communication tactics. Other work predicts Yelp business ratings from review text, estimates Reddit users’ locations without geotags, and examines power structures in news media.

Urban and mobility research is another major theme. Studies analyze group event scheduling through a dedicated mobile application, cluster partial mobility trajectories at scale, and map urban smellscapes using smellwalk observations and a smell-related dictionary. Crowd-sourced perceptions of beauty, quietness, and happiness are transformed into recommendations for emotionally pleasant city routes.

Typical methods include sparse learning, supervised machine-learning classifiers, text-based heuristics, sentiment or topic-related feature extraction, crowd-sourcing, mobile data collection, and scalable distributed clustering. Several studies combine online traces with surveys, reviews, or offline observations to validate predictions.

Recent directions emphasize parsimonious but informative digital traces, prediction from unstructured text, inference despite missing explicit labels or geotags, and scalable analysis of large behavioral datasets. The work also increasingly moves beyond conventional outcomes—such as votes or ratings—to subjective urban experiences, social diffusion, and system design.

abstracts x20|fb4e550cfbc9792b5f07c6a26f.text:
## Social Media Mining for Spatial, Political, and Urban Insights

This community studies how user-generated and social-media data can reveal human preferences, behavior, mobility, and perceptions of place. Political applications infer voter intention and topic preferences from Twitter likes, Facebook activity, and parliamentary voting networks. Urban research maps emotional, sensory, and functional characteristics through geotagged photos, tweets, check-ins, smellwalks, and crowdsourced judgments, including happiness, quietness, beauty, sound, smell, mood, and park exposure. Other work examines group event scheduling, online news influence and ranking, daily-deal diffusion, Yelp ratings, and Reddit user geolocation.

Typical methods combine machine learning and statistical modeling—including sparse learning, classifiers, latent Dirichlet allocation, negative-binomial regression, sentiment analysis, low-rank approximation, and signed-graph structural balance—with spatial analysis, trajectory clustering, network analysis, and probabilistic geospatial reasoning. Large-scale datasets and reusable infrastructures are prominent, including nearly a billion geolocated tweets and the 1.5-billion-tweet TweetsKB RDF corpus.

Recent trends emphasize parsimonious digital traces, inference without explicit geotags, scalable distributed processing, multimodal qualitative geospatial data, and applications that translate subjective urban experience into measurable maps and routing recommendations.

titles<=300|05f6e854d92ea2876e940bb008fe.text:
## Graph Representation and Analysis in Dynamic Social Networks

This community focuses on learning, modeling, and mining large-scale complex, social, and heterogeneous networks. Major themes include network representation learning and node/graph embeddings; link prediction and relationship inference; community detection, role and core–periphery discovery; temporal and multiplex network analysis; and applications such as fraud, anomaly, spam, recommendation, alignment, and social behavior analysis.

Typical methods include DeepWalk, node2vec, struc2vec, role- and community-based embeddings, matrix factorization, graph convolutional and attention networks, recurrent models, autoencoders, adversarial learning, and multimodal fusion of network structure, text, attributes, and knowledge bases. Probabilistic approaches include stochastic blockmodels, latent-space and membership models, graph grammars, Kronecker and attribute-based generators, and Bayesian trail analysis. Scalable graph mining relies on random-walk and wedge sampling, MapReduce/GPU processing, sparsification, indexing, sketches, and distributed algorithms for motifs, triangles, trusses, distances, and centrality.

Recent work emphasizes dynamic and continuous-time graphs, temporal motifs and event graphs, robust embeddings under evolving or missing data, heterogeneous and multilayer integration, explainable similarity and anomaly detection, and adversarial threats such as poisoning, de-anonymization, and attacks on graph embeddings. Evaluation, benchmarking, and principled graph sampling are also prominent.

titles<=300|5426a48cabc964cafb5f9b9da7c4.text:
## Information Retrieval: Neural Ranking, Context, and Reliable Evaluation

This community centers on information retrieval, especially learning to rank for web, product, enterprise, academic, biomedical, and conversational search. Major themes include neural relevance matching and passage/document reranking; query understanding, expansion, reformulation, and intent detection; personalized, session-based, mobile, and conversational search; and retrieval involving entities, knowledge graphs, tables, and scientific literature. Question answering—particularly non-factoid, multi-document, and knowledge-graph QA—is another substantial focus.

Typical methods combine BERT and other pretrained language models with interaction architectures such as Duet, PACRR, MatchPyramid, kernel pooling, attention, recurrent networks, and listwise, pairwise, or groupwise learning-to-rank objectives. Researchers also use embeddings, graph and hyperbolic representations, hashing, clustering, weak supervision, reinforcement learning, adversarial training, and multi-task learning. Query expansion commonly exploits word embeddings, Wikipedia, WordNet, pseudo-relevance feedback, and sequence-to-sequence generation.

Recent work emphasizes deep-learning benchmarks and toolkits, scalable production ranking, and contextualized retrieval. A strong methodological trend addresses biased clicks and online evaluation through counterfactual learning, propensity estimation, multileaving, bandits, and intervention-free position-bias correction. Interpretability, robustness to adversarial manipulation, privacy-preserving ranking, and factuality, objectivity, and credibility are also increasingly prominent.

abstracts x10|5426a48cabc964cafb5f9b9da7.text:
### Neural, Structured, and Dynamic Information Retrieval

This community centers on improving search and ranking across heterogeneous information needs and platforms. Core themes include relevance ranking, expert and dataset discovery, query understanding, mobile app selection, question answering, and web-content quality evaluation.

Typical methods combine representation learning with ranking and clustering. DeepRank models human-like relevance assessment by detecting relevant locations, estimating local relevance, and aggregating evidence. Other work uses locally trained embeddings and concept hierarchies for query expansion in heterogeneous bibliographic networks, while query2vec represents queries from the contexts of their top results and applies scalable Divide & Merge clustering. Neural language models, including BERT and MT-DNN, support answer filtering and reranking through language inference and question entailment. Traditional and alternative retrieval representations also remain relevant, including topology-preserving document signatures and bipartite ranking ensembles with specialized encoding and decoding.

The community increasingly addresses retrieval as a multi-stage, interactive process, proposing dynamic utility functions that incorporate user signals and overall search intent. It also expands beyond conventional web search toward unified mobile search, dataset search, and agent-like systems capable of answering complex questions. Overall, recent work emphasizes learned representations, domain adaptation, semantic understanding, and integrated retrieval pipelines.

abstracts x20|5426a48cabc964cafb5f9b9da7.text:
## Information Retrieval: Learning, Ranking, and Specialized Search

This community centers on improving information retrieval through learned representations, ranking models, and task-specific search systems. Major themes include document and passage ranking, query understanding, expert finding, web-quality and spam detection, dataset search, email and mobile-app search, and question answering. Several works address richer retrieval settings: heterogeneous bibliographic networks, dynamic multi-stage interaction, non-factoid questions, e-commerce intent, and large-scale time-series similarity search.

Typical methods include deep neural ranking architectures, semantic embeddings, query expansion, and learning-to-rank. Models capture local relevance, cross-document interactions, permutation invariance, or pairwise relationships. Systems also use multi-task learning, language inference, matrix factorization, kernel methods, support-vector machines, hashing/signatures, and scalable clustering. Ranking pipelines commonly combine candidate retrieval with later re-ranking, balancing quality and latency.

Recent work increasingly adopts pretrained language models, especially BERT, in multi-stage pointwise and pairwise ranking. Research also emphasizes weakly supervised or unsupervised settings, auxiliary query clustering, explainability through post-hoc interpretation, and benchmarks for passage retrieval. Search is broadening beyond web documents toward datasets, mobile applications, private email collections, and conversational or agent-based retrieval, with schema generation and structured metadata used to improve discoverability.

abstracts x20|05f6e854d92ea2876e940bb008.text:
### Dynamic and Intelligent Graph Mining

This community studies large-scale social, information, and knowledge graphs, emphasizing structure, dynamics, and practical inference. Major themes include temporal network characterization and forecasting, heterogeneous relationship prediction, community detection, social-network fusion, and urban-dynamics modeling. Knowledge-graph applications include triple scoring, entity normalization, and fact checking, while other work addresses fraud de-anonymization, privacy preference prediction, and relationship semantics.

Typical methods combine graph structure with node attributes, text, and external knowledge bases. Techniques include temporal event graphs, continuous-time prediction, metapath-guided cross-modal embeddings, dynamic and neural graph embeddings, predicate-path mining, ensemble scoring, and random-forest classification. Algorithmic studies develop local-information procedures, biased random walks and absorbing Markov chains, hop-doubling distance indexes, MapReduce triangle counting, and statistically guaranteed network sampling. Theoretical work analyzes clustering thresholds and properties of scale-free and community-guided random networks.

Recent directions favor representations that preserve temporal information and support robust future prediction, alongside deep embeddings for noisy or sparse content. Research also increasingly integrates multiple networks and modalities, scales analysis to massive graphs through distributed or indexed methods, and applies graph mining to trust, security, privacy, and fact verification.

abstracts x10|05f6e854d92ea2876e940bb008.text:
## Dynamic and Heterogeneous Network Intelligence

This community centers on representing, analyzing, and predicting behavior in complex information and social networks. Major themes include network representation learning, temporal graphs, heterogeneous relationship forecasting, social-network fusion, urban-dynamics modeling, and structural properties of real-world networks. It also addresses applications such as search-rank fraud attribution and knowledge-base triple scoring.

Typical methods combine graph structure with temporal, textual, behavioral, and geographic information. The Temporal Event Graph provides a static, lossless representation using inter-event times and two-event temporal motifs, while other work develops temporally robust representations and continuous-time relationship prediction. Heterogeneous-network studies use metapaths, cross-modal embeddings, and fusion across platforms. Predictive systems include ensembles of text- and knowledge-base scorers, refined through trigger-word detection, and Dolos, which uses fraudster traits and behaviors alongside min-cut dense methods for de-anonymization. Theoretical work analyzes local-information algorithms and proves clustering thresholds in community-guided random networks.

Recent directions emphasize preserving temporal information rather than aggregating it away, forecasting evolving heterogeneous relations, integrating multiple data modalities, and moving from detection toward attribution and identity-level analysis.

abstracts x20|d5affdbf39addf38736b9d3874.text:
## Temporal Graphs, Scalable Queries, and Network Dynamics

This community centers on modeling and analyzing networks whose interactions, structure, or node activity change over time. Major themes include temporal reachability, shortest paths, distances, latencies, journeys, connectivity, and time-aware centrality. Researchers also study information and opinion diffusion through dynamic monopolies, influence processes, media, and social ties.

Typical methods include temporal and link-stream formalisms; stream graphs extended to directed, weighted, and bipartite settings; sequences of static or time-varying graphs; and algebraic formulations using temporal quantities and semirings. Algorithmic work develops indexing, labeling, reachability oracles, landmark methods, hub acceleration, and vertex-centric parallel computation for large-scale distance and path queries. Analyses commonly combine structural metrics with temporal measurements and empirical interaction traces.

Recent trends emphasize scalable processing of massive real-world networks, including efficient construction and query answering, parallel execution, and time-aware centrality. The papers also move beyond static projections toward richer multilayer narrative models and detailed temporal applications, such as hospital contacts, knowledge mobilization, cryptocurrency transactions, and movie scripts.

abstracts x10|d5affdbf39addf38736b9d3874.text:
## Temporal Networks, Diffusion, and Scalable Graph Queries

This community studies how information, influence, and connectivity evolve across network structures and time. A major theme is diffusion: multi-level opinion spreading, dynamic monopolies, and colored-torus models investigate minimum initial activation or influence needed for network-wide adoption.  

Another strong focus is temporal-network analysis. Papers address reachability, time-respecting paths, distances, latencies, fastest paths, and temporal betweenness, emphasizing that static projections can conceal important temporal roles. Time-series analysis further examines changing network properties without requiring complete structural knowledge.  

The community also develops efficient graph-query infrastructure, including indexing for temporal reachability, single-source distance and shortest-path queries, reachability oracles, and landmark labeling. Typical methods combine graph-theoretic bounds, labeling and indexing schemes, shortest-path algorithms, temporal-complexity analysis, and parallel vertex-centric computation, including SIMD-oriented and batch execution models.  

A complementary direction enriches network representation: multilayer models capture characters and semantic elements in movie narratives rather than interactions alone. Recent trends therefore move from static graphs toward temporal and multilayer representations, while simultaneously pursuing scalable preprocessing and query algorithms for massive real-world networks.

titles<=300|d5affdbf39addf38736b9d38742f.text:
**Temporal and Dynamic Graph Analytics**

This community centers on modeling and querying networks whose edges, vertices, layers, or attributes evolve over time. Major themes include temporal reachability, shortest paths, distances, latencies, and centrality; stream, link-stream, multilayer, and time-varying graph formalisms; and analysis of structural change through temporal and dynamic graphlets, graphlets, alignment, and signal methods.

A strong systems focus targets scalable analytics on large or dynamic graphs. Typical methods include reachability and distance oracles, landmark labeling, hub acceleration, indexing, vertex-centric computation, distributed algorithms, query-plan optimization, window analytics, and algebraic or semiring-based formulations of temporal quantities. Work also addresses dynamic monopolies, opinion spreading, influence, and information emergence.

Applications span hospital contacts, mailing-list threads, media and gossip, cryptocurrency trading, trust-aware recommendation, movie ratings, social-network analysis, Git repositories, and scientific collaboration or challenge networks. Stream-based features and sentiment analysis support temporal recommendation.

Recent directions emphasize unified multilayer stream-graph models, layer centralities and time centrality, efficient analytics for evolving graphs, and principled comparisons of temporal networks. The community increasingly connects formal temporal semantics with practical, scalable indexing and distributed query processing.

titles<=300|2977b6f59f9e8a28167ef09022d0.text:
## Semantic Infrastructure for Web Archives and Scholarly Knowledge

This community studies how digital information can be modeled, preserved, synchronized, searched, and reused over time. Major themes include web archiving and “time travel” (Memento), archive coverage and profiling, rediscovery of missing pages, temporal coherence, archivability, URI persistence, and preservation of dynamic or deferred web content. A second focus is digital-library and repository architecture, including Fedora, aDORe, NSDL, OAI-PMH, ResourceSync, aggregation ecosystems, and interoperable access services.

Semantic scholarly communication is another strong theme: nanopublications, micropublications, scientific claims, provenance, annotations, linked data, contextualized information, and persistent references to changing resources. Applications include biomedical literature and data, mathematical software, manuscripts, and research repositories.

Typical methods combine standards-based system design with empirical evaluation of repositories and archives; crawling and focused collection; graph analysis; metadata aggregation; temporal queries; URI and cache analysis; and machine learning for ranking, classification, event detection, visual search, and page rediscovery. Case studies frequently use Wikipedia, social media, Common Crawl, Internet Archive, and national or institutional web collections.

Recent work trends toward large-scale, event-focused archive mining; human-assisted and decentralized preservation; richer provenance-centric knowledge graphs; persistent annotations; automated recovery of lost resources; and analytics infrastructure that connects archived web content with scholarly claims, software, and open research data.

abstracts x10|2977b6f59f9e8a28167ef09022.text:
### Semantic Organization and Long-Term Access to Digital Knowledge

This community studies how digital artifacts, scientific information, and web content can be modeled, preserved, aggregated, and retrieved over time. A central theme is representing artifacts through relationships and research life cycles rather than as isolated files, using persistent identifiers, semantic-web models, and formal organization of scientific claims. Repository architectures such as Fedora support heterogeneous, distributed objects, multiple disseminations, extensibility, and rights management.

Long-term preservation is addressed through durable storage designs, including VXA, which archives executable decoders with compressed content, and through practical acquisition and extraction of archived web pages. Web-archive research examines collection creation, memento accessibility, resource dating, user behavior, referral links, and search. Typical methods include architectural prototyping, metadata and aggregation modeling, evidence polling for estimated creation dates, large-scale access-log analysis, and empirical studies of hundreds of thousands of archived pages. Social-bookmarking data is used to improve temporal search and identify historically important resources.

Recent directions emphasize user-centered archive interfaces, domain- and organization-specific collections, richer contextual dissemination, machine-readable provenance, and formal scientific knowledge enabling aggregation, fact checking, consistency checking, question answering, and semantic search.

abstracts x20|2977b6f59f9e8a28167ef09022.text:
**Digital Preservation, Web Archives, and Semantic Scholarly Infrastructure**

This community studies how to preserve, represent, discover, and reuse evolving digital knowledge. Major themes include web archiving and temporal search; durable storage of compressed or heterogeneous digital objects; semantic modeling of scientific artifacts, claims, and research life cycles; and repository architectures supporting aggregation, dissemination, rights, and versioning.

Typical methods combine standards-based system design (OAIS, MPEG-21, SharedCanvas, persistent identifiers), empirical analysis of large collections and access logs, and evaluation with real archival datasets. Researchers use web crawling, HTTP acquisition and text extraction, social-media and bookmarking signals, lexical and title-based retrieval, and machine-learning models for predicting archival holdings. Caching and federated aggregation are investigated to improve archive performance, while web applications estimate resource dates and expose machine-readable evidence.

Recent work emphasizes freshness and longitudinal change, integrating social-web signals with focused crawling and temporal retrieval. Studies quantify link and annotation decay, disappearing resources, archival gaps, and “scholarly orphans” outside traditional preservation systems. Other directions formalize scientific claims for semantic search and automated reasoning, and develop modular repositories and virtual machines that make digital objects, codecs, and evolving linked data usable over long time spans.

titles<=300|f5236526824cd05bfc87df6156a6.text:
## Relational, Graph, and Data-Centric Analytics at Scale

This community studies scalable data management for relational, graph, array, stream, and machine-learning workloads. A central theme is query processing and optimization: worst-case-optimal, multiway, theta, spatial, and geometric joins; conjunctive-query enumeration and containment; factorized and compressed results; materialized-view maintenance; and cost-, selectivity-, or learning-based planning. Theoretical work emphasizes tractability, hypertree and submodular-width decompositions, functional dependencies, inequalities, updates, and communication costs.

Systems research develops high-performance engines and storage architectures, including columnar and LSM systems, adaptive indexing and database cracking, main-memory and heterogeneous hardware execution, MapReduce/Spark processing, array databases, and relational engines for graphs and machine learning. Graph themes include dynamic and streaming pattern matching, subgraph queries, graph analytics, compression, historical queries, and relational representations of graphs.

Typical methods include factorization, sketches and stratified sampling, approximate query processing with error guarantees, incremental and delta maintenance, static code generation, operator fusion, parallel and GPU execution, declarative languages, and probabilistic or reinforcement-learning-based optimization.

Recent trends connect databases with end-to-end machine learning, visual and video analytics, interactive exploration, data cleaning, provenance and versioning, privacy, cloud elasticity, and model-based or learned systems. Attention also shifts toward fast, approximate, continuously updated analytics over high-velocity data.

abstracts x10|f5236526824cd05bfc87df6156.text:
## Query Processing, Analytics, and Scalable Data Systems

This community centers on efficient query evaluation across relational, graph, visual, streaming, and distributed data. A major theme is join processing: mixed-integer linear programming is used to search left-deep plans, while worst-case-optimal parallel algorithms and single-round multiway joins address communication costs and correctness under distribution policies. Graph analytics is repeatedly translated into relational joins and SQL, including specialized hardware support through the Triejax architecture and evaluation on the Vertica column store.

Other work targets costly analytics workloads. Physical representations and hierarchical models reduce CNN-based image and video extraction costs; sparse tensors and functional dependencies support integrated machine learning over relational data; and MacroBase prioritizes unusual behavior in fast streams using reservoir sampling and heavy-hitters sketches. Systems research emphasizes practical performance and programmability, exemplified by the Scala-based LegoBase query engine and Vertica deployments.

Recent trends favor unifying diverse analytics with relational abstractions, exploiting optimization solvers, sketches, column stores, and specialized hardware, while explicitly managing parallel communication, consistency, and latency.

abstracts x20|f5236526824cd05bfc87df6156.text:
### Database Systems for Scalable Analytics

This community centers on advanced data management for analytical, distributed, and graph workloads. Core themes include query optimization and evaluation, especially join ordering, conjunctive queries, inequalities, communication costs, and correctness under parallel data distribution. Graph processing is frequently reframed as relational joins or SQL/Datalog programs, targeting both columnar databases and specialized hardware.

Typical methods combine formal complexity and communication analyses with practical systems research. Examples include mixed-integer linear programming for query-plan search, worst-case-optimal multiway joins, parallel algorithms, query compilation, and hardware-conscious execution. Approximation and statistical techniques support interactive exploration through maximum-entropy summaries, reservoir sampling, and heavy-hitters sketches. Other work applies model-based compression, functional dependencies, sparse tensors, and declarative abstractions to integrate machine learning with relational data.

The papers also address broader data-platform concerns: replication consistency, dataset version control, metadata cleaning and record linkage, recommendation objectives, and automated data-structure design. A notable trend is convergence between databases, graph analytics, and machine learning: systems increasingly seek end-to-end workflows spanning data preparation, querying, modeling, and visualization. Another trend is “abstraction without regret”—using high-level languages and declarative interfaces while retaining performance through compilation, specialized representations, parallelism, and hardware acceleration.

titles<=300|111a57ecbc5a35d8c92689477829.text:
### Networks, Influence, and Opinion Dynamics

This community studies how network structure shapes influence, information diffusion, collective beliefs, and controllability. A major theme is opinion dynamics: consensus, disagreement, polarization, social power, stubborn agents, bounded confidence, susceptibility, biased assimilation, backfire effects, homophily, and interactions across correlated topics. Signed and dynamic networks receive particular attention, including structural balance, trust–mistrust relations, state flipping, and evolving topology.

A second core theme is network centrality and navigation. Papers develop axioms and measures for PageRank, Katz, betweenness, accessibility, current-flow, absorbing-walk, criticality, distinctiveness, coverage, and node impact, often addressing edge addition, node removal, or network design. Random walks and shortest-path functionals support scalable search, diffusion analysis, personalized ranking, link prediction, and recommender systems.

Typical methods include Markov-chain and fluid models, matrix and spectral analysis, dynamical-systems convergence and asymptotics, optimization, approximation algorithms, sampling, distributed and vertex-centric computation, and empirical analysis of social-media or traffic data. Related work addresses influence estimation, active sensing, network inference, epidemic mitigation, recommendation auditing, information filtering, and crawling.

Recent trends emphasize billion-scale algorithms, dynamic graphs, partial-observation learning, network and opinion co-evolution, algorithmic control of polarization and diffusion, and auditing personalized information environments.

titles<=300|c9c2065a98ff1f6dddd27c797d61.text:
## XML Data Exploration, Distribution, and Structural Search

This community focuses on managing and querying XML data collections, with particular attention to structure-aware access and scalable organization. **DescribeX** addresses exploration and querying of XML Web collections, while **LiquidXML** investigates adaptive redistribution of XML content. The **ViP2P** platform extends this direction through XML views in peer-to-peer environments.

Typical methods emphasize structural representations and organization: **path summaries** and **path partitioning** support efficient processing in modern XML databases, while structural consistency constraints improve XML keyword search by eliminating spurious results. The papers collectively combine database indexing, XML views, content placement, and keyword-search techniques rather than treating XML as purely text.

Recent trends in this set move toward adaptive and distributed XML management—illustrated by content redistribution and peer-to-peer views—alongside increasingly precise structural search. Overall, the research seeks to make XML collections easier to explore, more efficiently partitioned and distributed, and more reliable for keyword-based retrieval.

abstracts x20|111a57ecbc5a35d8c926894778.text:
## Network Dynamics, Influence, and Social Systems

This community studies how network structure, interaction rules, and strategic behavior shape influence, opinions, information diffusion, and discoverability. Major themes include centrality and PageRank optimization; strategic rewiring and hiding in covert networks; opinion and belief evolution under biases, susceptibility, antagonistic links, multiple topics, and changing interpersonal relations; and navigation, node discovery, and traffic-based backbone extraction. Web crawling provides a complementary application involving large-scale data collection, indexing, accessibility, and vulnerability checking.

Typical methods combine graph theory, game theory, dynamical-systems and control analysis, stochastic processes, optimization, and asymptotic convergence proofs. Models include DeGroot, Friedkin–Johnsen, DeGroot–Friedkin, gossip interactions, signed graphs, logic matrices, random walks, and thermodynamic path functionals. Empirical and computational approaches analyze Italian Senate voting records, social-media propagation, recommendation feedback, and network traffic, often using feature selection, classification, and influence estimation.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic rather than static networks, including issue-dependent interactions, evolving signed graphs, and closed loops between opinions and personalized recommendations. There is also increasing attention to topic-specific user behavior, partial-observation estimation, strategic manipulation, and combining structural topology with functional usage data.

abstracts x10|c9c2065a98ff1f6dddd27c797d.text:
## XML Summaries, Search, and Distributed Data Management

This community focuses on efficient querying and organization of large, heterogeneous XML collections. A central theme is **structural summarization**: DescribeX declaratively represents complex document structures using XPath axes and constructs, while path summaries support access optimization and path-partitioned storage in modern XML databases.

A second major theme is **distributed XML management in peer-to-peer networks**. ViP2P uses DHT overlays and distributed materialized XML views to share and query document corpora. LiquidXML extends this direction through adaptive redistribution of possibly overlapping or redundant fragments, selecting storage locations to improve query performance.

Typical methods include declarative path and structural descriptions, XML path summaries, path partitioning, materialized views, DHT-based distribution, adaptive fragment placement, and experimental evaluation of access strategies. XML keyword search is addressed through structural-consistency techniques designed to eliminate spurious results beyond local LCA, SLCA, or MLCA filtering.

Overall, the work trends from centralized indexing and summarization toward heterogeneous, distributed, and adaptive XML infrastructures, while emphasizing globally informed query-result quality and performance optimization.

abstracts x10|111a57ecbc5a35d8c926894778.text:
## Network Influence, Opinion Dynamics, and Web Analysis

This community studies how network structure, individual influence, and strategic behavior shape information and opinions. Core themes include centrality and network formation, social power and dominance, consensus under signed or antagonistic interactions, biased and multi-topic opinion dynamics, covert-network detection, and the feedback between opinions and personalized recommendations. A related strand examines web crawlers, tracing their evolution from statistical collection and search indexing to accessibility and vulnerability assessment.

Typical methods combine game-theoretic models of link rewiring and strategic hiding with dynamical-systems analysis of consensus, equilibria, convergence, and stability. Researchers use graph Laplacians, centrality measures, signed networks, nonlinear state-dependent interaction models, and logic matrices for interdependent topics. Empirical work applies feature selection and voting-data mining to infer political affinities, while recommendation studies formulate closed-loop user–content dynamics.

Recent directions emphasize richer and more realistic settings: antagonistic or malicious recommendations, individual social biases, multiple logically coupled issues, strategic modification of interpersonal weights, scale-free influence, covert actors evading centrality-based detection, and adaptive recommender systems whose outputs both respond to and alter user opinions.

abstracts x20|c9c2065a98ff1f6dddd27c797d.text:
### XML Structure, Search, and Distributed Management

This community focuses on efficient querying and management of large, heterogeneous XML collections. A central theme is structural summarization: DescribeX provides declarative, XPath-expressive summaries for complex web collections, while research on path summaries develops practical construction and exploitation algorithms for XML databases. These summaries support query optimization and complement path-partitioned storage.

A second theme is distributed XML processing in peer-to-peer environments. ViP2P uses DHT overlays and distributed materialized XML views to share documents and answer arbitrary XML queries. LiquidXML extends this setting with adaptive redistribution of possibly overlapping and redundant fragments, selecting storage locations to improve query performance across peers.

Typical methods include XPath-based structural descriptions, path summaries, path partitioning, distributed materialized views, DHT infrastructures, adaptive fragment placement, and experimental evaluation of access and query-processing benefits. XML keyword search addresses a related usability problem: eliminating spurious results through structural consistency and global examination, beyond local LCA, SLCA, and MLCA heuristics.

Overall, the work trends from centralized indexing and summaries toward adaptive, distributed XML infrastructures, while increasingly emphasizing robust structural semantics and high-precision search.

abstracts x10|7a69d457bf4fcaf6b6ed3f8ffb.text:
### Database Reasoning Under Uncertainty and Provenance

This community investigates principled query processing over complex, distributed, and uncertain data. Major themes include query-answer causality and responsibility, abductive diagnosis, database repairs, view updates, and explanations for both query answers and non-answers. Provenance and data differencing support workflow reproducibility and lineage-based analysis.

A second major focus is probabilistic databases. Methods include knowledge compilation into decomposition trees, semiring and semimodule representations, and approximate lifted inference that evaluates a bounded set of database query plans and combines upper bounds. Work on uncertain-relation joins compares sorting, indexing, and materialized intermediate tables, using uncertainty statistics to select algorithms.

Additional themes include graph-pattern mining with constant and existential nodes, peer-to-peer query answering under semantic and exchange constraints, and trust-aware consistent answers. Across these areas, papers emphasize formal semantics, complexity analysis, tractability characterizations, and provable optimality, alongside experimental comparisons.

The research agenda is moving toward integrated management of heterogeneous information, uncertainty, text, code, streams, and workflows. It also increasingly favors database-native reasoning and explanation: approximate inference inside standard relational engines, explicit causes and responsibilities, and reproducible computational results.

abstracts x20|7a69d457bf4fcaf6b6ed3f8ffb.text:
**Probabilistic, Explainable, and Inconsistent Data Management**

This community studies advanced query processing when data are uncertain, inconsistent, incomplete, distributed, or richly annotated. Major themes include probabilistic databases and approximate inference; provenance, causality, responsibility, and data differencing for explaining query answers and non-answers; repairs and integrity management; and query answering across peers, conceptual dependencies, and belief-annotated databases. Additional work addresses graph-pattern mining, uncertain similarity ranking, XML access-control policy repair, workflow reproducibility, and MapReduce performance debugging.

Typical methods combine database-theoretic semantics with complexity analysis, rewriting, the chase, answer-set programs, provenance graphs, and abductive diagnosis. Probabilistic work uses semirings and semimodules, knowledge compilation, decomposition trees, safe query plans, Markov-style correlation representations, and database-native approximation. Systems also exploit indexes, sorting, relational intermediates, schema information, and statistics to improve scalability.

Recent trends emphasize moving beyond tuple independence toward complex correlations, aggregates, top-*k* ranking, and scalable approximate inference. Explanation is broadening from lineage to causal responsibility, why-not provenance, workflow reproducibility, and performance explanations. There is also increasing attention to actionable repairs—through active integrity constraints, policy correction, and causality-repair connections—and to integrating heterogeneous, uncertain, conflicting, and community-curated information.

titles<=300|c8634e3ae9cabd2c02f20cef5dfe.text:
## Collaborative Knowledge, Search, and Social Information Systems

This community studies how user-generated knowledge can be organized, searched, ranked, and reused. Major themes include Wikipedia and Wiktionary as structured knowledge sources; folksonomies, tagging behavior, vocabulary growth, and tag hierarchies; collaborative information seeking and social search; and expertise, influencer, and entity discovery in professional and social networks. Several works examine Chinese microblogs and the dynamics of attention, interests, opinions, and communities.

Typical methods combine graph and network analysis, including scale-free modeling, centrality, local dimension, backbone extraction, PageRank approximation, and bipartite-network analysis. Other recurring approaches include ontology matching, semantic similarity, entity disambiguation and linking, relational/XML database design, faceted and hierarchical classification, statistical information retrieval, learning-to-rank, recommendation, and visualization. Evaluation is addressed through search metrics, relevance assessment, clickthrough randomization, and experimental retrieval studies.

Recent directions emphasize multilingual and cross-source entity ranking, high-throughput linking on user-generated data, personalized and federated search, deep ranking models, and talent or expertise recommendation. The community also increasingly connects structured knowledge with dynamic social streams, collaborative archives, digital collections, and user-created communities for image and web search.

titles<=300|7a69d457bf4fcaf6b6ed3f8ffb3b.text:
## Database Semantics, Uncertainty, and Explainable Data Management

This community studies how databases can represent, query, repair, and explain imperfect information. Major themes include probabilistic and incomplete databases; provenance, lineage, and workflow reproducibility; causality, responsibility, diagnosis, and view updates; inconsistent data and integrity-constraint enforcement; and query answering over ontologies, graphs, XML, temporal, and peer-to-peer data. Data exchange, schema mappings, data quality, completeness, privacy, and ranking under uncertainty are recurring concerns.

Typical methods are highly theoretical and algorithmic: chase and finite-controllability arguments, Datalog and disjunctive rewritings, abductive diagnosis, repair programs, active integrity constraints, answer-set programming, and model-based diagnosis. Complexity dichotomies, tractability frontiers, reductions, and approximation analyses characterize query answering, resilience, responsibility, determinacy, and consistent answers. Provenance circuits, BDDs, knowledge compilation, tree automata, cycluits, model counting, and Shapley-style measures support explanation and uncertainty computation. Systems work explores lifted inference, probabilistic ranking, pruning, dynamic data structures, cloud-aware provenance, and database-backed statistical inference.

Recent directions emphasize scalable probabilistic processing, infinite and open-world uncertainty, structural tractability, and practical provenance tools. Causal database repair is increasingly connected to algorithmic fairness, while scientific workflow repeatability, hypothesis management, graph analytics, crowdsourcing, knowledge-base completeness, and streaming uncertain data broaden the application scope.

abstracts x10|c8634e3ae9cabd2c02f20cef5d.text:
### Collaborative Web Knowledge and Information Systems

This community studies how user-generated content can support information access, analysis, and decision-making. Major themes include Wikipedia and Wiktionary as dynamic knowledge sources: systems detect breaking news in Wikipedia, transform Wiktionary’s semi-structured entries into relational schemas, and provide densely annotated, multilingual entity-linking data.

A second theme is collaborative information seeking. Work develops taxonomies of collaboration based on intent, depth, concurrency, and location, investigates similarities among group-search participants, and explores how combined user profiles can improve retrieval and interfaces. Search evaluation is also examined through meta-evaluation and measures such as the Preference Identification Ratio.

Collaborative tagging receives substantial attention. Studies model vocabulary growth and allometric scaling, relating power-law behavior to heterogeneous user activity, while applications mine tags for product design and recommendation. Typical methods include large-scale log or snapshot analysis, statistical power-law modeling, structured extraction, entity linking, database transformation, and information-retrieval evaluation. Data-cube research adds multidimensional pruning through the diamond-dice operator.

Recent directions emphasize automated exploitation of large, richly annotated, multilingual datasets; near-real-time extraction from community platforms; and using collective behavior and metadata to improve search, analytics, and product decisions.

abstracts x20|c8634e3ae9cabd2c02f20cef5d.text:
### Collaborative Web Knowledge and Social Information Systems

This community studies how users collectively create, organize, search, and propagate information on the Web. Major themes include Wikipedia and Wiktionary as structured knowledge sources; collaborative tagging and folksonomies; social and group information seeking; semantic enrichment; and analysis of attention and influence in online networks.

Typical methods combine large-scale platform data mining with statistical and network analysis. Researchers examine power-law and allometric growth, vocabulary evolution, tag co-occurrence, similarity measures, category structure, and user behavior. Graph-based techniques include centrality measures, clustering, clickstream networks, and community formation. Other work develops practical systems and operators, including a Wikipedia-based breaking-news reader, relational extraction of Wiktionary entries, multidimensional “diamond dice” pruning, ontology matching through Wiktionary and SPARQL, and product design from desirable tags. Evaluation research also questions how search metrics correspond to user preferences.

Recent directions emphasize multilingual and machine-readable resources, exemplified by densely annotated Wikipedia linked to Freebase entities across languages. There is also increasing interest in forecasting behavior from streams, identifying influential or behaviorally similar users, improving collaborative search, and converting emergent social classifications into interoperable semantic and bibliographic knowledge structures.

titles<=300|b0c0c8272c5669287ef5278ffb33.text:
## Community Report: Complex Data Warehousing, Benchmarking, and Adaptive Optimization

This community focuses on engineering and evaluating data-management systems for complex, heterogeneous data. A dominant theme is XML warehousing and OLAP, including XML algebra, complex hierarchies, summarizability, fragmentation, join indexes, query optimization, and integration of web-derived data. Related work addresses object-oriented and document-oriented databases, asynchronous replication, CRUD performance, and clustering behavior.

A second major theme is physical-design automation in data warehouses: selecting indexes, bitmap join indexes, materialized views, and combined configurations. Typical methods include query and workload clustering, affinity-based and data-mining-based fragmentation, frequent-itemset mining, cost models, Markov analysis, and simulation. Clustering algorithms such as k-means are repeatedly evaluated for database organization and optimization.

Benchmarking is central, with generic tools and benchmarks for data warehouses, XML warehouses, object-oriented databases, text classification, Twitter keywords, and data processing. Discrete-event simulation and performance experiments are common evaluation techniques.

Additional applications include business intelligence, biomedical and archaeological warehouses, personalized medicine, and social-media event detection. Recent directions represented in the collection emphasize scalable text and document architectures, cloud-based optimization and pricing of shared optimizations, Web 2.0 OLAP and tag clouds, and automated, adaptive database administration.

abstracts x10|b0c0c8272c5669287ef5278ffb.text:
### Adaptive Data Management and Analytics

This community studies efficient management, analysis, and decision support over complex, heterogeneous, and rapidly changing data. Major themes include XML tree-pattern querying and optimization; XML data warehouses, fragmentation, OLAP summarizability, and web-based warehousing; dynamic index selection for evolving warehouse workloads; and business intelligence architectures tailored to small and medium-sized enterprises. A parallel stream addresses storage and performance in object-oriented databases through clustering policies.

Typical methods combine analytical models with empirical evaluation: tree-pattern matching frameworks, incremental frequent-itemset mining for workload-driven index selection, derived horizontal fragmentation, query-based techniques for correcting aggregation errors, and simulation or implementation-based comparisons of clustering algorithms. Text-oriented work emphasizes document-based, scalable architectures with preprocessing such as stemming, lemmatization, part-of-speech tagging, and named-entity recognition. The Twitter study extends this emphasis to social signals, detecting events through anomalies in mention-link creation rather than text alone.

Overall, the research trends toward adaptive and automated optimization, scalable processing of web and textual data, exploitation of structural and social relationships, and simpler or more lightweight solutions that reduce administrative overhead while supporting evolving workloads and complex data models.

abstracts x20|b0c0c8272c5669287ef5278ffb.text:
## Adaptive Data Warehousing, XML Analytics, and Data-Driven Optimization

This community focuses on building and optimizing decision-support systems for complex, heterogeneous, and evolving data. Major themes include XML data warehouses and OLAP, complex-data architectures, summarizability, fragmentation, benchmarking, and performance optimization through indexes and materialized views. Related work addresses scalable text analysis and large-scale classification, as well as event detection in social media.

Typical methods are workload-aware and data-mining-based. Researchers use frequent-itemset mining to select indexes, query clustering to choose materialized views, and affinity or derived horizontal fragmentation to distribute XML data. Query-based techniques address incorrect aggregation in complex hierarchies. Simulation and configurable evaluation frameworks measure clustering, buffer, prefetching, and database behavior under changing access patterns. Other studies develop reference architectures, benchmarks such as XWeB and LSHTC, and statistical mention-anomaly detection for Twitter events.

Recent trends emphasize automation and adaptability: database administration increasingly exploits workload mining; XML warehouses target irregular and multimodal data; and evaluation moves beyond static workloads toward dynamic behavior. Lightweight, scalable architectures for small enterprises and document-based systems for high-volume text further reflect the shift toward practical, large-scale analytics.

abstracts x10|444f4d4e29299e78fbb334aae0.text:
### Flexible, Fair, and Efficient Search over Complex Data

This community studies advanced data management, search, and recommendation systems under realistic constraints: imprecision, incomplete information, large-scale data, hidden interfaces, and competing user or societal objectives. One theme is richer database querying, including fuzzy relational models, flexible querying, concise relational object summaries, skyline queries over incomplete streams, and keyword search over structured data.

A second theme concerns web-scale retrieval and data acquisition. Work develops optimal algorithms for crawling hidden databases, third-party query reranking over public interfaces, and fast in-memory set intersection for information-retrieval workloads.

Efficiency is addressed through specialized algorithms and hardware-aware systems, including CPU–GPU hybrid acceleration for spatial cross-comparison in pathology images and worst-case-efficient set representations.

Fairness and diversity are increasingly prominent. Proposed methods quantify bias in ranked results, perform fairness-aware reranking, incorporate demographic representations into maximal marginal relevance, and use “antidote data” to improve polarization and fairness without directly modifying system algorithms or outputs. Overall, recent work trends toward socially responsible ranking and recommendation, while also emphasizing scalable processing of imperfect, heterogeneous, and externally controlled data.

titles<=300|444f4d4e29299e78fbb334aae097.text:
## Query Processing, Search, Compression, and Fair Ranking

This community centers on efficient information retrieval and analytical querying over large, heterogeneous, and dynamic data. Major themes include top-k, skyline, preference, ranking, similarity, and aggregate queries; hidden and web databases; graph, XML, social, bibliographic, biomedical, and location-based data; and OLAP and streaming systems.

Typical methods are algorithmic and systems-oriented: skyline and k-dominant processing, preference elicitation and revision, rank-aware aggregation, query reranking, crawling and sampling, view-size and aggregate estimation, and distributed or adaptive query execution. Extensive work targets compressed indexes and integer/bitmap representations using SIMD, vectorization, GPUs, sorting, wavelets, hashing, and in-memory data structures. Other approaches include learned query planning, approximate retrieval, nearest-neighbor and word-mover’s-distance methods, clustering, and game-theoretic or optimization-based models.

Recent directions emphasize responsible ranking and recommendation: fairness of exposure, disparate exposure, demographic satisfaction, diversity, polarization, bias auditing, and fairness-aware reranking. Search increasingly incorporates semantic representations, embeddings, neural passage retrieval, and k-nearest-neighbor methods, alongside graph and social-media analytics. Systems research continues toward scalable hybrid CPU/GPU execution, distributed streams, repetitive collections, hidden databases, and interactive large-scale analytics.

titles<=300|37f6d75de33bf3a46ffd4d88eec8.text:
## Entity Resolution, Data Fusion, and Human–Machine Curation

This community focuses on making heterogeneous, noisy data reliable and integrable. Core themes include entity resolution and consolidation, record linkage, schema and ontology matching, truth discovery, source reliability, data fusion, data cleaning, and knowledge-graph integration. A parallel strand studies crowdsourcing: task assignment, worker expertise, quality control, consensus, budget and latency optimization, and human-assisted joins, labeling, and graph search. Spatial crowdsourcing and web/deep-web extraction are recurring application areas.

Typical methods combine probabilistic and Bayesian inference, Markov logic, generative models, random forests, trust models, active and transfer learning, blocking and locality-sensitive hashing, embeddings, graph matching, and distributed or GPU similarity joins. Formal work develops dependencies, matching functions, Datalog reasoning, chase procedures, and complexity analyses. Systems emphasize interactive curation, query-time resolution, wrappers, spreadsheets, and reproducible pipelines.

Recent directions increasingly integrate deep learning with data curation and entity resolution, including semantic representations, learned string transformations, and low-resource transfer or active learning. Other trends emphasize scalable, schema-agnostic, incremental, and real-time processing; probabilistic holistic repair; adaptive human–machine collaboration; interpretable risk and data-quality metrics; and cleaning data for fair, robust machine-learning models.

abstracts x20|444f4d4e29299e78fbb334aae0.text:
## Efficient, Flexible, and Fair Data Retrieval

This community studies methods for improving retrieval, querying, indexing, and recommendation across relational, web, graph, spatial, and streaming data. Major themes include querying imprecise or incomplete data through fuzzy summaries and skyline methods; concise object summaries and aggregate skyline joins; and extracting data from hidden web databases through crawling and third-party reranking services.

Efficiency is central. Typical methods include specialized indexes and compressed representations, bitmap and set-intersection algorithms, SIMD and CPU–GPU parallelism, geometric pruning, and anytime top-k graph-pattern retrieval. Work on Hippo indexing, variable-byte encoding, n-gram hashing, and threshold functions targets lower storage, faster updates, and high-throughput query execution.

A substantial strand addresses fairness and social impacts in ranking and recommendation. Proposed techniques include fairness-aware reranking, demographic representations combined with maximal marginal relevance, antidote data, and consistency-based tag reranking. Complementary empirical work measures gender and age bias, including proxy effects in biography-based occupation classification.

Recent directions emphasize deploying socially aware retrieval methods without redesigning underlying systems, supporting user-specified ranking over public interfaces, and exploiting modern parallel hardware. The community also broadens classical database optimization toward real-world settings involving spatial pathology data, ride sharing, massive streams, fuzzy information, and graph-based search.

abstracts x10|37f6d75de33bf3a46ffd4d88ee.text:
### Reliable Data Integration and Entity Resolution

This community focuses on improving the quality, reliability, and scalability of data integration. Major themes include entity resolution (ER), entity consolidation and golden-record construction, data fusion across conflicting Web and enterprise sources, and automated discovery of syntactic patterns in database fields. Crowdsourcing is another prominent focus, including worker evaluation, fault-tolerant ER, spatial task assignment, and human–machine cooperation.

Typical methods combine probabilistic modeling, source-correlation analysis, voting and truth-discovery techniques, blocking and locality-sensitive hashing (including KLSH and DOPH), learned representations and deep learning, and rule-based match-and-merge pipelines. Several works formulate optimization problems that minimize human or requester cost while enforcing precision, recall, or confidence guarantees. Worker quality is assessed through statistically tight confidence intervals, while crowd input is treated as noisy and potentially contradictory.

Recent trends emphasize democratizing ER by reducing labeling, feature engineering, and parameter tuning; integrating deep representations for accuracy and efficiency; and introducing explicit quality control through human–machine systems. The community also moves toward scalable, probabilistic, and experimentally comparable solutions for heterogeneous data, unreliable sources, and real-world crowdsourcing settings.

abstracts x20|37f6d75de33bf3a46ffd4d88ee.text:
### Data Integration, Entity Resolution, and Trustworthy Data

This community focuses on integrating heterogeneous, noisy data and producing reliable, canonical information. Major themes include entity resolution and record linkage; data fusion and conflict resolution across Web, enterprise, scientific, and social-network sources; entity consolidation into “golden records”; and data-quality assessment through constraints, pattern discovery, and fact-checking. Crowdsourcing is treated both as a source of useful judgments and as a noisy process requiring worker evaluation and quality guarantees.

Typical methods combine probabilistic models for conflicting values and multiple truths, blocking and similarity joins for scalable matching, locality-sensitive hashing, partitioning, recurrence, and parallelism. Other work uses deep distributed representations for entities and database columns, learned regular-expression-like patterns, link-based evidence, and axiomatic discovery of order dependencies. Human–machine cooperation is optimized to meet precision, recall, or cost targets, while confidence intervals quantify worker reliability.

Recent trends emphasize automation and reduced expert effort: deep-learning-based, schema-agnostic, and progressive entity resolution; scalable linkage of millions of records; hybrid models that infer both the number and identity of truths; and targeted cleaning for fact-checking. The community also expands beyond static tables to spatial-temporal data, changing Web structures, and mobile spatial crowdsourcing.

titles<=300|de449020a4bc84c0a1fd957c417c.text:
## Graph Querying, RDF Systems, and Evolving Graph Data

This community centers on foundations, languages, and systems for querying and managing graph-structured data, especially RDF, SPARQL, property graphs, XML, and linked data. Major themes include SPARQL semantics, satisfiability, expressive power, optional patterns, negation, paths, provenance, incomplete and uncertain information, and ontology-mediated query answering. A parallel focus is interoperability: mappings among relational, RDF, XML, and property-graph models; query translation; schemas, shapes, validation, reification, and bidirectional evolution.

Typical methods include formal complexity and decidability analysis, relational-algebra and Datalog reductions, chase and dependency techniques, graph summarization, cardinality estimation, indexing, compression, incremental view maintenance, and distributed execution. Systems employ MapReduce, Spark, GPUs, HBase, adaptive partitioning, federated endpoints, streaming engines, and native graph databases. Benchmarks and empirical studies evaluate SPARQL workloads, federations, geospatial RDF, and social-network graphs.

Recent trends emphasize scalable and adaptive processing of large, distributed, streaming, and historical graphs; unified querying across RDF and property graphs; visual, keyword, example-based, and recommendation-oriented interfaces; and practical schema/shape management. Uncertainty, privacy, provenance, contextual knowledge, and approximate or bounded-response query answering are also increasingly prominent.

abstracts x10|de449020a4bc84c0a1fd957c41.text:
### Graph Data Management, Querying, and Structural Inference

This community investigates representations, query languages, optimization, and analysis for RDF, XML, and graph-based data systems.
