A central theme is efficient SPARQL processing, including optimization of OPTIONAL patterns (left outer joins), runtime optimization through incremental evaluation, and preference-aware querying via SPREFQL. Work on RDF semantics addresses incomplete or partially known information, while relational-to-RDF/OWL direct mappings use Datalog to establish information and query preservation.

Another theme is learning and extracting structure: deterministic regular expressions are learned from XML examples to infer DTDs or XSDs, and visual web-wrapper languages are formally compared. Provenance research applies graph segmentation and summarization to make evolving, versioned data-science provenance graphs more understandable.

The papers also examine graph-system foundations and practice. Gremlin is presented as a traversal machine and language executable across OLTP and OLAP graph systems, while graph-database research develops taxonomies of data organization and query designs for large, dynamic, richly attributed graphs.

Typical methods include formal semantics and proofs, language extensions and translations, query-plan optimization, incremental evaluation, machine learning from examples, graph summarization, and experimental performance evaluation. Recent trends emphasize runtime/adaptive optimization, scalable processing of evolving graph data, clearer expression of user preferences, and managing incomplete information and complex provenance.

abstracts x20|de449020a4bc84c0a1fd957c41.text:
### Graph Querying, Semantics, and Evolving Data Systems

This community focuses on querying, modeling, and optimizing graph- and Web-oriented data. A major theme is SPARQL and RDF: optimization of OPTIONAL patterns, runtime and summary-graph-driven query planning, federated evaluation at billion-triple scale, incomplete-information semantics, qualitative preferences, keyword/SPARQL hybrids, and translation between SPARQL and Gremlin. Related work studies RDF’s direct mapping from relational databases, preserving information and query answers, as well as analytical queries over Semantic Web data cubes.

A second theme concerns graph data management more broadly. Papers analyze graph database architectures and query models, define type systems and data-definition languages for property graphs, and present Gremlin’s traversal-machine foundations. Regular path and simple-path query complexity, uncertain-graph reliability maximization, and provenance-graph segmentation address theoretical and applied graph analysis.

Typical methods include formal semantics and complexity classification, Datalog-based mappings and update strategies, query rewriting and translation, structural or partition-based indexing, incremental/runtime optimization, approximation algorithms, and large-scale experimental evaluation. Other contributions learn XML schemas from examples and formally compare Web-wrapper languages.

Recent directions emphasize interoperability across RDF and property graphs, scalable federations and cloud services, schema and provenance management for evolving data, and richer query interfaces combining structured patterns with preferences or keywords.

titles<=300|a0cd285a9bf3f4f3cb659ec461a0.text:
### Keyphrase Extraction, Summarization, and Graph-Based Text Understanding

This community focuses primarily on extracting and organizing salient information from documents. Major themes include automatic keyphrase and term extraction, keyphrase indexing and visualization, information-rich passage retrieval, and conceptual representation of unstructured data. Applications span medical documents, broadcast news, scholarly communication, and news-story traffic prediction.

Typical methods combine linguistic processing with statistical, semantic, and graph-based techniques. Text denoising is used both for keyphrase indexing and for identifying informative passages. Ranking methods include personalized PageRank and folksonomy-graph adaptations for improved tag recommendation. Other work explores neural-network-based keyphrase extraction, hybrid extraction systems, and practical systems such as KEA. Summarization research addresses both single- and multi-document settings, including hierarchical approaches and privacy-preserving summarization and retrieval.

The community’s trajectory moves from practical automatic extraction and heuristic ranking toward richer semantic and neural methods. Graph structure is increasingly used to model relatedness, tags, and relevance. At the same time, research emphasizes controllable retrieval and summarization, including privacy preservation and the mathematical relationship between relevance and diversity in ranked results.

abstracts x10|a0cd285a9bf3f4f3cb659ec461.text:
### Keyphrase Extraction, Indexing, and Diverse Summarization

This community focuses on extracting and organizing salient concepts from documents, especially scientific, medical, broadcast-news, and online-news collections. Keyphrases support summarization, indexing, retrieval, browsing, classification, clustering, and conceptual representations.

Typical methods combine candidate generation with statistical and linguistic features such as term frequency, inverse document frequency, phrase position, and lexical patterns. Kea uses supervised machine learning to rank candidates, while hybrid medical extraction combines feature weighting with additional extraction strategies. Neural networks offer another supervised approach for scientific articles. Other work improves extraction indirectly through text denoising, semantic relatedness, and Personalized PageRank-based reranking. Keyphrase clouds and conceptual models extend extraction to multimedia monitoring and user-facing news applications.

The community also addresses system-level concerns. Privacy-preserving multi-document summarization uses Secure Binary Embeddings to enable approximate comparisons without exposing document contents. Research on expected *n-call@k* formally analyzes the relevance–diversity trade-off in result sets. Scholarly communication systems integrate automatic keywording and reference extraction into large open-access repositories.

Recent trends emphasize enhancing existing extractors rather than seeking a universal method, incorporating semantic and neural techniques, adapting to specialized domains, and connecting extraction with privacy-aware summarization and practical information services.

abstracts x20|a0cd285a9bf3f4f3cb659ec461.text:
## Keyphrase-Centered Retrieval, Summarization, and Privacy

This community focuses on extracting, organizing, and exploiting semantic information from large text collections. Keyphrase extraction is central, supporting indexing, summarization, browsing, clustering, news monitoring, and popularity prediction. Methods range from lexical candidate generation and feature-based machine learning (Kea), to neural networks, hybrid weighting schemes, and semantic graph ranking with Personalized PageRank. Text Denoising is used to identify information-rich sentences and improve keyphrase indexing and biomedical information extraction.

A second theme is document and passage summarization. Hierarchical combinations of single-document summaries extend summarization to multiple documents, while formal analysis of expected *n*-call@k characterizes the relevance–diversity trade-off. Privacy-preserving summarization and important-passage retrieval use Secure Binary Embeddings to hash keyphrase and bag-of-words representations, enabling approximate comparison without exposing document content.

Applications include broadcast and online news conceptualization, hourly story-traffic prediction using social, content, and stylometric features, and scholarly repository services such as automatic keywording and reference extraction. Graph-based recommendation is also explored through FolkRank adaptations for social tagging.

Recent directions emphasize semantic enhancement of existing extractors, neural and hybrid models, graph-based ranking, denoised representations, secure retrieval, and integration of extracted concepts into operational news and scholarly systems.

titles<=300|f845db77dac51a70af9056a641bc.text:
## Differential Privacy for Accurate, Context-Aware Data Release

This community centers on balancing privacy and utility in data publication, querying, mining, and learning. A major theme is accurate release of histograms, datacubes, contingency tables, range and summation queries, including high-dimensional workloads. Methods include hierarchical and multidimensional decompositions (PrivTree, DPCube, spatial decompositions), wavelet transforms, matrix and low-rank mechanisms, convex optimization, consistency boosting, adaptive workload selection, and sparse-vector variants.

A second focus is privacy-preserving mining and analysis: decision trees, frequent itemsets and graph patterns, regression, data cleaning, recommendation, record linkage, and data-stream mining. Local differential privacy supports point-of-interest recommendations, smart-device data collection, marginal release, and range queries.

The papers also address structured and sensitive settings, including trajectories, mobility, continuous location services, temporal correlations, social-media links, provenance views, search logs, unstructured data, and enterprise information. Non-differential privacy approaches include anonymization, slicing, perturbation, and \(l\)-diversity.

Recent directions emphasize adversarial and auxiliary-information attacks, reconstruction and composition risks, worst-case background knowledge, semantic and policy-aware guarantees, fairness alongside privacy, and privacy preferences. The community increasingly studies end-to-end systems, principled evaluation (DPBench), economic selection of epsilon, Bayesian inference, and mechanisms tailored to correlated, spatial, temporal, and high-dimensional data.

abstracts x20|f845db77dac51a70af9056a641.text:
### Differential Privacy for Useful Data Release

This community centers on privacy-preserving data publishing, analysis, and mining, with differential privacy as the dominant framework. Major themes include private histograms and sparse data release, hierarchical and geographic group-size estimation, high-dimensional and range-query answering, clustering, classification, recommendation, and graph/provenance protection. Several papers also examine privacy attacks and limitations of anonymization, including reconstruction, algorithm-aware adversaries, and the inability to prevent inferences already supported by public information.

Typical methods add calibrated noise to counts, query answers, thresholds, wavelet coefficients, or hierarchical decompositions. Other approaches use private partitioning, wavelet transforms, randomized perturbation, local differential privacy, surrogate graph nodes and edges, and provenance views. Utility is evaluated through query error, predictive accuracy, clustering quality, and recommendation performance.

Recent directions emphasize making privacy more application- and workload-aware: HDMM optimizes high-dimensional query error, while data-adaptive range-query methods privately learn useful partitions. Local differential privacy is applied to marginal release and successive point-of-interest recommendation. The community also increasingly studies societal consequences, notably fairness in private resource allocation, alongside refined analyses of sparse-vector mechanisms and the distinction between aggregate utility and risky individual reconstruction.

abstracts x10|f845db77dac51a70af9056a641.text:
## Privacy-Preserving Data, Queries, and Analytics

This community focuses on releasing and analyzing sensitive structured data while balancing privacy and utility. A dominant theme is differential privacy for statistical publication and data mining, including sparse contingency data, hierarchical group-size estimates, high-dimensional predicate queries, clustering, decision trees, and location recommendation. Related work examines provenance privacy in repeated public/private workflows, graph-query protection, and the limitations of group-based anonymization such as \(k\)-anonymity, \(l\)-diversity, and \(t\)-closeness.

Typical methods add calibrated noise to counts, use hierarchical decompositions or wavelet transforms, and optimize error across query workloads. Other approaches construct protected graph views with surrogate nodes and edges, propagate provenance views to conceal private outputs, or apply local differential privacy to user check-ins while preserving movement transitions. The papers emphasize that naïve noise addition, synthetic data, and anonymization can substantially reduce utility or still permit privacy breaches.

Recent directions prioritize utility-aware and workload-aware mechanisms: adaptive hierarchical estimation, high-dimensional query optimization, privacy-preserving machine learning and clustering, and application-specific local privacy for recommendation. Overall, the community is moving from generic perturbation toward structured algorithms that exploit sparsity, hierarchy, graph structure, and query or behavioral patterns.

titles<=300|c81d537a2179b330a40b47c0d5c6.text:
### Schema.org Semantics, Validation, and Knowledge-Graph Infrastructure

This community focuses on making web content and services machine-readable through Schema.org annotations. Major themes include defining tourism-specific domains, enabling tourism providers to publish complete semantic descriptions, and building the Tyrolean tourism knowledge graph. Several works extend annotations beyond static data to machine-readable Web APIs, action annotations, and automatic action processing.

A second theme is ensuring annotation quality and interoperability. Proposed methods include domain-specific semantic validation, verification and validation procedures, heuristics for publishing dynamic content, and a formal SHACL-based approach for customizing Schema.org. Semantify It addresses the practical creation, publication, and distribution of annotations through a dedicated platform.

The community also considers infrastructure for storing and processing large semantic datasets. Studies compare NoSQL systems with traditional databases for big-data analytics, examine NewSQL for scalable OLTP, and simulate big-data models on graph databases for wireless multimedia sensor-network surveillance.

Overall, the research trends from schema definition and tourism annotation toward formal constraint-based validation, dynamic and action-oriented semantics, platform-supported annotation workflows, and scalable graph or distributed database backends.

titles<=300|6348b6d808a57b58d1164d521eb6.text:
## Networks, Scholarly Influence, and Bibliometric Retrieval

This community studies complex networks as instruments for understanding science, society, and information. Major themes include scholarly impact and reputation; coauthorship, citation, co-contributorship, and academic genealogy; community detection and research-field mapping; and Wikipedia-based analysis of cultures, universities, political leaders, geopolitics, and gender. A parallel focus is bibliometric-enhanced information retrieval, including query and term suggestion, thesaurus and terminology mapping, personalized and expert search, exploratory browsing, visualization, and evaluation of digital-library services.

Typical methods include PageRank and Google-matrix analysis, weighted and personalized variants, centrality, spectral analysis, random walks, Markov chains, graphons, stochastic block models, modularity, clustering, and link prediction. Researchers combine these with neural networks, temporal embeddings, LSTM models, learning-to-rank, semantic similarity, reduced Google matrices, and large-scale log analysis. Network construction and data quality—especially author-name disambiguation, identifiers, and citation coverage—are recurring methodological concerns.

Recent work trends toward dynamic and predictive analysis: forecasting emerging technologies, author success, citation counts, and community growth; modeling temporal knowledge flows and career trajectories; and identifying rising scholars and important patents. There is also increasing attention to fairness and social structure, including gender asymmetries, prestige-driven inequality, cultural boundaries, and biases in scholarly evaluation and online platforms.

abstracts x20|6348b6d808a57b58d1164d521e.text:
## Network Analytics for Knowledge, Science, and Information Retrieval

This community studies large-scale information and scholarly networks, with emphasis on understanding structure, influence, communities, and information flow. Major themes include Wikipedia hyperlink networks and their multilingual, longitudinal evolution; university and geopolitical relationships; author coauthorship and citation networks; and the organization of knowledge for search and the Semantic Web.

PageRank, weighted PageRank, CheiRank, reduced Google matrices, and spectral analysis are recurring methods for ranking institutions, authors, and countries, and for identifying network interactions and communities. Bibliometric studies also use DBLP, Web of Science, and ACM data to examine scientific careers, venue populations, brokerage, closure, productivity, and citation impact. Author-name disambiguation is addressed through the validated semi-automatic seed+expand methodology.

Information-retrieval work focuses on knowledge maps, discipline-specific query expansion, relevance-assessment reliability, and behavioral signals such as mouse fixations. Other methodological contributions assess the stability and continuity of centrality measures, develop graphons for modeling massive networks, and evaluate MapReduce Apriori performance on Hadoop.

Recent directions include richer temporal and multilingual Wikipedia datasets, cross-cultural university ranking, fine-grained network-flow analysis through reduced Google matrices, scalable network modeling, and broader visual or interdisciplinary scientometric surveys.

abstracts x10|6348b6d808a57b58d1164d521e.text:
### Network Analysis for Knowledge, Science, and Information Systems

This community studies large, evolving networks as instruments for understanding knowledge, scholarly influence, and social or geopolitical relationships. Major themes include longitudinal, multilingual Wikipedia link graphs; citation and co-citation networks; computer-science communities and careers; and knowledge maps for information retrieval.

Typical methods are graph-based ranking and structural analysis. PageRank and its variants are applied to authors, institutions, and academic reputation, with attention to damping-factor sensitivity. Centrality measures are evaluated formally for stability and continuity in weighted graphs, motivating alternatives to unstable betweenness centrality. Reduced Google matrices extract geopolitical relations from Wikipedia. DBLP data support comparisons of productivity, population stability, and conference communities. Other methodological work develops graphons as nonparametric models for estimating and designing algorithms for massive networks. Retrieval studies assess human judgments using Fleiss’ Kappa and Krippendorff’s Alpha.

Recent directions emphasize richer data and more robust evaluation: complete revision-level, multilingual network datasets; principled validation of centrality and relevance assessments; and scalable statistical models for dense and sparse networks. The papers also extend network analysis beyond ranking toward cognitive and semantic phenomena, such as first-author bias in citation labels and guided exploration through knowledge maps.

abstracts x10|c81d537a2179b330a40b47c0d5.text:
### Semantic Web Publishing and Scalable Data Management

This community focuses primarily on making web content machine-readable through Schema.org annotations. Key themes include domain-specific semantic validation, selecting appropriate tourism types and properties, publishing dynamic data efficiently, and improving the online visibility of tourism providers. Several works extend annotation beyond static content to Web APIs, services, and actions, enabling automated agents and intelligent personal assistants to consume and process information.

Typical methods include defining domain specifications and vocabulary subsets, mapping heterogeneous data sources to Schema.org, generating and deploying annotations, applying context-dependent publication heuristics, and storing annotated content in graph databases. The Tyrol tourism projects demonstrate an end-to-end ecosystem: data collection, annotation, public knowledge-graph publication, and application scenarios. The Semantify platform addresses annotation creation, vocabulary selection, and distribution.

A notable recent trend is moving from annotation for search-engine optimization toward operational semantic infrastructure: machine-readable APIs, automatic action processing, and scalable publication of dynamic data. The community also includes complementary surveys of NoSQL and NewSQL systems, emphasizing database technologies for big-data volume, variety, velocity, and scalable online transaction processing.

abstracts x20|c81d537a2179b330a40b47c0d5.text:
## Schema.org Annotation, Validation, and Knowledge Graphs

This community focuses primarily on making Schema.org data more usable, reliable, and actionable. Core themes include domain-specific semantic validation, selecting appropriate tourism types and properties, publishing dynamic content efficiently, and annotating Web APIs and actions so automated agents can consume services. Several works target tourism, especially building semantic visibility and a public knowledge graph for the Tyrol region.

Typical methods include defining domain specifications and constraints, applying SHACL operators to generate formal domain patterns, and verifying annotations for syntactic correctness, completeness, and consistency with Web-page content. Other approaches use context-dependent publication heuristics to control scalability, latency, server load, and information disclosure. Platforms and data pipelines support annotation creation, source mapping, graph storage, distribution, and automatic action processing.

A recent trend is moving beyond static markup intended for search engines toward machine-readable services, intelligent assistants, and automated task completion. The community also explores scalable graph-based data ecosystems and broader big-data infrastructure, including graph databases for sensor-surveillance simulation and comparisons of NoSQL and NewSQL systems for high-volume, heterogeneous data management.

titles<=300|94814d5b1bdc426732ec4559482e.text:
**Scholarly Search, Bibliometrics, and Online Knowledge Networks**

This community studies how scholarly information is discovered, indexed, ranked, and evaluated online. A central theme is comparative assessment of Google Scholar, Web of Science, Scopus, Microsoft Academic Search, ResearchGate, and library catalogs, focusing on coverage, citation counts, indexing speed, overlap, languages, highly cited documents, and journal or institutional rankings. Researchers also examine Google Scholar Metrics and h-index reliability, including manipulation through merging, false papers, and other practices.

Open access is another major focus: studies measure green and gold availability, repository deposits, mandate compliance, institutional indicators, self-archiving, and publication-cost concerns. Search-engine research addresses retrieval effectiveness, query expansion, snippets, featured results, navigational and multilingual queries, user effort, task complexity, commercial intent, and evaluation frameworks.

Typical methods include large-scale bibliometric and webometric data collection, citation and coverage comparisons, systematic and scoping reviews, exploratory analyses, rankings, network analysis, community detection, clustering, visualization, sequence analysis, and temporal studies. Wikipedia, ResearchGate, university–industry links, and online collaboration serve as settings for analyzing collective behavior and reputation.

Recent work emphasizes open-access monitoring, language-sensitive and longitudinal Google Scholar analyses, academic “invisible web” resources, manipulation risks, fair ranking, and the changing availability of scholarly search platforms.

abstracts x10|94814d5b1bdc426732ec455948.text:
### Scholarly Metrics, Networks, and Efficient Information Retrieval

This community centers on quantitative methods for evaluating and navigating scholarly information. Major themes include citation analysis and journal or institutional benchmarking; comparisons among Google Scholar, Web of Science, and Scopus; webometric mapping of science-park and research infrastructures; and network-based analysis of scientific collaboration and communities. Library-material ranking is treated as a complex information-retrieval problem requiring multiple ranking factors.

Typical methods combine bibliometrics, citation counts, h-index measures, longitudinal and cross-disciplinary comparisons, web link analysis, and social-network analysis. Studies construct collaboration or institutional interlinking networks from sources such as Yahoo!, Bing, SocSciBot, and ResearchGate, then apply modularity-based community detection. Other work uses large citation datasets and correlation analyses to assess the coverage and reliability of scholarly search engines. Information-retrieval studies apply learning-to-rank for selecting evaluation topics and examine trade-offs between deep and shallow relevance judging.

Recent trends include growing reliance on Google Scholar for broad citation coverage and identification of highly cited documents, alongside systematic scrutiny of database coverage and metric validity. Evaluation is also shifting toward more intelligent, lower-cost construction of IR test collections, while network analyses increasingly consider geographic, ethnic, and cross-sectoral factors in collaboration.

abstracts x10|fc4521b7c8f85a9316f06b68ba.text:
### Learning- and Systems-Driven Data Management

This community spans database optimization, approximate analytics, scalable transaction processing, and emerging distributed data platforms. A major theme is applying deep learning to database decisions: MSCN estimates cardinalities under predicate and join correlations, while Neo generates query execution plans by learning from existing optimizers. Deep generative models are also used to approximate aggregate queries for interactive exploration.

Another strand addresses data-intensive applications. Video monitoring queries use approximate filters over detected objects and spatial relationships to accelerate declarative video-stream processing. Main-memory OLTP research targets parallel execution and resilience: predictive modeling helps optimize distributed transactions, while TARS enables parallel recovery with reduced logging overhead.

Blockchain and distributed databases form a newer systems focus. Blocklite provides a lightweight single-node emulator for experimenting with blockchain designs, and a comparative “twin study” examines how blockchain and distributed-database design choices affect system behavior. More established application-oriented work includes SkyServer’s public scientific-data access and relational backends for finite element analysis.

Recent trends emphasize learned components in query processing, approximate answers for interactive workloads, multicore recovery, and accessible experimentation infrastructure for blockchain systems.

titles<=300|fc4521b7c8f85a9316f06b68ba9e.text:
## Learning-Centric, Scalable Data Management

This community studies how database systems can become more scalable, adaptive, predictable, and accessible across analytical, transactional, scientific, spatial, streaming, and blockchain workloads. A dominant theme is learned data management: deep learning, reinforcement learning, generative models, Bayesian networks, and mixture models are applied to cardinality and selectivity estimation, cost modeling, join ordering, query optimization, indexing, partitioning, buffer management, view materialization, approximate query processing, and workload re-optimization. Learned indexes and neural representations also support similarity, DNA, spatial, and visual search.

A second major theme is high-performance transaction processing, including multicore OLTP, MVCC and serializability, recovery and logging, replication, distributed transactions, high contention, and predictable latency. Stream processing, HTAP systems, in-memory and log-structured storage, and hardware-conscious execution address continuous and mixed workloads.

Scientific and geospatial data management appears prominently through astronomy archives, spatial indexes, sensor data, finite-element databases, open science, metadata stewardship, and large-scale search. Blockchain research examines blockchain databases, permissioned systems, verifiable queries, consensus, sharding, and database integration.

Recent directions emphasize end-to-end autonomic optimization, energy efficiency, resilient and highly available distributed systems, learned representations, and tighter integration of databases with machine learning, scientific workflows, and blockchain infrastructures.

abstracts x20|94814d5b1bdc426732ec455948.text:
### Scholarly Impact, Discovery, and Research Networks

This community centers on measuring and organizing scholarly communication. A major theme is comparative bibliometrics: Google Scholar, Web of Science, and Scopus are evaluated for citation coverage, highly cited-document identification, journal rankings, institutional benchmarking, and citation longevity. Studies examine Google Scholar’s broad coverage, metadata and version-management problems, ResearchGate visibility and scores, and the relationship between citations, institutional characteristics, and academic collaboration.

A second theme concerns information retrieval and library discovery. Researchers investigate ranking factors for library materials, search-engine technologies for online catalogs, and learning-to-rank methods for selecting topics and reducing the cost of IR test-collection evaluation, including the deep-versus-shallow judging trade-off.

Typical methods include large-scale citation and web-data collection, longitudinal and cross-database comparisons, correlation analysis, bibliometric indicators such as the h-index and cited half-life, link analysis, social-network and modularity-based community detection, and statistical/model-selection approaches. Case studies cover science parks, nursing journals, Portuguese research units, ResearchGate, Wikipedia, and open-access availability.

Recent trends include expanded use of Google Scholar and academic social networks, systematic measurement of open access, more sophisticated search and ranking methods, and growing attention to the reliability, coverage, fairness, and practical consequences of research metrics.

titles<=300|6eb717ebcc512c74b41d8be3a83d.text:
### Weighted Bibliometric Indices and Author-Credit Allocation

This community studies extensions of research-impact metrics and principled ways to distribute credit among multiple authors. A central theme is the development of weighted indices for evaluating research quality when authorship is shared, including generalized linear, polynomial, and generalized geometric weighting schemes. One work addresses resequencing as a way to conform credit assignments to established authorship conventions.

A second theme concerns the mathematical relationships among bibliometric measures. The papers derive bounds and inequalities connecting the h-index, g-index, e-index, and generalized impact factor, with the aim of improving existing models. Complementing this theoretical work, another study analyzes generalized impact factors and related indices at the journal level.

Typical methods are analytical: defining generalized weighting formulas, comparing alternative credit-sharing schemes, and proving bounds or inequalities among indices. Overall, the research trends toward increasingly flexible, generalized models that account for author order and collaboration while seeking more rigorous and interpretable measures of individual and journal research impact.

abstracts x20|fc4521b7c8f85a9316f06b68ba.text:
## Data Management at Scale, with Learning and Distribution

This community spans database systems for increasingly large, heterogeneous, and data-intensive workloads. Major themes include learned query processing—cardinality estimation, approximate query processing, and neural query optimization—as well as scalable OLTP, concurrency control, recovery, and high-contention execution. Distributed data management is examined through blockchain systems, blockchain–database integration, and foundational issues of distribution, heterogeneity, and autonomy.

Typical methods combine system design with empirical evaluation: deep neural and generative models learn data distributions or execution plans; query batching exploits shared I/O and cache access; predictive models guide transaction execution; and parallel recovery, MVCC conflict repair, and specialized concurrency mechanisms improve transactional performance. Approximate filters support interactive video queries, while relational backends, public data platforms, and lightweight blockchain emulators demonstrate practical deployments.

The papers also address scientific and organizational data infrastructure, including petabyte-scale astronomy, finite-element databases, Jupyter-based reproducibility, data stewardship, and integration across database and file silos. Recent directions emphasize replacing hand-tuned database components with learned models, supporting interactive analysis over multimedia and massive scientific data, and augmenting existing systems rather than replacing them—particularly by adding blockchain layers or common representations across heterogeneous sources.

abstracts x10|6eb717ebcc512c74b41d8be3a8.text:
### Weighted Bibliometrics and Authorship Credit

This community focuses on refining research-quality metrics for papers with multiple authors and on clarifying relationships among citation-based indicators. A central theme is credit allocation: proposed policies include equal, positional, resequenced, arithmetic (linearly increasing or decreasing), polynomial, and generalized geometric weights. These schemes acknowledge that authorship conventions vary across disciplines and research groups, allowing evaluators to select or reorder authors and weights accordingly.

The resulting weighted h-indices and weighted citation h-cuts extend conventional h-index evaluations by incorporating individual contributions. Other work derives bounds and inequalities connecting h-index, g-index, e-index, and generalized impact factor directly from their definitions, without continuous-model assumptions, and tests them using citation data from five Price Medalists. A related line analyzes relationships among journal impact factor, h-index, and g-index using a time-window-free generalized impact factor, equivalent to citations per paper.

Overall, the research progresses from fixed credit-sharing policies toward flexible, parameterized weighting schemes, while also broadening analysis from author-level metrics to theoretical metric relationships and journal-level evaluation.

abstracts x20|6eb717ebcc512c74b41d8be3a8.text:
## Bibliometric Indices and Credit Allocation in Multi-Author Research

This community studies quantitative evaluation of research quality, with particular emphasis on citation-based indices and fair credit allocation among multiple authors. Core topics include extensions and relationships among the h-index, g-index, e-index, citation h-cuts, impact factor, and generalized impact factor. One line of work derives bounds and inequalities directly from index definitions, without assuming continuous citation models, and tests them using citation data from Price Medalists. Another analyzes relationships among journal impact factor, h-index, and g-index under a generalized, unlimited-time-window impact factor.

A major recurring theme is assigning authorship credit when disciplinary and group conventions differ. Proposed approaches include positionally or equally weighted indices, resequencing authors or weights, and flexible policies chosen by evaluators. Weight schemes developed across the papers include linearly increasing or decreasing arithmetic weights and polynomial (generalized geometric) weights. These schemes are compared with existing alternatives and incorporated into weighted h-indices and citation h-cuts.

Overall, the research trends from analyzing established bibliometric relationships toward customizable, generalized, and convention-sensitive evaluation frameworks for both authors and journals.

titles<=300|7b9decd28a65805f74edbf28c780.text:
### Diversification, Clustering, and Relaxed Similarity Search

This community studies how to improve search and spatial-query results through clustering, diversification, and controlled query relaxation. A central theme is producing result sets that balance relevance with coverage or dissimilarity, including context-based diversification for XML keyword queries, diversity in k-nearest-neighbor results, and DISC diversification based on dissimilarity and coverage.

Typical methods organize results or candidate structures into clusters: **Klustree** clusters answer trees returned by keyword search on graphs, while spatial techniques use k-d trees for approximate nearest-neighbor clustering and identify interesting dense regions. Query expansion and relaxation provide complementary strategies for broadening retrieval, particularly when combined with clustered results or similarity search.

Overall, the work moves beyond returning individually relevant items toward managing the composition of the entire result set. The emerging direction is integrated retrieval: combining approximate spatial search, clustering, query expansion or relaxation, and explicit diversity objectives to expose multiple relevant regions, answers, or interpretations rather than redundant results.

abstracts x20|b969b105b37f5be2accde1c02b.text:
## Categorical and Algebraic Foundations for Data Integration

This community develops mathematical foundations for databases, schema mappings, and data integration. A central theme is **functorial data migration**: schemas are modeled as categories (often finitely presented by graphs and path equations), instances as set-valued functors or algebraic theories, and schema morphisms induce adjoint migration operations such as \(\Sigma\), \(\Delta\), and \(\Pi\), corresponding to canonical projections, unions, joins, and related queries.  

A complementary line develops a dedicated **database category (DB)** whose objects are relational instances and whose morphisms are complex query computations rather than functions. This supports denotational semantics for view-based mappings, GLAV/LAV/GAV integration, matching, merging, and federation. Monads generalize database values to lists, sets, and null-like exceptions, while sketches, simplicial sets, and operads provide graphical or compositional representations for schemas, tables, queries, recursion, and wiring diagrams.  

Recent work emphasizes practical and interoperable systems: equational formalisms, graphical IDEs, the open-source FQL/Categorical Query Language, and case studies in supply chains and computational science. Algebraic property graphs extend the approach toward enterprise graph, relational, streaming, and microservice data, suggesting a trend from abstract categorical semantics toward usable cross-model integration tools.

abstracts x10|b969b105b37f5be2accde1c02b.text:
**Categorical and Algebraic Foundations for Data Integration**

This community studies database schemas, instances, mappings, and migration through category theory, algebra, and monads. A central theme is **functorial data migration**: schemas are modeled as categories (often finitely presented by graphs and path equations), instances as set-valued functors or initial term algebras, and schema morphisms induce adjoint migration operations such as \(\Sigma\), \(\Delta\), and \(\Pi\). These operations provide categorical accounts of projections, unions, joins, and related queries.

A second theme is the semantics of **view-based data integration**. The database category \(DB\) replaces ordinary functions with morphisms representing complex query computations, supporting interpretations of LAV, GAV, and GLAV mappings. Sketches, separation, federation, and matching/merging are used to analyze schema mappings and the expressive structure of this category.

Typical methods include equational and multi-sorted algebra, categorical semantics, adjoint functors, monads and Kleisli constructions, sketches, and simplicial database representations. Monads also model generalized field values, including lists, sets, and null-like exceptions.

Recent directions emphasize executable and visual formalisms: graphical IDEs, computer-supported manipulation of simplicial database “tiles,” and relational foundations that make categorical migration practical and accessible.

titles<=300|b969b105b37f5be2accde1c02b2d.text:
### Categorical and Algebraic Foundations for Data Integration

This community develops categorical and algebraic foundations for databases, data integration, and migration. A central theme is **functorial data migration**, treated through purely equational formalisms, relational foundations, Kleisli database instances, and denotational semantics for view-based mappings. Complementary work studies **database mappings** using monads, coinduction, and the theory of sketches, while algebraic approaches address integration, matching, merging, and structural properties of database categories.

The papers also extend these foundations beyond conventional relational databases. They examine table manipulation in **simplicial databases**, formulate **algebraic property graphs**, and use an operad of wiring diagrams to describe graphical database languages, recursion, and plug-and-play circuits. Categorical data integration is further connected to computational science.

Typical methods include category-theoretic semantics, functors and monads, sketches, equational reasoning, relational models, Kleisli constructions, coinduction, and operadic formalisms. The collection’s trajectory moves from foundational theory toward unified semantic accounts and practical deployment, while broadening the scope from database mappings to structured, graphical, computational, and scientific data integration.

titles<=300|9eccb258d5467e528504b76ba0bd.text:
### Distance-Aware Community Detection and Network Intelligence

This community centers on community detection and modularity-based analysis in complex social and spatial networks. A major theme is extending standard modularity to incorporate geographic distance, enabling the discovery of spatially near or geographically dispersed communities and modeling distance-dependent network structure. Related work develops latent-parameter, node-centric models for spatial networks.

A second theme concerns the theory and computation of modularity optimization. The papers examine the hardness of maximizing both standard and bipartite modularity, additive-approximation algorithms, approximation limits, and broader algorithmic approaches to network clustering.

Applications emphasize extracting actionable structure from large social networks. These include identifying small seed sets for viral marketing, detecting violent criminal gang members at an early stage, and using social-network intelligence to combat street-gang violence. The analysis of political violence in North and West Africa further applies distance and diffusion concepts to study the permeability and spread of violence across borders.

Overall, the work trends from general modularity theory toward distance-aware formulations, scalable approximation methods, and operational applications in marketing, security, and political-violence analysis.

abstracts x10|7b9decd28a65805f74edbf28c7.text:
### Diverse Search and Spatial Exploration

This community centers on improving search and exploratory analysis by addressing ambiguity, redundancy, and incomplete results. For XML and graph data, keyword queries are diversified across contextual interpretations, while relationship queries return ranked answer trees that can be clustered. Query expansion similarly uses clusters of search results to expose alternative meanings, supporting ambiguous and exploratory queries.

A second major theme is spatial data organization and retrieval. Approximate k-nearest-neighbor clustering uses k-d trees, while diverse KNN aims to avoid homogeneous result sets. Related work combines query relaxation—adding relevant results when too few are found—with diversification, explicitly trading off similarity and variety through greedy and clustering-based algorithms.

Typical methods include feature selection, result or answer-tree clustering, distance-based similarity and dissimilarity measures, spatial indexing, preference-guided exploration, and heuristic approximation for NP-hard subset selection. Coverage is an important criterion: DisC diversity seeks mutually dissimilar representatives that collectively represent the original results.

Overall, the research trends from basic relevance and nearest-neighbor retrieval toward context-aware, cluster-based, interactive, and multi-objective retrieval, balancing relevance, coverage, result quantity, and diversity.

abstracts x20|7b9decd28a65805f74edbf28c7.text:
## Diversified Search and Exploratory Data Analysis

This community focuses on improving search and exploration when relevance alone produces ambiguous, redundant, or insufficient results. A central theme is **result diversification**: methods seek dissimilar answers that cover different query contexts, semantic interpretations, or data regions. This appears in XML keyword search, graph relationship queries, KNN retrieval, similarity search, and DisC diversity, which formalizes diversity through dissimilarity and coverage.

Typical methods combine **clustering**, **feature selection**, similarity or distance functions, and heuristic optimization. XML search derives candidates from selected features and diversifies them by context; graph search clusters ranked answer trees. Other work clusters search results to support query expansion, uses K-d trees for approximate k-nearest-neighbor spatial clustering, and explores dense spatial regions through analyst guidance. Diversified KNN and similarity search explicitly balance proximity, relevance, and dissimilarity, with relaxation used to increase result counts when necessary. DisC diversification additionally studies computational hardness and approximation heuristics.

Recent trends emphasize integrated objectives rather than isolated ranking: combining query relaxation with diversity, supporting exploratory and ambiguous queries, and ensuring both coverage and non-redundancy across heterogeneous structured and spatial data.

abstracts x10|9eccb258d5467e528504b76ba0.text:
## Spatially Aware Community Detection and Network Intelligence

This community centers on community structure in social and spatial networks, especially how geographic distance changes connectivity, modularity, and organizational interpretation. Several papers extend or adapt modularity: distance-aware null models, spatially-near modularity for geographically cohesive groups, and distance modularity for geographically dispersed organizations. A latent-parameter, node-centric model addresses the unknown cost of distance in spatial-network formation.

A second theme is computational theory. The papers establish that maximizing bipartite modularity is NP-hard and develop additive-approximation algorithms for modularity maximization, complementing practical community-mining methods.

Applications emphasize security and social influence. Studies analyze the spatial and temporal diffusion of political violence, identify violent gang members using modified centrality and arrest metadata, and support law-enforcement intelligence through ORCA, including membership estimation, influential-seed detection, and subgroup discovery. Viral-marketing work develops scalable methods for selecting small seed sets that trigger network-wide adoption under tipping models.

Overall, the research trends from generic topology-based communities toward distance-sensitive, spatially interpretable structures, while combining scalable algorithms, approximation guarantees, and operational applications in violence prevention and network influence.

abstracts x10|d085f91ca7ae0047202fe4d132.text:
### Information Identity and Linked Data in Cultural Heritage

This community examines how libraries, archives, and museums can define, preserve, model, and publish information in changing digital environments. A central theme is the identity of information objects: one paper proposes carrier- and encoding-independent criteria based on discrete arrangements of finite numbers, while a literature review surveys disagreement over which digital characteristics—“significant properties”—should be preserved and whether they can be formalized.

A second major theme is the transformation of bibliographic metadata into machine-processable Web data. Studies critique the limitations of Entity–Relationship modeling for FRBR, FRAD, and RDA, and explore RDF as a more flexible foundation for representing entities, attributes, and relationships. One implementation applies this approach to a repository of master’s theses and doctoral dissertations, treating library metadata as potentially valuable independently of the resources it describes.

Typical methods include ontological analysis, conceptual-model critique, literature review, standards-based modeling, and implementation proposals. The community’s recent direction is pragmatic adoption of Semantic Web and Linked Data principles in cultural heritage institutions, alongside renewed attention to identity, preservation criteria, catalog structures, and the practical complexity of Web architecture and semantics.

titles<=300|36fb71879175b52bb59c633c4665.text:
### Social Trust, Networks, and Marketplace Recommendation

This community studies how social relationships, trust, and location shape information diffusion and consumer decision-making in online marketplaces. Key themes include social commerce, recommendation of products and categories, price and trust transmission, consumer choice, classifieds, and the influence of friends versus the broader crowd. Several works examine users becoming sellers and the role of social connections in marketplace participation.

Typical methods combine computational modeling, empirical studies, and recommender-system design. Rumor dissemination is analyzed through a computational model with a convergence theorem. Trust-based recommendation uses collaborative filtering and regular equivalence to exploit weak ties and address cold-start users. Other work develops scalable social recommender engines and integrates online social-network and location-based data for marketplace recommendations. Empirical research investigates social shopping information passing and behavior on the Beidian social-commerce site.

Overall, the research trends toward integrating multiple social signals—friendship, weak ties, trust, crowd influence, and geographic context—into recommendation and marketplace systems. The community also moves from theoretical analysis of diffusion and trust toward scalable, applied systems for online shopping, social commerce, and classified listings.

abstracts x20|36fb71879175b52bb59c633c46.text:
### Social Commerce, Trust, and Influence in Online Marketplaces

This community studies how social relationships shape online commerce, including product and category recommendation, information exchange, consumer choice, and the emergence of social-commerce platforms. A central theme is integrating marketplace behavior with social-network, location-based, trust, and communication data to improve recommendations and address collaborative-filtering sparsity and cold-start problems.

Typical methods include empirical analysis of large-scale marketplace and transaction networks (notably Taobao), examination of triads and directed closure, user studies on Mechanical Turk, and measurement studies of strong-tie commerce platforms such as Beidian. Recommender-system approaches use explicit or implicit trust, collaborative filtering, weak ties, and regular equivalence. Computational modeling is also applied to rumor dissemination, relating social homogeneity, trust, desires, and convergence. System-oriented work presents scalable, service-based recommendation architectures and a deployed classifieds platform emphasizing privacy, security, usability, ranking, and communication.

Recent trends move beyond ratings alone toward multimodal social signals and integrated marketplace–social–location data. They also emphasize strong-tie commerce, friends as sellers, and nuanced social influence: crowd ratings may outweigh friend recommendations, while negative friend opinions can be especially powerful.

abstracts x10|36fb71879175b52bb59c633c46.text:
### Social Influence, Trust, and Recommendation in Online Marketplaces

This community studies how social relationships shape information diffusion, consumer choice, and recommendation in online commerce. Major themes include integrating marketplace, social-network, and location-based data to recommend products and categories; understanding trust, advice, and social influence in purchasing; and analyzing social commerce where friends become sellers.

Typical methods combine large-scale marketplace and interaction-network analysis, including triads and directed closure, with user studies examining friend recommendations versus aggregate ratings. Recommender-system research develops trust-based and social collaborative-filtering models, including regular-equivalence techniques to exploit weak ties and address sparsity and cold-start problems. Other work presents computational rumor-dissemination models with convergence theorems based on social homogeneity and individual desires. System-oriented research includes the design and deployment of a privacy- and security-conscious classifieds platform and a scalable, REST-based social recommendation engine.

Recent trends emphasize combining multiple data sources rather than relying solely on ratings, measuring the differing effects of friends and crowds, and building scalable social-commerce infrastructures. Overall, the papers move from modeling social trust and influence toward integrated, empirically evaluated recommendation and marketplace systems.

abstracts x20|d085f91ca7ae0047202fe4d132.text:
### From Information Objects to Linked Cultural Heritage Data

This community examines how libraries, archives, and museums can identify, describe, preserve, and publish digital information objects despite changes in carriers, encodings, and representations. A central theme is the definition of object identity and the “significant properties” that preservation should retain. The papers also explore the transition from conventional cataloging and entity-relationship models toward machine-processable Semantic Web data.

Typical methods include ontological analysis of information objects; literature review and conceptual comparison of positions on significant properties; critique of ER-based bibliographic modeling; and implementation-oriented modeling using RDF, FRBR, and FRAD. Proposed applications include repositories for theses and dissertations, redesigned catalog structures and visualizations, and linked data environments for cultural-heritage institutions.

Recent trends emphasize treating library metadata as autonomous, reusable data rather than merely descriptions attached to resources. RDF is presented as a flexible alternative or complement to traditional cataloging frameworks, supporting links among entities and broader Web publication. At the same time, practical adoption remains tied to unresolved questions about identity, representation, preservation requirements, Web architecture, and the philosophical foundations of describing cultural objects.

abstracts x20|9eccb258d5467e528504b76ba0.text:
### Distance-Aware Community Detection and Network Intelligence

This community centers on community structure in social and spatial networks, with modularity as the dominant framework. Several papers extend modularity by incorporating geographic distance into null models or objective functions, enabling detection of communities that are either spatially cohesive or geographically dispersed. A related line develops latent-parameter models for spatial networks, where unknown distance costs influence edge formation.

A strong theoretical theme concerns the limits of modularity optimization. Work establishes that maximizing bipartite modularity is NP-hard and studies additive approximation algorithms, approximation limits, and provable guarantees for network clustering.

Applications emphasize security and public safety. Spatial and temporal diffusion models analyze political violence across North and West Africa, while gang-focused systems use social-network structure, metadata, modified centrality, classification, subgroup decomposition, and tipping-model influence analysis to identify violent members, influential actors, and criminal ecosystems. Viral-marketing research similarly seeks small seed sets that trigger network-wide adoption.

Overall, the research trends from topology-only community detection toward distance-aware objectives, spatial generative modeling, scalable algorithms, and theoretically justified approximations, alongside practical intelligence tools for intervention and prediction.

titles<=300|d085f91ca7ae0047202fe4d132cd.text:
### Semantic Web Approaches to Cultural Heritage Metadata

This community examines how libraries, archives, and museums can represent, preserve, and connect information in the Semantic Web. Its main themes include identifying information objects through ontological approaches; determining what scholarly materials should be preserved; treating library metadata as data; modeling repositories of master’s theses and doctoral dissertations; and linking cultural-heritage resources across the Web.

Typical methods are conceptual and analytical rather than empirical: literature review, ontology-based identification, RDF and metadata modeling, pragmatic examination of linked-data practices, and critical reflection on catalog structures and visualizations. Particular attention is given to RDF literals, entities, names, and the organization of catalog information.

A central concern is the shift from metadata as a local cataloging product to metadata as interoperable Web data. Recent directions emphasize linked-data implementation in libraries, archives, and museums, alongside efforts to rethink traditional catalog structures and visual representations. The literature also highlights an unresolved preservation question—what exactly should be retained and how existing scholarship addresses it—suggesting a gap between broad semantic-web ambitions and well-defined preservation practices.

titles<=300|ea758b5f358d7574da678ab0e481.text:
## Inferring User Attributes and Health Signals from Social Media

This community focuses on extracting latent demographic and personal attributes from social-media behavior, especially Twitter and Facebook. Key targets include gender, age, broader demographics, and human traits. The papers examine signals such as whom Twitter users follow—including celebrities—alongside Facebook status updates and other publicly available social-media content.

Typical methods involve machine-learning prediction, probabilistic inference, and latent-attribute modeling. Following patterns are used to infer age and gender, while status language supports inference of human traits. Several papers evaluate how accurately machine-learning systems can predict user demographics and review the broader methodological landscape of latent-attribute inference from Twitter.

A complementary theme is sentiment analysis for public-health applications. Twitter data are used to assess vaccination sentiment and its implications for infectious-disease dynamics and control, as well as to identify sentiment surrounding HIV-related medication side effects. Overall, the research connects user-level profiling with population-level health monitoring: demographic inference supplies behavioral context, while social-media sentiment offers signals relevant to vaccination, treatment experiences, and health communication.

titles<=300|cb4f466125c060562fdb105d6303.text:
### Streaming Event Intelligence for IoT

This community focuses on processing, interpreting, and managing event streams produced by distributed sensors, RFID systems, and the Internet of Things. Its central themes include complex event processing (CEP), stream consistency over time, scalable data acquisition, and distributed inference and query processing.

Typical methods include the definition of CEP foundations and SASE-style stream query languages; event-pattern detection over continuous streams; load shedding to manage processing pressure; and distributed techniques for acquiring sensor data with guaranteed time coherence. RFID tracking and monitoring illustrate how inference and queries can be executed across distributed data sources, while a data-centric IoT perspective frames the organization and use of heterogeneous sensor information.

Across the papers, the research trends toward real-time, scalable, and distributed stream analytics. Increasing attention is given to preserving temporal consistency, adapting processing under limited resources, and integrating acquisition, inference, and event-query mechanisms. Overall, the community connects foundational event-processing models with practical requirements arising from large-scale sensor and IoT deployments.

abstracts x10|6398ac20043aefe02bf9586ca9.text:
## Network Science for Scholarly, Software, and Online Systems

This community applies complex-network analysis to understand structure, evolution, and quality across diverse information systems. Major themes include scholarly communication—citation databases, multidisciplinary knowledge structures, researcher–topic relatedness, and coauthorship evolution—as well as software architecture, websites, social networks, and information networks.

Typical methods combine large-scale crawling or bibliographic retrieval with graph construction, statistical topology analysis, centrality measures, community detection, longitudinal visualization, and sampling experiments. Studies assess degree distributions, small-world and assortative properties, influential users, and network-based indicators of software design, reusability, vulnerability, efficiency, and controllability. Generative modeling is also used, including citation-dynamics models that reproduce common network properties and disassortativity. Comparisons of DBLP and CiteSeer highlight the importance of data provenance and database limitations.

Recent trends emphasize web-derived and autonomously collected data rather than only curated publication databases; frameworks for exploring emerging multidisciplinary fields; and scalable analysis through network sampling. Sampling research increasingly evaluates how exploration, expansion, and subgraph induction alter community structure and network properties. Evolutionary studies further suggest that global brokerage, measured by betweenness centrality, can become more important than local degree in scientific collaboration growth.

abstracts x10|ea758b5f358d7574da678ab0e4.text:
## Inferring Demographics, Traits, and Health Attitudes from Social Media

This community studies how publicly available social-media data can reveal latent user attributes and population-level health behavior. Core targets include gender, age, political leaning, personality, religion, race, IQ, and life satisfaction, alongside vaccination sentiment and HIV-treatment side effects.

Typical methods combine linguistic and behavioral signals with network context. Researchers use usernames, followers, tweets, retweets, status updates, celebrity-following patterns, and neighborhood structure. Approaches range from heuristics and hand-rated sentiment to language models, LIWC-based features, probabilistic inference, and machine-learning classifiers. Several studies emphasize language-independent signals, interpretable models, and combining content with social-network features. Datasets range from 100,000-node networks to over 100,000 users, enabling analysis at scale.

Recent trends move beyond isolated demographic prediction toward richer, multi-trait inference and public-health applications. Social-media measures are increasingly evaluated against external indicators, such as CDC vaccination estimates, and used to study spatial and temporal health sentiment, infectious-disease dynamics, and medication experiences. Reviews and methodological assessments highlight both the value of missing-data imputation and the broad applicability of these techniques in demography, business, legal investigation, and health research.

abstracts x20|ea758b5f358d7574da678ab0e4.text:
### Inferring Latent Attributes and Health Behaviors from Social Media

This community studies how publicly observable social-media data can reveal otherwise missing user attributes and population-level behaviors. Major themes include gender, age, personality, political identity, and other demographic or psychological traits, alongside vaccination attitudes and HIV-treatment experiences.

Typical methods combine linguistic and behavioral signals with network information. Researchers use usernames, followers, retweets, tweets, status updates, celebrity-following patterns, and neighborhood structure. Approaches range from heuristics and interpretable language models to probabilistic inference, machine-learning classifiers, dictionary-based linguistic features (such as LIWC), sentiment analysis, and hand-rated annotations. Several studies emphasize language-independent features and the value of combining content with social-network signals. Large datasets are common, including samples of approximately 100,000 Fotolog nodes and 101,853 social-media users.

Recent work extends prediction beyond gender toward age and multiple human traits, while applying inference to public-health questions. Spatio-temporal vaccination sentiment is validated against CDC vaccination estimates, and Twitter analysis identifies HIV medication side effects and sentiment. Reviews and methodological assessments also highlight the broader promise—and demographic-data limitations—of social-media research.

abstracts x20|6398ac20043aefe02bf9586ca9.text:
## Network Science for Complex Socio-Technical Systems

This community applies complex-network analysis to software, scientific knowledge, social interaction, and web infrastructures. Central themes include structural properties of real-world networks—small-world organization, scale-free degree distributions, disassortativity, mixing, community structure, and temporal evolution—as well as their implications for influence, collaboration, software quality, and knowledge discovery.

Typical methods construct networks from class dependencies, hyperlinks, coauthorships, citations, keywords, entities, online interactions, or web-search visibility. Researchers use centrality measures, preferential-attachment and citation-dynamics models, community and group-detection algorithms, network sampling and simplification, crawling, bibliometric databases, and longitudinal analysis. Comparative evaluation is common, particularly for sampling strategies, citation databases, simplification techniques, and detection algorithms. Network-based indicators are also proposed for software vulnerability, reusability, controllability, and scientific impact.

Recent trends emphasize dynamic and predictive analysis: forecasting social status, modeling evolving collaboration and social networks, predicting emerging knowledge relations, and studying interdisciplinarity through researcher–topic networks. Other developments include entity-level metrics, context-aware data integration, and frameworks for exploring multidisciplinary knowledge structures. Across domains, the literature increasingly addresses incomplete, heterogeneous, rapidly changing data while seeking scalable methods that preserve meaningful network structure.

### Network Science for Scholarly, Software, and Social Systems

This community applies complex-network analysis to understand structure, evolution, and impact across research, software, websites, social networks, and healthcare collaboration. Major themes include community structure and group detection; interdisciplinarity and knowledge organization; citation and collaboration dynamics; software-network architecture; and the reliability and consistency of bibliographic databases.

Typical methods involve centrality measures—especially betweenness—preferential-attachment and evolutionary models, multilevel and longitudinal analysis, network sampling and simplification, and comparative evaluation of community-detection algorithms. Researchers also use web-search and citation-network data to characterize topics, researchers, and databases, while matching and merging frameworks support integration across heterogeneous sources. Entity-level impact metrics extend analysis beyond papers and authors.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes temporal and dynamic perspectives: evolving social and scientific collaboration networks, changing knowledge structures, and genealogical or knowledge-graph features for literature-discovery prediction. Other emerging directions include context-aware data integration, statistical comparison of citation topologies, evaluation of sampling effects on detected communities, and network-based analysis of healthcare collaboration. Overall, the papers move from static structural description toward robust, longitudinal, and application-oriented network intelligence.

abstracts x10|cb4f466125c060562fdb105d63.text:
### Complex Event Processing for IoT and Streaming Systems

This community centers on processing continuous, heterogeneous event streams from RFID devices, sensors, and enterprise systems. A primary theme is complex event processing (CEP): expressing, correlating, filtering, and transforming low-level observations into meaningful, actionable events. Related work seeks a unified model connecting event processing, data streams, and asynchronous messaging while accommodating different workloads and consistency requirements.

Typical methods include specialized CEP languages and engines, pattern detection over real-time streams, distributed stream query processing, and inference integrated with querying. SASE demonstrates stream-based complex pattern detection for RFID data, while distributed RFID systems combine location and containment inference with query processing. Other work addresses scalable sensor joins, network utilization, latency, and guaranteed time coherence despite heterogeneous synchronization mechanisms. Load-shedding techniques are considered for graceful degradation under resource constraints, recognizing that CEP’s pattern queries differ from classical stream processing.

A notable trend is movement from application-specific and ad-hoc CEP frameworks toward theoretical foundations, generalizable abstractions, and integrated architectures. At the same time, growing IoT deployments drive research toward distributed scalability, cross-organizational sensing, temporal coordination, and data-centric integration of physical and digital entities.

abstracts x20|cb4f466125c060562fdb105d63.text:
### Foundations and Scalability of Complex Event Processing

This community studies how to process, correlate, and interpret heterogeneous event streams in real time, particularly for RFID and Internet-of-Things (IoT) applications. Key themes include unifying event processing, data streams, and asynchronous messaging; detecting meaningful patterns from high-volume sensor data; and supporting consistency, time coherence, and distributed execution.

Typical methods combine specialized event query languages with stream-processing architectures. SASE develops complex pattern specifications and real-time transformation of RFID streams. Distributed RFID systems integrate location and containment inference with query processing, while SENSE addresses scalable joins across distributed sensors with differing synchronization mechanisms and guarantees time coherence. Other work investigates load shedding tailored to CEP workloads, recognizing that conventional stream-processing techniques do not directly apply. Foundational research seeks formal models for CEP to replace ad hoc, example-driven frameworks.

Recent trends move from centralized processing toward scalable, distributed IoT infrastructures, while emphasizing principled semantics, resource-aware degradation, and reliable temporal integration. The broader direction is toward event-driven enterprise and physical-world applications that convert raw, continuous observations into actionable information.

titles<=300|6aead1cadbe98a6fae31b0ca4dc4.text:
## Cross-Modal Retrieval, Hashing, and Music Semantics

This community focuses on learning shared or aligned representations across heterogeneous modalities, especially for cross-modal retrieval, semantic search, and recommendation. A dominant theme is efficient deep hashing: works study deep cross-modal hashing, supervised fusion, triplet-based objectives, decorrelated codes, adaptive hash-code ranking, joint cluster-unary loss, and unsupervised CycleGAN-based hashing. These methods target compact, discriminative, and scalable representations for multimodal and visual search.

A second theme is cross-modal representation learning through joint embeddings, shared semantic spaces, correlation alignment, and deep cross-modal correlation learning. Applications include semantic cross-media and event retrieval, as well as audio–lyrics retrieval.

Music understanding forms a related application cluster. Papers explore lyrics-based genre classification with hierarchical attention, self-attentive genre classification for transparent recommendation, and deep modeling of music semantics using EEG regularizers.

Typical methods combine deep neural networks with metric or ranking losses, correlation-based alignment, attention mechanisms, adversarial cycle learning, multimodal fusion, and neuro-informed regularization. Emerging directions emphasize more adaptive ranking, disentangled or decorrelated codes, unsupervised learning, interpretable recommendation, and richer semantic alignment between modalities.

abstracts x10|6aead1cadbe98a6fae31b0ca4d.text:
### Cross-Modal Retrieval, Hashing, and Music Semantics

This community centers on efficient cross-modal retrieval and multimodal representation learning, especially for large-scale image, text, audio, video, and lyrics data. A major theme is deep hashing: studies address quantization loss, correlated bits, relative similarity, multi-view information, and the computational cost of pairwise or triplet-based supervision. Methods include adaptive Hamming-distance ranking, unary and triplet losses, decorrelation objectives, and unsupervised coupled CycleGAN hashing.

A second theme is learning shared representations across heterogeneous modalities. Joint embeddings and deep correlation-learning architectures project modalities into common spaces, with particular attention to temporal alignment between audio, lyrics, and other sequential data.

Several papers apply attention-based neural models to music understanding and retrieval. Hierarchical attention models classify lyrics across genre levels, while self-attention supports interpretable lyric and acoustic feature discovery for recommendation. Another direction incorporates listener EEG signals with audio to model music semantics beyond explicit tags.

Overall, the work trends from conventional supervised hashing toward deep, scalable, and unsupervised methods, while increasingly exploiting temporal structure, attention for interpretability, and perceptual or complementary multimodal signals.

abstracts x10|56f5755a79caa1b3a10f93ea6c.text:
### Recommender Systems Under Cold-Start and Marketplace Constraints

This community focuses on large-scale recommendation and ranking in e-commerce and travel marketplaces. Core themes include matching users with items or accommodations, optimizing destination recommendations for user preferences, and addressing the severe lack of reliable interaction history for new, infrequent, or changing users and items.

Typical methods combine latent-factor recommendation models with content-based prediction: convolutional neural networks infer item representations from descriptions when interaction-derived factors are unavailable. Deep learning is also examined for candidate generation and cold-start recommendation, alongside broader taxonomies of neural recommender methods. Marketplace-oriented work frames recommendation as a two-sided matching problem, balancing guests’ search constraints and providers’ desire for reach and revenue. Evaluation includes large-scale online experiments against production systems and conventional offline baselines.

A major recent trend is moving beyond the traditional, one-time cold-start setting. The “continuous cold start” problem emphasizes recurring sparsity, volatile interests, infrequent visits, and multiple user personas, challenging systems that depend on stable personal histories. Consequently, research increasingly favors content, contextual, and population-level signals and practical online validation over reliance on collaborative filtering alone.

abstracts x20|56f5755a79caa1b3a10f93ea6c.text:
**Recommendation Under Sparse and Changing User Signals**

This community focuses on recommender systems for large-scale e-commerce and travel platforms, with particular emphasis on personalization, marketplace matching, candidate generation, and cold-start conditions. One theme is optimizing travel-destination rankings from user preferences and comparing algorithms not only with standard offline baselines, but also with a production system through large-scale online experiments. Another addresses two-sided marketplaces: matching guests with suitable accommodations while helping providers reach valuable audiences.

Cold-start research includes model-based latent-factor recommendation, where convolutional neural networks predict item factors from descriptions when interaction data are unavailable. A survey organizes the emerging use of deep learning for candidate generation and cold-start recommendation, reflecting the field’s movement beyond traditional collaborative filtering.
