Recent work broadens the classical new-user/new-item problem into **continuous cold start**: even known users and items may provide sparse, outdated, or noisy signals because users visit infrequently, change interests, or exhibit multiple personas. These studies investigate personalization when user history cannot be trusted, leveraging broader interaction data rather than relying solely on individual histories. Overall, the community trends toward content-aware deep models, marketplace-wide signals, and rigorous online evaluation in real production environments.

titles<=300|56f5755a79caa1b3a10f93ea6c2c.text:
### Matching, Recommendation, and Continuous Cold Start

This community focuses on improving recommender systems when user preferences, items, or interactions are sparse or constantly changing. Core applications include travel-destination optimization based on user preferences and e-commerce recommendations beyond traditional movie-focused settings.

A major theme is **cold start**, addressed at both the initial-item/user stage and as a **continuous cold start** problem in e-commerce. The papers emphasize model-based approaches and deep learning, including their use for item cold start and candidate generation. Another central theme is **learning to match**, suggesting methods that learn compatibility between users, preferences, items, or destinations.

The community combines methodological research with surveys and application-oriented studies. Typical methods include preference-based optimization, learned matching models, model-based recommendation, and deep-learning techniques for candidate generation and cold-start handling.

Recent trends move from static, domain-specific recommendation—especially movie recommendation—toward dynamic e-commerce environments in which new items and changing interactions repeatedly challenge the system. This reflects a broader shift toward scalable candidate generation and learning-based methods designed to maintain recommendation quality under persistent data sparsity.

abstracts x20|6aead1cadbe98a6fae31b0ca4d.text:
## Cross-Modal Retrieval, Hashing, and Music Semantics

This community centers on efficient semantic retrieval across heterogeneous modalities, especially image–text, audio–lyrics, video, and multimodal visual data. A major theme is cross-modal hashing, which compresses content into binary codes for low-storage, fast large-scale search. Studies address discriminative ranking, multimodal views, bit decorrelation, relative similarity, efficient unary objectives, fusion supervision, and unsupervised learning.

Typical methods include deep neural networks that jointly learn features and hash codes, triplet and pairwise objectives, cluster-unary losses, correlation alignment, shared semantic spaces, and explicit semantic projections. Generative approaches such as coupled CycleGANs support unsupervised hashing, while query-adaptive ranking improves retrieval over multiple views.

A second theme is learning cross-modal temporal and sequential structure. Joint embeddings and two-branch correlation networks align modalities such as audio and lyrics, moving beyond static similarity. Music-focused work also explores hierarchical attention for lyric genre classification, self-attention for interpretable lyric and acoustic features, and EEG-regularized audio models that incorporate listeners’ perceptual responses.

Overall, the research trends from handcrafted-feature hashing toward end-to-end deep representation learning, richer correlation modeling, reduced dependence on labels, and greater attention to temporal alignment, interpretability, and perceptually grounded music semantics.

titles<=300|55f97b67d1a2eb5c227fdf63f7a3.text:
### Web Tables, Data Lakes, and Open-Domain Question Answering

This community studies how to make web and organizational data searchable, navigable, and useful for question answering. Core themes include defining comparable and searchable information on the web, organizing data lakes, and supporting queries over web or document tables—even when schemas are absent or dependencies must be inferred.

Typical methods use keywords to identify columns, discover patterns in knowledge bases, and compose table-based answers. Other approaches address scale through locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) for internet-scale domain search, while organizational methods improve navigation through data lakes. Knowledge bases are also used for automatic table completion, and web tables serve as evidence for open-domain question answering.

The field’s apparent recent direction is toward integrated, scalable, and schema-flexible systems: moving from table retrieval and keyword-based querying toward richer answer composition, dependency-aware document-table queries, knowledge-base-assisted completion, and open-domain QA. Overall, the papers connect information retrieval, data management, knowledge bases, and question answering around structured information found on the web.

abstracts x10|55f97b67d1a2eb5c227fdf63f7.text:
## Structured Search and Discovery over Web Data

This community focuses on making heterogeneous web and enterprise data searchable, comparable, and navigable. A central theme is answering natural-language and keyword queries with tables, including list, superlative, factoid, non-factoid, and multi-column requests. Related work retrieves knowledge-graph patterns for composing table answers and automatically completes user-specified tables from example rows and column descriptions.

Typical methods combine textual and semantic matching with table- and column-level features, machine-learning or neural similarity models, and graph-based representations. Knowledge graphs, RDF/SPARQL, and database dependencies support querying schemaless document tables without extensive manual schema mapping. For large-scale domain search, locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) indexes sets using Jaccard containment, while data-lake navigation is modeled as an attribute-subset graph optimized for expected user discovery.

Recent trends emphasize moving beyond isolated fact lookup toward richer structured answers and table generation, integrating web tables with knowledge bases, and reducing schema engineering. The work also increasingly addresses scale and usability: internet-scale domain indexing, probabilistic optimization of navigation structures, and unified definitions of ordered, multidimensional domains for precise comparison and search.

titles<=300|fb9dc5072b7f8aa6c1611f725ef9.text:
### Semantic and Interactive Methods for Historical Information Access

This community explores semantic modeling and direct representation as ways to organize and represent complex information, including mechanisms and repository contents. Several papers examine challenges in using semantic models to accurately capture mechanisms, suggesting attention to the limits and design issues of representational systems.

A major application area is historical and archival research. One paper applies machine learning to quantitative prosopography, while another uses text mining and coordinated models to improve access to digitized historical newspapers. These works extend computational methods to the analysis and discovery of people, texts, and historical records. The development of an interactive directory for Norfolk, Nebraska, in 1899–1900 further illustrates a focus on geographically and temporally specific historical information.

Typical methods include semantic modeling, direct representation, machine learning, text mining, coordinated modeling, and formative user-interface design. Overall, the community trends toward combining structured knowledge representation with automated analysis and interactive interfaces, enabling more effective exploration of digitized historical materials while addressing how faithfully models capture the underlying subject matter.

abstracts x10|fb9dc5072b7f8aa6c1611f725e.text:
## Semantic Modeling for Knowledge-Rich Historical and Cultural Information

This community develops rich semantic representations for artifacts, activities, mechanisms, people, and historical documents. A central theme is moving beyond document-centered storage and simple keyword search toward model-oriented repositories that directly represent entities, relationships, instances, scenarios, and state changes.

Typical methods include ontology and object-oriented modeling, frame semantics, hierarchies of aggregates and mechanisms, and semantic frameworks potentially implemented in programming environments such as XFO. These approaches are illustrated through Korean ceramic water droppers, scientific mechanisms, and proposed Human Activities and Infrastructures Foundry ontologies.

A second major theme is computational support for historical research. Machine learning is used to construct people gazetteers for quantitative prosopography, while text mining and coordinated models support richer exploration of digitized newspapers. Formative user-interface design is used to improve access to collections and encourage exploratory investigation of events, communities, and urban life.

Recent directions emphasize interactive, structured historical directories that connect entities and newspaper mentions, and repositories organized around rich semantic models rather than documents. Overall, the work trends toward integrated representations that connect cultural objects, mechanisms, people, and textual evidence while enabling more meaningful browsing and analysis.

abstracts x20|55f97b67d1a2eb5c227fdf63f7.text:
### Structured Discovery and Question Answering over Web Data

This community studies how to make heterogeneous web and enterprise data searchable, navigable, and directly useful for answering questions. A central theme is exploiting HTML tables and knowledge graphs to answer list, superlative, factoid, non-factoid, and multi-entity queries, including queries specified by column keywords or desired table patterns. Related work addresses automatic table completion from natural-language descriptions, column names, and example rows.

Typical methods combine textual and structural signals: query–table matching, column and schema analysis, knowledge-graph pattern discovery, entity joins, and candidate ranking. Neural semantic-similarity models are combined with table-specific and dominance features to improve precision and coverage. Semantic technologies such as RDF/SPARQL and database dependencies support querying schemaless document tables with limited manual schema mapping.

Another major theme is data-lake organization and domain search. Navigation structures model attribute sets as graphs linked by subset relationships and optimize expected table discoverability. Probabilistic user models guide organization design, while locality-sensitive hashing enables internet-scale search using Jaccard set containment. More foundational work proposes globally defined, ordered, multidimensional domains for comparable and searchable information.

Recent directions emphasize integrated table-centric retrieval, automated synthesis and completion, scalable approximate search, and combining semantic learning with structured representations to handle diverse, redundant, and weakly schematized data.

abstracts x10|8b4f63acc51f40dde78918effa.text:
## Interactive Ranking and Search-Page Understanding

This community studies how search systems can rank, compose, and evaluate results using users’ implicit interactions. A central theme is online learning to rank under limited or nonstandard feedback: list-level feedback, pairwise preferences in dueling bandits, and interaction signals gathered through interleaving. Methods include policy-gradient learning, Thompson sampling for scalable ranker selection, and null-space gradient descent for more efficient exploration.

Several papers address the difficulty of interpreting behavior in image and web search. They construct interaction-behavior models for two-dimensional image layouts and investigate image-search intents, recognizing that clicks and browsing patterns vary with presentation and user goals. Beyond individual clicks, neural encoder–decoder models predict sequences of user interactions.

The community also expands ranking beyond a simple linear relevance order. Complex-ranking approaches jointly infer item relevance and preferred display positions, while context-aware module embedding selects heterogeneous aggregated-search modules based on blue-link results and query context. Evaluation increasingly incorporates clicks, satisfaction, and immediate SERP value, accounting for no-click interactions that may still indicate success.

Overall, recent work trends toward richer feedback, behavior-aware and sequence-based modeling, scalable online experimentation, and ranking systems that jointly optimize content selection, layout, and user experience.

abstracts x20|fb9dc5072b7f8aa6c1611f725e.text:
## Rich Semantic Models for Historical and Cultural Knowledge

This community explores replacing document-centered information systems with richly structured semantic representations of objects, activities, mechanisms, people, and historical events. A central theme is model-oriented organization: ontologies extend beyond static entities to include instances, state changes, scenarios, aggregates, and mechanisms. Object-oriented modeling, frame semantics, and the proposed Semantic Modeling Framework (SMF), including Transitionals and hierarchies of Aggregates and Mechanisms, provide typical design approaches.

Applications emphasize cultural heritage and historical research. Human Activities and Infrastructures Foundry (HAIF) ontologies model artifacts, production processes, and aesthetic differences. Quantitative prosopography applies machine learning to construct people gazetteers from heterogeneous biographical and documentary sources. Historical newspaper projects combine text mining, coordinated models, exploratory search, formative user-interface design, and entity linking. An interactive Norfolk directory illustrates structured summaries connecting people and places across years and newspaper mentions.

Recent directions favor repositories with direct, semantically rich representations rather than collections of isolated documents. They also emphasize interactive access, richer relationships, and integration of computational extraction with human-centered interfaces for exploring historical communities, events, and urban life.

abstracts x20|8b4f63acc51f40dde78918effa.text:
## User-Centered Learning and Evaluation for Complex Search

This community studies how search systems can rank, assemble, and evaluate results using implicit user feedback, especially in image search and heterogeneous SERPs. A major theme is online learning to rank under realistic feedback constraints: list-level feedback, pairwise preferences in dueling-bandit evaluation, and efficient exploration of gradient space. Methods include policy-gradient learning, merged double Thompson sampling, interleaved comparisons, and null-space gradient descent.

A second theme is modeling user behavior beyond individual clicks. Work develops image-search interaction models that account for sparse clicks, two-dimensional layouts, and domain-specific behavior; investigates image-search intents; and predicts sequences of user interactions with encoder–decoder neural networks. Evaluation increasingly incorporates clicks and satisfaction, recognizing that non-clicks may reflect successful interaction with SERP features rather than dissatisfaction.

The community also addresses ranking in complex presentation settings, jointly inferring item relevance and display preferences, and constructing aggregated SERPs from blue links and heterogeneous modules. Context-aware module embedding uses top-ranked blue links to identify suitable modules.

Overall, research trends move toward scalable online experimentation, richer behavioral signals, intent- and satisfaction-aware evaluation, and context-sensitive optimization of multifaceted search-result pages.

titles<=300|8b4f63acc51f40dde78918effaa3.text:
### Online Ranking and User-Centered Web Image Search

This community studies online learning and evaluation for web and image search ranking. Core themes include optimizing relevance and display preferences, understanding why users search for images, and modeling interaction behavior through clicks, click sequences, attention, and satisfaction. Several papers address ranking in complex presentation layouts and aggregated search, including context-aware module embedding learning.

Typical methods combine online learning-to-rank with implicit user feedback, especially list-level feedback and click behavior. Exploration and evaluation are addressed through efficient gradient-space exploration and merge double Thompson sampling for large-scale online ranker testing. Behavioral and evaluation models use click-sequence analysis and models incorporating attention and satisfaction, while interaction models characterize web image-search behavior.

Recent trends emphasize moving beyond static relevance ranking toward adaptive, user-centered search experiences. The work increasingly treats presentation layout, module selection, and display preferences as ranking objectives alongside relevance. It also reflects a shift toward scalable online experimentation and richer behavioral signals, using bandit-style evaluation, efficient exploration, and context-aware representations to connect ranking decisions with user satisfaction.

titles<=300|77ac22c0b415ee6031b2a881984e.text:
### Big-Data Benchmarking and Stream Analytics

This community focuses on evaluating and improving systems for large-scale data processing. A central theme is benchmark-suite design: **BigDataBench** develops workloads derived from Internet services and web search engines, while **BDGS** provides a scalable big-data generator for benchmarking. Together, these works emphasize representative, scalable data and workloads rather than isolated microbenchmarks.

Another major theme is distributed stream processing. Multiple studies benchmark distributed stream-processing engines and systems, indicating interest in comparative evaluation of throughput, scalability, and execution behavior for continuous data streams. **StreamBox** extends this focus to hardware and memory architecture by exploring stream analytics on high-bandwidth hybrid memory.

The typical methods are benchmark construction, synthetic-data generation, workload customization, and comparative system evaluation. The tool framework for tweaking features in synthetic datasets suggests a methodological trend toward configurable and controllable data generation, enabling benchmarks to reflect different application characteristics.

Overall, the community trends toward more realistic Internet- and web-search-oriented workloads, scalable and tunable synthetic datasets, systematic benchmarking of distributed stream systems, and hardware-aware stream analytics using high-bandwidth memory.

abstracts x10|77ac22c0b415ee6031b2a88198.text:
## Big-Data Benchmarking, Generation, and Stream Analytics

This community focuses on making big-data systems measurable, scalable, and representative. A central theme is benchmark and dataset construction: BDGS targets application-specific generation across the four Vs—volume, variety, velocity, and veracity—while a feature-tweaking framework scales empirical datasets and preserves their characteristics. BigDataBench develops diverse workloads from Internet services and web-search engines, addressing confidentiality through industrial collaboration and an incremental benchmarking approach.

A second theme is evaluating distributed stream-processing engines. Frameworks compare Apache Storm, Spark, and Flink, emphasizing throughput, latency, windowed operations, and detailed performance characteristics rather than simple workloads.

Typical methods include synthetic-data generation, feature specification or extraction, workload suites, controlled scaling, and experimental comparisons on representative applications. Systems are assessed using performance metrics such as throughput and latency.

Emerging directions include broader and more application-specific benchmarks, support for changing workloads and heterogeneous data, and closer attention to hardware–software co-design. StreamBox explores hybrid DDR4/HBM memory for stream analytics, adapting data placement and computation to HBM’s limited capacity and preference for sequential, highly parallel access.

abstracts x20|77ac22c0b415ee6031b2a88198.text:
### Big Data Benchmarking and Stream Analytics

This community focuses on building representative, scalable benchmarks and improving the performance evaluation of big-data and stream-processing systems. Key themes include generating application-specific synthetic datasets that satisfy the 4V requirements—volume, variety, velocity, and veracity—and scaling empirical datasets while preserving their important characteristics. Benchmark suites target diverse workloads, data types, and rapidly changing systems, with particular attention to Internet services and web search engines where real data may be confidential.

Typical methods include configurable data generators, feature-based dataset transformation and tweaking, and benchmark suites derived from industrial workloads or web-search scenarios. For stream analytics, experimental frameworks compare distributed stream-processing engines such as Apache Storm, Spark, and Flink, emphasizing throughput, latency, and windowed operations. Detailed evaluations characterize performance across differing workloads and system capabilities.

Recent trends include moving beyond system-specific generators toward broader, application-oriented benchmarking; supporting more diverse and realistic workloads; and addressing the growing demands of streaming analytics. Hardware-conscious optimization is also emerging, exemplified by StreamBox’s use of hybrid DDR4 DRAM and high-bandwidth memory, which requires techniques to manage HBM’s limited capacity and favorably exploit sequential access and parallelism.

titles<=300|c9431770fc0167c08dee44e2f0c8.text:
## Social Media Sensing for Food, Health, Cities, and Politics

This community examines how digital traces—especially Twitter content, hashtags, and geolocated or finely grounded posts—can reveal social, urban, and public-health phenomena. Its themes include the global presentation of food (“foodporn”), information sources and needs in obesity and diabetes discussions, urban robustness and resilience worldwide, road-traffic monitoring, and interpretation of political discourse during India’s 2019 Lok Sabha elections.

Typical methods involve large-scale collection and analysis of social-media posts, discourse and hashtag analysis, identification of information sources and needs, and fine-grained geographic grounding of tweets. These approaches support both descriptive studies of online conversations and practical sensing systems, such as traffic monitoring.

Across the papers, a recurring concern is avoiding overly simplistic interpretations: hashtags are not necessarily judgmental, and online health discourse must be understood through its information ecology. The work also reflects a shift toward using social media as a real-time or near-real-time sensor for infrastructure and cities, while maintaining a global comparative perspective on food cultures and urban resilience.

titles<=300|9c993c58637bed53516400728f7d.text:
## Social Media Geolocation, Polarization, and Disinformation

This community studies two linked problems: inferring location from social-media activity and understanding politically polarized or misleading information online. Geolocation work examines Twitter geotagging behavior and develops convolutional and hierarchical neural networks for predicting users’ locations. It also addresses recovering the order of locations in trails when temporal observations are sparse.

A second major theme is political information ecosystems in the United States. Studies analyze polarization, partisanship, and junk-news consumption during elections, including the concentration of polarizing content in swing states. Other work investigates disinformation targeting U.S. military personnel and veterans, as well as junk-news activity on Facebook beginning with the 2018 midterm elections. An aggregator-based approach supports systematic collection and examination of such content.

Typical methods combine large-scale empirical analysis of social-media data, neural-network prediction, platform-specific content aggregation, and behavioral analysis of users and social bots. Recent trends emphasize intelligent bots, links between user preferences and news-diversity exposure, and increasingly focused investigations of election-related and national-security disinformation across platforms.

abstracts x10|c9431770fc0167c08dee44e2f0.text:
## Social Media as a Lens on Society, Health, and Cities

This community studies how large-scale social-media data can reveal cultural practices, public-health discourse, political communication, and urban conditions. Research themes include global food imagery and its concentration around sugary desserts; information quality, sources, and user needs in obesity and diabetes discussions; Twitter hashtags during India’s 2019 Lok Sabha elections; and real-time road-traffic monitoring.

Typical methods are computational social-science analyses of millions of posts: hashtag- and content-based measurement, citation/source analysis, user-behavior analysis, and geographic inference from textual features. The traffic-monitoring work develops QT2S, a system for fine-grained geolocation of tweets, while the urban-resilience study addresses how to connect institutional resilience initiatives with academic measurement and construct a comparative index of cities worldwide.

Recent trends emphasize using social platforms as continuous, large-scale sensing infrastructures: moving from descriptive analysis toward operational monitoring, finer geographic grounding, and explicit quantification. Across domains, the papers also interrogate biases and limitations in online data—including dominant food preferences, information quality, and the lack of consensus over how complex social or urban phenomena should be measured.

abstracts x10|9c993c58637bed53516400728f.text:
**Social Media Geolocation, Mobility, and Political Information**

This community studies how social-media data can reveal location, movement, user behavior, and information ecosystems. One major theme is Twitter geolocation: convolutional neural networks combine tweet text with profile metadata, while hierarchical neural models predict country before city and use character-aware embeddings to handle noisy language. Complementary empirical work examines geotagging behavior at massive scale, testing assumptions behind mobility and public-opinion research.

A second theme is political communication and misinformation. Studies analyze junk-news consumption, polarization, partisanship, and geographic concentration around US elections, including activity involving Russian, WikiLeaks, extremist, conspiracy, and military-focused sources. Methods include source dictionaries, user-network and ideological analysis, self-reported locations, and large-scale platform data. A junk-news aggregator further emphasizes systematic monitoring and transparency, particularly on Facebook.

The papers also investigate interventions and data quality. A controlled Weibo experiment uses benign social bots to examine whether user preferences affect news diversity. More generally, the community addresses incomplete observational data through location inference and recovery of movement order when timestamps have low temporal resolution.

Recent work trends toward hierarchical and noise-robust neural prediction, very large behavioral datasets, cross-platform misinformation analysis, and experimental approaches to information diversity.

abstracts x20|c9431770fc0167c08dee44e2f0.text:
## Computational Social Sensing for Society and Cities

This community studies how social-media data can reveal population behavior, public discourse, and urban conditions. Research themes include food culture and potentially unhealthy consumption norms, obesity and diabetes information ecosystems, urban robustness and resilience, road-traffic monitoring, and political communication during India’s 2019 Lok Sabha elections.

Typical methods rely on large-scale collection and analysis of user-generated content: nearly 10 million Instagram posts, 1.5 million health-related tweets, and extensive election- and traffic-related Twitter data. Researchers analyze hashtags, shared content, cited information sources, user behavior, and information needs. Textual features support fine-grained geolocation for traffic monitoring, while comparative and empirical analyses identify global patterns in food imagery and political discussion. Urban-resilience work focuses on clarifying concepts and developing quantification or index-based approaches.

Recent trends emphasize social media as a continuous, geographically sensitive sensing infrastructure. Studies increasingly move beyond simple topic counts toward assessing information quality, user needs, spatial grounding, and societal consequences. Global comparisons reveal standardized patterns—such as the widespread prominence of chocolate and cake—while political and infrastructural applications demonstrate the value of hashtag- and text-centered monitoring for real-time or event-focused analysis.

abstracts x20|9c993c58637bed53516400728f.text:
### Social Media Geolocation, Information Disorder, and Behavioral Analysis

This community studies how social-media data can reveal location, mobility, political information flows, and user behavior. One major theme is Twitter geolocation: researchers combine tweet text with profile metadata in convolutional neural networks, while newer models exploit geographic hierarchy by predicting country before city and use character-aware embeddings to handle noisy text. Complementary empirical work examines geotagging behavior at massive scale, challenging assumptions about whether geotagged users represent broader populations.

A second theme concerns junk news, disinformation, polarization, and partisan information consumption. Studies use curated source dictionaries, user self-reported locations, network analysis, and measures of ideological distribution to investigate Twitter activity around US elections and among military personnel and veterans. Work on Facebook extends this agenda by developing a junk-news aggregator and emphasizing transparency in otherwise closed platforms.

Other methods include controlled experiments with benign social bots on Weibo to test how content preferences affect news diversity and polarization, and formal approaches to recovering movement order when trails have insufficient temporal resolution.

Recent trends move toward richer neural architectures, large-scale behavioral validation, cross-platform analysis, and event-focused monitoring of misinformation, while retaining geographic and network-based explanations of online activity.

titles<=300|769bc3643b42ae3a54b03834729f.text:
## High-Dimensional Similarity Search: Toward Efficient and Scalable Indexing

This community focuses on approximate and exact-enough similarity search in high-dimensional spaces, especially cosine similarity and approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) retrieval. A major theme is improving the efficiency–accuracy–scalability trade-off: one work examines drawbacks of existing state-of-the-art locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) techniques for real-time processing and proposes solutions, while another develops an index for high-dimensional cosine-threshold queries with optimality guarantees.

The papers emphasize index-based methods, including multi-index hashing for cosine similarity and graph-based ANN search. The “HD index” targets the boundary between scalability and accuracy, whereas the “satellite system graph” seeks higher efficiency for graph-based ANN search. Collectively, the methods span hashing, specialized high-dimensional indexes, and graph structures, addressing both threshold queries and nearest-neighbor retrieval.

Recent trends point toward increasingly engineered search structures that support real-time operation, stronger theoretical guarantees, and improved scalability without sacrificing retrieval accuracy. The community is also exploring complementary design directions—hash-based and graph-based indexing—to push the efficiency frontier of high-dimensional search.

abstracts x10|769bc3643b42ae3a54b0383472.text:
### Scalable Similarity Search in High-Dimensional Data

This community focuses on efficient nearest-neighbor and similarity search over massive, high-dimensional datasets, motivated by the curse of dimensionality and the computational and storage costs of exact methods. Applications include image retrieval, document retrieval, image search, and mass spectrometry.

Typical methods are approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes and compact representations. Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) supports sublinear query processing, while multi-index hashing maps data to binary codes to reduce storage complexity. Inverted indexes and adaptations of Fagin’s Threshold Algorithm target cosine-threshold queries with optimality guarantees. Tree-based methods also remain active, including HD-Index, which uses hierarchical RDB-trees built on Hilbert keys for approximate \(k\)-NN search. Graph-based approaches improve ANN traversal beyond sparse NSG structures through the Satellite System Graph.

Recent trends emphasize pushing the scalability–accuracy and efficiency boundaries: addressing real-time limitations of established LSH techniques, providing formal optimality guarantees for cosine search, and designing indexes that perform well on massive, high-dimensional databases. The work reflects a shift toward specialized indexing structures—hash-based, tree-based, and graph-based—balancing query speed, accuracy, and storage overhead.

abstracts x10|42aaecdb8840afd09793727668.text:
### Resilient Database Storage and Recovery

This community investigates database reliability and performance as storage technologies evolve beyond the traditional DRAM–disk model. A central theme is recovery from failures at finer granularity: single-page failures are characterized as a fourth failure class, motivating a page recovery index, while instant restore enables read/write access during media repair by restoring segments on demand.

Several papers redesign recovery mechanisms for speed and concurrency. Techniques include transactional logging, propagation control, fine-granularity locking, partial rollbacks, snapshot isolation, and REDO-only recovery, with persistent database state maintained in a committed form.

Another major theme is integrating non-volatile memory (NVM) into database storage hierarchies. Proposed systems use multi-tier management across DRAM, NVM, and storage, and develop persistent buffer pools that allow CPU-level page access while supporting recovery. These approaches challenge the conventional separation between memory and storage and the assumption that data must first be migrated to DRAM.

Overall, the recent trend is toward hardware-aware database architectures that combine persistent memory, optimistic consistency, on-demand restoration, and highly granular, concurrent recovery to reduce downtime and improve efficiency.

abstracts x20|769bc3643b42ae3a54b0383472.text:
## High-Dimensional Similarity Search: Indexing, Hashing, and Graphs

This community focuses on efficient nearest-neighbor and similarity search over large, high-dimensional vector databases, motivated by image retrieval, document retrieval, image search, and mass spectrometry. A central challenge is the curse of dimensionality, which limits tree-based structures and makes exact or linear-time search impractical.

Typical methods use approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexing and compact representations. Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) supports sublinear queries, while multi-index hashing maps data to binary codes to reduce storage and accelerate cosine similarity search. Inverted indexes and adaptations of Fagin’s Threshold Algorithm target cosine threshold queries with formal optimality guarantees. HD-Index introduces hierarchical RDB-trees built on Hilbert keys for approximate k-nearest-neighbor search.

Recent work increasingly explores graph-based ANN indices, including improvements over NSG through the Satellite System Graph, aiming to reduce search paths while preserving efficiency. Overall trends emphasize real-time processing, massive-scale deployment, the scalability–accuracy tradeoff, and stronger theoretical guarantees alongside performance on real datasets.

titles<=300|de563ef109b476befd9996352500.text:
### Utility-Oriented Sequential Pattern Mining

This community focuses on discovering valuable patterns in sequence data rather than relying solely on occurrence frequency. Core themes include high-utility episodes, high-utility occupancy patterns, correlated utility patterns, trend information, and utility mining across multidimensional or multiple sequences. Several works address realistic variation through item-specific or individualized minimum-utility thresholds, while another studies utility analytics on uncertain data.

Typical methods are utility-based pattern-mining frameworks, including projection-based mining for sequence data and approaches designed for complex sequences. The papers also explore parallel sequential pattern mining, indicating attention to scalability and distributed computation. Survey papers consolidate developments in utility-oriented mining, parallel sequential mining, and privacy-preserving utility mining.

Recent trends emphasize broadening the setting in which utility is measured: from standard sequences to complex, multidimensional, uncertain, and multiple sequences; from uniform thresholds to varied or personalized thresholds; and from isolated utility to correlation and trend analysis. Privacy preservation and computational efficiency also emerge as important concerns, suggesting a shift toward practical, scalable, and application-oriented utility discovery.

titles<=300|42aaecdb8840afd09793727668ea.text:
### Resilient Database Storage and Recovery

This community focuses on making database storage systems resilient, fast, and efficient across diverse failure modes and persistent-memory technologies. A central theme is broadening failure models: one work defines and recovers from single-page failures as a distinct, fourth class of database failure, while another addresses instant restoration after media failure.

The papers develop mechanisms spanning the buffer and storage stack. Multi-tier buffer management is explored for systems combining volatile and non-volatile memory, alongside persistent buffer management using optimistic consistency. Recovery research emphasizes fine-granularity locking and fast redo-only recovery, suggesting designs that reduce coordination and avoid unnecessary undo work.

Overall, the community trends toward minimizing recovery and restoration latency while preserving correctness. It combines failure-specific recovery procedures with storage-system redesign, persistent or non-volatile buffering, optimistic techniques, and more selective locking. Together, these approaches aim to provide database systems that continue operating efficiently despite localized page faults, media failures, and the complexities of heterogeneous persistent storage.

abstracts x20|42aaecdb8840afd09793727668.text:
### Database Recovery and Storage for NVM-Era Systems

This community investigates database reliability and storage management as hardware increasingly combines volatile memory, non-volatile memory (NVM), and large storage devices. A central theme is expanding recovery beyond traditional system, media, and transaction failures by identifying **single-page failures** and introducing a page recovery index for efficient repair.

Typical methods integrate transactional logging, propagation control, fine-granularity locking, partial rollbacks, snapshot isolation, and redo-only recovery. One approach keeps persistent database state committed, enabling recovery to run concurrently with new transactions. For media failures, instant restore provides read/write access during repair and restores individual segments on demand, improving availability.

Several papers redesign buffer management for NVM. Proposed architectures use multi-tier hierarchies spanning DRAM, NVM, and storage, while persistent buffer pools treat NVM simultaneously as memory and storage, with optimistic consistency.

Recent trends move away from rigid memory–storage boundaries and lengthy, system-wide restoration. The work emphasizes fine-grained, demand-driven recovery; reduced downtime; direct CPU access to persistent pages; and recovery mechanisms adapted to faster, heterogeneous storage.

abstracts x10|de563ef109b476befd99963525.text:
**Utility-Oriented Pattern Mining in Complex Data**

This community focuses on discovering patterns that are valuable rather than merely frequent. Its central themes include high-utility episodes and sequential patterns in complex, time-ordered event data, with applications such as retail, e-commerce recommendation, click-stream analysis, route planning, and consumer-behavior analysis. Other themes extend utility mining through occupancy, item-specific minimum utilities, recency and trend information, multidimensional sequences, privacy preservation, and parallel processing.

Typical methods develop specialized efficient mining algorithms, including projection-based approaches such as ProUM and utility mining for complex sequences such as UMEpi. These methods seek to reduce the time and memory costs of mining large sequence databases. The community also studies alternative interestingness criteria—utility, occupancy, risk, recency, and item-specific thresholds—to overcome limitations of frequency and uniform minimum-utility thresholds. Surveys organize progress in utility-oriented, privacy-preserving, and parallel sequential mining.

Recent trends move beyond static, frequency-based pattern discovery toward richer and more realistic settings: complex event sequences, temporal databases, recent/trending high-utility patterns, multidimensional behavior, privacy-aware analytics, and scalable parallel computation.

titles<=300|fbf968444e25f96e8f6ab7f971b8.text:
### Knowledge Compilation, Width, and Probabilistic Query Counting

This community studies the structural and computational foundations of model counting, with particular emphasis on probabilistic databases and query evaluation. A central theme is the relationship between knowledge-compilation classes, circuit structure, and width parameters. The papers investigate how structural width influences compilation, and how compilation classes can characterize or explain such width.

A second theme is the difficulty of exact model counting. Work on lower bounds examines inherent limitations and derives applications to probabilistic databases, while another paper highlights limitations of applying propositional methods directly to query expressions. These results also inform the study of the intensional-versus-extensional conjecture, including progress on a special case.

Typical methods include structural and width-based analysis, comparisons among knowledge-compilation classes, lower-bound arguments, and complexity-theoretic applications to database queries. The collection also explores circuit constructions, especially deterministic decomposable circuits for safe queries.

Overall, the recent direction moves beyond negative results and structural characterizations toward constructive compilation techniques, while continuing to connect database semantics, exact counting, and the expressive limitations of propositional representations.

abstracts x20|de563ef109b476befd99963525.text:
## Utility-Oriented Pattern Mining in Complex Sequential Data

This community focuses on moving beyond frequency-based pattern mining toward patterns judged by utility—such as profit, importance, risk, cost, weight, or occupancy. A central theme is discovering high-utility episodes and sequential patterns in complex, temporal, multidimensional, and multi-sequence data, with applications including marketing, recommendation, clickstreams, IoT, route planning, and consumer analysis.

Typical methods develop specialized utility-mining frameworks and efficient algorithms designed to address the high memory and computational costs of sequence analysis. Projection-based mining, utility-aware search, and threshold strategies are prominent. The work also extends mining to high-utility occupancy patterns, correlated item patterns, item-specific or individualized minimum utilities, and recent/trend utility patterns. Surveys synthesize utility-oriented mining, privacy-preserving utility mining, and parallel sequential pattern mining.

Recent trends emphasize realism and scalability: handling uncertain IoT data, temporal recency, heterogeneous item importance, correlations among products, and multiple sequences with non-uniform thresholds. Parallel processing and privacy preservation respond to growing data volumes and sensitivity, while these richer utility models aim to produce more actionable and current knowledge than conventional support-based approaches.

abstracts x10|fbf968444e25f96e8f6ab7f971.text:
### Knowledge Compilation and Probabilistic Query Inference

This community studies exact probabilistic inference for unions of conjunctive queries (UCQs) over tuple-independent databases, focusing on the relationship between extensional (query-structure-based) and intensional (lineage-compilation-based) approaches. A central theme is identifying when lineage can be represented in tractable deterministic and decomposable circuit classes.

Typical methods include weighted model counting, inclusion–exclusion, lineage construction, and compilation into decision-DNNFs, deterministic DNNFs, structured NNFs, and OBDDs. The work systematically connects these knowledge-compilation classes with circuit width measures such as treewidth and pathwidth, providing both upper and lower bounds on representation size. It also shows that decision-DNNFs can be transformed into equivalent free binary decision diagrams with quasipolynomial overhead, yielding lower-bound tools for exact model counting.

Recent trends emphasize the limitations of purely propositional or grounded inference for query expressions and seek stronger structural guarantees. In particular, new techniques construct deterministic decomposable circuits in polynomial time for classes of “safe” UCQs, contributing to the broader effort to clarify the intensional–extensional complexity relationship.

abstracts x20|fbf968444e25f96e8f6ab7f971.text:
## Knowledge Compilation for Probabilistic Query Inference

This community studies exact inference for unions of conjunctive queries (UCQs) over tuple-independent probabilistic databases. A central theme is the relationship between **extensional inference**, which exploits query structure directly, and **intensional inference**, which compiles query lineages into tractable Boolean representations before computing probabilities.

Typical methods include inclusion–exclusion, weighted model counting, and knowledge compilation into deterministic and decomposable circuit classes such as decision-DNNFs, d-DNNFs, structured NNFs, and OBDDs. Several works connect these representations to structural parameters—including circuit treewidth and pathwidth—providing upper and lower bounds for translating bounded-width circuits into structured forms. Other results establish limitations of propositional model-counting approaches and relate decision-DNNFs to free binary decision diagrams with quasipolynomial overhead.

Recent work trends toward systematic comparisons between compilation classes and width measures, as well as constructing deterministic decomposable circuits in polynomial time for classes of “safe” queries. Overall, the papers seek to clarify when lineage-based compilation can match or complement direct database evaluation, while identifying the structural and representation-theoretic barriers to efficient exact inference.

titles<=300|737fbc51b6c6264882a9b0599b18.text:
## Context-Aware and Geographical POI Recommendation

This community focuses on personalized point-of-interest (POI) and venue recommendation, especially modeling users’ contextual, geographical, temporal, social, and category preferences. A central theme is extending collaborative filtering beyond standard matrix factorization: studies explore metric factorization, logistic matrix factorization, and collaborative ranking formulations.

Typical methods jointly incorporate location and time, including time-sensitive regularization, geographical-temporal matrix factorization, and multiple location-based similarities. Personalized ranking is repeatedly used for context-aware venue suggestion, emphasizing the ordering of candidate POIs rather than only rating prediction. Other approaches enrich representations through local geographical modeling, category-aware location embeddings, and social-centric scores.

The papers indicate a trend from generic collaborative models toward increasingly structured and personalized representations of mobility behavior. Recent directions emphasize combining several signals—local geography, temporal dynamics, social information, contextual conditions, and semantic categories—within unified or multi-phase models. Embedding-based approaches and logistic objectives complement factorization and ranking methods, suggesting movement toward more flexible representations while retaining collaborative recommendation foundations.

abstracts x10|737fbc51b6c6264882a9b0599b.text:
## Personalized POI and Venue Recommendation

This community studies personalized recommendation of points of interest and venues, primarily in location-based social networks. Its central themes are overcoming sparse check-in data and modeling users’ preferences together with geographical, temporal, contextual, social, categorical, and textual information.

Typical methods include matrix-factorization variants—metric factorization, logistic matrix factorization, and joint geographical-temporal models—as well as collaborative ranking models. These approaches incorporate location similarity, physical distance, popularity and activity changes over time, and geographical influence. Other work uses probabilistic mappings between user tags and location taste keywords, dimensionality reduction, venue content and reviews, and social-centric relevance scores for user modeling. Context-aware methods explicitly predict the appropriateness of locations under particular circumstances.

Recent trends move beyond conventional dot-product factorization and exact venue-history matching. Models increasingly exploit auxiliary signals to alleviate sparsity, including local geography, temporal dynamics, contextual appropriateness, social information, and venue categories. Neural representation learning is also emerging through category-aware POI embeddings that combine sequential and categorical information. Overall, the community progresses from generic collaborative filtering toward richer, context-sensitive ranking and embedding-based recommendation.

abstracts x20|737fbc51b6c6264882a9b0599b.text:
### Geospatial, Context-Aware Recommendation for POIs and Venues

This community studies personalized recommendation of points of interest and venues, primarily in location-based social networks. A central theme is improving sparse check-in-based recommendation by incorporating geographical influence, temporal behavior, popularity, user activity, contextual appropriateness, venue content, reviews, social signals, and categorical information.

Typical methods include matrix factorization and logistic matrix factorization, extended with metric distances, local geographical effects, and joint geographical-temporal modeling. Collaborative ranking models combine learning-to-rank with collaborative filtering and use multiple location similarities or time-sensitive regularization. Other work develops probabilistic mappings between user tags and location taste keywords, scoring functions for context-aware ranking, and social-centric user representations.

Recent trends move beyond conventional dot-product factorization toward more expressive distance-based models and neural representation learning. Category-aware location embeddings combine sequential and categorical POI information, while temporal and contextual models seek to represent when and where geographical influence matters. Across the papers, auxiliary contextual and social information is consistently used to alleviate sparsity and produce more personalized, context-sensitive suggestions.

titles<=300|0d3a79df98eb93213d2469135041.text:
### Explainable and Empirical Text Classification for Legal Review

This community focuses primarily on machine-learning methods for legal document review, especially text classification and predictive coding. A major theme is explainability: one framework and a case study examine how predictive-coding systems can make classification decisions more interpretable. Complementary empirical studies evaluate deep learning and compare convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with other learning algorithms.

Another recurring theme is methodological evaluation. Research investigates how preprocessing parameters affect predictive-coding effectiveness, emphasizing the practical consequences of text preparation choices. Across the legal-review papers, typical methods include empirical experiments, algorithmic comparisons, deep-learning models, CNNs, and explainability frameworks.

The apparent recent trend is a shift from assessing predictive performance alone toward more transparent and practically reliable systems. This includes analyzing preprocessing sensitivity and developing explainable predictive coding for legal workflows. A distinct but related paper applies Google Analytics to cybersecurity forensics, suggesting an expansion from legal text classification toward analytics-supported investigative applications.

abstracts x20|0d3a79df98eb93213d24691350.text:
## Explainable and Empirical Analytics for Legal Review and Cybersecurity

This community focuses primarily on machine-learning-assisted legal document review, especially predictive coding for identifying relevant or privileged electronically stored information. A central theme is improving trust and usability: explainable text-classification frameworks and case studies aim to help attorneys understand model decisions rather than treating systems as “black boxes.”

Typical methods include Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, deep-learning models, and Convolutional Neural Networks. Studies compare these algorithms using data from actual legal reviews, including documents of varied lengths, and evaluate how preprocessing parameters affect predictive-coding effectiveness. The work emphasizes empirical testing against the practical demands of large-scale review, where reducing cost and human effort is important.

Recent trends move beyond reliance on a single algorithm or fixed preprocessing configuration toward systematic comparisons, parameter evaluation, and deep-learning approaches. Explainability is becoming an important complement to predictive performance, addressing professional acceptance in legal settings.

A related cybersecurity-forensics study broadens the community’s data-analytics perspective by using archived Google Analytics web-traffic information—such as visitor location, timestamps, pages, and search keywords—to monitor and evaluate potentially malicious cyber activity.

abstracts x10|0d3a79df98eb93213d24691350.text:
### Explainable and Empirical Text Classification for Legal Review

This community centers on predictive coding and machine-learning-based text classification for legal document review, motivated by the need to reduce the cost and labor of processing large electronic-discovery collections. A major theme is explainability: several papers address the “black box” perception of classification systems and develop explainable predictive-coding approaches to help attorneys understand model decisions.

Methods include empirical comparisons among Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, and Convolutional Neural Networks. Studies evaluate these techniques on real legal-review datasets, including documents of varied lengths rather than only short texts. Other work investigates how preprocessing parameters affect predictive-coding effectiveness, challenging workflows that rely on fixed preprocessing settings and a single algorithm.

A clear recent trend is the movement beyond traditional LR and SVM baselines toward deep learning, particularly CNNs, while retaining empirical evaluation against established methods. At the same time, explainability and practical legal usability remain central concerns.

A related but distinct paper applies Google Analytics data to cybersecurity forensics. It treats web-traffic records—including visitor locations, timestamps, visited pages, and search keywords—as a source for monitoring and evaluating malicious cyber activity, extending analytics-based data analysis beyond marketing applications.

titles<=300|31fef80ec123140cb71831d4b005.text:
**Networks, Narratives, and Cast Dynamics**

This community studies fictional narratives through social and conversational network analysis. Core themes include extracting character networks from text and television, measuring structural properties of narrative communities, and examining how networks evolve across plots. Several works focus on *Game of Thrones*, including studies of network balance and whether network properties can predict deaths (“kills”). Other papers investigate specific narrative structures, such as the clique formed by the six protagonists of *Friends*.

Typical methods include surveys of character-network extraction, comparisons of narrative social-network extraction techniques, and dynamic conversational-network modeling (“narrative smoothing”). The community also develops resources, notably the *Serial Speakers* dataset of television-series dialogue. Network analysis is complemented by ecological modeling, used to study effective cast sizes in films through *The Avengers*.

Overall, the research moves from extracting and validating narrative networks toward richer temporal, comparative, and predictive analyses. Recent directions emphasize dynamic interaction patterns, reusable datasets, structural prediction of plot events, and modeling cast composition beyond static character graphs.

abstracts x10|31fef80ec123140cb71831d4b0.text:
## Computational Analysis of Narrative Social Networks

This community studies fictional narratives as evolving social systems, representing characters as nodes and interactions, relationships, or killings as edges. Main applications include plot summarization, subplot and role detection, classification, recommendation, and analysis of character prominence, causality, and social structure in novels, films, and television series.

Typical methods include static and temporal network analysis, dynamic conversational networks, and comparative evaluation of manual, co-occurrence-based, and machine-learning extraction. Studies of *Friends* and *Game of Thrones* examine changing relationships, prominence, balance, and mortality patterns, while kill prediction combines network properties with metadata and link-prediction approaches. Narrative analysis is also supported by annotated resources such as the Serial Speakers dataset, covering 161 episodes from three serial dramas.

Recent directions emphasize moving beyond static networks toward temporally evolving plots and automated extraction, while improving empirical foundations through method comparisons and multimedia datasets. Other work introduces quantitative measures of effective cast size using Shannon entropy and movie similarity using Jensen–Shannon divergence, extending network-oriented narrative analysis toward characterization, taxonomy, and recommendation.

abstracts x20|31fef80ec123140cb71831d4b0.text:
## Network Analysis of Fictional Narratives

This community studies fictional works—especially TV series and films—by modeling characters as nodes and their interactions or other relationships as edges. Main goals include narrative summarization, subplot and role detection, classification, recommendation, and comparison with real-world social dynamics.

Typical methods involve social-network analysis of manually extracted, co-occurrence-based, or machine-learning-derived character networks. Researchers examine static and temporal structure, causality, centrality, cliques, changing roles, and interaction dynamics across episodes and seasons. Dynamic conversational networks support analysis of evolving plots and season summaries, while kill networks and prior-character metadata enable link-prediction experiments. Network properties are also used to investigate cast prominence and fictional-world structure.

Recent work emphasizes temporal modeling of long-running series, predictive analysis of narrative events, and reproducible resources. The *Serial Speakers* dataset provides annotated speech data from 161 episodes of *Breaking Bad*, *Game of Thrones*, and *House of Cards*. Methodological comparison has become important, particularly in assessing how extraction choices affect downstream conclusions. Another trend extends beyond interaction graphs: entropy- and Jensen–Shannon-based measures estimate effective cast size and similarity between movies, supporting classification and recommendation.

abstracts x10|69ac4d445a4e94f30a3bdb66fb.text:
## Approximate Similarity Search: Graphs, Hashing, and Evaluation

This community focuses on efficient approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) retrieval across high-dimensional, binary, complex, and non-metric data. A central theme is neighborhood-graph indexing: one work studies how to merge existing \(k\)-NN graphs, while another applies graph search directly to non-metric or asymmetric distances and investigates index-specific modified distances.

Hashing remains a major approach. Locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) is extended through hybrid methods for faster high-dimensional near-neighbor reporting, addressing sensitivity to data and query-dependent parameters. Angular multi-index hashing targets cosine-similarity search over binary codes, avoiding exhaustive comparison through structured bucket lookup.

The papers also emphasize practical deployment and evaluation. IDEL integrates neural entity linking into the MonetDB relational database using Python user-defined functions and machine-learning libraries. ANN-Benchmarks provides standardized interfaces, datasets, parameter testing, quality measures, and visualization for comparing in-memory ANN algorithms.

Recent trends include moving beyond fixed metric assumptions, combining or adapting indexes to data distributions, supporting specialized representations such as binary embeddings, integrating neural retrieval workflows into databases, and establishing systematic, reproducible benchmarking practices.

titles<=300|69ac4d445a4e94f30a3bdb66fb7a.text:
### Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search and Graph-Based Retrieval

This community focuses on efficient similarity search in high-dimensional, complex, and non-metric spaces, with applications including database entity linking. A central theme is the construction and exploitation of neighborhood structures: merging k-nearest-neighbor graphs and using neighborhood graphs to support accurate, fast retrieval beyond conventional metric assumptions.

Hashing is another major approach. Hybrid locality-sensitive hashing targets faster near-neighbor reporting in high-dimensional spaces, while angular multi-index hashing enables fast cosine-similarity search in binary space. These methods emphasize reducing search cost while preserving retrieval accuracy.

The papers also connect approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) techniques to practical machine-learning systems. Neural embeddings are applied to entity linking, suggesting a trend toward embedding-based database integration and semantic matching. Finally, ANN Benchmarks provides systematic evaluation infrastructure, reflecting increasing attention to reproducibility and comparative assessment.

Overall, the recent direction combines graph-based indexing, specialized hashing schemes, and neural representations, alongside stronger benchmarking for measuring speed and accuracy across diverse retrieval settings.

abstracts x20|69ac4d445a4e94f30a3bdb66fb.text:
## Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search and Graph-Based Retrieval

This community focuses on efficient similarity search and retrieval across high-dimensional, binary, complex, and database-integrated data. A central theme is approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexing: one work addresses merging existing \(k\)-NN graphs, while another uses neighborhood graphs to support non-metric and asymmetric distances without requiring potentially harmful metrization or symmetrization. Hashing is another major approach, including a hybrid locality-sensitive hashing method for robust \(r\)-near-neighbor reporting under varying local densities and angular multi-index hashing for fast cosine-similarity search over binary codes.

The papers employ graph construction and traversal, locality-sensitive hashing, multi-index hash tables, approximate distance computations, and neural embeddings integrated into the MonetDB relational database through Python user-defined functions. Evaluation and reproducibility are emphasized through ANN-Benchmarks, which standardizes interfaces, datasets, parameter sweeps, and quality measures for comparing in-memory ANN algorithms.

Recent trends include combining or adapting indexes rather than constructing them from scratch, designing methods for challenging non-metric data, integrating neural retrieval into database systems, and developing more systematic benchmarking practices.

abstracts x10|e706578d985b755b46530ef9d0.text:
### Distributed Representations for Sparse Text and Music

This community explores learned vector representations for sparse, sequential, and semantically complex data. A central theme is overcoming the limitations of word-overlap methods such as tf-idf for very short, noisy texts from Twitter, Facebook, and Wikipedia. Proposed approaches aggregate word embeddings with inverse document-frequency weighting and use a median-based loss to reduce the impact of outliers, enabling robust, transferable similarity estimation.

The same representation-learning perspective is applied to music. Skip-gram word2vec with negative sampling produces distributed embeddings for folksong motifs, which are compared using cosine similarity and evaluated through melodic-similarity tasks. In music recommendation, recurrent neural networks model user behavior across multiple time scales, addressing temporal consumption patterns and the lack of explicit ratings. Sequence-to-sequence models are also explored for representing and recommending playlists, extending embedding methods from individual items to ordered collections.

Overall, the papers reflect a trend from surface-level matching toward dense semantic representations learned from context. Recent work emphasizes domain-specific embeddings, sequence and temporal modeling, robust aggregation, and evaluations based on practical similarity or recommendation tasks.

titles<=300|e706578d985b755b46530ef9d0c6.text:
### Representation Learning for Short Text and Music Recommendation

This community focuses on learning useful representations for sparse, short, and sequential content. Two papers address very short texts, emphasizing semantic similarity and representation learning through weighted aggregation of word embeddings. A related line applies distributed vector representations to folksong motifs, suggesting that learned embeddings can capture recurring musical patterns.

The remaining work targets personalized music discovery and playlist recommendation. Methods include recurrent neural networks for large-scale user modeling, with listening preferences represented across multiple time scales, as well as representation exploration for recommending playlists. Across the papers, typical techniques are distributed embeddings, weighted word-vector composition, recurrent sequence modeling, and representation-based similarity or recommendation.

The apparent recent trend is toward neural representation learning that unifies semantic or musical content with user behavior. The research moves from comparing short textual units and encoding motifs toward scalable, temporally aware personalization for music discovery and playlist generation.

abstracts x20|e706578d985b755b46530ef9d0.text:
### Distributed Representations for Short Text and Music

This community focuses on learning semantic representations for sparse, sequential, and culturally structured data. One major theme is semantic similarity for very short texts, especially social-media messages, where limited word overlap makes tf-idf methods ineffective. Approaches aggregate distributed word embeddings, often weighting them with inverse document frequency; a median-based loss is used to reduce the influence of outlier words. These methods are evaluated on paired Wikipedia and Twitter data and aim to work without context-specific retraining.

A second theme is representation learning for music discovery and recommendation. Skip-gram Word2Vec with negative sampling represents folksong motifs, with cosine similarity and a melodic-similarity evaluation used to assess whether embeddings capture contextual variation. For modern streaming services, recurrent neural networks model user listening histories across multiple time scales, addressing temporal behavior and the lack of explicit ratings. Sequence-to-sequence models are also explored for representing and recommending playlists, extending embedding-based methods beyond individual tracks.

Overall, the work trends from surface-level word overlap toward reusable distributed representations, while increasingly modeling context, sequence, temporal dynamics, and domain-specific similarity.

titles<=300|3bbd4cb7f44888ca3e0b8ee4500c.text:
### Interactive Analytics, Provenance, and Scalable Visualization

This community focuses on making data exploration and visualization interactive, scalable, and explainable. Its themes include algorithms for provisioning queries and analytics, provenance tracking for interactive visualizations, transparent scaling, browser-based analytics, and fine-grained lineage.

Typical methods are systems- and algorithm-oriented: query and analytics provisioning, mechanisms for capturing and exposing provenance, transparent scaling techniques, in-browser execution, and fine-grained lineage tracking designed to operate at interactive speed. The papers emphasize integrating these capabilities into interactive workflows rather than treating analytics, visualization, and provenance as separate stages.

A notable trend is movement toward increasingly immediate and user-facing analysis. Earlier concerns with provisioning and scaling are complemented by approaches that bring computation into the browser and make lineage available at fine granularity without sacrificing responsiveness. Overall, the work aims to combine performance, interactivity, and transparency across the analytics pipeline.

abstracts x10|3bbd4cb7f44888ca3e0b8ee450.text:
## Interactive Analytics, Provenance, and Scalable Visualization

This community studies systems that make data exploration interactive despite expensive computation, large datasets, and complex workflows. A central theme is **provenance and lineage**: provenance can express visualization interactions and support extensions to visualization systems, while fine-grained lineage captures relationships between individual workflow inputs and outputs for debugging, auditing, explanations, cleaning, and interactive analysis.

Another theme is reducing or relocating computation costs. **Compact provisioning** constructs a polynomial-size sketch for \(k\) hypothetical database scenarios, enabling queries across all \(2^k\) combinations of activated hypotheticals. For visualization, transparent scaling aims to let developers write browser-based applications naturally while automatically using back-end services when local storage or processing becomes insufficient.

Typical methods include provenance-based representations of interactions, sketches for scenario reuse, lineage capture optimized for interactive queries, and compiled query execution. Afterburner demonstrates in-browser analytics through a JavaScript analytical RDBMS using typed arrays and asm.js, with performance comparable to native MonetDB on selected queries.

Recent trends emphasize interactive-speed fine-grained lineage, browser-native execution, and transparent scaling: systems increasingly seek to combine rich interaction with reusable computation and infrastructure that adapts between front-end and back-end resources.

titles<=300|37cbcf1d08f34a76ac65f128bc27.text:
### Funding Acknowledgements, Collaboration, and Evidence-Based Research Management

This community examines how funding and acknowledgement data can illuminate research systems. Several papers focus on funding acknowledgements in Web of Science, addressing their characterization, analytical uses, limitations, and updated coverage. A related humanities study emphasizes how acknowledgement analysis can make otherwise invisible contributions and support broader assessments of scholarly work.

A major theme is extending collaboration analysis beyond authorship: combining author and acknowledgement information is used to reveal collaboration patterns and the wider structure of research support. Typical methods include bibliometric and database-oriented analysis, acknowledgement mining, comparative interpretation across research contexts, and explicit discussion of query design and data caveats.

The community also includes a decision-support perspective on research and development management. A data-driven evidential reasoning rule is applied to multiple-criteria R&D project selection, connecting research information with structured evaluation and prioritization.

Recent trends point toward more systematic use of acknowledgement data, improved understanding of its coverage and analytical constraints, integration of multiple signals of collaboration, and data-driven approaches for managing and selecting research projects.

abstracts x10|37cbcf1d08f34a76ac65f128bc.text:
## Funding Acknowledgements, Scholarly Credit, and Evidence-Based Research Evaluation

This community examines funding acknowledgements and broader acknowledgement practices as underused sources of information about research support, collaboration, and credit. Several studies characterize Web of Science funding-acknowledgement (FA) data, documenting variation by citation index, year, language, document type, discipline, and acknowledgement type. They emphasize persistent coverage gaps and biases, while noting improved collection in humanities and social sciences.

Typical methods include large-scale bibliometric and distributional analyses of indexed records, comparisons across databases and disciplinary contexts, and conceptual examination of acknowledgements as part of scholarly reward structures. Combining authorship with acknowledged individuals provides a broader measure of collaboration and reduces apparent disciplinary differences in team size.

A related methodological strand applies data-driven evidential reasoning to research-and-development project selection: expert assessments extracted from historical datasets are weighted by reliability and combined to rank projects, illustrated through a Chinese National Natural Science Foundation case.

Recent trends include the rapid growth of FA-based studies, increased attention to previously invisible contributions, integration of authorship and acknowledgement data, and more cautious interpretation of Web of Science indicators given uneven coverage.

**Funding Acknowledgements, Scholarly Credit, and Evidence-Based R&D Selection**

This community examines acknowledgements as an expanding source of bibliometric and collaboration data, alongside conventional authorship and citation measures. Studies emphasize that FA data can illuminate funding impacts and otherwise invisible contributions, particularly in the humanities, while also revealing disciplinary differences in credit attribution and collaboration.

Typical methods include large-scale bibliometric analysis of WoS records, distributional comparisons, and combined analysis of authorship and acknowledged individuals to broaden measures of research collaboration. The papers repeatedly identify coverage gaps, update effects, and analytical biases, recommending cautious interpretation. A recent trend is improved FA collection, including in the humanities and social sciences, and increased use of acknowledgements to make support networks and contributions visible.

A related methodological contribution applies data-driven evidential reasoning to multi-criteria R&D project selection, weighting expert evidence by reliability and demonstrating the approach through a National Natural Science Foundation of China case study.

**Supporting Completeness and Participation in Collaborative Knowledge Bases**

This community studies methods for expanding, structuring, and improving collaborative knowledge repositories, especially Wikipedia and Wikidata. A central theme is **knowledge-gap detection and completion**: recommending articles missing from one Wikipedia language edition but present in another, completing movie entities across multiple online knowledge libraries, and identifying underrepresented or incomplete classes in Wikidata.

A second theme is **editor assistance and personalization**. Systems recommend useful sections for Wikipedia articles and elicit newcomers’ interests through automatically mined questionnaires, enabling recommendations for articles to edit and editors to collaborate with. These approaches aim both to improve content quality and to convert new users into sustained contributors.

Typical methods include end-to-end recommendation pipelines, importance-based ranking, cross-language and cross-library entity matching, section recommendation, and statistical, non-parametric estimation of class cardinalities and completeness. The work combines automated mining of existing knowledge with schema- or ontology-based analysis and user-oriented recommendations.

Overall, the papers indicate a trend from merely organizing existing content toward proactive, data-driven support: finding what is missing, estimating how incomplete knowledge is, recommending concrete creation or editing actions, and tailoring onboarding to individual interests across increasingly diverse knowledge sources.

titles<=300|cd736e039a525e1b13bf61c0237a.text:
