It also emphasizes higher-order dependencies, multilayer and partially aligned networks, signed relations, explainable and fairness-aware recommendation, privacy, robust anomaly detection, and scalable tools and benchmarks for massive graphs.

titles<=300|cd76ecd348824eaa6ef922d29f8b.text:
## Multilayer Social Networks and Information Diffusion

This community centers on modeling social interaction as multiplex, multilayer, and dynamic networks. Major themes include community and group evolution, influential-user and blogger identification, node similarity and link prediction, network alignment, profile matching, and analysis of online–offline identities and ties. Information diffusion is studied through viral campaigns, innovation, opinion propagation, competing processes, epidemics, immunization, and influence maximization.

Typical methods combine graph-theoretic measures—centrality, shortest paths, similarity, entropy, mutual information, and PageRank—with community detection methods such as Louvain, Infomap, GED, and clustering-based approaches. Researchers develop multilayer generative, epidemic, branching-process, agent-based, and robustness models, alongside sampling and estimation techniques for large networks. Machine learning and language modeling support sentiment analysis, spam and deception detection, topic discovery, social recommendations, profile linkage, and text-enhanced group analysis.

Recent directions emphasize cross-platform identity resolution, online/offline and social–physical network integration, dynamic and heterogeneous data, and large-scale synthetic or mobile-derived datasets. Applications increasingly address misinformation and fact-checking, disease containment, mental health, professional behavior, education, and organizational knowledge diffusion. Visual analytics and user-guided crawling also support practical exploration of complex multilayer networks.

titles<=300|e96a7e712d7f0a3f605991363836.text:
## Social Networks, Misinformation, and Adversarial Behavior

This community studies how information, opinions, and harmful behavior spread through online social networks. Major themes include misinformation, rumors, fake news, clickbait, conspiracy narratives, political polarization, controversy, extremism, hate speech, cyberbullying, and online abuse. A parallel focus examines bots, sockpuppets, Sybil accounts, spam, crowdturfing, like farms, purchased followers, phishing, and manipulation of political discussion. Privacy, discrimination in advertising, search bias, information diets, and social bubbles address broader risks to users and platforms.

Typical methods combine graph analysis with machine learning and natural-language processing. Researchers use community detection, matrix factorization, spectral and latent-space embeddings, motif and structural features, temporal analysis, sentiment and linguistic modeling, supervised and ensemble classifiers, and crowdsourced labeling. Diffusion, contagion, influence-maximization, opinion-dynamics, and game-theoretic models explain propagation and intervention. Temporal network analysis and cross-platform measurement are common, alongside practical systems for bot, vandalism, rumor, clickbait, and fake-news detection.

Recent work emphasizes coordinated social-bot and disinformation operations, authenticity of online discussions, ideological echo chambers, contrarian-content exposure, demographic inequalities, and the interaction between social context and content. It also increasingly combines network structure, user behavior, and textual evidence for more robust detection and intervention.

titles<=300|fb31a001b8ff3ac71a0dd49e1ea8.text:
## Information Retrieval: Neural Ranking, Semantics, and Dynamic Search

This community centers on information retrieval (IR), especially relevance ranking, ad hoc and session search, query reformulation, and search quality. Major themes include neural semantic matching; entity, relationship, and knowledge-based retrieval; query expansion and vocabulary-gap reduction; web-content quality and spam detection; document clustering and similarity search; and retrieval from social, news, scientific, biomedical, and e-commerce collections.

Typical methods combine learning-to-rank, rank aggregation, probabilistic and term-based weighting, proximity and discourse features, graph and bipartite modeling, and multi-stage retrieval architectures. Neural approaches use word and entity embeddings, convolutional and recurrent networks, kernel pooling, MatchPyramid/PACRR-style interaction models, attention, reinforcement learning, generative models, and weak supervision. Knowledge resources such as Wikipedia, WordNet, knowledge graphs, entity links, and formula representations support semantic enrichment. Hashing, sketches, indexing structures, and searchable encryption address scale and privacy.

Evaluation is prominent, including LETOR datasets, ranking metrics, online interleaving and dueling-bandit methods, credibility/factuality assessment, and clustering baselines. Applications include event and microblog retrieval, exploratory and archive search, recommendations, question answering, expertise search, and vaccination or financial forecasting.

Recent directions emphasize end-to-end deep ranking, hybrid lexical–neural and temporal models, knowledge-aware representations, personalized and explainable retrieval, privacy-preserving model sharing, and efficient online evaluation.

titles<=300|90c4464d182125b9730a066f2d4e.text:
## Temporal Web Preservation and Semantic Scholarly Infrastructure

This community studies how web resources, digital objects, and scientific knowledge can remain discoverable, interpretable, and reusable as they change or disappear. Major themes include temporal web archiving and “time travel” through Memento, archive coverage and freshness, web-resource persistence, timestamping, synchronization, and recovery of missing pages. A second theme is digital-library and repository architecture, including Fedora, aDORe, NSDL, OAI-PMH, ResourceSync, persistent identifiers, format migration, and preservation policies.

The papers also develop semantic infrastructure for scholarly communication: linked open data, nanopublications, micropublications, provenance and versioning ontologies, contextualized claims, annotations, SharedCanvas, and interoperable aggregation systems. Web and scholarly data quality, schema matching, URI canonicalization, and orphan discovery are recurring concerns.

Typical methods combine focused and two-tier crawling, archive graph analysis, temporal queries, simulations, cache and policy evaluation, metadata aggregation, and structural/content extraction. Machine learning supports title- and image-based rediscovery, event detection, learning-to-rank, and breaking-news analysis; social links and Wikipedia activity provide contextual signals.

Recent work trends toward scalable archive access and extraction, event- and topic-focused collections, multimedia and manuscript annotation, human-assisted preservation, decentralized publication, persistent annotations, and long-term preservation of evolving linked data.

titles<=300|565178e5988d91800bae2f6d9b29.text:
**Scalable Data Management, Analytics, and Learning**

This community focuses on building scalable systems for querying, processing, and learning from large, heterogeneous, and evolving datasets. A central theme is query processing: worst-case-optimal, multiway, theta, spatial, similarity, and graph joins; conjunctive-query complexity, functional dependencies, inequalities, containment, and hypertree decompositions; and cost-based, adaptive, multi-query, and distributed optimization. Parallel execution emphasizes MapReduce, dataflow, shared-nothing and heterogeneous hardware, communication costs, skew handling, elasticity, and high-speed networks.

Graph data receives extensive attention, including graph databases, temporal and uncertain graphs, subgraph matching, graph streams, dynamic queries, pattern search, graph compression, and large-scale graph analytics. Systems also address arrays, time series, RDF, evolving data, provenance, versioning, and incremental or higher-order view maintenance.

Typical methods include factorized and compressed representations, sampling and approximate answers with guarantees, adaptive indexing and cracking, sketches, algebraic rewrites, static analysis, code generation, and probabilistic models. Machine learning is increasingly integrated into databases for feature engineering, relational learning, anomaly detection, data cleaning, recommendations, and in-database analytics.

Recent trends include interactive and progressive exploration, visual-query systems, lifecycle and dataset management, coordination-free or lock-avoiding consistency, privacy-preserving cloud analytics, multi-tenant resource sharing, and specialized engines combining relational, graph, array, streaming, and machine-learning workloads.

titles<=300|10c6220047316b19efb3628bbc48.text:
## Network Dynamics, Influence, and Scalable Graph Analysis

This community studies how structure, interaction, and information shape behavior in social and general networks. Major themes include opinion and belief evolution—especially polarization, consensus, disagreement, bounded confidence, homophily, susceptibility, trust/mistrust, and signed-network balance—as well as influence, social power, dominance, and community identity. A parallel focus is network measurement: centrality axioms and indices, betweenness, accessibility, criticality, backbone discovery, node impact, and knowledge segregation.

Typical methods combine dynamical-systems and Markov models with random walks, shortest-path and current-flow formulations, matrix factorization, spectral analysis, threshold models, and graph-theoretic inference. Optimization and control are prominent, including edge recommendation, node or relationship removal, epidemic mitigation, diffusion control, PageRank maximization, tagging, filtering, navigation improvement, and network design. Sampling, greedy methods, approximation algorithms, and genetic algorithms support difficult large-scale problems.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and signed networks, state-flipping and relative-interaction models, scalable billion-edge random-walk computation, fast top-\(k\) and restart algorithms, and guarantees for approximate methods. The papers also increasingly connect theory with observed traffic and social-media behavior through crawling, active sensing, system identification, recommender systems, and models of topic-specific online activity.

titles<=300|cd82617b4c010ecced4eabf438c8.text:
## Data Integration, Entity Resolution, and Human–Machine Data Quality

This community focuses on integrating heterogeneous, noisy, and conflicting data. Major themes include entity resolution and consolidation, record linkage, data fusion and truth discovery, linked/open/deep-web extraction, and knowledge integration. Closely related work studies data quality, anomaly detection, deduplication, matching dependencies, functional and differential dependencies, order dependencies, data exchange, and query answering.

Typical methods combine probabilistic and Bayesian models, source-reliability and trust estimation, graph matching, global constraints, Datalog, matching functions, and learned or unsupervised string transformations. Scalability is central: blocking, locality-sensitive hashing, inverted indexes, bitmap filters, embeddings, partitioning, parallel databases, GPU processing, and distributed systems support similarity joins and million-scale matching.

Crowdsourcing is used for labeling, conflict resolution, entity matching, data cleaning, truth assessment, query execution, and spatial task assignment. Research addresses worker reliability, adaptive question selection, jury formation, reproducibility, latency, incentives, and human–machine cooperation.

Recent directions emphasize holistic probabilistic repair, deep learning, transfer learning, active learning, collective and multi-source matching, contextual anomaly detection, and unified multi-model data management. The field increasingly combines automated inference with selective human intervention to improve reliability, coverage, and scalability.

titles<=300|8eb5a0b1170e81aafb23f65053bb.text:
## Collaborative Knowledge, Search, and Social Web Structures

This community studies how people collectively create, organize, search, and reuse knowledge on the Web. Major themes include Wikipedia and Wiktionary as multilingual knowledge sources; folksonomies, tagging behavior, vocabulary growth, tag hierarchies, and collaborative thesauri; and the evolution of classification systems such as UDC. A second focus is social and collaborative search, including expertise location, professional-network talent search, personalized and federated retrieval, preference prediction, and collaborative information seeking. Entity ranking, disambiguation, ontology matching, related-term search, and semantic coverage connect these systems to structured knowledge representation.

Typical methods combine information retrieval evaluation, clickstream and user-behavior analysis, learning-to-rank, graph and complex-network analysis, PageRank-like ranking, clustering, and power-law modeling. Systems work includes relational, XML, and native database indexing; SPARQL-accessible lexical resources; faceted classification; and interfaces for visual exploration.

Recent directions emphasize multilingual entity linking and global ranking, large-scale expert discovery, personalization, social attention and influence analysis, dynamic tagging communities, microblogging behavior during events, and integrating user-created communities and archives into search and discovery.

titles<=300|ed06e762afeaae7ecd925087dd01.text:
## Database Answers Under Uncertainty, Inconsistency, and Provenance

This community studies how databases can answer, explain, and repair queries when information is uncertain, incomplete, inconsistent, probabilistic, distributed, or semantically rich. Major themes include probabilistic databases and ranking; provenance, lineage, and workflow reproducibility; causality, responsibility, diagnosis, and view updates; consistent query answering and data repair; integrity constraints and data exchange; ontology-mediated and graph queries; and incomplete information, nulls, and schema mappings.

Typical methods are complexity and dichotomy analyses, reductions, chase and finite-controllability techniques, Datalog and disjunctive-Datalog rewriting, knowledge compilation, provenance circuits and graphs, BDDs, tree automata, belief propagation, Markov logic, abductive diagnosis, answer-set programming, and repair programs. Systems and algorithms target scalable uncertain-data processing, top-*k* ranking, similarity search, stream processing, MapReduce debugging, RDF and XML querying, and scientific workflow management.

Recent directions emphasize practical scalability and integration: approximate lifted inference over relational systems, read-once and dissociation-based evaluation, dynamic and cloud-aware provenance, probabilistic alignment and crowd data, causal inference from observational and multidimensional data, ontology-based access using expressive formalisms, and management of scientific hypotheses as uncertain data with predictive analytics. The papers also push toward explanatory interfaces, privacy via secrecy views, completeness assessment, and unified treatments connecting causality, repairs, provenance, and integrity maintenance.

titles<=300|885e9d95ce7c5f762fa724540e2d.text:
## Efficient Search, Ranking, and Analytics over Large Data

This community studies scalable data access, emphasizing fast indexing, compression, and query processing. A major theme is bitmap and integer-index engineering: Roaring bitmaps, word-aligned and difference coding, SIMD/vectorized decoding, hashing, wavelet histograms, and column/row reordering support high-throughput relational and multidimensional analytics. Related work targets in-memory SQL, OLAP, graph and relationship analytics, skyline and aggregate queries, sliding-window monitoring, cohort queries, and view-size estimation.

Another central theme is ranked and preference-aware retrieval. Papers address top-*k*, nearest-neighbor, similarity, skyline and skyline-join queries, result diversification, preference elicitation and revision, fuzzy summaries, and semantic optimization. Methods include probabilistic estimation, sketches, game-theoretic and signaling models, LP anonymization, embeddings and word mover’s distance, density-based clustering, and adaptive distributed processing.

The community also considers difficult data environments: hidden and evolving web databases, social and peer-to-peer systems, XML and linked data, scientific repositories, location services, and repetitive document collections. GPU/CPU hybrids, SIMD, MapReduce, distributed in-memory dataflow, and network-aware execution are recurring acceleration strategies.

Recent directions emphasize fairness in rankings, privacy rights, flexible and group preferences, scalable sponsored search, approximate retrieval, and browsing or sampling systems, alongside continued pursuit of trillion-scale, low-latency analytics.

titles<=300|6d4007bc65ac2c364739917e19ea.text:
## Graph Querying, RDF Management, and Semantic Web Data

This community focuses on querying, optimizing, and managing RDF, semantic-web, and property-graph data. A major theme is the foundations of SPARQL: multiset semantics, optional patterns, negation, satisfiability, well-designed queries, schema-aware answering, provenance, updates, and formal complexity. Regular and context-free path queries, navigational expressiveness, conjunctive queries, Datalog, and ontology reasoning provide complementary theoretical foundations.

Practical research targets scalable query processing through partitioning, compressed vertical storage, indexing, join-size estimation, adaptive execution, incremental evaluation, and query optimization. Distributed and federated systems use HBase, Spark, MapReduce, GPUs, replicated fragments, and adaptive partitioning, including RDF stream-processing engines. Benchmarking and workload analysis appear through gMark, SP2Bench, Geographica, query logs, and empirical studies.

The community also studies graph and data-model interoperability, including RDF/property-graph reconciliation, relational-to-RDF mappings, MongoDB, XML integration, XPath/XQuery, schemas, and shape expressions. Linked-data federation, web-scale querying, views, completeness, and data descriptions are recurring concerns.

Recent directions emphasize property-graph languages and traversal frameworks, visual and example-based querying, entity and expertise discovery, historical and streaming graphs, and interactive exploration. Uncertainty, anonymization, contextualized knowledge, annotated data, validation, and privacy extend graph querying beyond deterministic datasets.

titles<=300|e6d713220208038dc697358eb8ae.text:
## Keyphrase Extraction, Summarization, and Adaptive Information Selection

This community focuses on extracting salient information from documents and collections, especially keyphrases, important passages, and summaries. Core applications include medical and broadcast-news text, scholarly communication, and privacy-preserving multi-document summarization and passage retrieval.

Typical methods range from practical automatic extraction (KEA) and hybrid approaches to semantic graph techniques, including personalized PageRank and adaptations of FolkRank for tag recommendation. Text denoising is used both for keyphrase indexing and for identifying information-rich content. Neural networks introduce learned representations for keyphrase extraction, while hierarchical methods extend single-document summarization to multiple documents.

A second theme is adaptive selection under competing objectives. Contextual bandits support keyword selection for advertising on parked domains, and POMDPs model sequential selection of correlated advertisements. Mathematical analysis addresses the relationship between expected selection size and the relevance–diversity trade-off. Keyphrase clouds, traffic prediction for news stories, and scholarly communication protocols broaden the community’s applications.

Recent directions emphasize contextual and semantic modeling, graph-based relatedness, sequential decision-making, and privacy-aware processing, while retaining interpretable ranking, denoising, and diversity-control techniques.

titles<=300|b162e54fcee87e8d0d01718da01c.text:
### Web-Based Scholarly Evaluation, Search, and Online Knowledge Networks

This community studies how web platforms shape scholarly discovery, evaluation, and collective knowledge. A major theme is comparative bibliometrics: Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science, ResearchGate, and journal metrics are assessed through citation coverage, indexing speed, source overlap, h-index behavior, rankings, and highly cited documents. Several papers examine manipulation, article merging, false papers, ghost reputations, and the reliability of web-based indicators.

A second theme is information retrieval and search behavior. Researchers evaluate search engines using representative query samples, navigational and multilingual queries, result descriptions, commercial intent, query expansion, and simple versus complex search tasks. They also study academic search engines, library catalogs, the invisible web, and topic selection for low-cost test collections.

A third theme concerns online communities and networks, especially Wikipedia, university–industry relations, science parks, civil society, and online collaboration. Methods include network analysis, visualization, sequence analysis, clustering, temporal analysis, and finite-state or computational models of interaction and conflict.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes Google Scholar Metrics, language effects, open-access growth and mandate effectiveness, algorithmic fairness, and the fading or changing availability of academic search services.

titles<=300|22597ff7de49bf40a34f8366ea4d.text:
### Semantic Annotation and Scalable Data Management

This community spans two connected themes: semantic enrichment of web and tourism content, and database technologies for large-scale data processing. Several papers develop tourism-specific semantic models, including defined tourism domains, complete semantics for service providers, and validation of Schema.org annotations. The work emphasizes making web content machine-readable and enabling tourism services to exploit consistent domain knowledge.

A second line focuses on annotation infrastructure and automation. Proposed approaches include platforms for creating, publishing, and distributing semantic annotations, as well as automatic action processing based on annotated information. Typical methods therefore involve domain modeling, semantic annotation, validation, and service-oriented processing.

The database papers examine alternatives for big-data management, contrasting NewSQL systems for scalable online transaction processing with NoSQL databases for analytics. They emphasize classification, system characteristics, and comparative analysis. Graph databases are also applied to simulate big-data models for surveillance in wireless multimedia sensor networks.

Overall, the community trends toward combining structured semantics with scalable data platforms: improving annotation quality and reuse while addressing the transaction-processing, analytics, and graph-oriented requirements of increasingly large and heterogeneous datasets.

titles<=300|cc8ca84b6925da2824794ad20434.text:
## Bibliometric Network Science and Scholarly Information Retrieval

This community connects network analysis, bibliometrics, and information retrieval. Major themes include measuring scholarly influence through PageRank, citation counts, h-index variants, prestige/popularity, and multidimensional author metrics; analyzing coauthorship, citation, collaboration, and academic genealogy networks; and studying centrality, vulnerability, power, community structure, and influence diffusion in directed and weighted graphs.

Typical methods include Google-matrix and spectral analysis, personalized and seeded PageRank, Markov-chain and Ulam-network models, graphons, mean-field approximations, link prediction, clustering, label propagation, and efficient large-scale network algorithms. Empirical studies use DBLP, Web of Science, Scopus, patents, Wikipedia/Wikidata, social media, and digital-library logs.

Information-retrieval work emphasizes bibliometric-enhanced search, query and term expansion, thesaurus and terminology mapping, semantic similarity, learning-to-rank, expert and author recommendation, entity disambiguation, and interactive visualization. Knowledge maps and science models support browsing and contextualization.

Recent directions include dynamic and temporal influence ranking, personalized scholarly services, metadata enrichment, emerging-technology detection, cross-cultural and multilingual Wikipedia analysis, and evaluation of gender, prestige, and collaboration inequalities. There is also growing attention to data quality, author identifiers, uncertainty, and scalable systems for massive scholarly and social networks.

titles<=300|daab80fe035615d80cec72781cca.text:
### Diversified Search and Clustering for Structured Data

This community focuses on improving search-result quality by combining similarity, clustering, query expansion, relaxation, and diversity. The papers address keyword queries over XML data, keyword search on graphs, spatial clustering, and \(k\)-nearest-neighbor (kNN) retrieval.

Typical methods include context-based diversification for XML keyword queries; clustering graph-search answer trees with **Klustree**; and approximate kNN spatial clustering using k-d trees. Other work expands queries from clustered results or combines query relaxation with diversification to recover useful alternatives when exact matching is insufficient. Diversity is also treated directly in kNN result selection, with methods seeking representative results rather than merely the most similar ones. The DISC approach emphasizes dissimilarity and coverage as explicit criteria for result diversification.

Overall, the research trends from organizing retrieved answers through clustering toward integrated retrieval pipelines that balance relevance, coverage, and dissimilarity. The community also shows increasing interest in approximate and scalable techniques, particularly for spatial kNN search, while applying diversification across multiple data models—including XML, graphs, and general similarity-search settings.

titles<=300|34594f632b4d6c2544800eda6023.text:
### Differential Privacy for Data Publishing and Inference

This community centers on privacy-preserving data release, analysis, and mining, with differential privacy as the dominant framework. Major themes include private histograms, datacubes, contingency tables, range and linear queries, frequent-itemset and graph-pattern mining, spatial and trajectory data, search logs, and regression. A parallel strand studies anonymization, microdata, unstructured records, provenance views, links, and social-media data, often under strong background knowledge or adversarial information-fusion attacks.

Typical methods include hierarchical decompositions (PrivTree, multidimensional partitions, spatial decompositions), wavelet and low-rank mechanisms, matrix mechanisms, convex optimization, consistency post-processing, adaptive and workload-aware query answering, and sparse-vector techniques. Utility–privacy trade-offs are evaluated through accuracy, computational efficiency, composition, and principled benchmarks. Local differential privacy is applied to marginal release and smart-device data, while Bayesian inference, recommendation, record linkage, and data cleaning extend privacy beyond static tabular release.

Prominent recent directions represented here include policy-aware and personalized privacy, economic selection of epsilon, temporal-correlation protection, end-to-end parameter tuning, high-dimensional mechanisms, and simultaneous privacy and discrimination prevention. The literature also increasingly emphasizes formal privacy guarantees, reconstruction and composition attacks, and practical scalability.

titles<=300|b4e7895a0d5295320aa50b6720db.text:
### Social Signals for Marketplaces and Networks

This community studies how online social networks shape information diffusion, trust, consumer choice, and recommendation in online marketplaces. Several papers use social-network and location-based data to recommend products, categories, or items, while **SocRecM** focuses on a scalable social recommender engine. **Serefind** explores a social-networking website for classifieds, extending these ideas into marketplace infrastructure.

A second theme is social influence: *Swayed by Friends or by the Crowd* examines whether users respond more strongly to personal contacts or collective opinion. Related work analyzes the role of social networks in passing shopping information, the “price of trust,” and consumer decisions. Rumor dissemination is addressed through a computational model accompanied by a convergence theorem, indicating a formal approach to network dynamics.

Typical methods combine online behavioral, social, and geographic data; recommender-system design; empirical analysis of social influence and purchasing; and mathematical modeling with theoretical convergence guarantees. Overall, the research trends from understanding social effects and information spread toward practical, scalable marketplace recommenders and socially connected classified platforms.

titles<=300|f5f20dfa577202596db611f916b4.text:
### Categorical and Algebraic Foundations for Database Transformation

This community develops categorical and algebraic frameworks for database mappings, integration, and migration. Central themes include functorial data migration, database mappings, denotational semantics, and the structural properties of database categories. The papers connect these topics with monads, Kleisli database instances, theory of sketches, and purely equational formalisms.

Typical methods emphasize category-theoretic and algebraic modeling: database instances and mappings are treated through functors, monadic and Kleisli constructions, sketches, and equational reasoning. Relational foundations and matching and merging address how these abstractions describe practical data integration and structural database operations. Table manipulation in simplicial databases extends the scope toward higher-dimensional or simplicial representations.

Recent trends move from foundational theory toward richer formalisms and practical expression. The collection includes denotational accounts of view-based mappings, graphical and compositional approaches based on operads and wiring diagrams, and an explicit progression “from theory to practice.” Overall, the work seeks unified, compositional descriptions of database transformation, integration, recursion, and plug-and-play data-processing structures.

titles<=300|ebe24aec8ce427d1675802e465f5.text:
## Scalable Databases for Transactions and Scientific Data

This community focuses on building scalable, reliable, and efficient database systems for multicore, distributed, cloud, and scientific workloads. A major theme is transaction processing: concurrency control, MVCC and snapshot isolation, serializability, conflict repair, provenance, distributed transactions, logging, recovery, and highly available multi-datacenter execution. Another centers on storage and system architecture, including automatic and graph-based partitioning, replica placement, elastic and shared-nothing systems, main-memory databases, hybrid OLTP/OLAP designs, and hardware-conscious execution.

Scientific and spatial data management is also prominent. Papers address astronomy and observational-data infrastructures, finite-element and array data, metadata management, cross-matching, probabilistic joins, multidimensional and spherical indexes, and large geographic datasets.

Typical methods include predictive modeling, adaptive partitioning and logging, dependency logging, virtual snapshotting, cooperative scans, autonomic resource management, Paxos replication, relational backends, and specialized spatial structures such as hierarchical triangular meshes.

Recent trends emphasize cloud-scale and exascale data management, more predictable latency, energy- and eco-efficient database clusters, learned indexes, and distributed transactions that scale. The community also examines emerging systems including NoSQL consistency tradeoffs, private blockchains, and blockchain data processing.

titles<=300|4d671d5ccf0ef11148d3a0c10ad8.text:
### Social Media Inference and Public-Health Analytics

This community focuses on extracting latent user attributes and health-related signals from Twitter and other social-media data. A major theme is demographic inference, especially gender and age prediction. Studies examine gender prediction generally, infer age probabilistically from users’ followings, and use celebrity-following behavior to infer gender. A broader review considers methods for inferring latent attributes, while another paper evaluates how effectively machine learning can predict social-media demographics.

Typical methods include probabilistic inference and machine-learning models applied to users’ follow relationships, celebrity interests, and other observable social-media behavior. The papers emphasize assessing predictive performance and understanding what publicly visible activity reveals about users.

A second theme applies social-media analysis to health. One study assesses vaccination sentiment and discusses implications for infectious-disease dynamics and control. Another targets HIV-related medication side effects and sentiment using Twitter data. Together, these works indicate a trend from predicting individual demographics toward analyzing public-health attitudes, experiences, and signals at scale. The community therefore connects user-level inference with population-level health monitoring, while retaining a focus on Twitter-derived behavioral and textual evidence.

titles<=300|a2254c10634be1fec83e77780da6.text:
### Mobile Data and Computational Labor-Market Analysis

This community examines how mobile-phone and mobile-network data can reveal labor-market conditions and economic activity. Its themes span population-level “signatures” of unemployment, measurement of China’s economic activity, estimation of individuals’ employment status, and tracking employment shocks. One paper situates these efforts within complex-systems research and computational social science, linking labor markets to data-driven analysis of social dynamics.

Typical methods involve extracting behavioral or network indicators from large-scale mobile data, constructing measures of economic activity or employment, and using these measures to estimate individual status or monitor changes over time. The work combines empirical measurement with computational modeling and population-level tracking.

A notable trend is the movement from describing aggregate relationships—such as mobile signatures of unemployment and regional economic activity—toward more targeted employment-status estimation and near-real-time detection of shocks. Overall, the papers portray mobile data as a complementary source for labor-market monitoring, capable of capturing both broad economic conditions and localized or individual-level changes.

titles<=300|2f1c47850b23a3fd04349a412fe9.text:
### Complex Event Processing for Time-Aware IoT Streams

This community focuses on processing, interpreting, and querying continuous event streams, especially in complex event processing (CEP) and Internet-of-Things (IoT) settings. Core themes include the foundations of CEP, SASE (an event-processing language or framework), and the challenge of maintaining consistent streaming behavior through time.

Typical methods address event pattern processing, stream query evaluation, load shedding, and distributed inference. The papers also consider data-centric views of the IoT and RFID-based tracking and monitoring, linking stream processing with sensor-derived data and distributed query systems.

Recent trends emphasize practical scalability and responsiveness: reducing workload through load shedding, distributing inference and query processing, and addressing temporal consistency in ongoing streams. Together, the papers suggest a progression from establishing conceptual and language foundations toward resource-aware, distributed, and IoT-oriented stream analytics.

titles<=300|f146059bcfa79f97dc0bd896d008.text:
## Complex Networks for Science, Software, and Society

This community applies complex-network theory to understand structures and dynamics across software systems, scientific collaboration, citation databases, websites, healthcare partnerships, and social or information networks. A central theme is identifying communities, groups, and interdisciplinary connections, including how interdisciplinarity affects research impact and career trajectories.

Typical methods include graph construction from citations, hyperlinks, collaborations, and software dependencies; centrality measures such as betweenness; preferential-attachment and evolutionary models; community-detection algorithms; and network sampling, simplification, and group-structure analysis. Several studies empirically compare sampling strategies, clustering methods, online citation databases, and bibliographic topologies, while others quantify database consistency and entity-level impact.

The work increasingly emphasizes temporal and evolutionary perspectives: longitudinal social networks, multilevel and cross-time collaboration patterns, citation dynamics, and changing knowledge structures. Recent directions also connect network metrics with practical evaluation—measuring research influence, comparing scientific databases, characterizing multidisciplinary fields, and assessing how simplification or sampling alters observed structure. Overall, the papers combine methodological advances in network analysis with applications to the organization, reliability, and evolution of scientific and technical knowledge.

titles<=300|56331c095efe6890c7e675161abe.text:
## Educational Data Mining for Student Success

This community focuses on applying data mining and learning analytics to improve education. Its central themes are predicting student outcomes, identifying factors associated with academic performance, reducing dropout rates, and distinguishing high-performing students from underperformers. The papers also examine classroom teaching language, indicating interest in analyzing instructional practices alongside learner data.

Classification is the dominant method, used to predict dropout risk, performance, and performer/underperformer status. More broadly, the work emphasizes mining educational datasets to analyze student achievement and support performance improvement. The collection also includes a survey of learning analytics, suggesting an effort to consolidate the field’s concepts and applications.

The apparent trend is toward predictive educational analytics: moving from descriptive analysis of student performance toward early identification of at-risk or underperforming learners and targeted improvement. At the same time, the scope is expanding beyond student records to include classroom teaching language and broader learning-analytics perspectives.

titles<=300|205376ec285cc4f811c470b61725.text:
**Cross-Modal Learning for Music Semantics and Retrieval**

This community studies semantic understanding and retrieval of music through multiple modalities, especially lyrics and audio. One line of work focuses on music genre classification from lyrics, using a hierarchical attention network to model informative words and higher-level textual structure. A broader theme is learning shared representations across modalities: deep cross-modal correlation learning connects audio and lyrics for music retrieval, while deep cross-modal hashing targets efficient multimodal search. The community also develops discriminative representations for semantic cross-media retrieval, emphasizing alignment and separability between heterogeneous data types.

Typical methods are deep neural architectures for attention, correlation learning, representation learning, and hashing. These approaches seek either modality-invariant embeddings or compact codes that preserve semantic similarity across media. A distinctive direction introduces EEG regularizers into deep models, using neural responses to guide the modeling of music semantics beyond conventional content signals.

Overall, the work trends from single-modality lyric-based classification toward integrated, semantically grounded cross-modal retrieval. Current emphasis is on stronger audio–lyric alignment, discriminative shared representations, computationally efficient hashing, and incorporation of human neural feedback to improve semantic modeling.

titles<=300|f1499b4a7838dddb50bb75f22b07.text:
## Semi-Metric Networks for Adaptive Information Systems

This community studies network structures whose indirect connections can be stronger or more informative than direct links, with applications to recommendation, document analysis, knowledge management, and biological information extraction. A central theme is the use of **distance closures** and **semi-metric behavior** to identify hidden relationships in complex networks, particularly networks of documents and users/items.

Typical methods combine graph-based analysis with machine learning and biologically inspired models. The papers investigate semi-metric networks for recommender systems, use document-network structure to improve recommendations, and apply **word-proximity networks** with a novel linear model to uncover protein interactions in abstracts and other text. Another line develops **guided self-organization based on T-cell cross-regulation dynamics** for collective classification of textual documents. Distributed, biologically motivated designs are also proposed for adaptive knowledge management.

Overall, the work trends from theoretical characterization of network distances toward practical systems that exploit implicit, indirect, and semantically related connections. Recent emphasis appears to be on integrating network topology, textual proximity, adaptive classification, and biologically inspired distributed mechanisms to improve discovery, recommendation, and knowledge organization.

titles<=300|7a3e495b5727be6274ae3158469e.text:
### Verification of Data-Centric Artifact Systems

This community focuses on formal verification of artifact-centric business processes and relational data-centric dynamic systems. A central theme is ensuring correctness when processes manipulate persistent data, including settings with external services, hierarchical artifacts, and UML-based process models. The papers also study verification of query completeness over processes, connecting behavioral analysis with guarantees about available or generated information.

Typical methods combine formal modeling with automated verification. Colored Petri nets and relational databases are integrated through DB Nets, while artifact systems are analyzed using dedicated tools such as Verifas and the SPIN-based SpinArt verifier. UML artifact-centric models provide a higher-level representation for verifiable business processes. These approaches emphasize executable or tool-supported checking rather than purely informal analysis.

Overall, the work trends toward richer and more practical verification frameworks: from foundational combinations of databases and Petri nets, to scalable verification tools, external-service interactions, hierarchical artifact structures, and data/query-oriented properties. Together, the papers indicate a movement toward verifying complete data-aware processes across multiple abstraction levels.

titles<=300|a215593491ff392102fe392021e5.text:
## Network Diffusion, Influence, and Epidemic Intelligence

This community studies how information, opinions, rumors, innovations, and infections propagate through social, temporal, adaptive, and cyber-physical networks. Major themes include influence maximization and viral marketing; epidemic control, vaccination, curing, immunization, and protection; diffusion-source and rumor localization; and inference of network structure, transmission parameters, and propagation paths from cascades or partial observations.

Typical methods combine submodular optimization, greedy and approximation algorithms, adaptive and online learning, bandit feedback, stochastic optimization, optimal control, convex frameworks, and randomized sampling. Probabilistic models include independent-cascade, SIS/SIR/SIRS, Bass, Markovian, phase-type, threshold, and non-progressive diffusion models. Statistical and structural techniques include Bayesian inference, sparse recovery, spectral and random-matrix analysis, message passing, random walks, percolation, graph centrality, and Steiner-tree reconstruction.

Recent work emphasizes scalability to billion-scale and streaming networks, continuous-time and time-aware diffusion, dynamic and non-stationary graphs, partial timestamps and sparse observations, robustness to uncertainty and adversaries, privacy, competitive and complementary diffusion, and explanation-aware influence prediction. There is also growing attention to adaptive seeding, sequential interventions, multi-objective exposure and diversity, community structure, online experimentation, and integrated economic objectives such as revenue, profit, advertising, and crowdfunding.

titles<=300|d79d5d0743b72dafd283873b96c0.text:
## Recommender Systems: Graphs, Sequences, and Multimodal Personalization

This community focuses on personalized recommendation across products, news, media, scholarly resources, travel, music, fashion, and social platforms. Central themes include collaborative filtering and top-*N* ranking, sequential and session-based recommendation, cold-start and sparse-feedback settings, and the integration of content, reviews, tags, metadata, knowledge bases, and social or trust relationships. Researchers also study diversity, explainability, privacy, fairness, reputation, fraud, misinformation, and feedback effects.

Typical methods combine matrix and tensor factorization, Bayesian personalized ranking, neighborhood and diffusion algorithms, clustering, association rules, and graph-based ranking or random walks. Neural approaches include autoencoders, recurrent and self-attention models, factorization machines, embeddings, variational and generative models, graph convolutional networks, and reinforcement learning. Hybrid systems fuse collaborative, textual, visual, temporal, spatial, and contextual signals.

Recent trends emphasize deep sequential models, multimodal and cross-domain recommendation, knowledge- and social-aware representations, causal or deconfounded learning, robust and adversarial ranking, and online exploration through bandits or reinforcement learning. Scalability, streaming evaluation, synthetic interaction generation, interpretable recommendations, and systematic selection of recommendation algorithms are also increasingly prominent.

titles<=300|f792bdb972b373dbe19364b9e740.text:
## Network Science and Graph Representation Learning

This community focuses on methods for analyzing, modeling, sampling, and learning from large, dynamic, heterogeneous, and signed networks. Major themes include community detection and role discovery; link prediction and recommendation; centrality, similarity, and distance estimation; motifs, triangles, cores, trusses, and other higher-order structures; and anomaly, spam, fraud, and change-point detection. Applications span social, citation, communication, financial, web, biomedical, and knowledge graphs.

Typical methods combine random walks, graph sampling, MapReduce and distributed algorithms, spectral and matrix-factorization techniques, stochastic block models, latent-space and generative graph models, and probabilistic inference. Representation learning is especially prominent, including DeepWalk, node2vec, struc2vec, graphlets, meta-path and edge-semantic embeddings, dynamic embeddings, graph neural approaches, and feature propagation. Signed and multilayer networks receive substantial attention, particularly for balance, trust, antagonism, and recommendation.

Recent trends emphasize temporal and streaming graphs, continuous-time modeling, robust dynamic representations, heterogeneous information fusion, scalable and provable approximation, privacy and fairness, and explainable anomaly detection. The community also increasingly connects structural analysis with downstream prediction, while developing benchmark tools, repositories, and evaluation frameworks for large-scale graph mining.

titles<=300|ec2cc86529ae1ca13e24cc88d54d.text:
## Neural and Semantic Advances in Information Retrieval

This community centers on improving search relevance, ranking, and retrieval beyond lexical matching. Major themes include neural information retrieval and deep relevance modeling; query expansion, reformulation, and session search; semantic representations using word, entity, formula, and document embeddings; entity linking and relationship retrieval; and specialized search for biomedical literature, tables, archives, social media, products, ads, and conversations. Web-content quality, spam detection, credibility, factuality, and robustness to adversarial manipulation are recurring concerns.

Typical methods combine learning-to-rank, pairwise/listwise objectives, rank aggregation, kernel methods, probabilistic and language models, graph and bipartite modeling, clustering, hashing, and approximate-nearest-neighbor search. Neural approaches include CNNs, RNNs/LSTMs, attention, sequence-to-sequence query generation, kernel pooling, MatchPyramid, PACRR, reinforcement learning, GANs, and knowledge-resource or knowledge-graph integration. Weak supervision, online learning, bandit-based evaluation, multileaving, and privacy-preserving model transfer address practical deployment constraints.

Recent work trends toward end-to-end neural ranking, hybrid lexical–semantic and multi-stage architectures, contextual and personalized retrieval, conversational and proactive search, explainability, and slate optimization. Research also increasingly emphasizes unbiased online evaluation, efficient large-scale retrieval, semantic hashing, temporal and event-aware search, and retrieval applications that predict or recommend information needs.

titles<=300|3863f3aa760dde20734df86bb519.text:
### Social Media Integrity, Polarization, and Networked Influence

This community studies how information, opinions, and harmful behavior spread through online social networks. Major themes include misinformation, fake news, rumors, clickbait, conspiracy narratives, political manipulation, ideological polarization, echo chambers, and extremist or abusive communities. A parallel focus concerns inauthentic activity: social bots, spambots, trolls, sockpuppets, crowdturfing, purchased engagement, fake profiles, Sybil devices, and vandalism.

Typical methods combine graph analysis with machine learning and language processing. Researchers use community detection, matrix factorization, spectral and influence-based embeddings, link prediction, motif and clustering analysis, temporal models, diffusion and contagion models, and network centrality or communicability measures. Textual approaches include sentiment, stance, toxicity, demographic, and semantic analysis, alongside supervised, semi-supervised, ensemble, neural, and deep diffusive models. Crowdsourcing, honeypots, behavioral fingerprints, and longitudinal platform measurements support detection and validation.

Recent work emphasizes dynamic and cross-platform phenomena, including Russian and other political bot operations, the spread of low-credibility content, health misinformation, and interactions between mainstream and alternative communities. It also increasingly investigates interventions: contrarian exposure, balanced recommendations, fact-checking, bot-based mobilization, anti-Sybil defenses, randomized rankings, and tools for more inclusive or less polarized online discourse.

titles<=300|4d9efd619511f639fc4bfd804c69.text:
## Geospatial Social Media, Mobility, and Urban Intelligence

This community studies how social-media, mobile-phone, transaction, and location-based-service data reveal human behavior across space and time. Major themes include political opinion and election forecasting; user geolocation and toponym resolution; human mobility, migration, commuting, and international flows; urban boundaries, neighborhoods, deprivation, attractiveness, public-space use, and retail placement; and recommendations for routes, events, businesses, and points of interest. Several works examine online diffusion, follow and friendship formation, polarization, rumors, reviews, and reputation.

Typical methods combine sparse and supervised learning, grid-based and probabilistic classification, tensor factorization, topic modeling, sentiment and content analysis, and multimodal or feature-learning approaches. Graph methods address community detection, link prediction, centrality, influence, spatial interaction, and multilayer mobility networks. Trajectory compression, simplification, clustering, convoy discovery, pattern mining, and scalable spatiotemporal frameworks support movement analysis. Researchers also develop RDF corpora, entity-centric archives, visualization tools, and diffusion simulators.

Recent work emphasizes the 2016 U.S. election, real-time country and location inference, large-scale urban sensing, cross-source data fusion, and validation against polls or mobility models. Increasing attention is paid to sampling bias, noise, uncertainty, representativeness, and social segregation, alongside deeper learning and scalable analytics.

titles<=300|01356fa59da62439d86fff8062e6.text:
**Temporal Graphs, Reachability, and Network Dynamics**

This community centers on analyzing graphs whose topology, interactions, or attributes evolve over time. Major themes include temporal reachability and path queries, shortest-distance computation, centrality, influence propagation, dynamic monopolies, and opinion or information spreading. A parallel focus is modeling temporal interactions through stream graphs, link streams, temporal quantities, algebraic formulations, and semirings.

Typical methods emphasize scalable algorithm and index design: reachability oracles, distributed query processing, shortest-path accelerators, labeling schemes, graph indexes, query-plan optimization, and window analytics. Structural analysis uses dynamic graphlets, directed graphlets, network alignment, and temporal indicators. Empirical applications cover hospital contacts, mailing-list threads, social networks, knowledge mobilization, scientific collaboration and selection, and media or gossip networks.

Recent directions increasingly combine temporal structure with practical large-scale analytics: dynamic-graph indexing, distributed reachability, efficient window operations, and time-aware centrality. Recommendation is extended with trust, sentiment, content, and link-stream features, including movie-rating prediction. The papers also explore theoretical explanations of emergence and selection in scientific and algorithmic-information networks, suggesting a broader shift from static structural analysis toward temporal, evolving, and application-aware network intelligence.

titles<=300|b261e52ca53c9307acaada68d590.text:
### Data Mining for Prediction, Diagnosis, and Structural Analysis

This community examines data mining as a broad analytical and decision-support paradigm. Major themes include cancer diagnosis and prognosis, surveys of data-mining applications and feature scope, workforce prediction in the public-relations departments of Orissa blocks and panchayats, and multi-relational data-mining approaches.

The papers use data mining for both medical and administrative prediction tasks, while also exploring methodological foundations. Typical methods include predictive modeling for disease outcomes and worker-related estimates, comparative examination of applications and features, multi-relational analysis, and decomposition of quantitative Gaifman graphs as a tool for data analysis.

The collection reflects a movement beyond single-table or narrowly defined applications toward richer representations of data. In particular, multi-relational techniques and graph decomposition extend data mining to interconnected structures, while domain-specific studies demonstrate its practical use in healthcare and public administration. Overall, the community combines application-oriented prediction with surveys and structural methods aimed at broadening the scope and analytical capabilities of data mining.

titles<=300|77a3e87d49846ec41e880044f091.text:
## Networks, Influence, and Scalable Graph Analytics

This community studies how network structure shapes influence, opinions, diffusion, navigation, and collective behavior. A major theme is opinion and belief dynamics: consensus, polarization, disagreement, social bias, homophily, bounded confidence, susceptibility, threshold effects, and identity loss. Signed and trust–mistrust networks receive particular attention, including structural balance, state-flipping, social power, and convergent appraisals.

A second focus is centrality, accessibility, and node importance. Work develops axioms and measures based on degree, betweenness, absorbing walks, current flow, randomized shortest paths, coverage, criticality, and knowledge segregation. Random walks and PageRank support node discovery, similarity learning, recommender systems, navigation, optimal transport, and information-multiplicity analysis.

Typical methods include Markov chains, random-walk and path-functional formulations, matrix analysis, spectral techniques, dynamical-systems and asymptotic analysis, stochastic models, optimization, approximation algorithms, sampling, greedy methods, and genetic algorithms. Applications include epidemic mitigation, network design, edge recommendation, filtering, active sensing, and distributed inference.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and multilayer/interdependent networks, scalable computation on massive or billion-node graphs, fast approximate and exact top-\(k\) search, and guarantees for dynamic random-walk algorithms. The community also increasingly links personalization and recommendation to opinion formation, models evolving online behavior, and investigates control or obfuscation strategies for social and information networks.

titles<=300|5bacf2b7d8f292571a1f63d0044a.text:
## Scalable, Intelligent, and Scientific Data Management

This community centers on building scalable database systems for demanding transactional, analytical, and scientific workloads. A major theme is multicore and distributed OLTP: high-contention execution, transaction scheduling, partitioning, concurrency control, serializability, MVCC, snapshot isolation, recovery, replication, and geographically distributed consistency. Cloud and shared-nothing architectures emphasize elasticity, availability, dependency logging, and placement of data and replicas.

A second theme is scientific and spatial data management, including astronomy, finite-element analysis, physiological data, geo-tagged social data, multidimensional indexing, cross-matching observations, scientific metadata, and public data archives. Systems such as SkyServer, SkyQuery, the World Wide Telescope, and parallel image-search engines illustrate efforts to connect databases with online science and large-scale exploration.

Typical methods include specialized storage engines, relational and array extensions, log-structured and in-memory designs, hierarchical spatial indexes, graph-based partitioning, Paxos replication, snapshot and dependency-based recovery, and experimental workload benchmarking. Research also studies energy-performance tradeoffs and data infrastructures as socio-technical systems.

Recent directions include learned indexes and deep-reinforcement-learning-based query optimization, partitioning, and database administration; visual and notebook-centered exploration; autonomic resource management; eco-friendly database design; hybrid OLTP/OLAP systems; and blockchain-oriented consistency, storage, and data-processing platforms.

titles<=300|324ad91beecf4e41274a2e6c3a33.text:
### Personalization and Cold-Start Recommendation

This community focuses on learning personalized matches between users and items, with applications ranging from travel planning to e-commerce. One theme is optimizing travel destinations according to individual user preferences, framing recommendation as a preference-aware selection or optimization problem. Another is “learning to match,” emphasizing the discovery of suitable user–item relationships.

A dominant research concern is the item cold-start problem: recommending new items with limited or no interaction history. The papers explicitly investigate model-based approaches and deep learning to address this challenge. They also highlight the **continuous cold-start** setting in e-commerce, where new products repeatedly enter a changing marketplace and must be recommended promptly.

The methods represented include preference-based optimization, learned matching models, model-based recommendation, and deep-learning approaches. Recent work appears to move beyond traditional movie recommendation benchmarks toward practical e-commerce environments, emphasizing the ongoing—not one-time—nature of cold start. Overall, the community trends toward scalable personalization that can handle new items continuously while preserving relevance to changing user preferences.

titles<=300|452295f3af1317438b2848317581.text:
## Social Influence and Trust-Aware Recommendation

This community studies how social relationships, location, trust, and collective behavior shape online-marketplace recommendations and consumer choice. Several papers develop social recommenders that use online-network and location-based data to recommend products, categories, or marketplace items. **SocRecM** emphasizes scalability, while trust-based collaborative filtering addresses the cold-start problem through regular equivalence.

A second theme concerns social influence in purchasing and information sharing. The work examines whether users are swayed by friends or by the broader crowd, and models the “price of trust” in online shopping and consumer decisions. Rumor dissemination is treated computationally, with a formal model and convergence theorem for propagation through social networks.

The methods span recommender-system design, collaborative filtering, trust modeling, social and location data integration, behavioral analysis, and mathematical analysis of diffusion dynamics. **Serefind** extends these ideas to a social-networking website for classifieds.

Overall, the research trends toward combining recommendation with social context: moving beyond user–item interactions to incorporate network influence, trust, geography, scalability, and collective information dynamics.

titles<=300|2bae3f46a3f906ffbcf5376f97e3.text:
### Web-Scale Search and Data-Lake Organization

This community focuses on making large, heterogeneous information collections searchable, comparable, and navigable. One theme is establishing uniform definitions for web information, supporting consistent discovery across diverse sources. Several papers address table-oriented question answering: systems use keywords—especially column keywords—to locate relevant tables and compose answers by identifying patterns in a knowledge base.

A second major theme is data-lake organization. The work considers how to structure and optimize organizations so users can efficiently navigate large collections of datasets, emphasizing discoverability and practical access rather than isolated storage.

Typical methods include keyword-based retrieval, pattern matching over structured data, table and column indexing, and organization schemes designed for navigation. At web scale, locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) ensembles are used for efficient domain search, suggesting approximate similarity search as a strategy for handling very large collections.

Overall, the papers move from defining comparable web information and answering queries over individual tables toward scalable infrastructure for searching, organizing, and navigating entire data lakes.

titles<=300|6d93c82e3b401fedec7ed3e30f57.text:
### Ranking and Recommendation: Unbiased Evaluation and Interactive Optimization

This community focuses on improving ranking and recommender systems under realistic feedback and evaluation constraints. Core themes include learning-to-rank with biased user feedback, unbiased comparative evaluation of ranking functions, and the relationship between offline and online evaluation in small e-commerce settings. The papers also address how to obtain better evaluation data: active sampling is used to make large-scale information-retrieval assessment more efficient, while preference-elicitation interfaces collect dense datasets incorporating rich user information.

Typical methods combine statistical correction and comparative evaluation protocols with active data-collection strategies. Deep reinforcement learning is applied to optimize sponsored-search ranking policies, emphasizing sequential decision-making rather than static ranking alone. Interface design supports richer preference measurement for recommender research.

Overall, the work trends toward more reliable and resource-efficient evaluation, explicit treatment of feedback bias, and closer alignment between offline metrics and online behavior. It also reflects a shift toward interactive systems that learn from richer preferences, selectively acquire judgments, and optimize ranking strategies dynamically.

titles<=300|e897cb4e8d42fc694288ba814f85.text:
### Semantic Models and Interactive Access to Historical Information

This community explores how semantic modeling and direct representation can organize, describe, and improve access to complex information. One theme concerns foundational semantic-modeling practices (“semantic modeling with foundries”) and the challenges of using such models to represent mechanisms. Complementing these conceptual studies, “repositories with direct representation” focuses on representing information more directly within repository environments.

Applied work turns to digitized historical newspapers, combining text mining with coordinated models and formative user-interface design. The “interactive directory for Norfolk, Nebraska, 1899–1900” further illustrates a localized, historical-information application.

Typical methods include semantic modeling, mechanism-oriented analysis, direct repository representation, text-mining workflows, coordinated interface models, and formative user evaluation or design. Overall, the papers suggest a trend from developing modeling foundations toward practical systems for discovery and exploration. Recent emphasis appears to favor interactive, user-informed access tools that connect structured representations with digitized historical sources.

titles<=300|8907bd316aee075d62c8e545211d.text:
### Web Image Search: Learning, Evaluation, and User Interaction

This community studies how to improve and understand image search through online ranking, user behavior, and large-scale evaluation. A central theme is **online learning to rank**, particularly methods that use list-level feedback to optimize image filtering and ranking decisions. The papers also emphasize efficient experimentation: **merge double Thompson sampling** applies bandit-style sampling to evaluate large-scale online rankers while balancing exploration and reliable comparison.

A complementary line of work models searcher behavior. Interaction behavior models and click-sequence models aim to represent how users examine results, click, and proceed through search sessions. Another study addresses the motivations behind image searching, providing a user-centered perspective on query and interaction patterns.

Typical methods therefore combine online learning, Thompson-sampling-based experimentation, behavioral modeling, click-sequence analysis, and empirical studies of search motivations. Overall, the research trends from static relevance estimation toward adaptive ranking systems evaluated in realistic settings, with increasing attention to sequential interactions and the reasons users search for images.

titles<=300|2cfc5043aa33dce378cfa617c0a9.text:
### Multimodal Learning for Music Semantics and Retrieval

This community studies semantic understanding and retrieval of music through both textual and acoustic modalities. A central theme is lyric-based genre classification, including hierarchical attention networks and self-attentive genre classifiers. These models also support content-based feature exploration and more transparent music recommendation.

Several papers extend beyond single-modality classification toward audio–lyrics integration. Deep cross-modal correlation learning is used for music retrieval, while deep cross-modal hashing and discriminative representation learning target efficient semantic cross-media retrieval. These approaches emphasize learning shared or aligned representations across modalities.

Typical methods include hierarchical and self-attention mechanisms, deep representation learning, cross-modal correlation modeling, and hashing-based retrieval. The work also explores supervision beyond conventional labels: EEG regularizers are introduced for deep modeling of music semantics, suggesting interest in incorporating neural responses into representation learning.

Overall, the apparent trend is from lyric-focused genre prediction toward multimodal, semantically meaningful, and retrieval-oriented systems. Recent directions emphasize combining audio and lyrics, improving interpretability for recommendation, learning discriminative shared spaces, and using alternative semantic signals such as EEG.

titles<=300|c67d11950d35dcfbd67d7af18807.text:
### Big Data Benchmarking and Synthetic Workload Generation

This community focuses on constructing practical, scalable benchmarks for evaluating big-data systems. Its themes include broad big-data benchmarking, distributed stream-processing engines, and workload representation based on internet services and web search engines.

Typical methods combine benchmark suites with data-generation tools. **BDGS** provides a scalable generator for big-data benchmarking, while the synthetic-dataset framework enables controlled feature modification (“tweaking”) to study how dataset characteristics affect evaluation. **BigDataBench** develops benchmark suites grounded in workloads from internet services and web search, emphasizing application-representative data and tasks. Distributed stream-processing engines are assessed through dedicated benchmarking methodologies.

The apparent direction of the work is toward more realistic and adaptable evaluation: benchmarks increasingly draw from operational online services, while scalable generators and configurable synthetic data support reproducible experiments, controlled variation, and broader system comparisons. Collectively, the papers connect standardized benchmark suites with flexible workload construction for both batch-oriented big-data systems and distributed streaming platforms.

titles<=300|94b2e87fe2bd072da1aa511ec199.text:
### Artifact-Centric Process Verification and Relational Data

This community studies the modeling, management, and formal verification of data-aware processes and artifact systems. A central theme is the integration of relational data with dynamic systems: relational data-centric processes, artifact systems, and processes involving external services are examined for correctness and query completeness.

Typical methods combine database formalisms with established verification models. DB-nets unite colored Petri nets and relational databases, while UML is used to specify verifiable artifact-centric business processes. Dedicated tools include **VerifAS**, a practical verifier for artifact systems, and **SpinArt**, which applies the SPIN model checker to the same setting. The papers also address hierarchical artifact systems, extending verification beyond flat process structures.

Recent directions emphasize practical and scalable verification, richer system features, and tighter connections between process models and database semantics. In particular, the work progresses from foundational relational and artifact-centric modeling toward verification with external services, hierarchical organization, and explicit guarantees about query completeness.

titles<=300|95a65eb96b291c9dcc6c4f161dc3.text:
## Dynamic Topic Modeling and Social Sensing

This community centers on extracting evolving topics, events, opinions, and communities from large-scale textual and social-media streams. Major applications include disease and influenza surveillance, disaster response, civil-unrest and protest forecasting, sports and scheduled-event detection, tourism, autism research, public sentiment, and online-video popularity.

Typical methods include latent Dirichlet allocation and its extensions: hierarchical, dynamic, continuous-time, author-topic, coupled, limited-attention, multi-grain, and feature-conditioned models. Bayesian nonparametric processes, matrix/tensor factorization, graph and citation-network analysis, neural embeddings, incremental machine learning, and multi-instance learning support topic discovery, influence modeling, community detection, and temporal prediction. Spatial-textual clustering, burst detection, semantic filtering, optimal-route search, and submodular optimization address geographically localized events and mobility data. Summarization, question answering, visualization, ontology learning, and human-in-the-loop review methods improve interpretation and retrieval.

Recent work emphasizes scalable and real-time processing, including distributed inference, stream summarization, adaptive representations, and continuous-time models. Research increasingly combines Twitter, news, Wikipedia, citation networks, and other weak signals; integrates text with links, locations, trajectories, and multimodal social actions; and moves from retrospective topic and event analysis toward forecasting disease outbreaks, unrest, popularity, crowd behavior, and emerging trends.

titles<=300|61be34f5d30680be8217c3c6d3f6.text:
### Scientometrics, Research Evaluation, and Maps of Science

This community centers on measuring and visualizing scholarly and technological activity. Major themes include citation-based research evaluation; alternatives and extensions to the journal impact factor and h-index; percentile, field- and time-normalized indicators; and assessment of individuals, institutions, countries, journals, and programs. Considerable attention is given to fairness, uncertainty, statistical significance, interdisciplinarity, gender, collaboration, and unintended effects of rankings and national assessment exercises.

Typical methods include co-citation, bibliographic coupling, co-word and co-authorship analysis; aggregated journal-citation networks; science and patent overlay maps; clustering, community detection, topic modeling, and reference publication year spectroscopy (RPYS). Researchers compare full versus fractional counting, normalization schemes, databases such as Web of Science, Scopus, Microsoft Academic, Dimensions, and Mendeley, and validate indicators against peer review or expert judgments. Regression, bootstrap, network models, and visualization are also common.

Recent directions emphasize contextual and full-text citation analysis, semantic and semantometrics, deep-learning prediction and recommendation, large-scale database mining, author disambiguation, interactive maps, and methods for identifying emerging topics, breakthroughs, knowledge translation, and science–technology links.

titles<=300|a4bb7c6055dd0b7326f097e9b6a3.text:
## Community Detection in Complex, Dynamic, and Multilayer Networks

This community focuses on discovering and evaluating mesoscale structure in complex networks. Major themes include disjoint, overlapping, fuzzy, hierarchical, core–periphery, link, bipartite, directed, signed, attributed, multilayer, and temporal communities. Applications span social media, scientific collaboration, recommendation, epidemics, cyber threats, knowledge graphs, web services, mobility, and biological networks.

Typical methods include modularity and likelihood optimization; stochastic block models and mixed-membership models; spectral clustering, graph Fourier methods, eigenvector localization, and non-backtracking matrices; label propagation and local seed-expansion; random walks, personalized PageRank, heat kernels, diffusion, conductance, and flow; matrix factorization, embeddings, densest-subgraph and density-based clustering; and evolutionary, ensemble, ant-colony, biogeography, and other heuristic optimizations. Community quality is assessed with conductance, modularity, surprise, kappa, F-score, generalized agreement measures, ground truth, and detectability analyses.

Recent trends emphasize scalable and distributed processing of very large or streaming graphs, real-time detection and tracking in evolving networks, multilayer and heterogeneous structure, node attributes and covariates, and principled model-order and uncertainty assessment. Local and strongly localized methods, dynamic visualization, community profiling, influence-aware analysis, and methods for small or partially observed communities are also prominent.

titles<=300|053cd5c0694c2b61e42f38b937bb.text:
## Social Network Dynamics, Diffusion, and Collective Attention

This community studies how online and offline networks form, evolve, and shape behavior. Major themes include information, rumor, emotion, meme, product, and disease diffusion; popularity, virality, trends, and collective attention; influence, homophily, weak and strong ties, and community structure; and applications in crises, politics, crime, science, health, and recommender systems. A substantial strand addresses misinformation, malicious URLs, cyberbullying, privacy, overload, and anomalous or deceptive accounts.

Typical methods combine graph analysis and centrality measures with community detection, cascade reconstruction, diffusion and epidemic models, Hawkes and Poisson processes, survival analysis, stochastic differential equations, and agent-based simulation. Researchers also use temporal and multimodal data mining, sentiment and semantic representations, time-series analysis, deep learning, attention models, and observational causal inference. Optimization and control methods target campaigning, incentives, influence maximization, polling, and steering opinions.
