Recent directions emphasize microscopic and time-aware cascade prediction, multimodal popularity forecasting, multiplex and competing diffusion, dynamic and evolving communities, privacy-compliant prediction, early disaster and misinformation detection, and integrating social structure with content, geography, cognition, and offline behavior.

titles<=300|ef95ae8f5279fed09080f91d7210.text:
## Scientometrics, Research Assessment, and Academic Performance

This community centers on measuring and explaining research performance, with a strong empirical focus on Italian universities, national assessment exercises, recruitment, funding, and regional disparities. Major themes include bibliometric indicators and rankings; productivity, quality, impact, and efficiency; gender, age, seniority, and academic careers; collaboration, interdisciplinarity, internationalization, and university–industry links; and author-name disambiguation.

Typical methods combine citation and publication analysis with field and size normalization, fractional authorship, h- and g-index evaluation, journal-impact comparisons, DEA and other nonparametric efficiency models, stochastic and statistical models, multivariate and sensitivity analyses, benchmarking, cluster analysis, and network analysis. Peer review is frequently compared with bibliometrics, while uncertainty is addressed through funnel plots and citation-window analysis.

A substantial methodological strand develops author-identification systems using coauthor and citation networks, heuristic and semi-supervised learning, relative frequencies, and deep neural networks, including work on ethnicity and imbalanced training data. Other tools include recommendation systems based on keyword relationships and semantic multiplexes.

Recent directions emphasize fairer and more robust evaluation: accounting for gender, author order, team size, disciplinary differences, uncertainty, changing assessment rules, and labor inputs; detecting opportunistic behavior and ranking distortions; and linking research performance to technology transfer, spin-offs, and public–private collaboration.

titles<=300|771f2dc3229217aaba0450f47277.text:
## Scalable Data, Text, and Mathematical Information Systems

This community integrates database systems, information retrieval, machine learning, and mathematical knowledge management. Major themes include scalable data ingestion and analytics using Accumulo, D4M, Graphulo, SciDB, and distributed or cloud platforms; polystore and cross-platform query processing through BigDAWG and Rheem; and algebraic foundations based on relational lattices, associative arrays, linear/relational algebra, and tensor models.

A second focus is query optimization and prediction, including cardinality and resource-consumption estimation, adaptive re-optimization, shared and multi-query execution, caching, workload management, regret-based operator ordering, and performance-aware scaling. Graph analytics and provenance processing support large-scale scientific, cyber, and road-network workloads.

Information-retrieval research emphasizes text categorization, authorship attribution, topic modeling, feedback, clustering, semantic features, and document classification. Typical methods include Bayesian and nearest-neighbor models, association rules, genetic and evolutionary algorithms, deep learning, statistical estimation, and feature or dependency selection.

Mathematical search is a distinctive thread, covering formula repositories, LaTeX acquisition, formula indexing, rendering, context-aware representation, math-aware retrieval, question answering, and physics applications. Recent work trends toward integrated polystore architectures, server-side graph computation, learned and uncertainty-aware optimization, autonomous workload management, cloud cost sharing, and scalable math-aware search.

titles<=300|177a9ccc41aae1860f27264c8726.text:
## Scholarly Impact, Openness, and Digital Scholarly Communication

This community studies how scholarly work is discovered, used, shared, and evaluated beyond traditional citation counts. Major themes include altmetrics and social-media attention (Twitter, Mendeley, blogs, Wikipedia, policy documents, and online reviews); open access, repositories, preprints, and data sharing; usage-based indicators such as downloads, readership, library loans, and referral activity; and the evaluation of books, publishers, journals, institutions, and research groups. A related stream examines scholarly communication infrastructures, including author identifiers, digital libraries, citation and data indexes, and academic social networks.

Typical methods are large-scale bibliometric and webometric analyses, comparisons of altmetrics with citations and usage, surveys and case studies, network and co-readership analysis, text mining, sentiment analysis, OCR, metadata extraction, and statistical normalization of skewed or zero-inflated data. Recommender systems address papers, venues, reviewers, and conference assignments using citation, content, usage, and social signals.

Recent work emphasizes multidimensional and contextual impact, societal and policy influence, real-time tracking of trends and digital footprints, and institutional or field-normalized indicators. It also highlights data-quality, coverage, bots, bias, heterogeneity, and methodological problems in interpreting open-access and altmetric advantages.

titles<=300|f8da9c60583d6618ab99bcbcea15.text:
## Social Media Integrity, Manipulation, and Polarization

This community studies how information, opinions, and malicious behavior spread through online social networks. Major themes include misinformation and fake-news detection, rumor verification, clickbait, propaganda, political manipulation, extremist and hateful content, cyberbullying, spam, fraud, astroturfing, and social bots. Many papers examine polarization, echo chambers, controversy, segregation, collective attention, and the influence of partisan or state-sponsored communities across Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Gab, 4chan, and other platforms.

Typical methods combine graph and network analysis—community detection, centrality, motifs, diffusion and influence models, link prediction, matrix factorization, temporal analysis, and structural Sybil detection—with natural-language processing and machine learning. Features include linguistic style, sentiment, stance, user behavior, network structure, and social context; classifiers range from semi-supervised and ensemble models to neural and deep diffusive networks. Researchers also use honeypots, crowdsourcing, social sensors, causal inference, and platform-scale datasets such as Hoaxy, FakeNewsNet, and Truthy.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes interpretable and fairness-aware ranking, trustworthy-user and reputation systems, early-warning and real-time detection, cross-platform influence operations, and intervention strategies—fact-checking, exposure balancing, contrarian recommendations, bot-based mobilization, and defenses against coordinated manipulation.

titles<=300|2b576b8038558d120a531c277b4b.text:
## Recommender Systems: From Collaborative Filtering to Graph, Sequential, and Explainable Models

This community spans personalized recommendation across products, news, music, images, video, travel, academia, healthcare, and social media. Core themes include collaborative filtering and ranking; social, trust, and reputation-aware recommendation; sequential and session-based prediction; context, temporal, spatial, and behavioral modeling; and cold-start, long-tail, diversity, coverage, and privacy challenges.

Typical methods range from neighborhood models, matrix and tensor factorization, Bayesian personalized ranking, diffusion, random walks, association rules, and factorization machines to neural collaborative filtering, autoencoders, variational models, recurrent and convolutional networks, attention and self-attention, and reinforcement learning. Graph-based approaches use bipartite networks, knowledge graphs, graph embeddings, graph convolution, community structure, and heterogeneous relationships. Content and multimodal systems incorporate text, reviews, tags, metadata, audio, visual features, taxonomies, and linked data.

Recent directions emphasize deep and hybrid models, sequential recommendation, multimodal representation learning, adversarial robustness, causal and deconfounded recommendation, explainable reasoning, and fairness. Research also increasingly addresses exploration–exploitation, feedback loops, adaptive interaction, scalable serving, online experimentation, and evaluation in streaming or real-world systems.

titles<=300|c4ec4c16040beba2267917166cea.text:
## Graph Mining and Representation Learning in Dynamic Social Networks

This community studies the structure, evolution, and analysis of large social, information, biological, and knowledge networks. Major themes include community detection, role and core–periphery discovery, centrality and influence, signed and multiplex networks, link prediction, anomaly and fraud detection, and graph sampling. Temporal networks receive substantial attention through event graphs, dynamic stochastic block models, latent-space models, change-point detection, temporal motifs, and evolving embeddings.

Typical methods combine random walks, matrix factorization, spectral and tensor techniques, modularity optimization, motif and graphlet analysis, probabilistic generative models, and scalable approximation algorithms. Representation learning is especially prominent, including DeepWalk, node2vec, struc2vec, graph convolutional networks, heterogeneous-network meta-path embeddings, structural and role-aware embeddings, and content-enhanced or multimodal models. Applications include recommendations, scholarly knowledge graphs, spam and insider-trading detection, social status inference, network alignment, and epidemic simulation.

Recent trends emphasize dynamic and heterogeneous graphs, higher-order structure, uncertainty, negative and signed relationships, fairness and robustness, and learning from incomplete or streaming data. Scalability remains central, with distributed graph generation, sublinear sampling, efficient triangle and motif counting, compressed indexes, and high-performance analysis toolkits.

titles<=300|bf2c80edc7b637572ea3ed5d5414.text:
### Information Retrieval: Neural Ranking, Semantic Search, and Adaptive Evaluation

This community centers on improving information retrieval beyond keyword matching. Major themes include ad hoc, web, biomedical, ecommerce, social-media, mobile, scholarly, table, image, and conversational search; entity and relationship retrieval; question and passage answering; query expansion and reformulation; recommendation; and web-content quality and spam detection.

Typical methods combine learning-to-rank with deep semantic matching. Convolutional, recurrent, attention-based, kernel-pooling, listwise, and sequence-to-sequence models represent queries, documents, passages, and products. Word, entity, concept, formula, and knowledge-graph embeddings address vocabulary mismatch and support entity linking, expertise search, personalization, and semantic retrieval. Classical relevance models, term weighting, relevance feedback, graph methods, clustering, hashing, approximate nearest neighbors, and fusion remain important for efficiency and scale.

A strong methodological focus is reliable evaluation: unbiased and counterfactual learning to rank, propensity estimation, multileaving, bandits, online experimentation, robustness to adversarial manipulation, and metrics for relevance, credibility, factuality, objectivity, and diversity. Interpretability is explored through local explanations and visualization.

Recent directions emphasize end-to-end neural ranking, weak or adversarial supervision, neural pseudo-relevance feedback, joint search–recommendation optimization, reinforcement-learning query reformulation and result diversification, session and conversational search, time-aware retrieval, and privacy-preserving or resource-efficient deployment.

titles<=300|49b8a668d40153935db6e83e5f59.text:
## Geosocial Intelligence from Online Traces

This community studies how social-media, mobility, transaction, and communication traces reveal human behavior across space and time. Major themes include political opinion and election forecasting; geolocation and home-location inference; urban mobility, neighborhood structure, migration, and segregation; place attractiveness and retail-site selection; and urban experiences such as smells, sounds, parks, walkability, and public-space use. Additional work examines influence, polarization, diffusion, friendships, churn, event participation, and recommender systems.

Typical methods combine geospatial analysis with graph and network modeling, including community detection, signed and multilayer networks, centrality, link prediction, diffusion models, and spatial interaction analysis. Machine-learning approaches range from sparse learning, tensor factorization, probabilistic inference, clustering, and optimization to CNN/RNN, deep multiview learning, embeddings, and feature learning. NLP supports sentiment, topic, entity, rumor, and toponym analysis, while computer vision is applied to selfies and political imagery. Trajectory simplification, compression, pattern mining, and uncertain-query methods address large movement datasets.

Recent work concentrates on the 2016 U.S. election, fake news and rumor detection, political polarization, large-scale Twitter geolocation, multimodal behavioral modeling, and validation of platform bias. Researchers increasingly integrate heterogeneous sources and explicitly model uncertainty, scale effects, temporal dynamics, and data quality.

titles<=300|6e042eb1075e9c9bef95bf1f7467.text:
## Efficient, Fair, and Preference-Aware Data Retrieval

This community develops scalable methods for searching, querying, ranking, and analyzing large or complex data collections. Major themes include top-*k* and skyline queries; preference-aware, fuzzy, aggregate, and incomplete-data querying; hidden-web crawling and query processing; graph, XML, social-network, and linked-data retrieval; and OLAP over multidimensional or spatial data.

A prominent systems focus is performance engineering. Papers develop bitmap and inverted-index compression, integer and *n*-gram coding, hashing, sorting and column reordering, succinct and learned indexes, and fast set intersection. SIMD vectorization, GPUs, in-memory execution, MapReduce, distributed dataflows, caching, and adaptive algorithms are recurring methods. Approximation, sketches, sampling, and cost/quality tradeoffs support large-scale or streaming workloads.

Information retrieval research covers query variation, reranking, nearest-neighbor and embedding-based search, word mover’s distance, clustering, recommendation, and passage retrieval for biomedical question answering. Ranking is increasingly treated as a social and ethical problem, with work on exposure, attention, demographic disparities, diversity, coverage, privacy, and fair ranking schemes.

Overall, the collection trends toward hybrid architectures, learned and neural retrieval, approximate and multistage processing, GPU/SIMD acceleration, and socially responsible search and recommendation.

titles<=300|c100994e122e9db6423a0adc87fe.text:
## Scalable Data Management and Analytics

This community focuses on building scalable systems for querying, processing, and learning from large, heterogeneous data. Major themes include worst-case-optimal and multiway join processing; query optimization, indexing, materialized and incremental views; graph and RDF analytics; array and time-series management; and parallel, distributed, and cloud data systems. A closely related strand applies databases to machine learning, including sparse-tensor computation, relational learning, feature engineering, graphical models, and in-database analytics.

Typical methods combine theoretical complexity and size-bound analyses with practical systems research. Papers develop mixed-integer and cost-based optimization, hypertree decompositions, factorized representations, sketches and sampling, approximate query processing with error guarantees, adaptive indexing, code generation, operator fusion, and hardware acceleration. MapReduce, dataflow, shared-nothing, GPU, and main-memory architectures are recurrent implementation settings. Interactive exploration, visual analytics, provenance, versioning, data cleaning, and privacy address usability and governance.

Recent work trends toward unified relational–graph–array engines, native compilation for heterogeneous hardware, continuous and dynamic graph processing, incremental maintenance, elastic cloud execution, and approximate or progressive answers. The community also emphasizes machine-learning workloads, attention prioritization, collaborative data management, and systems that support evolving, streaming, and raw data.

titles<=300|8a5f596857b44cc184087dda75ed.text:
## Graph Querying, Semantics, and Scalable RDF Management

This community centers on the foundations and engineering of graph query languages, especially SPARQL over RDF, OWL, linked data, and property graphs. Major themes include SPARQL semantics and complexity; optional patterns, negation, federation, updates, provenance, completeness, and reasoning; regular and context-free path queries; and formal connections among SPARQL, relational algebra, Datalog, XPath/XQuery, Gremlin, and openCypher.

Typical methods combine formal analysis of expressiveness, satisfiability, tractability, containment, chase termination, and lower bounds with practical query optimization. Systems research explores summaries, indexes, vertical partitioning, compressed storage, cardinality estimation, join algorithms, incremental view maintenance, adaptive partitioning, MapReduce/Spark/GPU execution, and distributed or federated processing. Benchmarking uses synthetic generators such as gMark and workloads such as SP2Bench, alongside analyses of real query logs.

A second thread addresses interoperability and schema management across RDF, XML, relational, JSON, and property-graph models, including mappings, shape expressions, schema inference, and visual query interfaces. Provenance, uncertainty, privacy, annotations, and streaming data extend graph querying beyond static datasets.

Recent directions emphasize unified RDF/property-graph querying, web-scale federation and link traversal, scalable stream reasoning, learned or embedding-based query assistance, approximate evaluation, adaptive systems, and interactive exploration of heterogeneous graphs.

titles<=300|8c97ec0ff39e89eb14c09efcc236.text:
## Temporal Web Archives and Semantic Scholarly Infrastructure

This community centers on preserving, modeling, and exploiting evolving digital information. A major theme is web archiving: estimating resource age, measuring coverage and archivability, rediscovering missing pages, preserving deferred representations, and enabling time travel through Memento, timemaps, and temporal graphs. Related work studies synchronization, URI canonicalization, caching, persistence, and personal or decentralized archiving.

A second theme is digital-library and repository infrastructure. Fedora, aDORe, NSDL, OAI-PMH, ResourceSync, SharedCanvas, and related architectures support complex objects, metadata aggregation, interoperability, format migration, and long-term preservation. Research also addresses policies, storage formats, repository requirements, and human-assisted curation.

Semantic scholarship is another strong focus: nanopublications, micropublications, claims and evidence, provenance, annotation models, PAV, contextualized information, and diachronic linked data. These systems make scientific assertions, software, manuscripts, and biomedical resources computable and traceable.

Typical methods combine standards-based system design, ontology and data-model development, crawling and archive simulations, graph analysis, empirical repository evaluations, and machine learning for classification, ranking, event detection, and page recovery.

Recent directions emphasize scalable archive analytics, semantic layers over archives, social-media-informed focused crawling and news mining, multimedia and image extraction, persistent annotations, scholarly orphan discovery, decentralized publication, and more rigorous measurement of temporal coherence and web persistence.

titles<=300|d96bc1509c67d12cd42916be8f17.text:
## Network Science for Scholarly Discovery and Social Analysis

This community centers on applying network science to scholarly communication, information retrieval, and large-scale social or cultural systems. Major themes include PageRank and related centrality measures for ranking authors, papers, journals, universities, experts, and online entities; coauthorship, citation, corporate-board, patent, and political networks; and the distinction between prestige, popularity, influence, and scientific contribution. A parallel focus is bibliometric-enhanced information retrieval, including query expansion, terminology mapping, thesauri, topic contextualization, recommendation, exploratory search, and interactive visualization.

Typical methods include Google-matrix and reduced-Google-matrix analysis, weighted and personalized PageRank, spectral and Markov-chain techniques, graphons, stochastic block models, community detection, clustering, link prediction, mean-field approximations, and learning-to-rank. Studies also use temporal embeddings, LSTM models, social-media mining, Wikipedia/DBpedia/Wikidata, patent and citation databases, search logs, and user experiments. Name disambiguation, data quality, uncertainty, anonymization, and evaluation reliability recur as methodological concerns.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and multilayer networks, emerging-technology and author-career prediction, cross-cultural and gender analysis, interactive digital-library systems, scholarly knowledge graphs, and scalable analysis of massive networks.

titles<=300|3a7e382d6d995ad32365830fa178.text:
### Semantic Web Annotation and Scalable Data Infrastructures

This community focuses primarily on making web content and services machine-readable, with a strong emphasis on tourism. Research defines tourism domains, develops complete semantics for tourism providers, and builds the Tyrolean tourism knowledge-graph ecosystem. Schema.org is used to annotate domain content, web APIs, and actions, supported by domain-specific semantic validation and heuristics for publishing dynamic content.

A second theme is automation and infrastructure: annotation-based automatic action processing and *Semantify.it* address the creation, publication, distribution, and operational use of semantic annotations.

The community also examines database technologies for large-scale data management. Papers compare NoSQL systems, discuss NewSQL for scalable OLTP over big data, and simulate big-data models on graph databases for wireless multimedia sensor-network surveillance.

Typical methods include semantic modeling, schema-based annotation, validation, heuristic publication strategies, action processing, platform and ecosystem development, taxonomy-based database comparison, and graph-database simulation.

Recent trends point toward integrated knowledge-graph ecosystems, automated semantic actions, machine-readable APIs, and scalable combinations of structured annotations with graph, NoSQL, and NewSQL technologies.

titles<=300|fad589ace5e895939f4951e9f6ee.text:
## Community Report: Data Integration, Entity Resolution, and Crowdsourced Curation

This community focuses on making heterogeneous, web-scale data reliable and interoperable. A central theme is **entity resolution and consolidation**, including record linkage, deduplication, schema and ontology matching, matching dependencies, and graph-based integration. Closely related work addresses **data fusion and truth discovery**, resolving conflicts among multiple sources, estimating source and worker trustworthiness, and discovering multiple or context-dependent truths.

A second major theme is **data quality and curation**: cleaning inconsistent or incomplete data, detecting anomalies and unknown errors, repairing databases probabilistically, and supporting human-centric curation. Web extraction, wrapper repair, linked-data integration, knowledge graphs, and spreadsheet/table assistance extend these capabilities to practical settings.

Typical methods combine probabilistic and Bayesian inference, crowdsourcing and active learning, deep or transfer learning, graph matching, string transformations, global constraints, and Datalog-based reasoning. Scalable systems rely on blocking, locality-sensitive hashing, inverted indexes, partitioning, embeddings, GPUs, and parallel databases. Crowdsourcing research also studies task assignment, worker reliability, adaptive questioning, team formation, and budget- or latency-aware optimization, especially for spatial tasks.

Recent directions emphasize human–machine cooperation, holistic and self-driving data curation, deep-learning-based entity matching, selective verification, source-aware truth discovery, reproducible crowd analytics, and applications to linked, medical, urban, and open-web data.

titles<=300|8c324c61989c1db850ae587ef201.text:
### Differential Privacy for High-Dimensional, Structured, and Social Data

This community centers on privacy-preserving data publishing, analysis, and learning, with differential privacy as the dominant framework. Major themes include accurate answers to statistical, range, batch, linear, histogram, datacube, contingency-table, and high-dimensional queries; private data mining and machine learning; and protection of trajectories, locations, mobility, search logs, streams, graphs, links, and social-media data. Local differential privacy appears in marginal release, smart-device data collection, and range-query answering.

Typical methods include hierarchical decompositions, wavelets, multidimensional partitioning, matrix mechanisms, low-rank and convex optimization, mixture models, functional mechanisms, random walks, and adaptive or workload-aware query answering. Frequent-itemset and graph-pattern mining, decision trees, regression, recommendations, and record linkage receive specialized treatments. Privacy models also address sparse data, microdata, l-diversity, anonymization, provenance, policy-aware mechanisms, temporal correlations, composition, auxiliary information, and adversarial reconstruction.

Recent trends emphasize improving the privacy–utility–efficiency trade-off through consistency, end-to-end parameter tuning, modular algorithms, benchmarking, and universally utility-maximizing mechanisms. The literature increasingly considers realistic threats and background knowledge, personalized or population-level privacy, social and temporal structure, and the integration of privacy with fairness, semantic guarantees, and practical data exploration.

titles<=300|0b3b3170d1dc8fad0bee40a557bd.text:
## Online Learning and User-Centered Evaluation for Image Search

This community studies how to improve web image and general search ranking through online interaction data. Major themes include learning to rank from list-level feedback, relevance-aware presentation in complex layouts, and understanding why users search for images. Several papers model user behavior through clicks, click sequences, attention, and satisfaction, aiming to make search-result evaluation more realistic than simple relevance judgments.

Typical methods include online learning-to-rank algorithms, exploration of gradient space, and Thompson-sampling strategies for large-scale ranker evaluation. Interaction behavior models and click-sequence models are used to interpret browsing and engagement patterns, while evaluation models combine clicks with attention and satisfaction signals. The work also considers display preferences alongside topical relevance, reflecting the importance of how results are presented, not only which results are ranked.

Recent trends emphasize efficient and statistically informed online experimentation, including merged Thompson sampling and more targeted exploration. At the same time, evaluation is becoming increasingly user-centered by incorporating behavioral sequences, visual attention, and satisfaction into ranking and search-quality models.

titles<=300|dbccb2d3cbd520076544b461be97.text:
## Web-Based Scholarly Metrics, Search, and Online Knowledge Networks

This community centers on evaluating scholarly impact and information discovery through web-based data. A dominant theme is comparison of Google Scholar, Web of Science, and Scopus: coverage of highly cited documents, citation counts and speed, disciplinary and language variation, journal rankings, h-indices, and research-assessment applications. Many studies examine Google Scholar’s scale, metadata quality, institutional links, open-access evidence, and vulnerability to citation or h-index manipulation.

A second theme is information-retrieval evaluation. Research addresses topic selection for test collections, deep versus shallow judging, query expansion, search-result overlap, navigational and multilingual queries, result descriptions, commercial intent, credibility, and user effort across simple and complex tasks. Library catalogs and academic discovery are also considered.

A third theme concerns online scholarly and knowledge communities, including university–industry networks, ResearchGate reputations, Wikipedia collaboration and conflict, online social movements, and science-park interactions. Typical methods include large-scale citation and webometric analyses, API-based data collection, comparative benchmarking, network analysis, sequence analysis, clustering, finite-state modeling, and statistical tests such as Benford analysis.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes open-access measurement, low-cost bibliometric tools, multilingual and temporal analyses, fair ranking, manipulation detection, and the changing availability of academic search platforms.

titles<=300|e45bb494e402f71b9c4cbcac6c55.text:
## Scalable, Intelligent, and Scientific Data Management

This community focuses on building database systems that remain fast, reliable, and useful at extreme scale. Major themes include multicore and distributed OLTP, concurrency control, transaction recovery, replication, consistency, and high-contention execution. Work examines MVCC, snapshot isolation, serializability, dependency logging, adaptive logging, logical recovery, Paxos, and multi-datacenter transactions.

A second theme is scalable storage and query processing for cloud, social, spatial, and scientific data. Systems address partitioning, placement, indexing, arrays, multidimensional and geospatial search, probabilistic joins, batch processing, and hybrid OLTP/OLAP workloads. Astronomy and other scientific applications motivate large data archives, metadata management, observatories, event analysis, and reproducible open science.

Typical methods include specialized database architectures, shared-nothing clusters, distributed storage, replication protocols, graph-based partitioning, hierarchical spatial indexes, cooperative scans, virtual snapshotting, and adaptive query processing. Empirical performance, latency, energy use, and failure recovery are recurring evaluation criteria.

Recent work increasingly applies deep reinforcement learning and learned structures to join ordering, query optimization, administration, partitioning, and indexing. Other emerging directions include autonomic and predictable systems, energy-efficient clusters, visual and neural data exploration, blockchain databases, verifiable queries, and socio-technical stewardship of scientific and open data.

titles<=300|421ef63b7ac60e8b6174e899e849.text:
## Multimodal Semantic Retrieval and Music Understanding

This community focuses on learning shared, discriminative representations across modalities, especially for music retrieval and recommendation. A central theme is cross-modal alignment between audio and lyrics, supported by deep correlation learning and cross-modal hashing for efficient retrieval. Several works address semantic cross-media retrieval more broadly through discriminative representation learning and decorrelated hash codes.

Music understanding is another major focus, including genre classification from lyrics and self-attentive genre modeling for content-based, transparent recommendation. Attention-based architectures—particularly hierarchical and self-attention networks—are typical methods for capturing structure and salient semantic information in lyrics and music content. Deep neural models are also used to integrate heterogeneous modalities and produce compact retrieval codes.

A notable emerging direction is incorporating human-response signals: EEG regularizers are explored to improve the modeling of music semantics. Overall, the research appears to move from compact and decorrelated hashing toward deeper semantic modeling, stronger audio–lyric integration, attention-driven interpretability, and cognitively informed representations.

titles<=300|5ddb2fa22d4a89360c4e5de3748a.text:
## Network Diffusion, Influence, and Epidemic Control

This community studies how information, opinions, rumors, and infections propagate through social, temporal, multilayer, and cyber-physical networks. Major themes include influence maximization and marketing; epidemic prevention, vaccination, curing, and rumor blocking; diffusion-source localization; and inference of hidden network structure, transmission parameters, and propagation paths from cascades or partial observations.

Typical methods combine independent-cascade, threshold, SIS/SIR/SIRS, Bass, and adaptive diffusion models with submodular optimization, greedy and approximation algorithms, randomized sampling, random walks, spectral and moment analysis, message passing, sparse recovery, Bayesian inference, and agent-based simulation. Source detection frequently uses Jordan centers, likelihood or sample-path methods, partial timestamps, querying, and strategic source-obfuscation models. Large-scale systems motivate scalable, distributed, GPU-based, streaming, and billion-node algorithms.

Recent directions emphasize adaptive and online decision-making under myopic or partial feedback, nonstationary and time-varying networks, continuous-time and non-progressive diffusion, multiple competing or complementary cascades, and resource-constrained sequential seeding. The community also increasingly addresses robustness, uncertainty, fairness, privacy, explainability, heterogeneous opinions and thresholds, dependence between items, and the integration of representation learning, contrastive training, and empirical behavioral data.

titles<=300|78f8346afdada3965b9b891c8cfa.text:
## Unbiased and Adaptive Evaluation of Ranking Systems

This community focuses on learning and evaluating search and recommender rankings under imperfect feedback. A central theme is removing bias from user-derived signals, represented by unbiased learning to rank, unbiased LambdaMART, and unbiased comparative evaluation of ranking functions. Counterfactual learning to rank extends this goal to additive metrics and deep models, emphasizing evaluation and optimization from logged or otherwise biased interactions.

The papers use diverse methodological approaches: pairwise learning with LambdaMART, deep reinforcement learning for sponsored-search ranking, counterfactual estimation, and comparative evaluation protocols. Complementary work addresses how to obtain better evidence, including active sampling for large-scale information-retrieval evaluation and a preference-elicitation interface designed to collect dense recommender datasets enriched with user information.

A further theme is methodological validity: comparing offline and online recommender-system evaluation, particularly in small e-commerce settings. Overall, the apparent trend is toward more reliable, scalable, and interactive ranking research—combining debiasing, counterfactual and deep models with improved data collection and evaluation designs.

titles<=300|57224db01309158f4fd5aeb76073.text:
## Community Detection in Complex, Dynamic, and Multilayer Networks

This community focuses on detecting, evaluating, and interpreting mesoscale structure in complex networks. Major themes include disjoint, overlapping, fuzzy, hierarchical, core–periphery, link, bipartite, and hybrid node–link communities. Increasing attention is given to attributed, signed, directed, multiplex, heterogeneous, temporal, and spatial networks, with applications to social media, scholarly networks, web services, recommendation, epidemiology, cybersecurity, and team formation.

Typical methods include modularity and likelihood optimization; spectral clustering, graph Laplacians, non-backtracking matrices, and graph signal processing; stochastic block and latent-space models; matrix factorization and embeddings; label propagation; random walks, personalized PageRank, heat kernels, diffusion, and conductance; density-, truss-, triangle-, and subgraph-based techniques; and evolutionary, ant-colony, biogeography, and other ensemble or heuristic algorithms. Local, seed-based, distributed, streaming, parallel, and scalable approaches are especially prominent.

Evaluation is a central concern, involving modularity, conductance, surprise, stability, NMI, F-score, kappa, agreement measures, ground truth, detectability thresholds, phase transitions, and context-sensitive quality functions. Recent trends emphasize dynamic community tracking, multilayer integration, attributed and higher-order networks, automated model and resolution selection, debiasing, interpretability, and real-time analysis of large evolving graphs.

titles<=300|42280943ec44c6e0d08f128a9b3d.text:
## Social Media, Misinformation, and Network Integrity

This community centers on computational analysis of social media as a contested information environment. Major themes include fake news, rumors, disinformation, political manipulation, propaganda, conspiracy narratives, and misinformation during elections and health crises. Closely related work examines polarization, echo chambers, controversy, hate speech, trolling, cyberbullying, extremism, and online community conflict.

A second major focus is platform integrity: detecting social bots, trolls, sockpuppets, spam, crowdturfing, fake profiles, Sybil users, like farms, phishing, and coordinated campaigns. Several studies assess privacy, bias, fairness, discrimination, search and news-feed ranking, and unequal information exposure.

Typical methods combine network and diffusion analysis with machine learning. Papers use community detection, graph embeddings, link prediction, spectral and matrix factorization, motif and temporal analysis, influence modeling, causal inference, sentiment and stance detection, linguistic analysis, and crowdsourced or weak supervision. Deep, ensemble, transfer-learning, multimodal, and interpretable models support fake-news, clickbait, abuse, vandalism, and bot detection.

Recent trends emphasize state-sponsored information warfare, Russian influence operations, political advertising and microtargeting, multimodal deception, early-warning systems, and interventions that reduce polarization or misinformation. Researchers increasingly combine social context with content, pursue fairness-aware ranking and detection, and study coordinated manipulation across platforms.

titles<=300|5a75b11874e1505a49d62d611695.text:
### Geolocation, Political Polarization, and Junk News on Social Media

This community examines how social-media data reveal geographic behavior, political information flows, and disinformation. One research theme is location inference: convolutional neural networks are used to predict tweet geolocation, while large-scale empirical analysis characterizes geotagging behavior. Complementary work addresses reconstructing the order of locations in trails when temporal resolution is low.

A second major theme concerns political polarization and partisan media consumption. Studies investigate how social-media news and political information during the U.S. election became polarizing and concentrated in swing states, and how partisanship relates to junk-news consumption.

The community also focuses on junk news and coordinated disinformation. Research examines campaigns targeting U.S. military personnel and veterans, as well as junk-news dissemination on Facebook. Typical methods include deep-learning prediction, large-scale behavioral measurement, temporal-spatial reconstruction, comparative political analysis, and platform-specific aggregation of posts.

Recent work trends toward systematic monitoring of junk news and disinformation across major platforms, with particular attention to election periods, politically salient populations, and the geographic concentration of content and audiences.

titles<=300|74f6f04f766b7cd1d581ab103651.text:
## Recommender Systems: Personalization, Sequences, and Responsible Ranking

This community centers on personalized recommendation across products, music, news, videos, images, research papers, travel, and points of interest. Major themes include collaborative filtering and top-*N* ranking; sequential and session-based recommendation; social, trust, and knowledge-graph recommendation; and content-aware or multimodal personalization using text, images, audio, metadata, and reviews.

Typical methods range from neighborhood models, matrix and tensor factorization, Bayesian personalized ranking, diffusion, random walks, and probabilistic models to neural collaborative filtering, autoencoders, factorization machines, attention mechanisms, recurrent networks, self-attention, capsules, and graph neural networks. Hybrid approaches combine collaborative signals with semantic, visual, temporal, behavioral, or social features. Research also addresses cold start, sparse and implicit feedback, missing modalities, scalability, approximate retrieval, and online or streaming settings.

A strong strand studies sequential decision-making through reinforcement learning, bandits, exploration–exploitation, and conversion optimization. Recent directions emphasize transformers, memory-augmented and context-aware sequence models, cross-domain and multi-behavior learning, and richer user/item representations. Responsible recommendation is increasingly prominent, including popularity and exposure bias, fairness in two-sided platforms, diversity, robustness to shilling and adversarial attacks, privacy, explainability, and evaluation under realistic feedback.

titles<=300|9d9d8ee764441d2d0616fae2b7ae.text:
## Temporal and Dynamic Graph Analytics

This community focuses on modeling, querying, and analyzing networks whose structure, interactions, or attributes change over time. Major themes include temporal reachability, shortest paths, distances, latencies, and centrality, alongside diffusion processes such as opinion spreading, dynamic monopolies, trust, gossip, and influence.

Typical methods emphasize scalable graph algorithms and indexing: reachability oracles, landmark and hub labeling, shortest-distance indexes, distributed and vertex-centric computation, and performance guarantees for large dynamic graphs. Algebraic formulations using temporal quantities and semirings provide general analytical frameworks, while stream graphs, link streams, multilayer networks, dynamic graphlets, directed graphlets, and network alignment support richer structural representations. Time-series analysis and window-function optimization address temporal aggregation and query processing.

Applications include hospital contact networks, mailing-list discussions, movie scripts and ratings, social media recommendation, knowledge mobilization, and scientific collaboration or selection networks. Recent directions increasingly combine temporal and multilayer modeling, layer-aware centralities, dynamic graphlets, scalable window analytics, and exact query processing. The papers also show a trend toward integrating structural and temporal features with machine-learning-oriented recommendation and toward understanding how network evolution drives emergence, influence, and scientific or social outcomes.

titles<=300|59d5b71ed6297319e6bfae7ceb3d.text:
## Information Retrieval: Neural Ranking, Context, and Interaction

This community centers on improving information retrieval across web, enterprise, e-commerce, biomedical, social-media, mobile, and scholarly settings. Major themes include learning-to-rank and multi-stage retrieval; semantic matching and passage/document re-ranking; query understanding, reformulation, expansion, and suggestion; and entity-, table-, graph-, and knowledge-aware search. Question answering, conversational search, expert and dataset finding, recommendation, and complex answer retrieval form important application areas.

Typical methods combine traditional lexical weighting, relevance feedback, term proximity, and rank aggregation with word/entity embeddings, convolutional and recurrent networks, attention, interaction models, kernel pooling, and listwise or groupwise objectives. BERT and contextual language models increasingly support document and passage ranking. Weak supervision, adversarial training, reinforcement learning, hashing, approximate nearest-neighbor search, and graph embeddings address limited labels and scalability. Evaluation includes TREC-style benchmarks, online interleaving, bandits, counterfactual propensity correction, and specialized relevance, credibility, quality, and robustness measures.

Recent work emphasizes unbiased and counterfactual learning from logs, personalization and session context, conversational and proactive retrieval, explainable and interpretable neural ranking, knowledge-rich representations, and joint search–recommendation optimization. Applications increasingly target specialized collections, long-tail entities, scientific literature, tables, archives, health, and real-time event streams.

titles<=300|3aa934d4c8870819a50b32f24af4.text:
## Graph Learning for Dynamic and Heterogeneous Networks

This community focuses on understanding, representing, and predicting structure in large-scale social, information, citation, and financial networks. Major themes include network and node embeddings, link prediction, community detection, role and core–periphery identification, centrality, anomaly and fraud detection, and signed or multiplex network analysis. Temporal networks receive substantial attention, including evolving communities, dynamic stochastic blockmodels, temporal motifs, change-point detection, and time-aware link prediction.

Typical methods combine random walks, matrix factorization, spectral techniques, latent-space and blockmodel formulations, graph grammars, and probabilistic generative models. More recent work applies graph neural networks, attention, adversarial learning, multimodal fusion, and heterogeneous meta-path representations. Motif, wedge, truss, and graphlet statistics support higher-order structural analysis, while sampling, sparsification, indexing, and distributed algorithms address massive graphs.

Applications include recommendations, knowledge-graph reasoning, scholarly and product discovery, social status and tie-strength inference, spam and insider-trading detection, money laundering, and network alignment. Recent trends emphasize scalable and streaming analysis, temporal and higher-order representations, robustness against attacks and missing data, privacy and fairness, and unified evaluation frameworks for graph embeddings and link prediction.

titles<=300|0fb47680dbcac8375cf6f8869a09.text:
## Network Dynamics, Influence, and Scalable Graph Analysis

This community studies how information, opinions, influence, and epidemics propagate through social and other complex networks. A major theme is opinion and belief dynamics: consensus, disagreement, polarization, social balance, homophily, stubborn agents, biased assimilation, backfire effects, susceptibility, thresholds, and discrepancies between private and expressed opinions. Signed and time-varying networks receive particular attention, including state-flipping and relative-state models, interdependent topics, and evolving social power.

A second theme concerns measuring and optimizing network structure. The papers develop and axiomatize centrality measures based on degree, betweenness, random walks, current flow, accessibility, absorbing walks, and information; they also address node discovery, navigability, backbone extraction, edge addition, network obfuscation, and influence estimation from partial observations. Diffusion and epidemic control include relationship removal, spectral-radius reduction, edge recommendation, filtering, and characterization of multi-agent processes.

Typical methods are Markov chains, random walks with restart, matrix and dynamical-systems analysis, stochastic and threshold models, optimization, sampling, greedy and approximation algorithms, and graph-theoretic inference. Recent trends emphasize billion-scale computation, dynamic graphs, scalable personalization, online collective behavior, recommender feedback loops, active sensing, knowledge segregation, and practical web crawling and change detection.

titles<=300|4ec911ba55c8f9d24743eff30142.text:
## Scalable Data Management, Query Processing, and Analytics

This community focuses on building scalable systems and theory for querying, integrating, and analyzing relational, graph, array, document, and streaming data. A central theme is efficient join processing: worst-case-optimal, multiway, geometric, trie-based, skew-aware, and factorized joins, supported by bounds based on functional dependencies, hypertree decompositions, entropy, and submodular width. Query optimization includes cost-based planning, adaptive indexing, operator reordering and fusion, physical design, materialized-view selection, and incremental maintenance.

Graph data receives extensive attention through relational graph engines, graph pattern matching, subgraph search, triangle enumeration, dynamic and historical graphs, graph streams, and distributed graph analytics. Systems such as EmptyHeaded, Ringo, Pregelix, AsterixDB, and Vertica illustrate efforts to unify declarative databases with graph and large-scale computation.

Other recurring methods include approximate query processing, sketches, sampling, probabilistic databases, factor graphs, compression, and progressive visualization for interactive exploration. The community also develops database-centric machine learning, including relational learning, feature engineering, declarative ML workflows, and in-database inference.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and streaming workloads, cloud and heterogeneous hardware, high-speed networks, adaptive and learned optimization, collaborative/versioned data management, privacy and security, and tighter integration of databases with machine learning and visual analytics.

titles<=300|054f3e20a7aea3243e48961131d5.text:
## Data Management at Scale: Learning, Concurrency, and Scientific Infrastructure

This community spans scalable database systems for analytical, transactional, spatial, scientific, and blockchain workloads. A central theme is **learning-augmented data management**: deep learning and reinforcement learning are used for cardinality estimation, join ordering, query optimization, workload re-optimization, buffer management, indexes, and visual exploration. Generative models support approximate query processing and data synthesis.

Another major focus is **high-performance and distributed transaction processing**, including multicore OLTP, contention-aware scheduling and partitioning, MVCC, serializability, snapshot isolation, replication, recovery, and predictable latency. Work on cloud and multitenant systems explores elasticity, availability, consistency trade-offs, and distributed data placement.

The papers also address **scientific and spatial data infrastructures**, with astronomy serving as a recurring application domain. Methods include relational and array databases, probabilistic joins, spatial and multidimensional indexes, hierarchical triangular meshes, metadata management, and open-data practices.

A growing theme is **blockchain as a data-management platform**, covering consistency, verifiable queries, execution, interoperability, and architectural analysis. Recent directions emphasize learned indexes and optimizers, autonomous administration, HTAP and IoT systems, energy-efficient databases, visual/neural data management, and stronger integration between databases, reproducible science, and open research infrastructures.

titles<=300|c278924a1f2b3c691dc6cc69f8af.text:
## Utility-Oriented Sequential Pattern Mining

This community focuses on discovering valuable rather than merely frequent patterns in sequential data. Core themes include high-utility episode and sequence discovery, utility mining across multiple or multidimensional sequences, and utility-driven trend analysis for intelligent systems.

Typical methods emphasize utility-based pattern evaluation, including projection-based mining (ProUM), item-specific or individualized minimum-utility thresholds, and approaches designed for complex sequences. The collection also addresses practical constraints and data characteristics through parallel sequential pattern mining, privacy-preserving utility mining, and mining over uncertain data.

Survey papers consolidate the foundations of utility-oriented pattern mining, privacy-preserving techniques, and parallel sequential mining, while the research papers extend utility analysis beyond conventional frequency-based measures. Overall, the field is trending toward more flexible and realistic settings: varied thresholds across items or sequences, multiple data dimensions and sequence collections, uncertainty-aware analytics, scalable parallel processing, and extraction of trends with direct relevance to intelligent systems.

titles<=300|1f3603a13af051e669eb432d54b0.text:
### Unbiased and Counterfactual Learning for Ranking Evaluation

This community focuses on making ranking and recommender-system learning and evaluation reliable despite biased user feedback. A central theme is modeling position and examination bias, including methods for estimating bias without intrusive interventions and through intervention harvesting. Several works develop unbiased learning-to-rank algorithms, spanning pairwise approaches such as Unbiased LambdaMART and counterfactual methods for additive metrics and deep models.

The papers use a range of methods: bias-aware statistical estimation, counterfactual learning, pairwise ranking algorithms, deep reinforcement learning for sponsored-search strategy optimization, and comparative evaluation of ranking functions. Evaluation is considered both offline and online, including studies of small e-commerce systems and active sampling for large-scale information-retrieval assessment.

The community also addresses data collection: preference-elicitation interfaces aim to create dense recommender datasets enriched with user information. Overall, the research trends toward reducing dependence on biased implicit feedback, estimating bias with fewer or no intrusive interventions, extending unbiased objectives to deep and metric-specific models, and improving the scalability and realism of ranking evaluation.

titles<=300|0ba95505f94e805f65f7ef09967f.text:
### Web-Scale Table Search and Data-Lake Organization

This community focuses on making heterogeneous web and data-lake content comparable, searchable, and navigable. A central theme is answering table-oriented queries when schemas are incomplete or absent: systems use column keywords, keyword composition, and discovered dependencies to identify relevant tables and assemble answers. Related work studies how to organize data lakes and optimize their structure for effective exploration and navigation.

Typical methods include knowledge-base pattern discovery, keyword-based table retrieval, schema-free query processing over document tables, and locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) ensembles for internet-scale domain search. Together, these approaches emphasize scalable indexing and search across loosely structured collections rather than reliance on fixed schemas.

Recent trends move toward schemaless and dependency-aware querying, broader integration of web tables with data lakes, and organizational techniques that support efficient human or system navigation. Overall, the papers suggest a progression from defining comparable web information and retrieving tables toward large-scale, structured access to heterogeneous repositories.

titles<=300|9ec9fc426e7d05d7d1502813899f.text:
### Knowledge Compilation, Width, and Exact Query Counting

This community studies the structural and computational foundations of knowledge compilation for model counting and database queries. A central theme is the relationship between compilation classes and width parameters: the papers connect knowledge-compilation guarantees to structural properties of instances and clarify how width governs tractability. Another major focus is exact model counting, including lower bounds and their consequences for probabilistic databases. The work also examines query expressions, emphasizing limitations that arise when database problems are treated solely through propositional methods.

Typical methods are theoretical: relating circuit representations to width measures, proving complexity lower bounds, analyzing the expressive limits of propositional encodings, and developing decomposable circuit constructions. The papers particularly emphasize deterministic decomposable circuits and their applicability to safe queries.

Overall, the research trends from foundational correspondences between compilation classes and structural width, through impossibility results for exact counting, toward more database-aware circuit frameworks. This suggests a shift from simply compiling queries propositionally to identifying structural conditions and circuit representations that support reliable, tractable counting.

titles<=300|be1dc573f37fdf1d7fd542ede5a7.text:
### Context-Aware Recommendation and Venue Ranking

This community focuses on personalized recommendation of points of interest (POIs) and venues, extending collaborative filtering beyond conventional matrix factorization. Core themes include exploiting context, time, location, social signals, and venue categories to improve ranking quality and address users’ changing preferences.

Typical methods formulate recommendation as personalized or collaborative ranking rather than explicit rating prediction. They incorporate multiple location-based similarities, social-centric scores, temporal regularization, and category-aware location embeddings. Several works use multi-stage or two-phase models, suggesting separate treatment of preference learning and time-sensitive ranking. Metric factorization represents a broader methodological direction for modeling interactions with richer relational structure than standard matrix factorization.

The research progresses from general context-aware venue recommendation toward increasingly structured representations of place and user behavior. Location is modeled not only through geographic similarity but also through learned embeddings and multiple complementary similarities. Time-sensitive collaborative ranking captures temporal dynamics, while social information provides additional signals for venue suggestion. Overall, the papers indicate a trend toward combining collaborative, geographic, contextual, temporal, categorical, and social evidence in unified personalized ranking systems.

titles<=300|55fe4777487030b9736ccd131138.text:
### Big-Data Benchmarking and Synthetic Workloads

This community focuses on evaluating big-data systems through representative, scalable, and configurable workloads. Its main themes include benchmark-suite design, distributed stream-processing performance, and synthetic data generation. Several papers present benchmark suites derived from internet services and web-search engines, aiming to capture realistic application and data characteristics. Others address benchmarking distributed stream-processing engines and systems, emphasizing comparative evaluation of their behavior under streaming workloads.

Typical methods include constructing workload suites, generating large synthetic datasets, and running controlled experiments across distributed processing platforms. A dedicated tool framework supports feature-level modification of synthetic datasets, enabling researchers to tune workload characteristics for different benchmarking scenarios. The BDGS work emphasizes scalable generation, while BigDataBench emphasizes benchmarks grounded in real-world service and search-engine patterns.

The recent direction represented by these papers is toward more systematic and reproducible evaluation: combining realistic application-inspired benchmarks with scalable synthetic generation and configurable dataset features. Streaming systems receive particular attention, suggesting growing interest in performance evaluation for continuous, distributed data processing rather than only batch-oriented big-data workloads.

titles<=300|0728eb290a952db094f31a6c3296.text:
### Social Similarity and Mobile Friend Recommendation

This community studies how social and behavioral information can support user similarity estimation and friend or content recommendation. Key data sources include publicly disclosed Facebook profiles, texting data, and interactions among users in physical proximity. The papers explore both latent similarity—inferring commonalities from communication behavior—and explicit or psychologically grounded similarity for recommending friends.

Typical methods involve analyzing user profiles, comparing patterns in text messaging, estimating similarity in proximity-based mobile social networks, and incorporating psychometric characteristics into recommendation models. Several works emphasize decentralized or collaborative systems, where nearby users contribute to recommendations without relying entirely on centralized infrastructure.

A clear trend is the progression from analyzing static, publicly available social information toward richer behavioral and contextual signals, especially communication patterns and physical proximity. The community also moves toward more personalized recommendations by combining social similarity with psychological traits, while investigating mobile and decentralized settings for real-world, user-collaborative recommendation.

titles<=300|65430f8598bcc2a4da98880a60ce.text:
### Multimodal Representation Learning for Retrieval and Music Understanding

This community focuses on learning shared, discriminative representations across modalities for efficient semantic retrieval. A major theme is **cross-modal retrieval and hashing**, including deep cross-modal hashing, decorrelated codes, triplet-based objectives, joint embeddings, and discriminative semantic representations. These methods aim to align heterogeneous data while supporting compact retrieval codes.

Music-oriented work applies multimodal learning to **audio, lyrics, genres, and recommendation**. Hierarchical and self-attentive networks are used for lyrics-based genre classification and content-based feature exploration, while deep correlation learning connects audio and lyrics for music retrieval. Another direction incorporates EEG regularizers to improve the modeling of music semantics.

Typical methods include deep neural networks, attention mechanisms, metric-learning objectives, correlation learning, shared embedding spaces, and hashing-based indexing. The papers also explore unsupervised learning, notably through a coupled CycleGAN hashing network, reducing dependence on paired or labeled data.

Overall, the research trends from basic cross-modal alignment toward more discriminative, compact, interpretable, and weakly or unsupervised representations, with increasing emphasis on semantic understanding and practical multimedia retrieval.

titles<=300|410f35c0f866075a59ae8c63c321.text:
**Adversarial Attacks and Defenses in Social-Network Inference**

This community studies how graph-analysis algorithms can be manipulated to obscure or distort network structure. A central theme is attacking community detection and link prediction, particularly when these tasks rely on node-similarity measures. The papers examine genetic-algorithm-based attacks on community detection, manipulation of similarity scores, and attacks designed to reduce the ability of link-prediction algorithms to infer hidden relationships. A related concern is attack tolerance: how users can hide their social relations from inference in a network.

Typical methods are adversarial graph perturbations, manipulation of node similarities or links, and evolutionary or genetic search procedures for selecting effective changes. The work treats privacy protection as a strategic problem against algorithms that reconstruct missing or concealed connections.

A notable trend is the shift from studying offensive attacks and their effectiveness toward targeted defense. In particular, evolutionary perturbations are used not only to attack link prediction but also to defend selected targets against link-prediction-based attacks. Overall, the papers trace an arms race between structural manipulation, privacy-preserving concealment, and algorithmically optimized defense.

titles<=300|c5852a70a24b9973e19bcfc23c26.text:
## Information Retrieval: Neural Ranking, Context, and Conversational Search

This community centers on improving information retrieval across web, enterprise, biomedical, e-commerce, academic, mobile, and social-media settings. Major themes include relevance ranking and passage retrieval; query understanding, expansion, reformulation, and intent detection; personalization and recommendation; entity, table, dataset, and expert retrieval; conversational and question-answering systems; and web-content quality, spam, credibility, and adversarial robustness.

Typical methods combine learning-to-rank, pairwise/listwise/groupwise optimization, ranking aggregation, axiomatic regularization, and online or counterfactual learning from clicks and logs. Neural approaches use CNNs, RNNs, attention, interaction architectures, kernel pooling, Siamese or dual embeddings, and BERT-based contextual representations. Weak supervision, pseudo-relevance feedback, word/entity embeddings, knowledge graphs, graph models, reinforcement learning, adversarial training, hashing, and approximate nearest-neighbor search support scalable retrieval. Evaluation emphasizes TREC-style benchmarks, ranking metrics, unbiased online experimentation, multileaving, interpretability, and efficiency.

Recent work shifts from keyword matching toward deep semantic and contextual ranking, especially BERT passage/document re-ranking and knowledge-enhanced retrieval. There is growing focus on conversational search, session context, proactive recommendations, complex and non-factoid answers, and query reformulation. Parallel trends address deployment concerns: scalable production systems, privacy-preserving learning, weakly supervised data, fairness/unbiased evaluation, explainability, robustness, and combining search with recommendation.

titles<=300|188ab2a8137b2a9eb2b77dadf76f.text:
### Web Tables, Knowledge Bases, and Data-Lake Search

This community studies how to organize, discover, and query heterogeneous web and document tables at scale. A central theme is establishing uniform definitions for comparable and searchable web information, enabling table search and structured retrieval. Several works focus on answering table queries through column keywords, keywords that compose table answers, and schemaless queries over document tables with dependencies. Knowledge bases support both pattern discovery and automatic table completion, linking incomplete tabular content with existing structured information.

A second theme concerns data-lake management: organizing large collections and optimizing their structure for efficient navigation. At internet scale, locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) ensembles are used for domain search, suggesting an emphasis on approximate, scalable retrieval rather than exhaustive comparison.

Overall, the research trends from foundational web-table comparability toward integrated systems for semantic search, query answering, completion, and data-lake navigation. Typical methods combine keywords, dependencies, knowledge-base patterns, hashing-based indexing, and organizational strategies for heterogeneous, schemaless data.

titles<=300|176f316568aa0a33f8b1198049d9.text:
## Learning-Centric, Distributed Data Management

This community spans database systems, scientific data infrastructures, and emerging blockchain databases. Major themes include scalable OLTP/HTAP, multicore and main-memory execution, distributed transactions, replication, recovery, concurrency control, partitioning, and cloud storage. Query processing is another core focus, particularly cardinality/selectivity estimation, join ordering, indexing, spatial search, approximate processing, and workload-driven re-optimization.

A defining methodological trend is learned data management. Papers apply deep learning, Bayesian models, mixture models, generative models, embeddings, and deep reinforcement learning to cardinality estimation, cost modeling, query optimization, partitioning, index construction, buffer management, scheduling, view materialization, and database administration. Learned indexes and adaptive structures are evaluated through specialized benchmarks and performance-oriented system designs.

The community also develops systems for scientific and geospatial workloads, including astronomy archives, metadata management, spatial indexing, visual exploration, data integration, and reproducible/open science infrastructures. Blockchain research addresses verifiable queries, auditability, consensus, sharding, interoperability, and blockchainified database systems.

Recent work increasingly combines machine learning with self-managing databases, predictable latency, energy efficiency, and approximate analytics. Transaction research emphasizes high contention, multiversion consistency, scalable distributed recovery, asynchronous replication, and heterogeneous hardware. Blockchain databases and cross-system data access represent a growing intersection between distributed database principles and decentralized infrastructures.

titles<=300|f9f1e1303604fcdc7735cb4c5a8a.text:
### Computational Analysis of Narrative Character Networks

This community studies fictional narratives through networks of characters and their interactions, spanning television series, films, and recurring case studies such as *Game of Thrones* and *Friends*. Core themes include extracting social networks from narrative text, character centrality and group structure, plot evolution, and cast-size organization.

Typical methods include surveys of character-network extraction and analysis, comparisons of alternative narrative social-network extraction techniques, and dynamic or “smoothed” conversational networks for tracking changing relationships across episodes. Network properties are also used predictively, as in forecasting deaths or kills in *Game of Thrones*, while clique analysis examines tightly connected ensembles such as the six central characters in *Friends*. An ecological-modelling perspective is applied to effective cast sizes in films, illustrated through *The Avengers*.

The research appears to be moving from static network description toward methodological validation, temporal modelling, prediction, and modelling narrative ensembles at multiple scales. Overall, the papers combine computational network analysis with close attention to how stories organize characters, interactions, and evolving casts.

titles<=300|0352cbfd7616226f484b69bc1d56.text:
### Personalized and Context-Aware POI Recommendation

This community focuses on recommending points of interest (POIs) and venues through personalized ranking models. A central theme is extending collaborative filtering beyond standard matrix factorization, including metric factorization, logistic matrix factorization, and collaborative ranking approaches.  

Methods incorporate diverse contextual signals: geographic proximity and multiple location-based similarities, temporal dynamics, user context, venue categories, and social information. Local geographical regularization and location embeddings model spatial preferences, while category-aware embeddings capture semantic relationships among venues. Social-centric scores provide an additional basis for venue suggestion.  

The papers also emphasize ranking-oriented objectives rather than only rating prediction. A joint two-phase, time-sensitive regularized collaborative ranking model addresses changing preferences and temporal effects, while personalized context-aware models integrate situational information into venue ranking.  

Overall, the research trends from basic factorization toward richer, multi-signal recommendation systems that combine collaborative behavior with geography, time, categories, context, and social cues. The progression also suggests increasing interest in representation learning and specialized regularization for more personalized and location-sensitive POI recommendation.

titles<=300|fab9dd21604a22fbe408955fd5c9.text:
### Acknowledgements, Collaboration, and Evidence-Based Research Decisions

This community centers on extracting scholarly and organizational insight from funding and acknowledgement data. Several papers characterize funding acknowledgements in Web of Science and examine how acknowledgement-based queries should be designed, emphasizing interpretation challenges and caveats. Another study applies acknowledgement analysis in the humanities to make otherwise invisible forms of contribution and support more visible.

A complementary theme is collaboration measurement: combining authorship with acknowledgements reveals patterns that authorship data alone may miss. Across these studies, typical methods include bibliographic database analysis, structured querying, acknowledgement-text analysis, and comparison of authorship and acknowledgement relationships.

The community also includes a methodological application to R&D project selection. This work uses a data-driven evidential reasoning rule to address decisions involving multiple criteria, extending the broader emphasis on extracting and integrating evidence for evaluation.

Recent directions point toward broader use of acknowledgement data, more cautious and transparent query interpretation, integration of multiple scholarly signals, and data-driven approaches to complex research-management decisions.

titles<=300|0f5bbfa7472cada4212421198d21.text:
### Research Software, Reproducibility, and Scholarly Impact

This community focuses on recognizing, documenting, and evaluating research software within computational science. A central theme is the role of software and its dependencies in research citation graphs, alongside the broader challenge of measuring software impact through conventional citations. The examination of the **lme4** R package illustrates these measurement difficulties at the level of a specific, widely used research tool.

Other papers address the infrastructure and language needed for sustainable, reproducible research. The **Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS)** is discussed through its design and first-year review, while the **ReScience Initiative** represents an approach to sustaining computational science. Work on terminologies for reproducible research highlights the importance of shared concepts and precise vocabulary.

Typical methods include analysis of citation graphs, focused examination of software citation practices, journal design and review assessment, initiative-level discussion, and terminology clarification. Taken together, the papers indicate a trend from treating software as an auxiliary research product toward treating it as a citable, reviewable, reproducible, and sustainable scholarly contribution.

titles<=300|c35a2349fe60d40b3c60c27f4fca.text:
**Scalable Systems for Video Analytics**

This community studies data-management systems for querying and analyzing large-scale visual data, including stored video, streaming cameras, and autonomous-camera deployments. A central theme is making video analytics efficient enough for exploratory and machine-learning workloads without requiring exhaustive processing of every frame.

Typical methods include approximate query processing, neural-network-based video query acceleration, specialized data stores, and access mechanisms designed for large visual datasets. The papers emphasize system-level support for efficient retrieval and analytics rather than treating video solely as raw media.

Collectively, the work moves from standalone querying toward integrated infrastructure: systems that manage visual data, support machine-learning workloads, and operate over continuously arriving camera streams. Approximation and model-based processing emerge as practical ways to reduce the cost of exploratory queries, while dedicated storage and access layers address scale. The recent direction is toward unified platforms capable of serving both historical video analytics and real-time or streaming-camera queries.

titles<=300|fbed98d108f5cf1d1e5b221ed231.text:
### Learning and Evaluating Ranking Systems Under Bias

This community focuses on reliable ranking for search, advertising, and recommendation systems. Key themes include optimizing sponsored-search rankings with deep reinforcement learning; estimating and correcting position or examination bias; counterfactual learning to rank; and unbiased comparative evaluation of ranking functions.

Typical methods combine interventions and intervention harvesting to identify context-dependent examination behavior, alongside approaches that estimate position bias without intrusive interventions. Counterfactual learning methods target additive ranking metrics and extend to deep models. Evaluation is treated as a sampling problem, with active sampling proposed for large-scale information-retrieval experiments. The community also addresses data collection through preference-elicitation interfaces designed to gather dense recommender datasets enriched with user information.

Recent trends point toward less intrusive and more scalable evaluation, replacing or complementing explicit interventions with observational and counterfactual techniques. At the same time, ranking optimization is becoming more adaptive through deep reinforcement learning, while evaluation and dataset construction increasingly emphasize efficiency, user context, and reduced bias.

titles<=300|b958327072722835515dd55a51e7.text:
### Network Representation Learning and Evolving Graph Analysis

This community centers on extracting structure, semantics, and dynamics from large-scale social, information, biological, financial, and web graphs.
