This community focuses on building high-performance data systems for increasingly large, dynamic, and heterogeneous workloads. Major themes include parallel and distributed query processing; worst-case-optimal, multiway, geometric, and skew-aware joins; cardinality estimation and cost-based optimization; and materialized-view maintenance, factorization, compression, and adaptive indexing. Graph analytics and graph streams are prominent, including pattern matching, triangle counting, graph search, visualization, and relational engines for graph processing. Other recurring areas include main-memory OLTP, concurrency control, recovery, replication, consistency, cloud elasticity, and energy-efficient infrastructure.

Typical methods combine theoretical complexity and size bounds with systems research and experimental benchmarking. Common techniques include MapReduce, dataflow and shared-nothing architectures, multicore and GPU execution, sampling and sketches, approximate query processing, static analysis, code generation, and incremental maintenance. Machine learning is increasingly used for cardinality estimation, workload management, query optimization, data cleaning, and visual exploration, including deep learning and reinforcement learning.

Recent trends emphasize learned and autonomic database components, interactive and progressive analytics, unified relational/array/graph processing, streaming and evolving data, collaborative provenance and versioning, and resource-aware execution across heterogeneous hardware and cloud environments.

titles<=300|0bcb7fa91e04c588f30d214976c4.text:
## Social Networks, Influence, and Polarization

This community studies how social networks shape opinions, choices, information diffusion, and collective behavior. Major themes include consensus, disagreement, polarization, social balance, influence, and opinion evolution—often with signed, heterogeneous, dynamic, or multilayer interactions. A related stream examines controversy, partisan slant, echo chambers, ideological segregation, and exposure to contrarian content on Twitter, Facebook, and other social media.

Other work addresses recommendation and competitive diffusion, including product choice, popularity bias, social ties, privacy-preserving influence, information multiplicity, and causal evaluation of recommender systems. Network structure and infrastructure are also central: link prediction, backbone and event discovery, crawling, navigability, node criticality, communicability, accessibility, and numerous centrality measures.

Typical methods combine dynamical-systems and Markovian models (DeGroot, Friedkin–Johnsen, bounded-confidence, threshold, Bayesian, and fluid models) with signed-network analysis and stochastic processes. Algorithmic approaches include spectral embedding, random walks, randomized shortest paths, matrix formulations, sampling, nonnegative matrix factorization, greedy and approximation algorithms, genetic optimization, and network design or edge modification.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes evolving and topic-specific social media, empirical measurement of controversy and political discourse, scalable graph algorithms, privacy and intervention, causal recommendation analysis, and controlling polarization, epidemics, diffusion, and information exposure.

titles<=300|de5507d51ccc939ecee9e0b27c68.text:
## Algebraic Foundations and High-Performance Big-Data Systems

This community links formal database theory with scalable data-processing infrastructure. A major theme is unifying relational, array, matrix, graph, spreadsheet, SQL, NoSQL, and NewSQL data through associative arrays, LARA, relational lattices, non-distributive lattices, and polystore mathematics. Work also studies query languages and semantics for semi-structured, JSON, visual, tree, MongoDB, and web-extraction data, including Datalog, guarded negation, conjunctive queries, and predicate calculus.

Systems research emphasizes high-throughput ingestion and analytics. D4M and Accumulo support sparse associative-array computation, provenance capture, cyber-data pipelines, and very large insert rates. Graphulo brings server-side sparse matrix multiplication and graph algorithms to BigTable-style databases, while BigSparse targets external graph analytics. BigDAWG develops a polystore architecture spanning heterogeneous engines, with tensor-based models, releases, demonstrations, and on-demand computing through Supercloud. SciDB, Vertica, and LogInson provide additional large-scale database and loading contexts.

Typical methods include algebraic modeling, formal expressiveness and lower-bound analyses, benchmarking, schema and language design, and implementation-driven performance evaluation. Recent trends move toward integrated polystore systems, configurable and semi-structured query languages, tensor and graph processing, cloud/HPC deployment, and increasingly capable D4M releases.

titles<=300|370d566f027578afe2336896f4da.text:
## Reliable, Uncertain, and Integrated Data Management

This community studies how to answer queries and maintain data quality when databases are incomplete, inconsistent, uncertain, heterogeneous, or crowd-generated. Major themes include probabilistic databases and uncertain data; data integration, fusion, truth discovery, and source reliability; entity resolution and matching dependencies; integrity constraints, repairs, and consistent query answering; and provenance, causality, diagnosis, explanations, and view updates. Ontology-mediated access, schema mappings, RDF/graph querying, data exchange, and incomplete information form another substantial strand.

Typical methods combine database theory—chase procedures, Datalog, constraint reasoning, repair semantics, complexity dichotomies, finite controllability, and knowledge compilation—with probabilistic inference, Bayesian and Markov models, belief propagation, provenance circuits, and approximation algorithms. Systems work emphasizes relational implementations, parallel and cloud processing, query optimization, blocking, transfer learning, active learning, and human-in-the-loop cleaning. Crowdsourcing is used for entity matching, labeling, truth assessment, joins, routing, and task assignment, often with quality and reliability models.

Recent work trends toward scalable, practical systems for massive probabilistic and linked data, holistic and deep-learning-assisted cleaning, human–machine cooperation, cloud-aware reproducible workflows, graph and RDF integration, causal and “why/why-not” explanations, and unified approaches connecting uncertainty, provenance, repairs, and knowledge fusion.

titles<=300|cc3e50c97dd1948bcb0914c82aa8.text:
## Social, Semantic, and Preference-Aware Data Search

This community studies intelligent search and ranking across relational, web, RDF, XML, social, and hidden databases. Major themes include top-*k*, skyline, preference, and aggregate queries; efficient query processing and optimization; semantic integration using Wiktionary, WordNet, Wikipedia, ontologies, and linked open data; and indexing or summarizing large, distributed, and streaming collections.

A second strong theme is collaborative tagging and folksonomies. Papers analyze vocabulary growth, tag similarity and hierarchies, semantic coverage, user attention, influence, expertise, and the evolution of classification systems. Related work investigates social search, microblogging behavior, complex networks, location forecasting, and information diffusion.

Typical methods include graph and network analysis, machine learning for query planning, reranking, entity resolution, and blocking, as well as clustering, wavelet and sketch summaries, probabilistic or approximate algorithms, MapReduce, GPU acceleration, encryption, and linear/integer programming. Game-theoretic models also appear in collaboration, querying, and marketplaces.

Recent trends emphasize fairness and diversity in rankings, including exposure, disparate exposure, image fairness, and fair ranking schemes. Other newer directions include privacy-aware social networks, dynamic and hidden-web databases, scalable semantic retrieval, and richer user-preference modeling.

titles<=300|2c8ed99dbafe649e64a24902acf3.text:
## Community Report: Ranking, Search, and Network Intelligence

This community centers on ranking and information retrieval through network science, especially PageRank, Google matrices, centrality, and their extensions. A major empirical domain is Wikipedia: studies rank articles, entities, universities, experts, and multilingual content while examining cultural relations, political leadership, editing behavior, conflict, collective memory, and breaking news. Related work applies network analysis to Twitter, Bitcoin, professional networks, collaborations, street systems, sports, nonprofits, and geopolitics.

Typical methods include spectral analysis of Google matrices, personalized and seeded PageRank, reduced Google matrices, Ulam networks, centrality and subgraph-walk measures, graphons, clustering, randomization, temporal modeling, and critical-node detection. Information-retrieval studies use learning-to-rank, query expansion, federated and personalized search, XML databases, entity linking, clickthrough logs, relevance assessment, and user studies. Text and multimedia retrieval incorporate lexical, semantic, sentiment, visual, graph, WordNet, and Wikipedia features.

Recent directions emphasize temporal and dynamic networks, multilingual and cross-cultural entity ranking, fair and credibility-aware ranking, deep ranking models, large-scale expertise discovery, and low-cost evaluation. Wikipedia increasingly functions as both a searchable knowledge base and a sensor for social dynamics, news, norms, and collective behavior.

titles<=300|a245b5f09901616a659f726d8837.text:
### Scholarly Information Networks and Bibliometric Retrieval

This community studies scholarly communication as an interconnected information, collaboration, and knowledge infrastructure. Major themes include author-name disambiguation and identity resolution; coauthorship, citation, and impact analysis; academic expert and researcher recommendation; and bibliometric enhancement of information retrieval. Researchers also examine digital-library search behavior, query and term suggestion, thesaurus and terminology mapping, personalization, relevance assessment, and interactive visualization.

Typical methods combine bibliometric and network analysis—centrality, PageRank, clustering, longitudinal and multilayer-network models—with information-retrieval techniques such as query expansion, learning to rank, rank aggregation, semantic similarity, and citation-network exploitation. Large-scale deduplication and disambiguation use blocking, coauthor networks, semi-supervised learning, and deep neural networks. Studies frequently rely on DBLP, arXiv, Web of Science, Scopus, social-science search logs, and other harvested open data, alongside user studies and evaluation test collections.

Recent trends emphasize scalable and data-aware analysis, richer author identifiers and metadata enrichment, science models for contextualized browsing, and interactive visual search. The literature increasingly treats retrieval as a socio-technical practice, integrating social networks, semantic multiplexes, research data archives, open-science tools, and recommender systems. Attention is also shifting toward reproducibility, data reuse, text reuse and plagiarism detection, and measuring usefulness in real search sessions.

titles<=300|afe00c24cea44033f7a1a4b1a11c.text:
**Differential Privacy and Privacy-Preserving Data Analysis**

This community centers on differential privacy (DP) for releasing, querying, and mining sensitive data. Major themes include accurate range, histogram, datacube, contingency-table, and high-dimensional query answering; private data publishing and anonymization; and privacy-preserving mining, classification, regression, frequent-itemset and graph-pattern discovery. Applications cover search logs, mobility and trajectories, spatial data, smart devices, recommendations, social networks, and provenance views.

Typical methods include hierarchical decompositions (PrivTree and spatial variants), wavelet transforms, multidimensional partitioning, consistency postprocessing, matrix and low-rank mechanisms, convex optimization, adaptive and workload-aware query answering, and local DP. Researchers also study composition, sparse-vector variants, approximate versus exact DP, privacy-budget selection, and policy-aware mechanisms such as Blowfish. Anonymization work addresses background knowledge, reconstruction, adversarial information fusion, record linkage, and privacy breaches, alongside formal guarantees including \(k\)-anonymity and \(l\)-diversity.

Recent directions emphasize utility and scalability for high-dimensional and batch workloads, end-to-end parameter tuning, modular and reusable frameworks (Ektelo, DPBench), and local DP for decentralized collection. Other emerging concerns are temporal correlation, semantic and provenance guarantees, discrimination prevention, Bayesian inference, and balancing individual versus population privacy.

titles<=300|93ab66471f5798a44b791a1a1cd4.text:
## Scientometrics, Research Assessment, and Academic Inequality

This community focuses on measuring and explaining research performance, especially in the Italian university and higher-education system. Major themes include institutional, national, regional, disciplinary, and individual productivity; university rankings; research funding and efficiency; peer review versus bibliometrics; and the consequences of national assessment exercises such as VQR and scientific habilitation.

Typical methods combine publication and citation indicators, field and time normalization, fractional and author-order counting, highly cited researcher measures, h- and g-indexes, and statistical or stochastic productivity models. Data-envelopment analysis, non-parametric efficiency estimation, regression, clustering, network analysis, funnel plots, and sensitivity analyses are widely used. Several studies address author-name disambiguation, uncertainty, citation-window effects, ranking distortions, and opportunistic behavior.

A second major strand examines collaboration, interdisciplinarity, internationalization, university–industry links, technology transfer, team size, and the relationship between collaboration and impact. Gender inequalities receive sustained attention through analyses of authorship, recruitment, careers, collaboration, and the contribution of star scientists. Other work studies age, seniority, academic rank, migration, nepotism, and regional divides.

Recent directions emphasize fairer, uncertainty-aware, field-sensitive evaluation; alternative counting and scaling rules; territorial and institutional benchmarking; and the risks of simplistic performance-based funding and composite indicators.

titles<=300|591f8c3e27f734a616a11bd4058a.text:
### Empirical Methods for Legal Review and Cybersecurity Forensics

This community focuses on empirical applications of machine learning and information-retrieval techniques to legal document review, with a related interest in analytics for cybersecurity forensics. Core themes include comparing machine-learning and keyword-based approaches for prioritizing documents, applying deep learning to legal text classification, and improving predictive coding effectiveness.

Typical methods are experimental evaluations on document-review tasks, comparing alternative models, keyword methodologies, active-learning strategies, and preprocessing parameters. The studies emphasize measurable effectiveness rather than purely theoretical contributions, examining how model choice, iterative labeling, and text preparation influence review outcomes.

Recent trends include movement from traditional keyword search toward deep learning and predictive coding, while retaining interest in active learning to reduce annotation effort and improve classification. Another trend is systematic analysis of preprocessing choices, recognizing that pipeline configuration can substantially affect results. Beyond legal review, the use of Google Analytics for cybersecurity forensics suggests growing attention to applying operational web analytics and data-driven investigation techniques in security contexts.

titles<=300|ea2f1da4e8d48b90359d0d5404af.text:
**High-Performance Data Management for Scientific, Spatial, and Collaborative Analytics**

This community focuses on scalable data systems that make large scientific, spatial, textual, and social datasets queryable and interactive. Major themes include multidimensional and relational OLAP, scientific metadata and event processing, astronomical data services, spatial indexing and cross-matching, graph and cohort analytics, and collaborative information seeking.

Typical methods emphasize compact representation and hardware-conscious execution: bitmap, Huffman, VByte, and integer compression; Roaring bitmaps; SIMD, CPU/GPU hybrid processing, and vectorized decoding; cache-aware and in-memory analytics; relational backends for arrays and finite-element data; and specialized indexes such as HTM, spatial trees, universal indexes, and repetitive-string structures. Query optimization includes view-size estimation, column/row reordering, histogram-aware sorting, adaptive or query-driven algorithm selection, and multi-stage retrieval tradeoffs. Distributed dataflow, batch processing, probabilistic joins, and cloud systems support scale.

Recent work trends toward petabyte- and exascale scientific management, trillion-cell interaction, low-latency event analysis, real-time and in-memory SQL, and highly repetitive or compressed data. Alongside performance engineering, the community increasingly studies user groups, collaboration, query variation, and systems that enable nonexperts to explore complex data.

titles<=300|3d991a42b891e536bbd48f86f182.text:
### Complex Event Processing for Streaming and IoT

This community focuses on detecting, querying, and interpreting meaningful patterns in high-volume event streams, particularly for sensor networks, RFID systems, and the Internet of Things. Core research addresses the foundations of complex event processing (CEP), the SASE model, and a vision for consistent stream processing over time.

Typical methods include event-pattern languages and query plans, automata-based detection—especially lazy chain automata—join-query optimization, and distributed inference and query processing. These techniques aim to reduce computation while preserving timely and semantically meaningful results. Load shedding is explored as a resource-management strategy for handling overload in CEP systems.

The papers also emphasize a data-centric view of IoT, where heterogeneous observations are transformed into higher-level events and used for tracking and monitoring. Overall, the research trends from foundational models and formal processing mechanisms toward scalable, distributed, and adaptive stream analytics. Efficiency, consistency, optimization, and robust operation under continuous and potentially overloaded data flows are recurring priorities.

titles<=300|9d228dc923e71388a062c3487354.text:
### Social Diffusion, Influence, and Online Popularity

This community studies how information, opinions, behaviors, rumors, and products spread through social and socio-physical networks. Major themes include influence maximization and viral marketing; diffusion-source localization and network inference from partial cascades; popularity, hashtag, video, and topic lifecycle prediction; opinion dynamics, complex contagion, and competing cascades; and the effects of communities, geography, attention, emotions, and network structure. Applications span Twitter, YouTube, Reddit, Facebook, crowdfunding, mobile sensing, disasters, health, advertising, and misinformation.

Typical methods combine epidemic, SI/SIR, Bass, logistic, point-process, Hawkes, survival, and stochastic-differential models with graph algorithms for centrality, submodular optimization, sampling, network design, and source detection. Bayesian inference, sparse recovery, causal analysis, polling, agent-based simulation, and temporal or multiplex network models are also prominent. Machine-learning approaches increasingly use recurrent and attention-based deep models, latent-factor methods, multimodal content features, and contrastive training for cascade and popularity prediction.

Recent work emphasizes adaptive, online, robust, and nonstationary influence optimization; real-time prediction; partial observability and hidden nodes; privacy-compliant estimation; misinformation mitigation; higher-order and competitive diffusion; and integrating social, topical, temporal, geographic, behavioral, and visual signals.

titles<=300|3b3a55f6aabf539b6bbd91fae7ef.text:
### Scientometrics, Research Evaluation, and Mapping Science

This community focuses on measuring, visualizing, and explaining scholarly and technological activity. Major themes include citation-based evaluation of journals, articles, researchers, institutions, and countries; critiques and extensions of the journal impact factor, h-index, SNIP, CWTS indicators, I3, percentile measures, and newer prestige, diversity, creativity, and contextual-impact metrics. A recurring concern is fairness: field and time normalization, fractional counting, multiple authorship, uncertainty, statistical significance, interdisciplinarity, and differences between clinical and basic research.

Typical methods include co-citation, bibliographic coupling, co-authorship and journal–journal citation networks; science-overlay maps; clustering and community detection; RPYS and algorithmic historiography; text mining and visualization; regression, simulation, bootstrap, and distributional modeling; author disambiguation; and citation prediction using neural networks. Studies frequently compare Web of Science, Scopus, Microsoft Academic, Dimensions, Mendeley, and F1000 data.

Recent trends emphasize open and alternative data, full-text and semantic indicators, AI-assisted classification and summarization, interactive maps, research recommender systems, and prediction of breakthroughs or future performance. The literature also increasingly examines globalization, collaboration diversity, gender, funding, peer review, university rankings, technology transfer, patents, and the unintended effects of research assessment systems.

titles<=300|f69a5c10ea52d5d707edf4e95970.text:
## Dynamic Mining of Social, Scholarly, and Spatial Data

This community studies methods for extracting evolving knowledge from large-scale text, social-media, scholarly, and geospatial data. A major theme is **dynamic topic discovery**, including hierarchical, continuous-time, coupled, author–topic, limited-attention, and feature-conditioned LDA models. These methods track emerging topics, trends, communities, and links across document streams.

A second focus is **real-time event and disease surveillance**. Twitter and news are mined for sports events, disasters, epidemics, public sentiment, breaking news, and localized bursts. Spatial-textual clustering, semantic filtering, incremental learning, interaction graphs, and timeline generation support detection and situational awareness.

The community also addresses **scholarly information extraction and recommendation**: citation and text-reuse analysis, author contributions, metadata and reference parsing, hypothesis generation, semantic publishing, knowledge graphs, and personalized paper or related-article recommendation. Wikipedia is used for multilingual growth, timelines, navigation analysis, hyperlink completion, and disease monitoring.

Typical methods combine Bayesian generative models, matrix/tensor factorization, graph algorithms, Markov chains, density-based clustering, submodular optimization, probabilistic reasoning, and neural embeddings. Recent directions emphasize scalable distributed processing, continuous-time and online inference, deep learning for indexing and clustering, user-level modeling, and integration of content, links, behavior, and spatial-temporal signals.

titles<=300|591e72055ccd508531066ebb5149.text:
## Community Detection and Network Structure

This community centers on detecting, evaluating, and interpreting mesoscale structure in complex networks. Major themes include disjoint, overlapping, fuzzy, hierarchical, role-based, core–periphery, link, bipartite, attributed, directed, multilayer, and temporal communities. Applications span social media, mobile-phone and criminal networks, scientific literature, biological and neuronal systems, web services, urban networks, and epidemic control.

Typical methods include modularity and its multislice, adaptive, surprise- and likelihood-based variants; spectral and matrix-factorization approaches; stochastic block and mixed-membership models; label propagation (including LabelRank, SLPA, and role-based variants); random walks, personalized PageRank, heat kernels, diffusion, Markov stability, and flow methods; local seed expansion, conductance optimization, truss and dense-subgraph methods; and scalable parallel, streaming, distributed, and MapReduce algorithms. Graph embeddings, manifold learning, tensor methods, and ensemble optimization extend these techniques to heterogeneous data.

Evaluation is a major concern, with work on quality functions, detectability and phase transitions, ground truth, benchmarking, overlapping-community agreement, stability, and visualization. Recent trends emphasize dynamic and multilayer networks, real-time event and community tracking, attributed and higher-order graphs, local and strongly localized detection, principled generative models, and applications involving influence, recommendation, misinformation, cybersecurity, and criminal-network analysis.

titles<=300|a85f622a8c3ebd9a4b1d89ca11b1.text:
## Dynamic Networks, Graph Representation, and Social Structure

This community focuses on learning from complex, heterogeneous, signed, multilayer, and time-evolving networks. Major themes include network representation learning and graph embeddings; link prediction and recommendation; community detection, role and core–periphery discovery; anomaly, fraud, spam, and change-point detection; network alignment and similarity search; and analysis of social influence, interaction dynamics, and temporal motifs. Applications span social media, scholarly and knowledge graphs, recommender systems, finance, cybersecurity, epidemiology, and online behavior.

Typical methods include random walks and matrix factorization (DeepWalk, node2vec, LINE, PTE), structural and role-aware embeddings (struc2vec, graphlets, diffusion wavelets), spectral methods, stochastic block models, latent-space and point-process models, and graph convolutional or other neural architectures. Heterogeneous-network work frequently uses meta-paths, meta-graphs, side-information fusion, and multimodal evidence. Evaluation emphasizes scalable similarity, ranking, link prediction, and anomaly detection, though several papers question benchmark validity and realism.

Recent trends include continuous-time and event-based modeling, dynamic and multilayer embeddings, higher-order and simplicial representations, inductive and scalable learning, robust handling of sparsity and imbalance, signed-network analysis, explainable anomaly detection, and adversarial or privacy-related concerns.

titles<=300|4fe5a38f8ff5a2c9d44231105aba.text:
## Text Classification and Math-Aware Information Retrieval

This community centers on intelligent retrieval, organization, and analysis of textual and mathematical information. Major themes include text categorization and authorship attribution; hierarchical, skewed, multilingual, and semi-structured document classification; relevance feedback and technology-assisted review; and visualization, navigation, recommendation, and quality estimation for digital collections.

A distinctive research strand develops mathematical information retrieval, including formula repositories, mathematical-language processing, notation namespaces, formula indexing, query-result merging, and comparisons of presentation- versus content-based search. Related work addresses scalable search, textual context for formula representation, Wikipedia integration, rendering, and math-aware question answering.

Typical methods include multinomial and naïve Bayes models, k-nearest-neighbor and k-medoids clustering, association rules, term-class relevance measures, semantic relations, topic models, feature selection, genetic and evolutionary optimization, graph and edit-distance metrics, segmentation, annotations, and machine-learning approaches to sentiment and opinion extraction. Evaluation commonly emphasizes precision, recall, high-recall review, robustness, reliability, and scalability.

Recent trends move toward semantic and context-aware representations, adaptive or personalized search interfaces, automated acquisition and indexing, social-media and web analysis, richer mathematical repositories, and integrated systems combining classification, visualization, recommendation, and question answering.

titles<=300|959b9d70e24cdb0fc3a28546bf65.text:
## Scientometrics and Research Assessment in Higher Education

This community focuses strongly on evaluating universities, researchers, disciplines, and national research systems, with Italy as the principal empirical setting. Major themes include bibliometric measurement, productivity and impact, institutional rankings, national assessment exercises (especially VQR), research funding, academic recruitment and career advancement, and university–industry technology transfer.

Studies examine citation counts, journal impact factors, h- and g-indexes, highly cited researchers, fractional and order-sensitive authorship, field and size normalization, citation windows, and uncertainty in rankings. They frequently compare bibliometric indicators with peer review, identify distortions and opportunistic behavior in assessment exercises, and model efficiency using DEA, stochastic methods, multivariate statistics, clustering, and sensitivity analysis.

A second cluster investigates collaboration, interdisciplinarity, internationalization, mobility, team size, co-authorship, and their relationships with productivity and impact. Gender differences in authorship, collaboration, recruitment, promotion, and research performance are recurring concerns, alongside effects of age, seniority, rank, and academic specialization.

Recent directions emphasize more robust and equitable assessment: accounting for uncertainty, disciplinary heterogeneity, author identity and contribution, evaluator–researcher cognitive distance, territorial strengths, public–private alignment, and qualitative definitions of research impact. The literature is notably critical of simplistic rankings and performance-based funding in noncompetitive higher-education systems.

titles<=300|4da042dfc60343026cbccc27b3e6.text:
### Scholarly Impact, Open Access, and Research Analytics

This community studies how scholarly impact is measured, communicated, and amplified across traditional and digital channels. Major themes include altmetrics and societal impact; comparisons of Google Scholar, Web of Science, Scopus, Mendeley, and social-media indicators; open-access citation and usage advantages; preprints and repositories; book and publisher evaluation; and scholarly information behavior. Related work examines Twitter, ResearchGate, Wikipedia, policy documents, downloads, readership, and hyperlinks as traces of attention and influence.

Typical methods are large-scale bibliometric and webometric analyses, citation and readership-network mapping, coverage and correlation studies, surveys, case studies, and field-normalized or zero-inflated indicators. Researchers also develop recommender systems for papers, venues, reviewers, and experts; metadata extraction and reference disambiguation tools; scholarly search portals; peer-review management systems; ontologies; and social-network or text-mining models. Google Scholar manipulation, data quality, source heterogeneity, and ranking validity receive sustained scrutiny.

Recent trends move toward multidimensional, real-time, and contextual research evaluation: combining citations, usage, social attention, and policy mentions; tracing digital footprints; predicting future citations or policy impact; assessing books and institutions; and studying emerging platforms. Open science infrastructure—preprints, self-archiving, research data, persistent identifiers, and community repositories—continues to reshape scholarly communication and evaluation.

titles<=300|74ceeb41d120f4dff8909c07f4c7.text:
## Multilayer Social Networks, Communities, and Information Diffusion

This community centers on modeling and analyzing social systems as multiplex, multilayer, multidimensional, and interconnected networks. Major themes include community and group evolution, social roles, influential users and bloggers, identity resolution across platforms, and diffusion of information, opinions, innovations, epidemics, and competing cascades. Applications span social media, blogospheres, telecommunications, virtual worlds, organizations, recommender systems, public health, and scholarly communication.

Typical methods combine graph algorithms and statistical modeling: centrality, ranking, modularity, Louvain and Infomap clustering, parameter-free pruning, shortest paths, layer similarity, robustness analysis, and epidemic or branching-process models. Researchers also use temporal graphs, dynamic and agent-based models, convex optimization, association rules, record linkage, profile matching, network alignment, text and sentiment analysis, sampling and estimation, and large-scale parallel processing. Synthetic network generation, diffusion-aware crawling, and inferred network construction support evaluation and data acquisition.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes temporal and multilayer dynamics, inter-layer coupling, competing diffusion, layer/node attacks, and content-aware propagation. It also trends toward integrating online and offline data, resolving identities across heterogeneous platforms, extracting networks from activity traces, and developing practical methods for massive datasets and visual analytics.

titles<=300|9f15716517601438ea51a38cc813.text:
## Epidemic Spreading, Control, and Self-Healing Networks

This community studies how infections, computer viruses, and failures propagate through complex, temporal, adaptive, socio-technical, and interdependent cyber-physical networks. Core questions include epidemic thresholds, stability, extinction and elimination difficulty, outbreak cost, topology-dependent infection behavior, and the accuracy of exact versus approximate SIS/SIR/SIRS models.

Typical methods combine Markov-chain formulations, deterministic dynamics, message passing, random-matrix and Laplacian spectral analysis, moment closure, local structural information, and phase-type transmission models. Optimization is central: convex programs, resource-allocation models, switching strategies, greedy centrality protection, vaccination, awareness investment, curing, and containment policies are evaluated under uncertainty and worst-case scenarios. Several works establish performance limits, lower bounds, tighter thresholds, and efficient or approximate policies.

A strong parallel theme concerns resilient interdependent cyber-physical systems, using message passing, error-correction ideas, and bio-inspired protection-resource allocation to support self-healing. The research increasingly emphasizes temporal and activity-driven networks, adaptive state-dependent behavior, awareness, and network data rather than static topologies alone. Recent directions also integrate robustness to uncertainty, dynamic interventions, local sampling, and scalable spectral or moment-based analysis for large networks.

titles<=300|0e5c53bfee6dce7a83387c420ff0.text:
## Social Media Networks, Misinformation, and Online Influence

This community studies how information, opinions, and harmful behavior spread through online social networks. Major themes include misinformation and rumor detection, political polarization and manipulation, social bots and trolls, fake engagement, extremism, hate speech, cyberbullying, and online abuse. Other substantial areas address crisis response, public-health communication, elections, censorship, privacy, fairness, gender and demographic inequality, and network security.

Typical methods combine graph analysis with machine learning and natural-language processing. Researchers use community detection, clustering, matrix factorization, centrality and influence measures, motif and entropy analysis, link prediction, and temporal or evolutionary network models. Classification and ranking systems identify bots, spam, clickbait, rumors, toxic content, fake profiles, and emergency information, often using linguistic, sentiment, propagation, and user-profile features. Agent-based, contagion, threshold, and differential-equation models investigate influence and emotional dynamics. Many studies introduce datasets, monitoring platforms, visualization tools, and real-time detection systems for Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Wikipedia, Gab, forums, and livestreaming services.

Recent directions emphasize multimodal and cross-platform analysis, early warning and interpretable detection, state-sponsored influence campaigns, coordinated inauthentic behavior, fairness in feeds and advertising, and interventions such as fact-checking, contrarian recommendations, bots for public health, and defenses against Sybil and astroturfing attacks.

titles<=300|e01d960eccb8b51daafceea60e43.text:
## Network Science at Social-Media Scale

This community studies the structure, evolution, sampling, and analysis of large social and complex networks. Major themes include link prediction and tie-strength inference; community, core, motif, and hierarchy discovery; centrality, ranking, navigability, and influence; graph sparsification and robustness; and diffusion, contagion, competing products, epidemics, and security. Many papers examine online platforms, communication, collaboration, mobility, trade, and bipartite or attributed networks.

Typical methods combine random walks, respondent-driven and stratified sampling, streaming and sublinear algorithms, sketching, MapReduce, and distributed computation. Wedge, edge, butterfly, graphlet, and clique sampling support motif and subgraph estimation, while sampling-based approximations target betweenness, closeness, PageRank, degree distributions, and graph size. Generative approaches include preferential attachment, stochastic Kronecker, multiplicative-attribute, geometric, latent-variable, grammar-based, and community-structured models. Spectral methods, modularity, k-core and nucleus decompositions, matrix completion, machine learning, and game-theoretic or agent-based models are also common.

Recent work emphasizes dynamic and evolving graphs, graph streams, higher-order structure, attributed and multilayer networks, privacy-preserving analysis, scalable distributed tooling, and principled guarantees. Applications increasingly address spam and unsafe content, privacy attacks, political violence, cyber/infection response, viral marketing, and cross-platform behavior.

titles<=300|18e8f371e4c8ccd5b8791551bfea.text:
## Geospatial Social Media Intelligence

This community studies how location-based and user-generated data reveal human geography, mobility, urban activity, and social structure. Major themes include tweet and document geolocation; home, country, and multiple-location inference; migration and diaspora analysis; mobility trajectories, commuting, and inter-urban interaction; and urban functional regions, boundaries, attractors, deprivation, walkability, smells, sounds, and public-space use. Other strands examine influence, polarization, news targeting, disinformation, friendships, segregation, and community structure, alongside applications in retail placement, business zones, event participation, recommendations, and economic resilience.

Typical methods combine geotagged Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, Flickr, Yelp, check-ins, mobile-phone records, call-detail data, weather, and planning or transaction data. Approaches include CNNs, deep multiview learning, feature learning, grid classification, tensor factorization, probabilistic inference, total-variation optimization, self-organizing maps, network analysis, influence models, and graph/community detection. Trajectory work emphasizes uncertainty handling, pattern mining, querying, compression, and scalable spatiotemporal frameworks.

Recent trends move toward deep and multimodal geolocation, real-time and country-scale inference, confidence-aware estimation, sparse-data reconstruction, and integration of social traces with mobility models. Increasingly, research targets global comparative scaling, urban planning, social good, and fine-grained behavioral signatures.

titles<=300|24371df87e3b6541949bd97e21d0.text:
## Network Analytics for Politics, Knowledge, and Culture

This community applies graph-based computation to large-scale social, knowledge, and information networks. A central theme is **ranking and influence**: PageRank, Google matrices, reduced Google matrices, spectral analysis, and multidimensional ranking are used for academic reputation, universities, Wikipedia articles, geopolitical ties, world literature, Bitcoin, and cultural interactions. Wikipedia and Wikidata serve as major multilingual resources for studying historical leaders, political relations, terror networks, editing behavior, collective memory, and cross-cultural boundaries.

A second major theme is **signed and political networks**. Structural balance, frustration indices, graph partitioning, integer programming, binary optimization, and spectral methods analyze voting behavior, European Parliament and congressional votes, ideological communities, disagreement, and political fragmentation.

A particularly prominent application is the **2016 U.S. presidential election**, studied through Twitter likes, follows, retweets, rumors, political language, gender, polarization, supporter migration, and multimodal classification. Related work examines Japanese and Brazilian elections.

Typical methods include network construction, PageRank-based diffusion and influence analysis, reduced-matrix and Ulam-network techniques, temporal and sequence analysis, clustering, computer vision, text classification, and social-media plausibility checks. Recent directions emphasize dynamic and time-aware analysis, multilingual and cross-cultural comparison, fairness-preserving summarization, bot and editor distinctions, and integrating social, textual, and multimedia evidence.

titles<=300|1277ffb18d0473fcbdf232f186ea.text:
### Recommender Systems: From Collaborative Filtering to Robust, Contextual Intelligence

This community spans core collaborative filtering and ranking, including matrix factorization, Bayesian personalized ranking, factorization machines, neighborhood methods, diffusion, graph-based ranking, and scalable distributed implementations. Hybridization is central: systems combine ratings with text, reviews, tags, images, audio, metadata, taxonomies, knowledge graphs, social ties, trust, and heterogeneous item relations to address sparsity and cold start.

Sequential and session-based recommendation is a major theme, using Markov chains, recurrent and self-attentive networks, context trees, temporal models, and multi-timescale user representations. Reinforcement learning and contextual or multi-armed bandits support exploration, online interaction, page-wise recommendation, advertising, and profit-aware objectives.

Deep learning trends include neural collaborative filtering, autoencoders, variational and adversarial models, neural autoregressive methods, attention, embeddings, and cross-domain transfer. Graph and knowledge-based approaches increasingly support explainable reasoning and social recommendation.

The community also emphasizes robustness and societal concerns: shilling and adversarial attacks, privacy, fairness, diversity, popularity bias, feedback loops, selection bias, causal impact, and multi-stakeholder objectives. Recent work further develops evaluation frameworks, realistic online and streaming settings, active learning, causal/deconfounded recommendation, and interpretable or visually explainable systems.

titles<=300|72f254c5fbf64ea2f352cfb09235.text:
## Data Quality, Integration, and Causality in Uncertain Databases

This community focuses on making heterogeneous, incomplete, inconsistent, and crowdsourced data usable and trustworthy. Major themes include entity resolution and deduplication; data fusion and truth discovery across web, linked-data, medical, and peer-to-peer sources; schema matching and mapping composition; web extraction and wrapper repair; and data cleaning under matching, functional, denial, and other integrity constraints.

A substantial theoretical strand studies consistent query answering, database repairs, causality, responsibility, diagnosis, abduction, and view updates. It characterizes tractable and intractable cases, complexity dichotomies, chase procedures, repair semantics, aggregate and numerical constraints, nulls, incomplete data, and uncertain databases. Frequent-itemset, episode, dependency, and association-rule mining extend these concerns to probabilistic or constrained data.

Typical methods combine probabilistic and Bayesian inference, source-trust models, active learning, transfer learning, deep learning, blocking and signatures, graph matching, Datalog/ASP rewriting, and repair-based algorithms. Crowdsourcing is used for labeling, joins, entity resolution, truth discovery, task assignment, and quality assessment, often with confidence, budgets, spatial constraints, or human–machine cooperation.

Recent trends emphasize scalable and real-time systems, holistic probabilistic repair, collective and multi-source entity matching, deep-learning-assisted curation, reproducible crowd processing, privacy-preserving mining, causal explanations, and integrating trust, provenance, uncertainty, and data quality into unified knowledge-fusion pipelines.

titles<=300|2329cda52747af7d79bb7a0a37e8.text:
## Graph Querying, RDF Management, and Dynamic Graph Analytics

This community centers on graph data management, with a strong emphasis on RDF, SPARQL, linked data, and the reconciliation of RDF with property graphs. Major themes include SPARQL semantics, satisfiability, negation, optional patterns, property paths, federated querying, provenance, schema and shape languages, and interoperability with XML, relational databases, and Gremlin.

Typical methods combine formal complexity and expressiveness analysis with practical query optimization. These include join reordering, cardinality and selectivity estimation, summaries, sketches, signatures, partitioning, compression, adaptive indexing, incremental view maintenance, and distributed execution over Spark, HBase, clusters, and cloud platforms. Benchmarking and workload generation—particularly through gMark, SP2Bench, Geographica, and query-log studies—are recurring evaluation strategies.

A second major strand addresses reachability, regular and context-free path queries, shortest paths, subgraph matching, and graph pattern matching. Many systems target temporal, streaming, uncertain, probabilistic, or multi-relational graphs, using matrix multiplication, sparse matrices, reinforcement learning, approximation, and specialized indexes.

Recent directions emphasize large-scale and continuously changing graphs: RDF stream reasoning, dynamic graph search, continuous aggregate and pattern queries, historical graph storage, adaptive distributed engines, and query-aware partitioning. Provenance, reproducibility, privacy, entity linking, visual exploration, and example-based or recommendation-driven querying further broaden graph analytics toward interactive and trustworthy data use.

titles<=300|aa2484631ac73e225928671b0100.text:
### Network Inference, Graph Signals, and Dynamic Social Networks

This community studies how network structure and signals can be inferred, reconstructed, and exploited in noisy, incomplete, multilayer, and evolving settings. A major theme is **graph signal processing**, including graph Fourier transforms based on spectral projectors, graph filters and the z-Laplacian, diffusion and superposition distances, sampling and reconstruction of bandlimited or smooth signals, variation minimization, localization, and dictionary learning.

A second theme is **network inference and reconstruction** from unreliable measurements, consensus dynamics, spectral templates, structural regularity, relational data, and heterogeneous errors. Methods include spectral clustering, low-rank models, matrix completion, generalized hypergeometric ensembles, graph filtering, distributed autoregressive moving-average filters, and task-focused model selection.

**Link prediction and community discovery** use clustering coefficients, node similarity, entropy, mutual information, asymmetric clustering information, and generalized communities. Other work addresses centrality sensitivity, influence, rumor and infection spreading, and graph-based optimization.

Applications emphasize social and human networks: mobility, proximity sensing, personality, mental health, attendance, recommendation, and event propagation. Recent directions increasingly incorporate time, temporal bipartite networks, evolving-network behavior, dynamic trend prediction, multilayer similarity, smartphone sensing, scalable randomized or distributed algorithms, and robustness to uncertainty and measurement noise.

titles<=300|de3620f8bef8098b6ddaa84b1ffe.text:
## Information Retrieval: Neural Ranking, Entities, and Reliable Evaluation

This community centers on improving search quality across web, mobile, biomedical, social-media, e-commerce, email, tables, and scientific literature. Major themes include ad hoc retrieval and relevance ranking; entity-oriented search, linking, disambiguation, and knowledge-graph integration; question answering and answer-passage retrieval; query understanding, reformulation, expansion, and session search; and personalized recommendation and venue or product suggestion.

Typical methods combine probabilistic and language-model retrieval, term weighting, relevance feedback, data fusion, graph and centrality methods, clustering, hashing, approximate nearest-neighbor search, and learning-to-rank. Neural approaches are especially prominent: CNN, RNN/LSTM, attention, interaction and kernel-pooling models, dual and distributed embeddings, semantic matching, reinforcement learning, and deep listwise or groupwise ranking. Weak supervision, pseudo-relevance feedback, adversarial regularization, and knowledge-rich representations address limited labels and vocabulary mismatch.

A strong methodological thread concerns evaluation: unbiased and counterfactual learning-to-rank, propensity correction, multileaving, bandit-based online testing, active sampling, and metrics for credibility, factuality, satisfaction, and robustness. Recent work trends toward end-to-end neural and hybrid lexical-semantic ranking, explainable and privacy-preserving systems, conversational and proactive search, table and data-lake retrieval, and integrating clicks, context, entities, temporal signals, and user preferences.

titles<=300|5d1fd3ca66889a0833a57690d2a4.text:
## Community Report: Social Search, Ranking, and Preference-Aware Data Systems

This community studies information discovery across web, social, and structured data. Major themes include search-engine evaluation and user behavior; Wikipedia, Wiktionary, folksonomies, and collaborative tagging; expertise and talent search; hidden-web crawling and federated retrieval; and querying semi-structured, incomplete, and distributed databases.

Typical methods combine information retrieval and learning-to-rank with query expansion, reranking, entity linking, ontology matching, semantic similarity, and graph-based ranking. Database research emphasizes top-k, skyline, preference, aggregate, probabilistic, and order-incomplete queries, often using indexes, approximation, monitoring, and distributed processing. Social studies model tagging, attention, influence, collaboration, and talent flows through complex networks, clustering, game theory, and stochastic processes. Evaluation uses representative query samples, clickthrough logs, relevance judgments, demographic comparisons, and user studies.

Recent work increasingly addresses fairness in rankings and exposure, including disparate exposure, differential satisfaction, unbiased preference collection, and fair Wikipedia ranking. Other trends include deep ranking for search verticals, GPU-accelerated similarity, scalable high-dimensional retrieval, multilingual entity ranking, semantic navigation of linked data, and personalized or federated search. The community also moves toward privacy-aware social analytics and systems that integrate human-generated labels, expertise, and collaborative signals into retrieval.

titles<=300|4e563d7ca54d0d707317885462d8.text:
### Complex Data Warehousing, Benchmarking, and Adaptive Optimization

This community focuses on managing and analyzing complex, heterogeneous, and web-derived data. A major theme is XML data warehousing and OLAP, including XML schemas and tree patterns, fragmentation, join indexes, indices, summarizability, rollup operators, query optimization, and the XWeb/X-WACODA architectures. Physical design is another central topic: papers study joint and separate selection of indexes, materialized views, bitmap join indexes, query clustering, cost models, replacement strategies, and database auto-administration.

The community also investigates object-oriented and document databases, emphasizing clustering, CRUD performance, dynamic behavior, simulation, and generic benchmarking tools. Benchmark construction is prominent, spanning data warehouses, distributed stream processing, big-data systems, text classification, keyword/document search, and synthetic data generation.

Typical methods include clustering (especially k-means and affinity-based approaches), query- and data-mining-based selection, discrete-event simulation, cost modeling, Markov analysis, pattern-tree and algebraic operators, and large-scale benchmark suites.

Recent directions emphasize scalable big-data and web-search benchmarks, cloud-based optimization and pricing, document-oriented and asynchronously replicated systems, social-media event detection and response clustering, temporal-community modeling, and complex biomedical, archaeological, and personalized-medicine warehouses.

titles<=300|1e2a883816d217217773bd00a521.text:
## Temporal Archives, Semantic Preservation, and Scholarly Data

This community studies how digital objects, web resources, and scientific knowledge can be preserved, modeled, and rediscovered over time. Major themes include temporal web archiving and “time travel” through Memento, archive coverage and freshness, deferred representations, URI persistence, synchronization, and recovery of missing or orphaned resources. A second focus is semantic and provenance-rich scholarly communication: nanopublications, micropublications, annotations, claims and evidence, data citation, ORCID-based discovery, and diachronic linked data.

Typical methods combine repository and digital-library architectures (Fedora, DSpace-like systems, NSDL, OAIS, OAI-PMH, ResourceSync, and ARChiving formats), ontology and metadata modeling, semantic-layer construction, graph analysis, and empirical studies of archived web collections. Search and discovery use focused crawling, event- and topic-based subcollections, timeline summarization, entity relatedness, structured queries, text mining, and learning-to-rank or classifier-based approaches. Human-assisted curation and collaborative annotation complement automation.

Recent work trends toward scalable archive analytics (ArchiveSpark), cross-lingual and event-centric exploration, multimedia and manuscript annotation, persistent references to changing linked data, decentralized publication and archiving, and adaptive preservation policies. Attention increasingly shifts from merely storing content to measuring temporal coherence, accessibility, provenance, reproducibility, and practical scholarly use.

titles<=300|72900ce52ff1cedbb649a371ca48.text:
## Scalable, Intelligent Data Management and Analytics

This community centers on building scalable database systems for analytical, graph, probabilistic, and machine-learning workloads. Major themes include query optimization and execution—especially join ordering, worst-case-optimal and multiway joins, parallel processing, materialized views, adaptive indexing, compression, and cost/resource estimation. A substantial line of work studies uncertain and probabilistic data, including lifted inference, factor graphs, knowledge compilation, provenance, approximate answering, and integrity constraints.

Graph processing is addressed through relational graph engines, triangle enumeration, graph pattern joins, interactive visualization, and historical graph queries. Other recurring topics include stream and complex-event processing, time-series management, OLTP concurrency and recovery, distributed transactions, cloud storage, and MapReduce/Spark-style systems.

Typical methods combine worst-case and structural query analysis, hypertree and tree decompositions, factorized representations, sampling and sketches, randomized algorithms, static program analysis, and specialized parallel hardware. Learning-based approaches use deep learning, sparse tensors, statistical models, and deep reinforcement learning for cardinality estimation, join ordering, workload management, indexing, and database administration.

Recent trends emphasize learned and autonomic optimizers, database–machine-learning integration, interactive/progressive exploration, shared and heterogeneous execution, privacy and verifiability, energy efficiency, and predictable performance in distributed and cloud systems.

titles<=300|ee03f979eaf1eb3f0d28ff39445a.text:
## Scholarly Networks, Bibliometrics, and Enhanced Information Retrieval

This community connects bibliometrics, information retrieval, and network science for analyzing and improving scholarly communication. Major themes include author-name disambiguation; coauthorship, citation, and thematic networks; scholarly impact, reputation, and expert ranking; emerging-technology and literature-trend detection; and digital-library search and visualization.

Typical methods are graph-based: PageRank and personalized PageRank, centrality measures, community detection, stochastic block models, label propagation, modularity, link prediction, and citation-network analysis. Author disambiguation uses blocking, initials and relative-frequency heuristics, supervised and semi-supervised learning, deep neural networks, citation and coauthor evidence, and entity matching. Information-retrieval studies employ query and term expansion, thesaurus and terminology mapping, learning-to-rank, bibliometric-enhanced retrieval, recommendation, rank aggregation, and interactive or visual interfaces. Evaluation draws on user logs, interactive retrieval experiments, relevance assessments, test collections, and data-quality analysis.

Recent work trends toward scalable and distributed processing, including Hadoop and data-aware network algorithms; temporal and dynamic modeling of collaboration, influence, and knowledge flows; machine learning for author identification, community growth, and emerging technologies; and richer scholarly metrics distinguishing prestige, popularity, contribution, and entity impact. Open science, research-data stewardship, persistent identifiers, semantic-web representations, and visual analytics increasingly support reproducible scholarly infrastructures.

titles<=300|21d835800d154762df1b99f73266.text:
### Opinion, Influence, and Diffusion in Dynamic Social Networks

This community studies how opinions, beliefs, trust, and social power evolve over networked populations. Major themes include consensus, disagreement, polarization, community identity, knowledge segregation, social balance, and the distinction between expressed and private opinions. Models address signed trust–mistrust ties, homophily, biased assimilation, bounded confidence, thresholds, susceptibility, social biases, random actions, and heterogeneous belief systems.

Typical methods are dynamical-systems and Markovian analyses of DeGroot, Friedkin–Johnsen, threshold, and bounded-confidence models; asymptotic and convergence analysis; graph-theoretic characterization of diffusion and influence; and control or intervention through interpersonal-weight adjustment, obfuscation, and network modification. Random and time-varying graphs, relative interaction matrices, state flipping, and weakly connected networks support robustness studies. Other work focuses on inference and sensing, including partial-observation influence estimation, system identification, distributed inference, active sensing, and social learning.

Recent directions emphasize signed and dynamic random networks, coupled opinion–recommendation feedback, evolving topology and social power, stochastic effects, and data-driven online behavior. YouTube studies examine engagement, popularity forecasting, sensitivity, and metric dependence, while newer work connects social sensing with interactive decision-making and collective behavior.

titles<=300|d499b18390ad1e2543cecbd2a35c.text:
## Differential Privacy for Structured Data Publishing

This community centers on privacy-preserving data release, querying, mining, and analysis. Differential privacy is the dominant framework, with work spanning histograms, datacubes, contingency tables, range and linear queries, high-dimensional statistics, spatial and temporal data, trajectories, mobility, search logs, social networks, graphs, and smart-device data. Related approaches include anonymization, \(l\)-diversity, local differential privacy, policy-aware and Blowfish privacy, provenance sanitization, encryption, and privacy-preserving record linkage.

Typical methods develop adaptive, workload-aware, and optimization-based mechanisms: hierarchical decompositions (PrivTree and spatial variants), wavelets, multidimensional partitioning (DPCube), matrix mechanisms, low-rank approximations, convex optimization, consistency boosting, and functional mechanisms for regression. Other studies address frequent-itemset and graph-pattern mining, decision trees, recommendation, data cleaning, entity resolution, and semantic or integrity guarantees. Evaluation emphasizes privacy–utility trade-offs, accuracy, efficiency, composition, and adversarial attacks using auxiliary information or sensitive reconstruction.

Recent trends include local and noninteractive privacy, end-to-end parameter tuning, principled benchmarking (DPBench), temporal-correlation protection, personalized and policy-tunable guarantees, and simultaneous privacy, fairness, and utility. The literature also increasingly studies practical deployment in transportation, social media, enterprise, and mobile sensing data.

titles<=300|d7d649c4c11553f48ca1abb884ab.text:
## Social, Semantic, and Temporal Recommendation

This community studies recommendation and information discovery in social, tagging, marketplace, and educational settings. A major theme is cognitive-inspired tag recommendation: models incorporate memory activation, forgetting, frequency, recency, semantic context, and temporal hashtag reuse, with user studies examining acceptance and confirmation bias. Other work targets robust recommendation under sparsity, cold start, long-tail effects, and competing objectives such as accuracy, novelty, and coverage.

Social and contextual signals are central. Systems exploit friendship, crowd influence, trust, location, sentiment, and online behavior for product, category, item, job, and spatial recommendations. Graph-based methods include collaborative filtering, regular equivalence, link analysis, random surfing, and scalable social recommendation engines. Semantic Scholar mining, topic modeling, item embeddings, and geographical sparse additive generative models provide additional personalization and behavioral analysis.

A second cluster addresses large-scale stream and archive processing: similarity joins and searches over endless or set streams, entity-centric news and tweet exploration, and RDF corpora of annotated tweets. Political applications model sentiment, opinion polling, entity popularity, and hashtag behavior using aggregation, topic modeling, and visualization.

Recent directions emphasize cognitively grounded temporal modeling, richer semantic and social context, scalable streaming infrastructure, and evaluation beyond accuracy toward real-world folksonomy structure, coverage, novelty, and user value.

titles<=300|d23844ad896f58e5f99e9486f1d7.text:
## High-Performance Scientific Data Management and Retrieval

This community focuses on making massive, heterogeneous datasets queryable, compressible, and interactive. Major application areas include astronomy and spatial science, pathology, finite-element analysis, scientific metadata, social-network geography, document collections, and OLAP/business analytics.

Typical methods combine relational, multidimensional, array, graph, and key-value data models with specialized indexing. Bitmap indexes, spatial structures (including zones and hierarchical triangular meshes), repetitive-string indexes, universal and learned indexes, and cohort/query-processing techniques support fast search and analysis. Compression is central: variable-byte, Huffman, difference, word-aligned, and Roaring bitmap schemes are optimized through sorting, value/column/row reordering, and SIMD vectorization. Fast set intersection, hashing, nearest-neighbor classification, and retrieval-stage algorithm selection further improve performance.

Systems research emphasizes in-memory SQL, GPU and CPU/GPU hybrid execution, distributed dataflow, probabilistic joins, parallel databases, and database-backed scientific workflows. Several papers address usability through SQL generation, collaborative OLAP, browsing, sampling, and public scientific portals.

Recent trends move toward exascale and petabyte-scale management, cloud-based low-latency event analysis, modular data management, learned index compression, trillion-cell interaction, and highly optimized vectorized libraries. Overall, the work bridges database systems and scientific discovery while prioritizing throughput, scalability, compression, and interactive response.

titles<=300|bf831d33b88061fec3e8d8d6cad8.text:
## Scalable Similarity Search, Joins, and Dynamic Indexing

This community focuses on efficient similarity search and large-scale indexing across vectors, sets, strings, spatial data, biosequences, and moving objects. Core problems include approximate and exact nearest-neighbor search, similarity and containment joins, edit and local-alignment matching, entity linking, and selection or ranking under team context.

Typical methods emphasize partitioning and hashing: locality-sensitive hashing (including Bayesian, adaptive, hybrid, and covering variants), angular multi-index hashing, velocity-based partitioning, and two-dimensional spatial strategies. Inverted indexes, bitmap filters, sketches such as KMV, embeddings, source coding, and learned indexes are used to reduce search and verification costs. Distributed and hardware-accelerated processing is prominent, including MapReduce, cloud architectures, GPUs, and generic inverted-index frameworks. Specialized systems address spatio-textual search, visual instance search, and moving k-nearest-neighbor queries.

Recent trends include learning- and embedding-based indexing and joins, robustness and contextual outlier detection, adaptive hypothesis testing, and scalable systems targeting billion-vector collections. The papers also stress practical evaluation through benchmarking, total-recall guarantees, durability under dynamic updates, and faster verification for exact similarity processing.

titles<=300|0157f9dea362d88da24d5f3155bd.text:
**Twitter Mining for Organizational, Health, and Political Insights**

This community centers on computational analysis of Twitter and other social-media content to study public discourse and support prediction. Major themes include: social-media use by organizations, illustrated by a case study of U.S. northeastern public and state libraries; characterization of diseases and disorders discussed by gay users; analysis of negative tweets concerning obesity, diet, diabetes, and exercise; and measurement of public opinion on economic issues during U.S. presidential elections.

Typical methods involve mining and computational content analysis of tweets, identifying topics and negative or opinion-oriented content, and characterizing patterns within particular populations or issue domains. The political studies extend these descriptive approaches toward predictive analysis, examining whether Twitter activity can improve the predictability of U.S. presidential elections.

Overall, the papers suggest a progression from documenting how organizations and communities use social media, to extracting health-related and public-opinion signals, and increasingly to testing whether those signals can forecast electoral outcomes.

titles<=300|07d9999e7cc3b92ed4d3a0093377.text:
## Machine Learning for Legal Review and Cybersecurity Forensics

This community focuses primarily on empirical applications of machine learning to legal document review, especially predictive coding and text classification. Research examines keyword-based methods, deep learning, and active-learning strategies for identifying relevant documents in privilege review and broader legal-review projects.

Typical methods include comparative empirical evaluations of classification approaches, experiments with active-learning strategies, and analysis of how preprocessing parameters affect predictive-coding effectiveness. A related case study investigates explainable text classification, emphasizing explainable predictive coding and the interpretability of review decisions.

Across the papers, the main concerns are classification performance, workflow effectiveness, parameter sensitivity, and transparency. Recent trends move beyond accuracy-oriented evaluation toward deep-learning approaches, systematic optimization of preprocessing and active-learning choices, and explainability for legal practitioners. One paper extends the community’s applied analytics perspective to cybersecurity forensics, using Google Analytics as a supporting source of investigative information.

titles<=300|d55603ab0bd36cb5138a3062f58f.text:
**Views, Rewritings, and the Limits of Query Determinacy**

This community studies database views and the extent to which queries can be determined, reconstructed, or maintained from them. A central theme is the fundamental undecidability of determinacy: several papers establish undecidability for conjunctive queries, using structured counterexamples such as red spiders and rainworms, and for regular path queries, including attempts to escape red-chain constructions.

The typical methods are formal reductions and carefully designed graph/query gadgets that encode hard decision problems. These results emphasize intrinsic limitations rather than merely algorithmic inefficiency. Complementary work investigates constructive alternatives, particularly Datalog rewritings of regular path queries using views, which provide a rule-based mechanism for expressing query answers from available view information.

The community also revisits the view update problem, connecting query answering with the challenge of propagating updates through derived views. Overall, the papers trace a tension between expressive query languages and the feasibility of reasoning with views: undecidability results delineate the boundary, while Datalog-based rewritings and renewed analyses of view updates seek usable frameworks within that boundary.

titles<=300|cc9aec344e9d23366ff27375a88c.text:
### Diffusion Sources, Epidemics, and Network Intervention

This community studies how contagions, rumors, information, and failures spread through complex, temporal, adaptive, multilayer, and cyber-physical networks—and how to infer or control them. A central theme is source localization: identifying single or multiple infection, rumor, or information sources from partial timestamps, sparse observations, queries, sensors, or incomplete cascades. Methods include Jordan centers, shortest-path and time-respecting paths, statistical inference, sample-path analysis, cascade reconstruction, Steiner-tree sampling, network infusion, and online observer placement. Robustness to transmission variance, untruthful answers, limited budgets, and source obfuscation is emphasized.

A second major theme is epidemic analysis and intervention. Work develops exact SIS/SIR/SIRS models and approximations using random matrices, spectral bounds, moment closure, phase-type transmissions, percolation, and simulation. Control strategies include vaccination, curing, awareness investment, protection switching, resource allocation over time and degree classes, containment, network dismantling, and targeted protection. Studies also quantify epidemic, attack, and uncertainty costs and derive lower or necessary-and-sufficient budget bounds.

Recent directions increasingly address temporal and adaptive networks, external agents, contact adaptation, competing spreading processes, multilayer cyber-physical systems, and synergistic dynamics. There is also growing focus on scalable inference, provable guarantees, robustness, and realistic network data such as airline and social networks.

titles<=300|0584c1a930e7ef5e43e520bf9f30.text:
## Bibliometrics, Science Mapping, and Scholarly Impact

This community focuses on measuring, mapping, and evaluating scientific activity. Major themes include citation and altmetric indicators; author, journal, institutional, and national rankings; research evaluation and peer review; interdisciplinarity, collaboration, and internationalization; and the evolution of fields, topics, and technological domains. Scholarly communication through Twitter, Mendeley, ResearchGate, Wikipedia, downloads, library loans, and web links is examined alongside conventional citations.

Typical methods include citation-network analysis, co-citation and co-authorship mapping, journal–journal relations, community detection, overlay maps, text mining, topic and keyword analysis, and reference publication year spectroscopy. Researchers develop and compare h-index variants, percentiles, normalized citation scores, SNIP, I3, RCR, P100, beamplots, and multidimensional or fractional indicators. Statistical modelling, regression, effect sizes, neural networks, author disambiguation, and recommender systems support prediction and evaluation.

Recent trends emphasize responsible and fairer assessment, field and time normalization, fractional counting, uncertainty and validity testing, and triangulation with peer review. The literature increasingly compares Web of Science, Scopus, Microsoft Academic, Dimensions, Google Scholar, and social-media data, while exploring open access, real-time topic detection, AI-assisted peer review, and the societal impact of research.

titles<=300|b98de194ff24bea8e82341d66010.text:
## Dynamic Topics and Social Sensing

This community centers on extracting evolving knowledge and events from large text and social-media streams. A major theme is dynamic topic modeling: LDA, HDP, author-topic and limited-attention models are extended with time, hierarchical structure, arbitrary features, embeddings, tensor factorization, and continuous-time processes to track topic birth, evolution, and emergence. These methods support timeline construction, news and event detection, stream summarization, query expansion, and content recommendation.

A second theme treats Twitter, Wikipedia, reviews, and video platforms as real-time sensors. Studies infer public sentiment, user interests, influence, engagement, popularity, disasters, sports events, and infectious-disease outbreaks. Typical approaches combine semantic filtering, incremental learning, interaction or diffusion graphs, probabilistic epidemiological models, power-law verification, and time-series forecasting.

The community also mines scholarly communication through citation and paper-evolution graphs, text reuse and plagiarism detection, author and community modeling, knowledge-graph construction, and biomedical hypothesis generation. Recommendation, semantic indexing, question answering, and ontology learning connect these analyses to decision support.

Recent directions emphasize scalable and online inference, neural embeddings and deep learning, cross-source alignment between news and social media, geo-temporal and cross-lingual analysis, and tighter integration of content, links, and temporal dynamics.

titles<=300|8eb57c2d2baaa6a1b4c4a1abd7aa.text:
## Community Detection in Complex, Dynamic, and Multilayer Networks

This community centers on detecting, evaluating, and interpreting mesoscale structure in complex networks. Major themes include disjoint, overlapping, fuzzy, bipartite, directed, signed, attributed, spatial, temporal, and multilayer communities, alongside core–periphery structures, role communities, link communities, and small local groups. Applications span social media, mobile and online dating networks, scientific collaboration, political violence, epidemics, cybersecurity, events, and information retrieval.

Typical methods include modularity optimization and resolution modelling; spectral, random-walk, personalized-PageRank, heat-kernel, flow, and conductance-based techniques; label propagation; density-, truss-, and subgraph-based algorithms; matrix and tensor factorization; stochastic block models and other generative approaches; hierarchical, ensemble, evolutionary, and bio-inspired optimization; and machine-learning or manifold methods. Local, distributed, streaming, and parallel algorithms address large-scale computation.

A strong methodological focus is evaluation: quality functions, conductance, stability, surprise, information-based scores, external classification, benchmark datasets, null models, detectability, phase transitions, and model selection. Recent work increasingly targets dynamic and multilayer networks, real-time community tracking, attributed and higher-order structures, uncertainty, privacy, incomplete graphs, and scalable local detection. There is also growing emphasis on community profiling, visualization, role identification, and linking detection with influence, recommendation, prediction, and intervention.

titles<=300|2a87c5fecfc4c5673646664fac38.text:
## Text Mining, Semantic Retrieval, and Mathematical Information Access
