This community focuses on scalable text analysis and specialized information retrieval, especially for mathematical content. Major themes include document clustering, hierarchical and short-text classification, authorship attribution, opinion-spam and sentiment analysis, keyword extraction, and corpus visualization. Mathematical information retrieval is prominent, covering formula repositories, formula rendering and representation, LaTeX acquisition, query-result merging, context-aware formula search, mathematical question answering, and applications to Wikipedia and physics.

Typical methods combine probabilistic and discriminative learning with k-means/k-medoids, k-trees, naïve Bayes, nearest-neighbor models, association rules, term-class relevance, feature selection, semantic relations, ontologies, and topic models. Graph and tree methods support link analysis, edit-distance comparison, hierarchical classification, and web-scale clustering. Hashing and signatures—including supervised, self-taught, density-sensitive, topic-aware, and multi-granularity approaches—target fast similarity search for text, images, and time series.

Recent work trends toward deep and discrete representation learning, scalable streaming and parallel indexing, semantic and contextual enrichment, and improved evaluation metrics. The community also increasingly addresses personalized, adaptive, and interactive search, automated scientific-document acquisition, digital-library recommendations, and reliable quality estimation for large heterogeneous collections.

titles<=300|8e3f3fae3755980af4e153280837.text:
### Social Networks, Influence, and Information Diffusion

This community studies how social networks form, evolve, and shape the spread of information, opinions, emotions, behaviors, and popularity. Major themes include community structure and identity; strong and weak ties, centrality, structural diversity, rich clubs, and network resilience; influence maximization and viral marketing; cascade dynamics, complex contagion, and competing diffusions; and the prediction of engagement, trends, hashtags, videos, news, and user churn. Applications span Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Reddit, Instagram, mobile-phone networks, online games, MOOCs, crises, public health, crime, and political discourse.

Typical methods combine graph mining and community detection (including Louvain methods), centrality and entropy measures, diffusion and epidemic models, Hawkes and Poisson processes, survival analysis, Bayesian and sparse network inference, agent-based and stochastic simulations, and optimal control. Supervised and deep-learning approaches increasingly integrate temporal, semantic, sentiment, image, and social signals. Experiments, observational analyses, surveys, and field studies address causal influence, recommendation, and social advertising.

Recent work emphasizes continuous-time and multiplex diffusion, early warning and real-time forecasting, neural cascade models, attention and cognitive biases, hidden-network inference, privacy-compliant prediction, intervention and steering, and socially beneficial applications such as disaster response, health, education, and low-resource communities.

titles<=300|db2976aba912328d877edd0b15dc.text:
### Dynamic and Heterogeneous Graph Representation Learning

This community centers on learning, analyzing, and applying representations of complex graphs, especially dynamic, multilayer, heterogeneous, and social networks. Major themes include network and node embedding, link prediction, graph similarity and alignment, community detection, role discovery, anomaly detection, and temporal network modeling. Applications span recommender systems, fraud and money-laundering detection, cybersecurity, scientific and patent networks, knowledge graphs, online communities, road networks, and health or crowdfunding data.

Typical methods combine random walks, matrix factorization, spectral and diffusion techniques, graphlets and motifs, centrality and curvature measures, latent-space and stochastic block models, and increasingly deep learning. Graph convolutional, attention, recurrent, variational, adversarial, and multimodal models are used to incorporate node attributes, text, semantics, edge labels, and temporal information. Evaluation frameworks and studies of link-prediction reliability are also prominent.

Recent work emphasizes continuous-time and event-based graphs, temporal embeddings, change-point and streaming anomaly detection, scalable similarity search, and representation learning across multiplex or aligned networks. Other emerging directions include robustness and security—adversarial attacks, poisoning, privacy, and fraud detection—as well as higher-order structure, hypergraphs, signed networks, and models that preserve structural roles alongside semantic content.

titles<=300|104c877ce2b7469eea2fe2691816.text:
**Scientometrics, Research Assessment, and Academic Inequality**

This community focuses on measuring research performance at individual, departmental, university, regional, and national levels, with Italy as the dominant empirical setting. Major themes include bibliometric indicators (citations, h- and g-indexes, journal impact factors, highly cited papers), productivity and efficiency, university rankings, national research assessment exercises, funding allocation, and academic recruitment. Considerable attention is given to gender, age, seniority, academic rank, nepotism, career advancement, and the persistence of “star” scientists. Collaboration is examined through coauthorship networks, internationalization, interdisciplinarity, team size, university–industry links, and technology transfer.

Typical methods include citation and publication analysis, regression and multivariate stochastic models, data envelopment analysis, nonparametric efficiency estimation, network and community analysis, clustering, sensitivity analysis, funnel plots, benchmarking, and comparisons between peer review and bibliometrics. Methodological concerns include author disambiguation, fractional authorship, field and size normalization, citation-window choice, self-citation and gaming, ranking uncertainty, and the treatment of author order.

Recent work trends toward open and scalable infrastructure (OpenCitations and book citations), prediction of long-term impact, refined measures of territorial strengths and interdisciplinarity, integrated evaluation decision systems, and critical scrutiny of performance-based funding and assessment distortions.

titles<=300|339abde551563b020cf249431a7c.text:
## Multiplex Social Networks, Diffusion, and Online Identity

This community centers on analyzing social systems as multilayer, multiplex, temporal, and heterogeneous networks. Major themes include community and group evolution, influential-user and blogger identification, centrality and ranking, link prediction, social roles, network alignment, and profile identity matching across platforms. Other prominent applications address information diffusion, viral campaigns, epidemics, innovation, competing spreading processes, immunization, and influence in virtual worlds and telecommunication networks.

Typical methods combine graph mining and network science with multilayer centrality, modularity, stochastic block models, Louvain and Infomap clustering, tensor decomposition, branching processes, dynamical systems, agent-based models, and robustness analysis. Researchers also use association-rule mining, language models, sentiment and text analysis, probabilistic data fusion, record linkage, and large-scale parallel matching. Sampling and synthetic-network generation support analysis when observations are incomplete or massive.

Recent directions emphasize temporal and dynamic multiplex modeling, interlayer similarity and entanglement, layer/node attacks, diffusion-aware sampling, and unified representations of online identities. There is increasing integration of network structure with content, endorsements, behavioral traces, and heterogeneous data, alongside practical concerns such as fake-news fact checking, spam and deception detection, disease containment, and scalable cross-platform identity resolution.

titles<=300|52a6d35090a492451503cdccb870.text:
## Data Integration, Quality, and Crowdsourced Knowledge

This community centers on making heterogeneous, incomplete, uncertain, and conflicting data usable. Major themes include entity resolution and deduplication; data fusion and truth discovery; integrity constraints, repairs, and consistent query answering; schema and ontology matching; provenance, causality, and explanations; and crowdsourcing for labeling, cleaning, ranking, and spatial task assignment. A related stream studies crisis-oriented social media, including emergency detection, geolocation, aid ranking, and disaster management.

Typical methods combine probabilistic and Bayesian inference, Markov logic, generative and deep learning, transfer and active learning, blocking and locality-sensitive hashing, similarity joins, graph matching, Datalog/ASP rewriting, database repairs, abduction, and complexity analysis. Human–machine workflows use confidence, adaptive questioning, redundancy, early stopping, and risk-aware task selection. Systems address web extraction, linked data, RDF, probabilistic databases, and scalable GPU or distributed processing.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes holistic and explainable data curation, learning-based entity resolution with limited human effort, semantic and contextual data quality, approximate dependencies, fairness-aware repair, and reproducible benchmarks. Social-media applications are moving toward multimodal, real-time, multilingual, and location-aware emergency intelligence, while truth discovery expands to medical and knowledge-graph settings.

titles<=300|93c33f2051d088f256f0da8bae0c.text:
### Social Media Misinformation, Manipulation, and Political Dynamics

This community studies how information, opinions, and harmful behavior spread through online social networks. Major themes include fake news, rumor and disinformation detection; political polarization, elections, propaganda, and ideological echo chambers; social bots, trolls, sockpuppets, Sybils, spam, astroturfing, and coordinated manipulation; and online abuse, hate speech, cyberbullying, and extremist content. Additional work examines popularity, collective attention, emotional contagion, trends, emergencies, censorship, privacy, and demographic inequalities.

Typical methods combine network and temporal analysis with machine learning. Studies use retweet, follower, propagation, and interaction graphs; community detection, motif analysis, centrality, and dynamic models; linguistic, sentiment, stance, image, and profile-feature analysis; and supervised, semi-supervised, unsupervised, sparse, causal, and deep-learning approaches. Researchers also develop datasets, platforms, dashboards, honeypots, and real-time systems for rumor, bot, spam, clickbait, and fake-news detection, alongside interventions such as fact-checking, edge recommendation, targeted debunking, and bot-based public-health messaging.

Recent work increasingly focuses on state-sponsored influence campaigns, Russian interference, microtargeted political advertising, multimodal and multilingual deception, early-warning and causal detection of pathogenic accounts, interpretable and fairness-aware moderation, and modeling misinformation as a dynamic, polarized network process.

titles<=300|ed6d7035776624c1bdc93ea5a9b2.text:
### Geosocial Networks, Signed Graphs, and Urban Behavior

This community studies how online social activity and mobility data reveal social structure, human behavior, and urban dynamics. Major themes include signed and directed networks—balance, negative ties, influence, reciprocity, core–periphery structure, community detection, link prediction, node relevance, and political polarization. A second focus is urban and spatial computing: trajectories, mobility patterns, smell and sound maps, walkability, deprivation, retail placement, optimal routes, and crowd or event detection. Other work analyzes recommendations, adoption, diffusion, venue popularity, and business ratings using Yelp, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Foursquare, Wikipedia, and mobile-phone data.

Typical methods combine graph mining and network models (modularity, spectral methods, stochastic block models, structural balance, integer programming, graph convolution), probabilistic and Bayesian inference, Markov chains and hidden Markov models, spatial-textual clustering, trajectory compression, and optimization. Surveys and axiomatic approaches complement empirical analyses.

Recent trends move toward scalable streaming and distributed algorithms, deep representation learning and transfer learning, multimodal or composite networks, uncertainty-aware trajectory and geospatial modeling, and fine-grained social sensing. Applications increasingly address public health, elections, gender and cultural inequalities, urban planning, transportation, and business intelligence.

titles<=300|deaab89628af5f978c848c697de8.text:
## Geospatial Social Media, Mobility, and Scalable Data Systems

This community centers on extracting geographic, demographic, and socioeconomic structure from large-scale digital traces. Major themes include Twitter and social-media geolocation; home, country, and multiple-location inference; urban activity, neighborhoods, boundaries, commuting, migration, and mobility networks; and relationships between spatial context, segregation, attractiveness, consumption, sentiment, and health behavior. Related work studies demographic and latent-attribute inference, including age, gender, socioeconomic status, and human traits, as well as misinformation, polarization, influence campaigns, and political communication.

Typical methods combine convolutional, deep, multiview, and grid-based classifiers; probabilistic inference, total-variation minimization, tensor factorization, matrix completion, Ising models, and generic machine learning; and network analysis, scaling laws, spatial interaction models, and spatiotemporal analysis. Researchers rely on geotagged tweets, check-ins, photographs, mobile-phone and transaction records, Facebook, Flickr, Wikipedia, and news data, often validating mobility and location models across cities and countries.

A substantial systems strand addresses the infrastructure required for these analyses: spatial indexing, relational and array databases, distributed and cloud processing, scientific metadata, astronomical archives, privacy-preserving publication, and large-scale cross-matching. Recent trends emphasize deep learning, real-time and low-latency event detection, sparse-data location timelines, global and multimodal mobility estimation, and applications to resilience, public health, migration, and social good.

titles<=300|947702c956a82b93a10b2f9735b8.text:
## Recommender Systems: Deep, Sequential, and Responsible Personalization

This community centers on personalized recommendation across products, music, news, videos, travel, education, research papers, fashion, and social platforms. Major themes include collaborative filtering and ranking; session-, sequence-, and context-aware recommendation; cold-start and sparse-feedback problems; multimodal content using text, images, audio, and reviews; social, trust, and knowledge-graph recommendation; and group, cross-domain, and reciprocal recommendation.

Typical methods range from matrix and tensor factorization, Bayesian personalized ranking, factorization machines, clustering, association rules, and probabilistic graphical models to neural collaborative filtering, autoencoders, recurrent and self-attention models, memory networks, graph neural networks, and embeddings. Reinforcement learning, contextual and multi-armed bandits, meta-learning, and Markov models address online adaptation, exploration, advertising, and sequential decisions. Approximate similarity search, binary codes, product embeddings, and distributed systems target scalability.

Recent directions emphasize transformers and self-attention for next-item and session recommendation; hybrid multimodal and knowledge-aware representations; explainability through reviews, taxonomies, and knowledge graphs; and robustness against adversarial or fraudulent users. Fairness is increasingly addressed through popularity-bias mitigation, exposure and representation objectives, fair reranking, and multi-stakeholder perspectives. Evaluation is also expanding toward bandit feedback, streaming settings, business value, reproducibility, and real-world deployment.

titles<=300|67293348d254d6cec018d2684585.text:
## Information Retrieval: Neural Ranking, Personalization, and Interactive Search

This community focuses on improving information retrieval across web, enterprise, biomedical, e-commerce, social-media, mobile, and dataset settings. Core themes include document, passage, answer, product, ad, entity, table, and image ranking; query understanding and reformulation; query expansion; question answering; recommendation; and web-content quality and spam detection.

Typical methods combine learning-to-rank with neural representations and interaction models, including CNNs, RNNs, attention, kernel pooling, dual and duet embeddings, listwise and pairwise objectives, and BERT-based multi-stage re-ranking. Word, entity, graph, table, hyperbolic, and contextual embeddings address vocabulary gaps and semantic matching. Weak supervision, pseudo-relevance feedback, knowledge graphs, entity linking, and external resources such as Wikipedia and WordNet are common.

A substantial line of work studies online learning, multileaving, bandits, counterfactual and unbiased ranking, propensity estimation, click and position-bias correction, and efficient evaluation. Personalization uses user context, query history, temporal and geographic signals, and task models.

Recent work emphasizes BERT and contextual neural ranking, knowledge-rich and graph-augmented retrieval, conversational and session-based search, reinforcement learning for reformulation and ranking, explainability, robustness, and joint search–recommendation systems. Dataset, table, and data-lake search are also increasingly prominent.

titles<=300|bd5aa9f34a59b296220973b9672a.text:
## Google Scholar, Scholarly Search, and Research Evaluation

This community centers on bibliometrics and academic search, especially the coverage, reliability, and evaluation uses of Google Scholar in comparison with Web of Science and Scopus. Studies examine citation counts, h-indexes, journal and university rankings, highly cited documents, citation aging, reference growth, source coverage, indexing speed, language effects, and open-access indicators. A recurring concern is the validity and credibility of metrics, including manipulation through merging articles, false papers, over-optimization, and Goodhart’s law.

Typical methods include large-scale comparative citation analyses, bibliographic and webometric data mining, benchmarking research units, systematic comparisons across disciplines and countries, and analyses of Google Scholar profiles and APIs. Information-retrieval work evaluates search engines using representative query samples, retrieval effectiveness, result descriptions, snippets, user effort, task complexity, and query expansion. Other studies use citation contexts and networks to rank articles, summarize papers, recommend literature, and model scholarly or university–industry connections.

Recent directions include assessing Google Scholar as a low-cost research-assessment tool, measuring open access through combined data sources, studying academic search-engine overlap and the decline of Microsoft Academic Search, improving citation-based summarization and recommendation, and extending evaluation to software, reproducible research, Wikipedia, and online scholarly communities.

titles<=300|22daa8dfb756a730c15ca6b70c83.text:
## Databases, Search, and Fair Social Information Systems

This community studies advanced querying and information discovery across relational, graph, XML, semi-structured, distributed, and hidden-web databases. Major themes include top-\(k\), skyline, preference, ranking, similarity, and aggregate queries, often under incomplete, uncertain, fuzzy, dynamic, or changing-preference data. Query processing emphasizes efficient indexing, approximate nearest-neighbor search, progressive and adaptive algorithms, streaming, middleware, peer-to-peer systems, and query planning.

A second strong focus is semantic and social information organization. Papers investigate collaborative tagging, folksonomies, vocabulary and tag-hierarchy growth, Wikipedia and Wiktionary integration, ontology matching, semantic search, expert recommendation, and browsing of linked or scientific data. Typical methods include graph and network analysis, relational learning, fuzzy logic, game-theoretic models, clustering, word and image similarity, and data integration.

More recent work emphasizes responsible search and recommendation: fairness of exposure and attention, disparate exposure, demographic satisfaction, diversity, privacy, and antidote data for reducing polarization. These studies develop learning-to-rank, reranking, auditing, and representation-based methods. Overall, the trajectory moves from efficient query and index design toward interactive, semantic, socially aware, and fairness-constrained information systems.

titles<=300|68c0fa40ef442e40a2181019b5f3.text:
## Networks, Signals, and Social Influence

This community studies how information, beliefs, and behaviors evolve over complex, signed, directed, and time-varying networks. A major theme is opinion dynamics: consensus, disagreement, polarization, social power, homophily, stubbornness, biased assimilation, backfire effects, bounded confidence, thresholds, and random actions. Signed networks receive particular attention through structural balance, trust–mistrust relations, state flipping, and opinion separation. Related work examines recommendations, social ties, expressed versus private opinions, knowledge segregation, and influence in online platforms.

A second theme is graph signal processing. Papers develop graph Fourier transforms, spectral projectors, graph filters, diffusion and superposition distances, sampling and reconstruction methods, variation minimization, localization, dictionary learning, and coherent-structure discovery. These tools support inference and analysis of signals and processes on networks.

Typical methods include spectral analysis, consensus and Friedkin–Johnsen/DeGroot-style models, stochastic and Bayesian formulations, dynamical-systems analysis, causal inference, graph filtering, spectral clustering, distributed optimization, and active or structured sampling. Network topology is inferred from consensus dynamics, spectral templates, and partial observations.

Prominent directions include dynamic and multilayer networks, heterogeneous susceptibilities and thresholds, scalable spectral algorithms, joint learning of topology and signals, and data-driven analysis of social-media influence and collective behavior.

titles<=300|36386505dafaa7692913e812d510.text:
**Graph Querying, Integration, and Scalable Knowledge-Graph Processing**

This community centers on the foundations and systems of graph data management, especially SPARQL over RDF and its convergence with property-graph models. Major themes include SPARQL semantics, complexity, satisfiability, negation, optional patterns, property paths, regular and context-free path queries, query determinacy, and ontology-mediated answering. A parallel focus is federated, distributed, and linked-data querying, including source selection, query planning, replicated fragments, endpoint divergence, and relational/XML interoperability.

Typical methods combine algebraic and relational reformulations with cost-based query optimization, heuristic reordering, cardinality estimation, graph summaries, partitioning, vertical compression, and adaptive indexing. Reachability and shortest-path work uses landmark labeling, sketches, hubs, pruning, and dynamic indexes. Large-scale execution relies on MapReduce, Spark, GPUs, vertex-centric computation, distributed stream engines, and incremental view maintenance. Formal approaches draw on category theory, monads, chase-based reasoning, dependencies, and regular datalog.

The papers also address provenance, data completeness, schema evolution, shapes, validation, annotated data, and graph view maintenance. Recent directions emphasize temporal and dynamic graphs, streaming RDF, graph analytics and OLAP, scalable federation, property-graph/SPARQL interoperability, benchmark generation, and practical graph query languages and systems.

titles<=300|06396bedb101e49cdd18f7136dee.text:
## Scalable Analysis, Sampling, and Modeling of Complex Social Graphs

This community focuses on understanding, measuring, and generating large-scale social, information, web, citation, software, and communication networks. Major themes include graph sampling and inference; community, core, hierarchy, and dense-subgraph discovery; centrality, influence, link prediction, and network classification; motif, triangle, graphlet, and clique statistics; sparsification; and privacy, security, diffusion, and attribute inference.

Typical methods combine random walks, respondent-driven and egocentric sampling, wedge and edge sampling, stratified and streaming techniques, capture–recapture estimation, and sampling-based approximations with quality or bias analysis. Scalable computation is central, using MapReduce, distributed and GPU algorithms, external-memory processing, parallel counting, and network-analysis toolkits. Structural methods include spectral and algebraic techniques, k-core/k-truss/nucleus decompositions, convex optimization, graph neural networks, and motif-based measures.

A second strong line develops generative models: Kronecker, multiplicative attribute, random geometric, preferential-attachment, grammar-based, latent-group, and community-structured models, often evaluated against real networks’ degree distributions, clustering, motifs, hierarchy, and dynamics. Recent work increasingly addresses temporal, attributed, multilayer, bipartite, spatial, and streaming graphs, alongside dynamic community evolution, indirect links, realistic graph generation, scalable motif profiles, and privacy-aware or task-driven sampling.

titles<=300|27dd3236eb0f765012b18578ad82.text:
## Semantic Preservation and Temporal Web Knowledge

This community focuses on preserving, modeling, and searching evolving digital information. A major theme is web archiving: estimating coverage and resource age, rediscovering lost pages, improving crawl freshness, handling deferred representations, and enabling time travel through Memento, archives, and temporal query languages. Related work studies archivability, fixity, format migration, synchronization, caching, and preservation policies.

A second theme is semantic scholarly communication. Nanopublications, micropublications, provenance ontologies, scientific claims, data citation, persistent identifiers, and linked open data are used to represent relationships among evidence, publications, datasets, software, and research entities. Repository and aggregation architectures—including Fedora, NSDL, OAI-PMH, DPLA, SharedCanvas, and related federation models—support interoperable digital objects and metadata.

Typical methods combine standards-based system design with focused crawling, archive mining, entity and event extraction, temporal graphs, ranking, text and image mining, schema matching, and supervised or adaptive machine learning. User studies and evaluation measure search strategies, temporal coherence, accessibility, coverage, persistence, and citation impact.

Recent work trends toward large-scale semantic layers over archives, provenance-rich and decentralized publication, human-assisted curation, collaborative annotation and search, social-media-informed discovery, reproducible data citation, and knowledge graphs connecting scholarly resources across time.

titles<=300|2449501cff78807a6ec2feed0126.text:
### Community Report: Learning-Enhanced, Scalable Data Management

This community studies scalable query processing and analytics across relational, graph, probabilistic, streaming, and multidimensional data. Major themes include join ordering and worst-case-optimal joins; cardinality, selectivity, and resource-cost estimation; query optimization; transaction processing and recovery; indexing, compression, and main-memory execution; provenance, versioning, and explanations; and privacy, security, and consistency in distributed databases.

Typical methods combine formal complexity analysis and lower bounds with practical systems research. Papers develop mixed-integer programming, cost-based and adaptive optimization, worst-case and factorized join algorithms, SIMD/GPU acceleration, MapReduce and shared-nothing parallelism, sampling and sketches, bitmap and integer compression, and specialized storage structures. Probabilistic databases use knowledge compilation, factor graphs, MCMC, lineage, and approximate inference. Graph workloads are addressed through relational engines, streaming algorithms, graph pattern matching, and transactional graph stores.

A strong recent trend is learned data management: deep models estimate cardinalities, optimize joins, manage workloads, tune indexes, and support machine-learning inference. Related work integrates SQL with machine learning, linear algebra, and neural video or image analytics. Systems increasingly emphasize interactive exploration, progressive and approximate answers, adaptive execution, workload-aware resource management, energy efficiency, and heterogeneous hardware, while maintaining provenance, correctness, privacy, and predictable performance.

titles<=300|ec10d96de90c75b7b30cf1456f89.text:
## Influence and Diffusion in Social Networks

This community centers on influence maximization: selecting seeds, allocating coupons or advertising, and designing networks to maximize information, product, opinion, or revenue diffusion. Major themes include adaptive and online seeding, competitive and complementary cascades, rumor and misinformation blocking, opinion polarization, elections, immunization, and non-progressive or time-dependent diffusion. Work also studies sequential and multiphase seeding, active friending, influencer marketing, and balancing spread, speed, diversity, exposure, and fairness.

Typical methods include submodular optimization and greedy approximation, adaptive policies under partial or myopic feedback, stochastic and robust optimization, bandits, investment and game-theoretic models, and centrality-based targeting. Random walks, PageRank, shortest-path and current-flow measures support influence estimation and node ranking. Sampling, sketches, distributed computation, GPU methods, embeddings, representation learning, and deep learning address large-scale graphs. Several papers infer diffusion or causal influence from incomplete observations and use evidential or reliability-based models.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic, continuous-time, multilayer, heterogeneous, and nonstationary networks; model-free and learning-based influence maximization; billion-scale exact or near-optimal algorithms; and practical constraints involving privacy, adversarial behavior, fairness, time-critical propagation, overexposure, and limited network information.

titles<=300|16ad3e0b6409b7d457e16c7b643a.text:
## XML and Ontology-Driven Semantic Search

This community focuses on two related directions: querying and managing XML collections, and improving text retrieval through ontologies and semantic associations.

XML research addresses exploration and querying of web collections, adaptive content redistribution, XML views in peer-to-peer systems, and efficient database organization through path summaries and path partitioning. Keyword search is refined by structural-consistency techniques that eliminate spurious results.

The information-retrieval work combines keywords with ontological features, named entities, and WordNet. Typical methods include generalized vector-space models, ontology-based query expansion, latent ontological features, and query-oriented spreading activation over semantic networks. These approaches aim to capture related concepts and entities beyond exact keyword matches.

Overall, the research trends from basic ontology and keyword integration toward richer semantic representations: latent relationships, named-entity associations, and activation-based search. In parallel, XML systems emphasize adaptive distribution, peer-to-peer views, structural summaries, and reliable structure-aware retrieval. Together, the papers seek search systems that are both semantically expressive and robust to the organization and structure of underlying collections.

titles<=300|d3ad68cc13b4ecdb6183bafd7461.text:
## Complex Data Warehousing, Benchmarking, and Event Streams

This community focuses on managing and analyzing complex, heterogeneous, and streaming data. A major theme is XML data warehousing and OLAP, including fragmentation, join indexes, indexing, query optimization, summarizability, pattern-tree rollups, and the joint selection of indexes and materialized views. Related work addresses warehousing complex web, archaeological, biomedical, and personalized-medicine data, as well as metadata and knowledge integration.

A second strong theme is database performance engineering. Papers study dynamic index and materialized-view selection, query clustering, cost models, cloud optimization pricing, adaptive re-optimization, clustering in object-oriented and document databases, and automated administration. Numerous benchmarks and simulation frameworks evaluate warehouses, OODBs, document stores, stream engines, and big-data systems, often using synthetic data generators and workload-focused tools.

Event and stream processing is another central area, covering complex event detection, Twitter anomaly tracking, RFID and sensor monitoring, load shedding, query optimization, stream consistency, and distributed processing. Typical methods include clustering, data mining, simulation, benchmark construction, lazy-chain automata, and scalable document architectures.

Recent directions emphasize scalable big-data benchmarking, distributed stream processing, real-time social-data analysis, cloud-based optimization, and machine-learning methods for text classification and top-k inference.

titles<=300|7a9e1a8258ebddb739b621965d61.text:
### Utility-Aware Pattern and Association Mining

This community studies methods for discovering, representing, and evaluating patterns in graphs, sequences, event streams, and relational data. A central theme is moving beyond frequency toward utility: revenue-maximizing recommendations, high-utility episodes, trend information, individualized or item-specific thresholds, complex sequences, multi-sequence mining, and uncertain data. Episode mining is prominent, including closed, strict, simultaneous, serial, and compressed episodes, as well as free-rider screening.

Typical methods emphasize compact or informative representations, such as closed and non-derivable itemsets, generic bases of association rules, pattern-collection summarization, and subsequence-constrained sequence mining. Projection-based utility mining and dual-partition models address computational efficiency and screening. The community also investigates approximate query answering for inconsistent databases and statistical significance assessment for association rules.

Recent directions emphasize scalability and deployment: parallel sequential pattern mining, MapReduce-based social content matching and n-gram computation, and revenue-oriented recommendation. Other emerging concerns include privacy-preserving utility mining, uncertainty-aware analytics, varied or personalized utility thresholds, and mining associations in graphs and relational settings. Overall, the work broadens pattern mining from frequency-based discovery toward utility, compression, robustness, statistical validity, and large-scale analytics.

titles<=300|e26cd3b77549a90438532f5fb92a.text:
### Graph-Based Recommendation and Ranking in Social Systems

This community centers on recommender systems formulated as graphs: user–item, user–tag, tripartite, bipartite, trust, social, and heterogeneous information networks. Major themes include collaborative filtering and ranking, tag recommendation, reputation and trust evaluation, social-commerce and location-aware recommendation, trend/popularity prediction, and domain applications such as food, recipes, travel, health, books, television, and jobs.

Typical methods include diffusion, random walks, heat conduction, similarity-based neighborhood models, iterative filtering and ranking, matrix and tensor factorization, topic modeling, meta-path sampling, embeddings, graph projection and backbone extraction, clustering, and GPU-based or distributed computation. Researchers also address spam and manipulation, cold starts, sparse data, rating-bound effects, diversity–accuracy tradeoffs, explanations, privacy, and scalable deployment.

Temporal and cognitive modeling is prominent: studies incorporate recency, frequency, semantic context, forgetting, memory activation, attention, curiosity, and evolving-network dynamics, especially for tag reuse and trend prediction. Social influence is examined through friendships, weak ties, trust, crowds, and information diffusion.

Recent directions emphasize integrated user–item–tag and heterogeneous graphs, robust and objective reputation ranking, personalized context-aware recommendations, social and marketplace data, embeddings beyond accuracy optimization, selective privacy, and practical health or intervention-oriented systems.

titles<=300|5c0a17013f94a923bf3a0b52802b.text:
## Algebraic and Polystore Foundations for Scalable Data Systems

This community develops mathematical, database, and systems foundations for high-throughput big-data analytics. A central theme is the **associative-array and relational-lattice perspective**, unifying spreadsheets, matrices, graphs, SQL, NoSQL, NewSQL, predicate calculus, and relational algebra. Work on LARA, LaraDB, relational semantics, lattice axioms, and algebraic conditions for adjacency arrays supplies formal models and computational kernels.

A second theme is **scalable storage and ingestion**, especially with Accumulo and D4M. Studies address schema design, database operations, provenance ingestion, cyber-data pipelines, log transformation, and performance at very high insert rates. Graphulo extends this infrastructure with server-side sparse matrix multiplication and graph algorithms, supported by benchmarking.

A third theme is **polystore and heterogeneous analytics**. BigDAWG provides architecture, releases, demonstrations, tensor-based models, and relational-algebraic foundations for querying across database engines. Related work examines SciDB, Vertica, HPC import, and on-demand cloud database computing.

Typical methods include algebraic modeling, system architecture and implementation, benchmark-based evaluation, sparse matrix and graph computation, and large-scale application studies such as pathogen identification and social-network analysis.

Recent trends emphasize richer D4M capabilities, integrated graph and relational processing, tensor data models, provenance management, and database platforms supporting flexible, distributed big-data pipelines.

titles<=300|77698ee32b2f4a9f457950d3680d.text:
## Scholarly Networks, Retrieval, and Open Science

This community studies scholarly communication as an interconnected system of authors, papers, citations, institutions, reviewers, repositories, and users. Major themes include author-name disambiguation and identifier coverage; bibliometric indicators of influence, prestige, reputation, and research performance; coauthorship, citation, patent, and corporate networks; and community detection, centrality, growth, vulnerability, and knowledge-flow analysis.

A substantial strand develops bibliometric-enhanced information retrieval: query and term suggestion, terminology mapping, classification, ontology and thesaurus use, exploratory and visual search, personalization, session analysis, and expert, paper, and reviewer recommendation. Peer-review infrastructure and paper assignment are recurring applications.

Typical methods include PageRank and related ranking models, centrality and community-detection algorithms, stochastic and temporal network models, citation mining, log and usage analysis, controlled vocabularies, knowledge graphs, supervised and semi-supervised learning, learning-to-rank, neural models, and interactive visualizations.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes open access, preprints, self-archiving, repository use, data stewardship, preservation, and usage-based or alternative impact metrics. It also explores deep learning for disambiguation, temporal embeddings and link prediction, semantic and multiplex networks, large-scale scholarly data integration, and reproducible open-science tools such as Jupyter and digital research-data archives.

titles<=300|a5b1f4192241442de054f527bf4c.text:
## Keyphrase Extraction, Summarization, and News Text Understanding

This community focuses on extracting salient information from documents and organizing it for search, indexing, recommendation, and news aggregation. Keyphrase research spans practical automatic extraction (KEA), medical-document extraction, semantic relatedness and Personalized PageRank (SemRe-Rank), semantic connectivity (SCAKE), multipartite graphs, neural networks, text denoising, and folksonomy-graph adaptations for tag recommendation. Several works address indexing and conceptual representation of noisy or unstructured text.

Summarization is another major theme, including efficient single-document summarization, word-embedding-based quality measurement, hierarchical multi-document summarization, privacy-preserving multi-document summarization, and privacy-preserving important-passage retrieval. Related generation tasks include automatic title construction using dependency trees and semi-automatic title systems, as well as keyphrase-cloud generation.

News applications include categorization, keyphrase extraction for aggregation systems, broadcast-news analysis, and hourly traffic prediction of news stories. The papers also consider scholarly communication protocols and the mathematical relationship between expected n-call-k behavior and relevance–diversity trade-offs.

Overall, the research trends from rule- and feature-oriented extraction toward semantic, graph-based, neural, and embedding-based methods, while increasingly emphasizing scalability, diversity, denoising, privacy preservation, and integrated information access.

titles<=300|cb7421cc8a13227e1f61948dadf6.text:
## Differential Privacy for Private Data Release and Analysis

This community centers on privacy-preserving data publishing, querying, and mining, with differential privacy as the dominant framework. Major themes include accurate release of histograms, datacubes, contingency tables, sparse data, trajectories, spatial regions, and high-dimensional query workloads. Local differential privacy is applied to smart-device data, recommendations, search logs, marginal release, and location or spatiotemporal event protection.

Typical methods include hierarchical and multidimensional decompositions (PrivTree, DPCube), wavelet and low-rank mechanisms, matrix mechanisms, convex optimization, adaptive and workload-aware query answering, consistency boosting, and functional mechanisms for regression. Research also covers privacy composition, temporal correlations, auxiliary information, reconstruction and adversarial attacks, Bayesian inference, and principled evaluation.

A parallel line studies anonymization, including \(k\)-anonymity, \(l\)-diversity, slicing, microdata publication, unstructured data, provenance sanitization, and privacy-preserving record linkage. Secure querying uses federated databases, oblivious processing, encrypted databases, and secure hardware.

Recent directions emphasize local and policy-aware privacy, utility–privacy tuning, continuous spatial and trajectory data, fairness-aware decisions, privacy-preserving recommendations, semantic guarantees, and practical systems and benchmarks for efficient end-to-end deployment.

titles<=300|171bd711af61c2c11f9e6df2b217.text:
## Network Science, Wikipedia Mining, and Personalized Search

This community studies large-scale networks through spectral analysis, centrality, ranking, and information retrieval. A major focus is the Google matrix and PageRank—including reduced Google matrices, Ulam networks, dynamical attractors, localization, delocalization, and applications to Wikipedia, Twitter, Bitcoin, the Web, geopolitics, cultural relations, terrorism, universities, and historical figures. Researchers also examine centrality, communicability, subgraph structure, graphons, uncertainty, link prediction, navigability, clustering, and evolving-network dynamics.

Wikipedia and related knowledge graphs serve as rich multilingual data sources for entity ranking, cross-cultural and historical analysis, language clustering, social interaction, editing behavior, breaking-news detection, and collective memory. Complementary work analyzes DBLP, academic careers, faculty hiring, talent mobility, professional networks, urban street networks, and online collaboration.

Typical methods combine matrix and spectral techniques, PageRank variants, graph embeddings, graphons, temporal and sequence analysis, statistical and semantic text processing, learning-to-rank, deep ranking, entity linking, and XML/database retrieval. Applications emphasize personalized expertise and talent search, federated search, summarization, and preference prediction.

Recent trends include scalable and language-agnostic analysis, multilingual and cross-cultural modeling, dynamic and temporal networks, fairness and inequality in academic and knowledge systems, robust centrality and uncertainty, and integration of graph structure with behavioral, textual, and social signals.

titles<=300|1fb80dffeea98b11681a1731f10a.text:
### Schemas, Validation, and Semantic Data Integration

This community studies how schemas, annotations, and query languages make heterogeneous web and graph data more structured, interoperable, and machine-processable. A major theme is XML schema inference and validation, including deterministic and restricted regular expressions, unordered XML, XML twig queries, type-based document projection, and schema-guided stream scheduling. Work on XPath and tree-pattern queries addresses containment, rewriting, logical operators, provenance, and DAG pattern matching, often focusing on tractability and completeness.

A second theme concerns RDF and semantic annotations. Shape Expressions, SHACL, formal validation, code generation, and customization approaches aim to align intended and actual RDF content. Several papers develop Schema.org methods for dynamic-content publishing, domain-specific validation, machine-readable APIs, automated action processing, and tourism knowledge graphs, supported by annotation platforms and ecosystem-building efforts.

Typical methods include formal semantics, complexity analysis, schema learning, heuristic algorithms, query rewriting, code generation, and empirical studies over XML and schema collections. Additional work examines tabular web data and scalable database architectures, including NewSQL, NoSQL, and graph databases.

Overall, the research trends toward automated schema discovery, stronger validation, executable semantic annotations, and integrated infrastructures for structured web and streaming data.

titles<=300|1334b3d6abdf6a02a9377245d934.text:
## Social Media, Networks, and Applied Knowledge Discovery

This community studies how social-media and text networks reveal users, communities, attitudes, expertise, and risky behaviors. Major themes include identifying gang members on Twitter, characterizing social identity and cohesion, analyzing attitudes toward China, and examining UK drill music. Public-health applications are prominent, including multimodal detection of illicit drug activity on Instagram, monitoring drug interactions and reactions, image analysis, and analyses of electronic health-record disparities.

Typical methods combine network analysis with machine learning and language processing: word embeddings, sentiment-trajectory analysis, multimodal analysis, collective classification, guided self-organization, word-proximity networks, and linear models. Several papers develop or apply semi-metric networks, distance closures, and biologically motivated distributed designs. Recommendation and information access are addressed through Pinterest–Twitter recommendation, document-network methods, hashtag-centric immersive search, digital-archive mining, and search-ranking comparison.

Recent trends emphasize fine-grained, multimodal, and domain-specific analysis—especially health, drugs, and social harms—alongside increasingly sophisticated network representations for recommendation, search, and knowledge management.

titles<=300|5989554f7fe84a542ad206dd0a36.text:
### Natural-Language Interfaces for Rich Database Exploration

This community focuses on making structured data accessible through natural-language queries. A central theme is bridging the semantic gap between user language and database representations, including SQL schemas, entity graphs, biological knowledge, and measurement units.

Typical methods include mining SQL query logs to learn how users express database needs, developing end-to-end neural models that translate natural-language questions into database queries, and incorporating domain knowledge for more expressive retrieval over biological databases. The work also addresses result interpretation and interaction: generating preview tables for entity graphs can help users understand available information before querying, while QUnits emphasizes querying with explicit units and quantitative meaning.

Overall, the research trends from conventional schema- and log-oriented interfaces toward neural, knowledge-rich, and more user-oriented systems. Beyond producing executable queries, these systems increasingly aim to support heterogeneous data, domain-specific semantics, units, and exploratory previews, narrowing the gap between natural-language requests and usable database results.

titles<=300|8df4a61800fb39f9f632aff22fe8.text:
### Network Diffusion, Social Contagion, and Online Popularity

This community studies how information, opinions, behaviors, diseases, and products spread through social and cyber-physical networks. Major themes include diffusion-source localization from partial or noisy observations; epidemic modeling, containment, vaccination, and awareness investment; influence maximization and campaigning; and the co-evolution of network structure, content, and user behavior. A substantial strand examines popularity, virality, engagement, hashtags, videos, memes, news, crowdfunding, and fashion across Twitter, YouTube, Reddit, Instagram, and other platforms.

Typical methods combine network science with stochastic modeling: SIR and related epidemic processes, branching and logistic/Bass models, point processes and Hawkes processes, survival analysis, random matrices, stochastic differential equations, and master-equation approximations. Source and network inference use Bayesian estimation, sparse recovery, message passing, partial timestamps, observer placement, and graph motifs. Empirical studies increasingly employ temporal, multiplex, adaptive, spatial, and heterogeneous networks, while machine-learning work uses recurrent models, attention mechanisms, graph neural networks, contrastive learning, and multimodal signals.

Recent trends emphasize continuous-time and time-varying diffusion, early prediction of cascades and popularity, hidden or competing cascades, semantic and behavioral context, intervention under uncertainty, privacy, misinformation and cyberbullying control, and applications for public health, social good, and recommender systems.

titles<=300|b930aa29f5201546b89b57b8e58e.text:
## Dynamic Topic and Social-Sensing Analytics

This community centers on mining evolving text, networks, and user-generated data. A major theme is dynamic topic discovery: latent Dirichlet allocation, hierarchical and infinite topic models, author–topic models, chained dimensions, continuous-time processes, matrix/tensor factorization, and embedding-space methods are used to track topic birth, death, evolution, and emerging trends. These models support scientific literature analysis, news monitoring, ontology learning, and hypothesis generation.

A second theme is real-time social sensing. Twitter and related streams are mined for event detection, sentiment, public opinion, sports moments, disasters, epidemics, influenza, Ebola, dengue, autism, and localized phenomena. Typical methods include incremental machine learning, Bayesian latent-variable models, semantic filtering, time-series forecasting, user-level aggregation, and fusion of news with social media.

Graph-based research examines hyperlinks, citations, communities, influence, navigation, mobility, and information transmission. Markov chains, PageRank variants, Bayesian trail comparison, fluid-limit models, graph factorization, and knowledge graphs are common. Applications include Wikipedia structure, scholarly retrieval, recommendation, and urban taxi trajectories.

Other recurring methods address summarization, question answering, semantic annotation, plagiarism and text reuse, and visualization. Recent directions emphasize scalable online processing, deep neural embeddings, knowledge-graph construction, spatial-temporal event understanding, and integration of heterogeneous behavioral, textual, and network signals.

titles<=300|075ad1774af2c99eb32bc133d9a1.text:
## Scientometrics, Scholarly Networks, and Research Impact

This community studies how science, technology, and scholarly communication can be mapped, evaluated, and predicted. Major themes include bibliometric indicators (h-index, i3, percentiles, crown indicators, SNIP, impact factor), field normalization, fractional counting, and fair assessment of researchers, institutions, journals, and publishers. A parallel focus examines citation, coauthorship, co-citation, patent, and collaboration networks to identify communities, research fronts, intellectual roots, emerging technologies, and influential scientists.

Typical methods combine network analysis, visualization and overlay maps, community detection, clustering, citation-context analysis, statistical modeling, and comparison of bibliographic databases such as Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, Microsoft Academic, Dimensions, and Mendeley. Author-name disambiguation, reference cleaning, embeddings, text mining, recommender systems, and deep neural networks support large-scale retrieval, profiling, and citation prediction.

Recent work increasingly evaluates altmetrics—including Twitter, Facebook, Mendeley, downloads, and online reviews—against citations, peer judgment, and societal impact. Open access, repositories, preprints, and digital usage traces are examined as influences on visibility and citation advantage. Other growing directions include dynamic and real-time mapping of hot topics, machine-learning prediction of productivity and breakthroughs, multidisciplinary and international collaboration, responsible metrics, and the effects of rankings and assessment systems on research behavior.

titles<=300|d57bc4cdfb77480b752080b2597c.text:
## Social Media Intelligence, Misinformation, and Fairness

This community studies online social networks as arenas for political communication, collective behavior, manipulation, and information disorder. Major themes include fake-news and rumor detection, clickbait, toxic or extremist content, social bots, trolls, spam, fake accounts, and coordinated campaigns. Many papers examine elections, polarization, echo chambers, propaganda, censorship, and opinion dynamics, particularly around U.S. elections, Brexit, Cambridge Analytica, and Russian interference.

Typical methods combine graph and temporal analysis with machine learning and natural-language processing. Researchers use community detection, nonnegative matrix factorization, embeddings, topic and sentiment modeling, stance and credibility classification, sparse and causal learning, anomaly and outlier detection, propagation modeling, and agent-based or game-theoretic models. Network structure, retweets, likes, followership, linguistic features, images, and crowd signals support prediction and measurement. Several works develop datasets, monitoring platforms, dashboards, and real-time detection systems.

Recent trends emphasize interpretable and weakly supervised misinformation detection, geometric deep learning, cross-lingual and cross-platform analysis, and early-warning systems. Fairness is increasingly central, encompassing search, ranking, recommendation, summaries, ad delivery, and social-network timelines. Research also shifts toward adversarially robust bot detection, intervention and mitigation, causal inference, and understanding coordinated state-sponsored or paid influence operations.

titles<=300|f95e1d5d1c79e028d8c19798bc85.text:
## Community Detection in Complex, Dynamic, and Multilayer Networks

This community centers on community discovery and network structure, spanning disjoint, overlapping, fuzzy, link, bipartite, attributed, signed, multiplex, and temporal communities. Major themes include evaluating partition quality, detectability and phase transitions, core–periphery organization, centrality and influence, vulnerability, diffusion, and the relationship between communities and weak or strong ties. Applications cover social media, mobile-phone and criminal networks, scientific collaboration, online dating, voting, transportation, and information cascades.

Typical methods include modularity optimization and Louvain-style algorithms; spectral clustering, graph Fourier methods, and eigenvector localization; stochastic block models and Bayesian inference; label propagation; random walks, PageRank, heat kernels, and flow-based local expansion; density, truss, conductance, and manifold-based clustering; and optimization, ensemble, and machine-learning approaches. Quality is assessed with modularity, conductance, kappa, F-score, stability, and overlapping-community metrics.

Recent directions emphasize scalable, parallel, streaming, and distributed detection; local and seed-based discovery; dynamic community tracking; multilayer and heterogeneous graph integration; structure- and semantics-preserving representations; privacy-aware detection; uncertainty and incomplete-network inference; and higher-order structures such as simplicial complexes and curvature.

titles<=300|a92fef44e0c2ce580e4eb7958298.text:
## Text Mining and Mathematical Information Retrieval

This community centers on automated text understanding, classification, and search, with a distinctive emphasis on mathematical language and formulae. Research addresses text categorization, authorship attribution, opinion-spam and sentiment detection, subject indexing, document-type classification, and hierarchical or personalized retrieval. Mathematical information retrieval spans formula repositories, math-aware search engines, combined text–formula queries, formula rendering, notation namespaces, semantic mappings, and question answering.

Typical methods include multinomial and naïve Bayes models, k-nearest-neighbor and k-medoids hybrids, association rules, term-class relevance measures, vector and similarity search, feature and keyword selection, topic models, ontological and semantic relations, tree-edit distance, graph metrics, and evolutionary optimization. Segmentation, annotations, and corpus visualization support web-page evaluation, navigation, and recommendation.

Recent directions emphasize integrating mathematical equations with textual context: formula embeddings, joint topic–equation models, improved formula representations, and math-aware QA. The literature also trends toward scalable web and digital-library infrastructure, including automated scientific-document crawling, open mathematical repositories, Wikipedia indexing, robust rendering, and interfaces designed around mathematicians’ information needs. Social-media analysis and multilingual classification broaden the application scope.

titles<=300|039daf7f857c108e7d0fff23dd9a.text:
## Multilayer Social Networks, Diffusion, and Identity

This community centers on modeling and analyzing social systems as multilayer, multiplex, dynamic, and heterogeneous networks. Major themes include community and group evolution, social roles, centrality and influence, link prediction, network alignment, and relationships spanning online and offline platforms. A substantial body of work studies information diffusion, epidemics, rumors, innovations, complex contagions, competing processes, immunization, and seed selection across interconnected layers.

Typical methods include graph and multilayer-network measures, Louvain and Infomap clustering, temporal and evolutionary models, branching processes, epidemic thresholds, game-theoretic and agent-based simulations, association-rule mining, tensor decomposition, graphlets, probabilistic data fusion, and optimization-based centrality. Sampling, synthetic-network generation, robustness analysis, and visual analytics support large-scale investigation.

Another prominent direction is cross-platform identity resolution and record linkage, using embeddings, graph neural networks, profile matching, stylometry, browse logs, and temporal graphs. Applications include recommender systems, genealogy, human resources, spam and deception detection, sentiment analysis, fact checking, and social-media crawling.

Recent trends emphasize scalable and automated analysis: massive profile matching, heterogeneous-information-network anomaly detection, learned representations, multilayer datasets, network alignment, and integrated text–network modeling. Work also increasingly examines content visibility, cross-posting, online/offline coupling, and coordinated strategies for information campaigns and misinformation control.

titles<=300|685f098fd8b56fb53e380a3ab188.text:
## Social Networks: Structure, Inference, and Diffusion

This community studies how online and mobile social networks form, evolve, and shape behavior. Major themes include network structure—degree distributions, community formation, mixing, rich-club and core–periphery organization, ego networks, resilience, and social homophily—and the biases these structures create, especially friendship-paradox, sampling, measurement, and demographic inequalities.

A second focus is information, influence, and contagion: diffusion during disasters and planned events, social sensing, epidemics with awareness, influence maximization, popularity and engagement forecasting, and the separation of social influence from personal preferences. Social learning, cooperation, deviant communities, emotional interaction, and competition in games extend these questions to collective behavior.

Typical methods combine large-scale analysis of Facebook, Twitter, mobile-phone, YouTube, Pinterest, Airbnb, Yelp, and gaming data with graph statistics, power-law and likelihood models, sampling theory, temporal network analysis, classifier-based inference, semi-supervised learning, and stochastic or agent-based simulations. Researchers also use controlled experiments, filtering algorithms, copulas, and optimization.

Emerging directions emphasize multimodal user and transaction data for demographic, credit, churn, and health-risk prediction; privacy and audience controls; dynamic and resilient networks; and real-time crisis monitoring. Attention to fairness, offline bias, data incest, and interpretable network inference is increasingly prominent.

titles<=300|693722fbe834d5a507594f4e8b9e.text:
## Recommender Systems: Sequential, Neural, Fair, and Explainable Personalization

This community centers on personalized recommendation across music, news, products, fashion, movies, travel, social activity, and advertising. Major themes include collaborative filtering and top-*N* ranking; session-based and sequential recommendation; cold-start and missing-modality settings; contextual, social, trust-aware, and cross-domain recommendation; and multimedia and knowledge-graph enhancement.

Typical methods span matrix and tensor factorization, Bayesian personalized ranking, Markov chains, hidden Markov models, factorization machines, metric learning, and neighborhood models. Neural approaches are prominent, including autoencoders, recurrent and convolutional networks, attention and memory networks, graph neural networks, transformers such as BERT4Rec, and generative or adversarial models. Reinforcement learning and contextual or multi-armed bandits address online recommendation, exploration, advertising, diversification, and revenue optimization.

Recent work increasingly addresses popularity, exposure, selection, and fairness biases; robustness to adversarial attacks and feedback loops; explainability through knowledge graphs, rules, interpretable factors, and calibrated explanations; and business-aware objectives such as price, profit, and conversion. Other trends include richer multimodal content, long- and short-term behavioral modeling, repeat-aware sessions, cross-domain transfer, scalable retrieval, and more rigorous offline, streaming, interactive, and reproducible evaluation.

titles<=300|edc91fa06c15131deeec1a37126f.text:
## Graph Representation Learning for Dynamic, Heterogeneous Networks

This community centers on learning representations of complex networks and applying them to prediction, ranking, recommendation, anomaly detection, and alignment. Major themes include temporal and evolving graphs; heterogeneous, multiplex, signed, attributed, and multilayer networks; community detection and role identification; and knowledge-graph, social-network, citation, transaction, and interaction analysis.

Typical methods include random walks (DeepWalk, node2vec, metapath- and motif-guided walks), matrix and tensor factorization, spectral and eigenvector techniques, latent-space and stochastic block models, graph kernels, graphlets, and graph coarsening. Deep learning is prominent, particularly graph convolutional, attention, recurrent, variational-autoencoder, adversarial, and multimodal architectures. Link prediction, graph similarity, network alignment, centrality, clustering, and change-point or anomaly detection are recurring tasks.

Recent work emphasizes dynamic and continuous-time modeling, temporal motifs and event graphs, scalable streaming analysis, and representations that preserve both local structure and global topology. Other trends include content and side-information fusion, multi-faceted node representations, robustness to missing data and perturbations, adversarial attacks and defenses, privacy, explainability, and more rigorous evaluation frameworks for embeddings and link prediction.

titles<=300|13691287fbc0497a44a6870d160c.text:
### Data Management Under Uncertainty, Inconsistency, and Human Input

This community studies how to query, integrate, repair, and explain heterogeneous, uncertain, and conflicting data. Major themes include probabilistic databases and incomplete information; consistent query answering, integrity constraints, repairs, and data exchange; provenance, causality, responsibility, diagnosis, and view updates; and ontology-mediated, temporal, XML, RDF, and knowledge-graph querying.

A substantial focus is data integration and quality: entity resolution, record linkage, schema and ontology matching, truth discovery, source reliability, data fusion, functional and matching dependencies, and approximate dependency discovery. Crowdsourcing is used for entity matching, labeling, ranking, spatial task assignment, expert finding, and knowledge acquisition, often through human–machine cooperation and adaptive question selection. Similarity joins, top-\(k\) search, vector retrieval, and scalable indexing address large-scale matching and retrieval.

Typical methods combine complexity and tractability analyses with chase and Datalog rewriting, SAT/model counting, knowledge compilation, probabilistic inference, graph matching, blocking and hashing, optimization, and learned or generative linkage models. Systems emphasize scalable query processing, cleaning pipelines, provenance debugging, and interactive exploration.

Recent directions connect these foundations to causal inference and algorithmic fairness, holistic and probabilistic cleaning, machine-learning-assisted validation, explainable data quality, secure exploration, and practical big-data integration platforms.

titles<=300|51e4132c04366512b2a1df6c3cf5.text:
## Urban Social Sensing, Mobility, and Utility-Aware Graph Mining

This community combines **social-media and location-based analytics** with scalable data mining. Major themes include understanding urban life—smells, walkability, deprivation, cultural boundaries, venues, events, political activity, gender preferences, and business development—from Yelp, Instagram, Twitter, Facebook, Flickr, Foursquare, WeChat, Reddit, call-detail records, and mobile applications. Closely related work addresses trajectory management: compression, uncertain-location inference, subtrajectory clustering and joins, convoy discovery, route recommendation, optimal facility placement, and traffic monitoring.

A second strong theme is **pattern and graph mining**. Papers study association rules, utility-oriented and privacy-preserving mining, sequential and serial episodes, constrained sequence discovery, graph pattern matching, temporal subgraph isomorphism, centrality, PageRank, and contextual or relationship-aware graph queries.

Typical methods include density- and probabilistic clustering, spatial-textual retrieval, MapReduce and distributed algorithms, deep learning and embeddings, submodular optimization, recommender systems, statistical significance testing, and simulation.

Recent directions emphasize deep and network-based behavior prediction, scalable processing of uncertain and streaming data, socially informed urban planning and business decisions, and analysis of collective identity and activism—including election communication, *MeToo*, and Fridays for Future. Reliability, privacy, explainability, and the effects of social influence also receive increasing attention.

titles<=300|b6b3ecfe3682db31dae9168244c0.text:
## Geospatial Social Computing and Crisis Intelligence

This community studies how online and mobile traces reveal location, mobility, demographics, social structure, and collective behavior. A dominant theme is geolocation: inferring tweet, user, home, country, or document locations from text, networks, activity patterns, weather, and sparse or non-geotagged data. Related work maps urban neighborhoods, functional regions, commuting, migration, tourism, spatial interaction, and global mobility using Twitter, check-ins, photographs, Facebook, Flickr, and mobile-phone records.

A second major theme is crisis and disaster intelligence. Studies detect events and sub-events, rank emergency alerts, extract locations and keyphrases, classify relevant or multimodal posts, summarize situational information, forecast unrest, and support flood, fire, haze, and disease management.

Typical methods include convolutional, hierarchical, graph, self-attentive, ensemble, and other deep-learning models; grid-based classification; toponym resolution; tensor factorization; optimization; network analysis; distant supervision; sentiment and semantic analysis; and scalable spatiotemporal pipelines. Evaluation, annotation bias, privacy, and uncertainty receive increasing attention.

Additional strands address Wikidata/Wikipedia quality and vandalism detection, knowledge-base completeness, recommendation and team formation, scientific communities and careers, influence campaigns, and cultural assimilation. Recent work emphasizes multimodal data, higher-resolution and real-time inference, cross-source mobility models, explainability, robustness, and privacy-aware geolocation.

titles<=300|fa8ef577ad9a509bab7789ffc6fe.text:
## Scalable Analysis and Modeling of Complex Social Networks

This community focuses on understanding the structure, dynamics, and applications of large social, information, citation, software, and interaction networks. Major themes include centrality, ranking, link prediction, community and core–periphery structure, roles, hierarchies, diffusion, influence, homophily, reciprocity, and network similarity. Many studies examine motifs, graphlets, triangles, cliques, butterflies, and higher-order structure, while others analyze signed, bipartite, multilayer, temporal, spatial, and attributed networks.

Typical methods combine random-walk and respondent-driven sampling, graph sketches, wedge and edge sampling, sparsification, sublinear estimation, MapReduce, distributed and GPU computation, and spectral or modularity-based algorithms. Generative approaches include preferential attachment, Kronecker and multiplicative-attribute models, random geometric and intersection graphs, stochastic grammars, rewiring, and constrained random graph generation. Machine learning is used for link prediction, classification, visualization, role discovery, graph embeddings, transfer learning, and neural estimation of centrality.

Recent work emphasizes streaming and evolving graphs, scalable motif and triangle counting, unbiased or task-driven sampling, graph reconstruction from partial observations, realistic graph generation, higher-order and heterogeneous modeling, and integrating topology with node attributes, language, geography, and negative ties. Applications span recommendations, misinformation and memes, security, education, political violence, scientific recognition, and online communities.

titles<=300|d4550fc2dfa3921cd22545dd14e9.text:
## Graph Data Management, Querying, and Scalable Analytics

This community focuses on the foundations and systems of graph data management, especially RDF, SPARQL, linked data, and property graphs. Major themes include SPARQL semantics, satisfiability, complexity, negation, optional patterns, paths, provenance, views, schema evolution, and mappings between relational, RDF, XML, and property-graph models.

A substantial body of work addresses query optimization and execution: federated-source selection and routing, join ordering, cardinality estimation, summaries, partitioning, indexing, adaptive execution, incremental view maintenance, and translation to relational algebra. Reachability, regular and context-free path queries, subgraph matching, similarity search, and shortest-path processing are recurring analytical problems.

Typical methods combine formal language and database theory with system building and empirical benchmarking. Techniques include graph summarization, sketches, compression, labeling and landmark indexes, matrix multiplication, MapReduce/Spark/GPU execution, reinforcement learning, and distributed or main-memory architectures. Benchmarks and workload generators such as gMark, LDBC, Geographica, SP2Bench, and BigDataBench support evaluation.

Recent directions emphasize temporal, streaming, and dynamic graphs; continuous complex-event and window analytics; adaptive and cloud-aware systems; machine-learning-assisted planning; scalable RDF stream reasoning; and interoperability between SPARQL and property-graph languages such as Gremlin and openCypher.

titles<=300|c37c56f0fb2c6953b3cc5a63cd8f.text:
## Information Retrieval: Neural Ranking, Context, and Reliable Search

This community centers on information retrieval and ranking across web, enterprise, e-commerce, biomedical, social-media, mobile, and academic search. Major themes include neural relevance matching and passage/document reranking; query understanding, reformulation, expansion, and intent detection; personalization and conversational search; and retrieval over entities, knowledge graphs, tables, and heterogeneous bibliographic networks.

Typical methods combine learning-to-rank—including pairwise, listwise, groupwise, counterfactual, and online approaches—with deep architectures such as BERT, CNNs, RNNs, attention, kernel pooling, interaction networks, and embedding-based models. Weak supervision, click logs, relevance feedback, auxiliary tasks, and reinforcement learning support training. Graph embeddings, entity linking, metapaths, and quasi-knowledge graphs extend retrieval beyond keywords. Hashing, locality-sensitive methods, nearest-neighbor graphs, inverted indexes, and learned indexes address scalability.

Recent work emphasizes contextual and conversational retrieval, neural passage ranking, multi-stage ranking, query-aware personalization, and retrieval for complex or non-factoid questions. There is also growing attention to unbiased online evaluation, propensity estimation, multileaving, interpretability, robustness, reproducibility, and efficient deployment. Applications increasingly include product search, sponsored search, tables, clinical evidence, social events, and data lakes.

titles<=300|fe13ed730526bd93cdd51fe07fdc.text:
## Data Management for Scalable, Learned Analytics

This community spans database theory, query processing, and systems for large-scale analytical workloads. Core themes include join ordering and worst-case-optimal joins; cardinality, cost, and resource estimation; query optimization, enumeration, containment, and rewriting; factorized representations; and tractable processing of conjunctive, Datalog, XQuery, RDF, and graph queries.

Typical methods combine relational algebra, hypertree and structural decompositions, functional dependencies, sketches, sampling, indexing, materialized views, and probabilistic or approximate query processing. Systems research emphasizes parallel and distributed execution, MapReduce, multicore and shared-memory architectures, columnar and LSM storage, serverless infrastructure, heterogeneous processors, and graph-relational engines. Transaction topics include MVCC, serializability, recovery, coordination avoidance, replication, and scalable OLTP.

A prominent recent direction is learned data management: deep models for cardinality estimation, selectivity, indexes, workload management, physical design, join ordering, and database administration, often using reinforcement learning. Other growing themes include declarative end-to-end machine learning, in-database inference, feature engineering, neural video and visual analytics, and learned representations for search.

The community also increasingly addresses interactive and streaming analytics, uncertainty, privacy, provenance, data cleaning, approximate answers with guarantees, and cloud-scale resource sharing.

titles<=300|9066d4017078b544f9793300b345.text:
## Social Influence, Opinion Dynamics, and Network Optimization
