This community studies how information, opinions, products, and epidemics spread through social and other interaction networks. Major themes include influence maximization and viral marketing; competitive, complementary, and multi-cascade diffusion; misinformation and rumor blocking; opinion formation, polarization, controversy, and structural balance; and network centrality, reliability, navigability, and topology design. Applications include advertising, elections, cyberbullying, recruitment, recommendation systems, epidemic mitigation, and team formation.

Typical methods combine graph algorithms, diffusion and threshold models, independent-cascade and linear-threshold processes, Markov chains, random walks, percolation, dynamical systems, and control theory. Optimization is dominated by greedy and adaptive-greedy strategies, submodular maximization, approximation algorithms, sampling and reverse-reachability methods, integer programming, spectral and embedding techniques, and online learning or bandit approaches. Empirical work analyzes Twitter, parliamentary votes, traffic, hashtags, and field experiments.

Recent trends emphasize scalable and exact billion-scale algorithms, dynamic and nonstationary networks, continuous-time and time-critical spreading, partial or myopic feedback, robust and uncertain optimization, and multi-round or sequential seeding. The literature increasingly incorporates fairness, privacy, explainability, confirmation bias, heterogeneous susceptibility, signed and multiplex networks, and opinion-aware or welfare-oriented objectives.

titles<=300|8342000f9f08fc21f911083456d0.text:
### Scholarly Information Retrieval, Semantics, and Research Data

This community studies scholarly information access across digital libraries, repositories, and academic search engines. Major themes include bibliometric-enhanced retrieval; query and term recommendation; research-paper and algorithm recommenders; personalization and user modeling; and interactive, visual, and exploratory search. A second strong focus is knowledge organization: thesauri, SKOS, classification systems, terminology networks, cross-concordances, linked data, and semantic heterogeneity. Many papers address research-data discovery, citation, preservation, metadata, stewardship, and digital infrastructures, alongside open science and semantic publishing.

Typical methods combine citation, co-author, usage-log, and session analysis with relevance judgments, online living-lab evaluations, user studies, eye tracking, and visualization assessment. Systems employ supervised learning, embeddings, neural title simplification, hybrid and meta-learning recommenders, query expansion, reference parsing, information extraction, entity linking, and scalable Hadoop-based processing. Evaluation emphasizes usefulness, ranking effects, bias, position, inter-rater agreement, coverage, and temporal behavior.

Recent work trends toward large-scale scholarly recommender services, per-instance algorithm selection, data-citation and repository analytics, automated metadata enrichment, and machine-readable knowledge systems. Interactive maps, heat maps, contextual browsing, and socio-technical studies increasingly connect retrieval technology with scholarly practices and infrastructure stewardship.

titles<=300|3ad8ce5d0b535a22f936eee185a7.text:
### Wikipedia, Search, and Social-Web Network Intelligence

This community studies large-scale knowledge and interaction networks, especially Wikipedia, Wiktionary, collaborative tagging systems, Twitter/Weibo, LinkedIn, and the broader Web. Major themes include ranking and influence, multilingual and cross-cultural relations, information retrieval, ontology and entity linking, expertise and talent discovery, and the evolution of online collaboration and attention.

Typical methods are graph mining and network science: PageRank and Google matrices, reduced Google matrices, spectral analysis, centrality and influence measures, community detection, clustering, link analysis, temporal and sequence modeling, and agent-based opinion models. Researchers also build relational, XML, and semantic-web databases; exploit Wiktionary, Wikipedia categories, Wikidata, tags, and social signals; and apply learning-to-rank, query expansion, personalization, federated search, and multimedia fusion. Evaluation emphasizes retrieval effectiveness, user behavior, relevance judgments, credibility, and search-task difficulty.

Recent directions include multilingual and cross-cultural mining, fairer and two-dimensional ranking, temporal detection of breaking news and social movements, professional-network talent-flow and expertise search, and identification of influential or critical nodes. Deep ranking models, vertical and personalized search, entity disambiguation, and structured knowledge resources increasingly complement classical graph algorithms.

titles<=300|209a40c9c15163409ca2f1581eb2.text:
## Data Warehousing, Distributed Databases, and Blockchain Data Systems

This community focuses on managing, querying, and optimizing complex data at scale. A major theme is XML warehousing and OLAP, including structural query preferences, tree-pattern matching, summarizability, fragmentation, join indexes, and query-performance optimization. Related work studies materialized-view and index selection, workload clustering, bitmap and join indexes, cloud cost models, and dynamic warehouse tuning.

A second theme concerns database architecture and performance: object-oriented and document databases, multimodel systems, distributed storage, replication, placement, sharding, autonomic resource management, and benchmarking. Energy-aware database design and comparisons of “wimpy” clusters with powerful servers are recurring concerns.

Blockchain research increasingly treats blockchains as data-processing and database platforms, addressing atomic commitment, smart-contract execution, resilient consensus, forkable storage, verifiable queries, interoperability, auditing, and permissioned-chain performance.

Other topics include dataset versioning, provenance, collaborative analysis, metadata and data-quality frameworks, historical graphs, web and biomedical warehouses, and social-stream event detection. Typical methods include clustering, simulation, benchmarking, query-log mining, cost modeling, graph partitioning, adaptive indexing, and machine learning for classification and transformations.

Recent work trends toward blockchain/database convergence, verifiable and forkable storage, scalable permissioned systems, energy efficiency, reproducible dataset management, and neural or weakly supervised text analytics.

titles<=300|4a0caffe464c857ea59aacd07b7c.text:
### Scalable Data Systems, Semantics, and Algebraic Analytics

This community studies scalable data management across relational, NoSQL, graph, array, and polystore systems. Major themes include high-throughput ingestion and processing with Accumulo, D4M, Graphulo, SciDB, and distributed database platforms; database-as-a-service, NewSQL, and multi-tenant storage; and analytics over sparse matrices, graphs, provenance, logs, sensor data, and scientific datasets.

A second theme is formal data representation and interoperability. Work develops associative-array, tensor, relational-lattice, and relational-algebra foundations, including semantics connecting databases, predicate calculus, matrices, and graphs. Polystore architectures and query systems integrate heterogeneous engines and support on-demand computation.

Schema and semantic-web research addresses XML schema inference, deterministic and restricted regular-expression learning, XPath and twig-query optimization, RDF validation, SHACL, Schema.org annotations, machine-readable APIs, and tourism knowledge graphs. Provenance tracking, workflow dependencies, and semantic annotation verification are recurring applications.

Typical methods combine algebraic and lattice-based modeling, formal semantics, complexity and tractability analysis, schema learning, query rewriting, type-based projection, code generation, benchmarking, and large-scale systems experimentation.

Recent trends emphasize billion-scale updates and ingestion, server-side graph algorithms, tensor-based polystore models, automated semantic annotation and validation, cloud/supercomputer database services, and integrated platforms for discovering, publishing, and analyzing heterogeneous structured data.

titles<=300|e2e37dbde6ce5c2c80c3f491ddcb.text:
## Social Networks, Information Diffusion, and Collective Attention

This community studies how online social networks form, evolve, and shape the spread of information, opinions, emotions, behaviors, and popularity. Major themes include influence and contagion; information cascades and rumor diffusion; community structure, multiplex and heterogeneous ties; weak and strong ties; collective intelligence and opinion dynamics; and social-media engagement across Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Reddit, Instagram, and mobile platforms. Applications include emergencies, elections, health and disease monitoring, cyberbullying, misinformation, recommender systems, marketing, social commerce, and online communities.

Typical methods combine large-scale network analysis with diffusion and epidemic models, Hawkes and Poisson processes, survival analysis, stochastic control, agent-based simulation, and causal inference. Researchers infer hidden network structure, sources, infection times, influence, and adoption from partial temporal observations, using sparse recovery, Bayesian inference, graph motifs, centrality, entropy, and community detection. Machine-learning approaches increasingly include temporal models, attention mechanisms, recurrent and coupled graph neural networks, contrastive learning, and multimodal content analysis for forecasting popularity, engagement, cascades, and trends.

Recent work emphasizes continuous-time and multiplex diffusion, co-evolution of networks and content, hidden nodes and competing cascades, information overload, intervention and influence maximization, socially grounded prediction, and integrating social, topical, geographic, sentiment, and behavioral signals.

titles<=300|0ad7db8c63a08c88724d2bd2e07b.text:
## Scalable Analytics for Scientific, Spatial, and Collaborative Data

This community explores high-performance data management for very large scientific, spatial, textual, graph, and social datasets. Major themes include multidimensional/OLAP databases, analytic column stores, relational backends for finite-element and astronomical data, and large-scale scientific metadata and event processing. Spatial research addresses indexing, cross-matching observations, geometric search, geographic-region classification, and vehicle sharing.

A strong methodological focus is compact, fast indexing: bitmap and inverted indexes, Roaring bitmaps, hierarchical triangular meshes, universal and compressed indexes, and multidimensional data structures. Compression and query execution are optimized with SIMD/vectorization, GPU–CPU hybrids, in-memory processing, sorting and attribute/row/column reordering, hashing, and distributed dataflow. Work also covers probabilistic joins, histogram-based estimation, caching, and cohort queries.

Another thread concerns human-facing access: natural-language-to-SQL systems, semantic query interfaces, preview tables, collaborative search and OLAP, and group-aware information seeking.

Recent trends emphasize exascale and petabyte-scale infrastructure, cloud-based low-latency scientific analysis, parallel and GPU-enabled execution, analytics over graphs and entity relationships, and increasingly efficient compressed representations. The community also moves toward integrated, full-lifecycle scientific platforms and practical tools for interactive exploration.

titles<=300|fa6b7d2433bc72df96e62697e2c2.text:
### Mobile Phone Data for Urban Dynamics and Public Health

This community centers on using mobile-phone-derived mobility data to understand population dynamics, urban activity, and disease risk. Its papers examine social events in time-varying mobile-phone networks, characterize the “city pulse” of Buenos Aires, and survey broader mobility-analysis approaches based on mobile-phone datasets.

A second major theme is public health, particularly Chagas disease in Argentina. The studies investigate how mobility data can support analysis of disease spread and identify areas with potentially high prevalence. Together, these works connect observed human movement patterns with epidemiological questions and geographic risk assessment.

Typical methods involve constructing and analyzing mobile-phone mobility or contact graphs, studying their temporal variation, and relating movement patterns to locations, events, or disease prevalence. Spatial analysis is central to detecting potentially affected areas.

The collection suggests a progression from descriptive urban and network analysis toward applied epidemiological modeling. It also reflects increasing interest in combining large-scale mobility datasets with public-health surveillance to infer disease propagation and prioritize regions for investigation.

titles<=300|8e20bf4d6143607fde6d756c357a.text:
### Network-Based Recommendation and Robust Ranking

This community centers on graph-based recommender systems and information filtering. A dominant theme is collaborative ranking on user–item, user–tag, and other bipartite or tripartite networks, with attention to sparse data, cold starts, rating bounds, similarity correction, diversity, and accuracy. Social ties, trust, reputation, influence, and heterogeneous relationships are repeatedly used to improve personalization.

Typical methods include diffusion and heat-conduction processes, random walks, iterative local or global ranking, neighborhood and KNN models, matrix and tensor factorization, clustering, meta-path sampling, topic models, ontologies, and feature-based hybrids. Network projection, backbone extraction, community structure, and link prediction support both recommendation and graph analysis. Robust variants address malicious nodes, spam, biased ratings, and reliable reputation scores.

Applications span news, books, travel, fashion, movies, trade, and especially food and health, including recipe personalization, nutrition, fitness, and just-in-time interventions. Temporal modeling is important for trend and popularity prediction, evolving networks, sessions, and repeat consumption.

Recent directions represented here emphasize diversity–accuracy tradeoffs, privacy-preserving and causal evaluation, adaptive and context-aware recommendation, explanations and objective ranking, distributed computation, and analysis of polarization, junk news, and social-bot effects on information consumption.

titles<=300|e0922ca20320fcac5369a307d1a2.text:
## Privacy-Preserving Data Management and Analysis

This community focuses on enabling useful data publication, querying, mining, and learning while protecting individual, group, and organizational privacy. Differential privacy is the dominant theme, covering histograms, range and summation queries, datacubes, contingency tables, trajectories, spatial data, search logs, graphs, frequent patterns, regression, recommendations, and Bayesian inference. Work emphasizes privacy–utility trade-offs, composition, auxiliary information, background knowledge, temporal correlations, and principled evaluation.

Typical methods include hierarchical decompositions (PrivTree, spatial and multidimensional partitions), wavelets, matrix mechanisms, low-rank and convex optimization, consistency constraints, sparse-vector variants, adaptive and workload-aware query answering, and local differential privacy. Several papers develop frameworks and benchmarks for reusable or policy-aware private computations.

A parallel line studies traditional anonymization and disclosure control, including \(k\)-anonymity, \(l\)-diversity, slicing, microdata and unstructured-text anonymization, provenance sanitization, and adversarial attacks. Secure querying uses federated databases, encrypted databases, secure hardware, oblivious processing, and partitioned security.

Applications increasingly involve mobility, continuous location services, social media, recommendations, smart devices, and fairness. Entity resolution and record linkage use blocking, probabilistic signatures, grams, and scalable parallel processing. Recent directions emphasize local and spatiotemporal privacy, privacy under correlations, policy and semantic guarantees, fairness, federated analysis, and scalable high-dimensional utility.

titles<=300|e382d465cec367a2262b30cc60b7.text:
## Graph, Semantic, and Context-Aware Recommendation

This community centers on recommender systems and information filtering across scholarly literature, social media, marketplaces, education, tourism, music, news, jobs, and entertainment. Major themes include collaborative, content-based, hybrid, context-aware, trust-aware, and group recommendation; cold-start, sparsity, diversity–accuracy, novelty, privacy, reputation, spam, and explanation; and personalization using ratings, tags, clicks, social ties, location, time, and behavioral signals.

Typical methods combine matrix and tensor factorization, latent-variable and topic models, neural networks and autoencoders, recurrent models, reinforcement learning, probabilistic and maximum-entropy models, association rules, fuzzy logic, and optimal design. Graph and network approaches are especially prominent, including diffusion, random walks, neighbor ranking, bipartite and tripartite projections, community detection, stochastic block models, embeddings, trust propagation, and heterogeneous-information-network meta-paths.

A substantial strand addresses scholarly recommendation and infrastructure: citation and author-topic modeling, metadata and contribution extraction, citation matching, literature knowledge graphs, related-article datasets, semantic annotation, and recommender APIs or living labs. Topic modeling, summarization, ontology learning, semantic similarity, and information retrieval support document understanding.

Recent work increasingly emphasizes deep and meta-learned models, embeddings, temporal and session-aware prediction, online and multifaceted evaluation, explainability, fair or risk-aware ranking, selective privacy, and explicit optimization of exploration, coverage, novelty, and user utility.

titles<=300|e23fc351656ff944dfeee0526e77.text:
### Resilient Database Systems for Emerging Storage

This community focuses on database reliability and performance across non-volatile memory, persistent memory, and heterogeneous storage systems. A central theme is extending traditional failure models: single-page failures are characterized as a distinct fourth class of database failure, while media-failure recovery is addressed through instant restore mechanisms.

Typical methods combine redesigned buffer managers, storage-aware data placement, and specialized persistent-memory I/O primitives. Multi-tier buffer management and persistent buffer management aim to coordinate volatile and persistent data while supporting optimistic consistency. Heterogeneity-aware management exploits the differing capabilities of hybrid storage technologies rather than treating storage as uniform.

Recovery research emphasizes reducing restart cost and limiting work after failures. Fine-granularity locking enables fast redo-only recovery, and instant restoration targets rapid availability following media faults. Across the papers, system designs integrate concurrency control, buffering, persistence, and recovery more tightly.

The emerging trend is toward database architectures tailored to diverse memory and storage technologies. Rather than relying on conventional block-oriented assumptions, these systems exploit persistence, tier-specific performance, and finer-grained failure handling to improve recovery speed, availability, and resource utilization.

titles<=300|d99f1017907c5b142db6397a063f.text:
### Community Detection in Complex, Dynamic, and Multilayer Networks

This community centers on identifying, evaluating, and interpreting structure in complex networks. Major themes include disjoint, overlapping, fuzzy, hierarchical, role-based, and core–periphery communities; attributed, directed, signed, bipartite, multiplex, and temporal networks; and applications to social media, communication, mobility, scientific, financial, political, and biological data.

Typical methods combine modularity optimization and its multilayer or distance-aware extensions with stochastic block models, graph spectra, spectral clustering, and likelihood or Bayesian inference. Label propagation, Markov stability, random walks, personalized PageRank, heat kernels, flow and conductance methods support local and scalable discovery. Density-based clustering, trusses, k-cores, manifold learning, total variation, evolutionary optimization, QUBO, and ensemble approaches address dense, overlapping, or noisy structure. Evaluation emphasizes quality functions, partition agreement, visualization, detectability, model selection, and robustness to missing or adversarial information.

Recent work increasingly targets evolving and streaming graphs through dynamic stochastic blockmodels, incremental label propagation, temporal segmentation, event graphs, and community tracking. Other trends include multilayer integration, node attributes and link dynamics, distributed/parallel/GPU implementations, real-time analysis, privacy-preserving detection, and improved centrality and core–periphery analysis.

titles<=300|d54183c24321ae624a8df9ef0d08.text:
## Multilayer Social Networks, Diffusion, and Identity

This community centers on modeling and analyzing social networks as multilayer, multiplex, multidimensional, and evolving systems. Major themes include community and group evolution; influential-user and centrality analysis; information, opinion, rumor, epidemic, innovation, and competing-process diffusion; and robustness under attacks or immunization. A second strong theme is identity resolution across online, offline, phone, and browsing networks, including profile matching, record linkage, genealogical reconstruction, and network alignment. Other recurring topics are social recommendation, sentiment and topic mining, fake-news detection, blog ranking, and information retrieval.

Typical methods include multilayer graph models, centrality and similarity measures, shortest paths, graphlets, clustering with Louvain and Infomap, GED-based group comparison, temporal graphs, association-rule learning, convex optimization, probabilistic data fusion, language models, stylometry, embeddings, and graph neural networks. Researchers also use sampling, synthetic-network generation, agent-based modeling, branching processes, and large-scale parallel matching.

Recent directions emphasize integrating temporal, textual, behavioral, and cross-platform evidence; analyzing online–offline and social–physical interactions; improving identity linkage with embeddings and GNNs; studying layer entanglement and network robustness; and developing diffusion-aware sampling, visual analytics, and practical strategies for epidemics, rumors, campaigns, and misinformation.

titles<=300|96c032de9a14d9b912626b97400d.text:
### Online Social Networks: Misinformation, Manipulation, and Polarization

This community studies how information, opinions, identities, and abuse spread through online social networks. Major themes include political communication and elections; fake news, rumors, clickbait, and conspiracy narratives; social bots, trolls, sockpuppets, spam, and coordinated manipulation; polarization, echo chambers, controversy, and community structure; and privacy, bias, fairness, and security. Applications also address health communication, extremism, cyberbullying, fraud, and crowdsourced platforms.

Typical methods combine graph mining with natural-language processing and machine learning. Researchers use community detection, matrix factorization, signed and dynamic-network models, diffusion and cascade analysis, relational event models, social embeddings, stance and sentiment classification, linguistic and visual analysis, and supervised, semi-supervised, and causal inference. Sampling, weak social supervision, crowd signals, honeypots, and user-profile or behavioral features support detection tasks. Several works develop datasets, repositories, dashboards, and systems such as Hoaxy, BotOrNot, FakeNewsNet, and CED.

Recent work increasingly examines state-sponsored influence campaigns, Russian and other political manipulation, coordinated or camouflaged bots, cross-platform behavior, and misinformation during elections and public-health events. It also emphasizes early detection, interpretability, adversarial robustness, fairness-aware ranking and summarization, and interventions that reduce harmful diffusion or connect opposing communities.

titles<=300|13ff33dfce8a2ab304b5761f5d5e.text:
### Recommendation Systems: Sequential, Graph-Based, and Responsible Personalization

This community focuses on personalized recommendation across music, news, products, fashion, travel, medicine, jobs, and social platforms. Major themes include collaborative filtering and ranking, session- and sequence-aware next-item prediction, playlist continuation, cross-domain and cold-start recommendation, and modeling complementary or heterogeneous item relations. Researchers also study popularity, exposure, fairness, bias, diversity, explainability, robustness, and business objectives such as revenue and advertising conversion.

Typical methods span matrix and tensor factorization, Bayesian personalized ranking, factorization machines, metric learning, Markov and hidden Markov models, recurrent and convolutional networks, autoencoders, transformers, and reinforcement learning. Graph neural networks, knowledge graphs, social and trust signals, reviews, text, images, audio, taxonomies, and multimodal embeddings provide richer representations. Bandits support exploration, online learning, and contextual recommendation, while adversarial training and poisoning studies address robustness.

Recent work emphasizes deep sequential modeling with long- and short-term interests, bidirectional transformers, memory and attention mechanisms, graph-based architectures, meta-learning, and scalable production systems. Evaluation is increasingly scrutinized through studies of sampling, offline bias, reproducibility, bandit feedback, calibration, and business value. Fairness-aware reranking, popularity-bias mitigation, interpretable knowledge-graph reasoning, and conversational or interactive recommendation are prominent emerging directions.

titles<=300|267399016782ed30b27692586de0.text:
## Networked Knowledge, Cities, and Social Behavior

This community studies how large-scale digital traces reveal structure, influence, culture, and behavior. A major theme is Wikipedia, Wikidata, and knowledge graphs: researchers analyze multilingual link networks, historical and biographical relations, completeness, navigation, editing conflict, gender bias, and vandalism. PageRank, Google-matrix spectra, reduced Google matrices, centrality, ranking, and network robustness are recurring tools.

A second theme concerns cities and mobility. Geotagged tweets, check-ins, Flickr, taxi trajectories, phone records, and urban sensors support research on smellscapes, walkability, deprivation, cultural interaction, event detection, retail placement, route recommendation, and urban resilience. Spatial-textual clustering, trajectory mining, Markov models, Bayesian hypothesis testing, and scalable distributed algorithms are typical methods.

Other work examines social influence, political communication, collective action, reputation, and gender or cultural asymmetries on Twitter, Instagram, Facebook, Yelp, and Reddit. Recommendation systems address food, recipes, venues, events, businesses, and routes, using ontologies, ingredient networks, topic models, graph representations, and ensemble learning.

Recent directions emphasize deep and representation learning, temporal and heterogeneous networks, multimodal evidence, fine-grained prediction, scalable streaming systems, and theoretically informed analyses of online movements, elections, misinformation, and collaborative knowledge production.

titles<=300|803937234bbab97bf38b8de5c8e1.text:
## Data Quality, Uncertainty, and Trustworthy Data Management

This community studies how to integrate, clean, query, and explain heterogeneous, uncertain, and conflicting data. Major themes include entity resolution and consolidation; truth discovery and data fusion; probabilistic and incomplete databases; integrity constraints, repairs, and consistent query answering; provenance, causality, responsibility, and query explanations; and crowdsourced data collection and quality control.

Typical methods combine database theory with probabilistic inference, knowledge compilation, Datalog, SAT/model counting, chase procedures, repair programs, and complexity analysis. Practical systems use blocking, similarity joins, embeddings, locality-sensitive hashing, graph matching, Bayesian and Markov models, random forests, neural models, and distributed or GPU processing. Human–machine workflows, active labeling, task assignment, and source-trust models are widely used to improve entity matching and truth assessment.

Recent directions emphasize scalable and progressive processing, deep and transfer learning for entity resolution and cleaning, holistic probabilistic repair, and integration of crowdsourcing with automated inference. The scope is also expanding toward causal inference and algorithmic fairness, data markets and pricing, knowledge-graph integration, schema and ontology evolution, explainable auditing, and reliable analytics over massive linked, temporal, and uncertain datasets.

titles<=300|701609d90314e1de10ddb5ca1613.text:
### Mapping Knowledge Translation in Biomedical Research

This community examines how biomedical knowledge develops from basic research into clinical applications, patented technologies, and drug or biomaterial innovation. Major themes include HIV/AIDS research fronts and their evolution, Ebola research shaped by basic clinical and patent knowledge, cancer drug development, and dental biomaterials R&D.

A recurring focus is the relationship between research domains and translation pathways: health problems are connected to ad hoc drug design, while liposomal doxorubicin provides a case for tracing knowledge translation and innovation. Comparisons between liposomes and metallic nanostructures further highlight differences in how cancer-related technologies move across research and application contexts.

The papers primarily use science-mapping and knowledge-structure approaches, including analysis of research fronts, hierarchical organization, part–whole relations, adaptive specialization, and linkages among basic, clinical, translational, and patented knowledge. Case-based mapping is used for specific technologies and disease areas.

Recent directions emphasize integrated views of translational research rather than isolated stages. The community increasingly studies how emerging fronts connect across levels, how technological platforms follow distinct translation trajectories, and how bibliometric structures can reveal innovation processes in biomedical and clinical research.

titles<=300|36feab458d1f285ec86c7257abcb.text:
## Social Media Intelligence for Location, Mobility, and Crisis Response

This community centers on extracting geographic, temporal, behavioral, and topical intelligence from social media and related digital traces. A major theme is user and post geolocation, including home-country-city inference, toponym resolution, geotagging, hyperlocal mapping, and privacy-preserving location publishing. Closely related work models urban mobility, migration, commuting, visited places, spatial interactions, and city attractiveness using Twitter, mobile-phone, Flickr, check-in, and economic data.

Another strong focus is crisis and public-health intelligence: detecting disasters, sub-events, epidemics, influenza, dengue, and fires; ranking emergency information; summarizing situational awareness; and supporting first responders. Studies also examine sentiment, disease communities, elections, polarization, junk news, influence campaigns, and misinformation.

Typical methods include convolutional and hierarchical neural networks, ensemble classifiers, word embeddings, semantic filtering, distant supervision, topic models (dynamic, hierarchical, continuous-time, and clustered LDA), tensor/matrix factorization, probabilistic models, differential equations, graph algorithms, community detection, and visual analytics. Evaluation, annotation bias, and uncertainty are recurring concerns.

Recent directions emphasize real-time and scalable processing, high-resolution and country-level prediction, multimodal integration with imagery and news, cross-source mobility inference, dynamic event evolution, epidemic forecasting, and privacy-aware or adversarially robust social-media analytics.

titles<=300|51de14857344838e9acc27687edf.text:
## Network Representation Learning and Dynamic Graph Mining

This community centers on learning, comparing, and analyzing complex networks, especially social, heterogeneous, temporal, multilayer, and knowledge graphs. Major themes include node and network embeddings, link prediction, community detection, node classification, role and centrality discovery, graph alignment, similarity search, and network sampling. Applications span fraud and spam detection, money laundering, cyber intrusion, recommendations, social status and tie-strength inference, scholarly and citation analysis, health, and human mobility.

Typical methods include random walks (DeepWalk, Node2Vec, structural and biased walks), matrix factorization, spectral and topological techniques, motif and graphlet analysis, probabilistic and generative graph models, and graph neural networks. Heterogeneous methods frequently exploit metapaths, attributes, side information, multimodal evidence, and attention. Large-scale processing emphasizes MapReduce, distributed and streaming algorithms, approximate counting, graph coarsening, and sublinear sampling.

Recent work increasingly addresses evolving graphs through temporal embeddings, dynamic link prediction, change-point and anomaly detection, and models combining recent changes with global structure. Other trends include robust and adversarial embedding, privacy and de-anonymization, signed and multilayer networks, higher-order structure, interpretable representations, and unified frameworks connecting community detection with representation learning. Evaluation, benchmarking, and principled sampling remain recurring concerns.

titles<=300|df094dab86954f63dc54062f015c.text:
## Graph Data Management and Querying

This community centers on the foundations, systems, and applications of graph data management. Major themes include SPARQL/RDF semantics and optimization; federated, distributed, and cloud-based querying; RDF–property-graph interoperability; graph databases and query languages; and knowledge-graph integration, provenance, and schema evolution.

A substantial theoretical strand studies conjunctive, regular, and context-free path queries, reachability, navigational expressiveness, satisfiability, determinacy, chase termination, finite controllability, and ontology-mediated query answering. Practical work develops join reordering, cardinality estimation, summaries, indexes, partitioning, compression, adaptive storage, incremental view maintenance, and workload-aware optimization. Typical methods include graph summarization and sketches, landmark and labeling indexes, matrix and GPU computation, MapReduce/Spark, relational-algebra translations, benchmarking, and empirical analysis of query logs.

Other recurring topics are streaming and temporal graphs, continuous pattern matching, dynamic shortest paths, subgraph isomorphism, and large-scale graph analytics. Systems address federated endpoints, RDF streams, distributed graph stores, and interactive exploration. Provenance and workflow reproducibility form a parallel theme.

Recent work trends toward unified graph models and algebraic foundations, RDF/property-graph translation, adaptive and learning-guided optimization, contextual and annotated knowledge graphs, natural-language and visual query interfaces, and scalable processing of dynamic, heterogeneous, and billion-node graphs.

titles<=300|19360994186a2520fa333d47546b.text:
## Information Retrieval Ranking, Neural Matching, and Fair Search

This community centers on learning to rank and relevance modeling across web, enterprise, e-commerce, academic, legal, biomedical, mobile, and conversational search. Major themes include ad hoc and passage retrieval, query expansion and reformulation, entity- and knowledge-graph search, personalization, recommendation, and question answering.

Typical methods combine traditional retrieval and term-based techniques—relevance feedback, language models, field weighting, graph methods, hashing, and approximate nearest-neighbor indexing—with neural representations and interaction models. BERT, CNN/RNN architectures, attention, kernel pooling, dual embeddings, listwise and groupwise scoring, and weak or distant supervision are widely used. Online settings employ counterfactual learning, propensity estimation, multileaving, bandits, reinforcement learning, and click-feedback modeling.

A substantial strand addresses evaluation, interpretability, robustness, and efficiency, including axiomatic regularization, explainable ranking, diagnostic tools, fast indexing, and reproducible evaluation. Fairness is increasingly prominent, covering bias in representations and feedback, disparate exposure, diversity, and fairness-aware re-ranking.

Recent work trends toward contextual and conversational search, multi-stage BERT re-ranking, neural–graph integration, personalized product and sponsored search, and learning from noisy or limited supervision. Attention also shifts toward reliable online evaluation and equitable ranking outcomes.

titles<=300|d2c97b08dfee9cf89c36b6bf323b.text:
## Information Retrieval, Scholarly Data, and Knowledge Infrastructures

This community centers on information retrieval (IR) across web, scholarly, library, social-science, and professional-search settings. Major themes include bibliometric-enhanced retrieval; query and term expansion; thesauri, SKOS, classification, knowledge organization systems, and terminology mapping; entity and document ranking; personalization; and exploratory, interactive, and visual search.

A second strong theme is research-data stewardship: dataset discovery and citation, metadata enrichment, reproducibility, digital archives, linked data, and the infrastructures supporting scientific data sharing and reuse. Papers also address database systems for scientific, spatial, XML, and multidimensional data, including distributed and petabyte-scale processing.

Typical methods combine user studies, relevance assessment, click and session-log analysis, test-collection evaluation, bibliometric and informetric analysis, supervised and learning-to-rank models, query-expansion and recommendation techniques, ontological modeling, and visualization. Engineering contributions describe relational, native XML, parallel, federated, and spatial indexing systems.

Recent directions emphasize neural title simplification and deep ranking, personalized and federated search, fair and credible ranking, featured snippets, large-scale professional-network search, linked-data mappings, automated dataset-reference detection, and interactive visual interfaces. Evaluation increasingly considers usefulness, bias, inter-rater agreement, user effort, complex tasks, and the quality and provenance of research data.

titles<=300|0ed129f2c37cba310c1bc49c81f8.text:
## Scalable Search, Analytics, and Social-Web Data Management

This community studies efficient retrieval, querying, and analytics over large, heterogeneous, and evolving data. Major themes include top‑\(k\), skyline, preference, ranking, and similarity queries; OLAP and multidimensional databases; hidden-Web crawling and estimation; graph and social-network analysis; information retrieval; and collaborative tagging, recommendation, and social search.

Typical methods emphasize performance-oriented data structures and systems: compressed bitmap and inverted indexes, variable-byte and Huffman coding, SIMD/vectorized decoding, GPU acceleration, in-memory and distributed execution, caching, sketches, sampling, and approximate algorithms. Work also develops learning-based query planning, probabilistic view-size estimation, geometric and density-based methods, graph centrality and clustering, ontology matching, semantic search, and formal treatments of incomplete data, preferences, and fuzzy summaries.

The community increasingly connects database technology with Web and social applications. Recent directions include scalable approximate nearest-neighbor and cosine search, high-throughput graph and relational analytics, streaming and sliding-window monitoring, hidden-database aggregation, semantic navigation of linked data, and richer collaborative information seeking. Social tagging research has expanded toward influence, attention, expertise, vocabulary evolution, recommendation, privacy, and behavioral modeling, while systems research continues pushing compression and indexing toward billion-scale and interactive workloads.

titles<=300|54df1f7405f15b3f2e738eeebe91.text:
## Scalable, Learned, and Approximate Data Management

This community studies high-performance data systems spanning relational, graph, array, RDF, document, and streaming workloads. Major themes include query optimization and join processing—especially worst-case-optimal, multiway, geometric, factorized, and parallel joins—along with cardinality, cost, resource, and workload estimation. A substantial line of work integrates machine learning into databases through learned indexes, learned optimizers, deep cardinality models, reinforcement-learning-based plan selection, and declarative end-to-end ML systems.

Approximate and progressive analytics are also prominent, using sampling, sketches, wavelets, generative models, probabilistic databases, deterministic error bounds, and visualization-aware techniques. Systems research addresses main-memory and multicore execution, GPUs and reconfigurable hardware, high-throughput ingestion, LSM storage, caching, recovery, concurrency control, distributed transactions, and cloud resource management.

Other recurring applications include graph analytics and RDF, time-series and spatial data, visual exploration, video and IoT monitoring, provenance, and scientific data. Typical methods combine relational algebra, factorization, hypertree decompositions, MapReduce, stream processing, adaptive indexing, code generation, and specialized storage layouts.

Recent directions emphasize learned and autonomous database administration, cross-platform and polystore optimization, approximate query services for cameras and large data, declarative data science, model management, and tighter integration of database engines with deep learning and interactive analytics.

titles<=300|dfecbba69dc6210165af47de7116.text:
## Networks, Opinions, and Graph Signal Dynamics

This community studies how network structure shapes information, beliefs, influence, polarization, and collective behavior. A major theme is opinion dynamics: consensus, disagreement, stubbornness, susceptibility, bounded confidence, biased assimilation, backfire effects, random actions, homophily, and multi-topic or interdependent beliefs. Signed-network research focuses on structural balance, frustration, partial balance, trust–mistrust relations, polarization, and network formation.

Graph signal processing provides a second foundation, including graph Fourier transforms, spectral projectors, graph filters, diffusion distances, smoothness and variation, sampling, reconstruction, localization, and dictionary learning. These tools support community detection, centrality estimation, topology inference, and analysis of spatiotemporal or irregular-network signals.

Typical methods include spectral analysis, Laplacian-based modeling, dynamical systems, Markov and threshold processes, optimization and integer programming, binary programming for frustration, distributed algorithms, random sampling, and inference from consensus or observed signals. Applications include parliamentary votes, Twitter propagation, recommendations, news diversity, cyber-social networks, and influence campaigns.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and multilayer networks, unknown or changing topology, confirmation bias and filter bubbles, personalized recommendation feedback loops, social bots, knowledge segregation, and active control. Work increasingly addresses intervention—leader selection, opinion maximization, polarization mitigation, competing influence investment, and auditing recommendation systems—alongside scalable and inexact spectral algorithms.

titles<=300|1fd08b015deda1b6068f3803d1ec.text:
### Streaming Similarity Search and Join Estimation

This community focuses on similarity operations over continuously arriving, potentially endless data streams. Its main themes include top-\(k\) similarity joins over set streams, streaming similarity self-joins, and estimating the sizes of similarity joins and self-joins in streaming environments.

Typical methods emphasize stream-oriented processing and approximate estimation rather than exhaustive comparison. Locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) is explicitly used for similarity-join size estimation, suggesting hash-based techniques for handling large or continuous data. The work also addresses similarity search over endless streams, including “fishing” for relevant items as data arrives.

Recent directions represented in these papers combine practical streaming search with analytical estimation: systems seek to retrieve the most similar pairs, support self-join queries, and predict join cardinalities under continuous data arrival. Overall, the community moves toward scalable similarity processing that can operate online, limit computation through top-\(k\) retrieval or hashing, and quantify join sizes in dynamic stream settings.

titles<=300|be528ee1b9bc27deba27c8789268.text:
## Web Tables, Dataset Search, and Intelligent Data Access

This community focuses on discovering, extracting, organizing, and exploiting heterogeneous web data—especially HTML tables, datasets, catalogs, and deep-web content. Major themes include dataset and scientific-table search; semantic table retrieval and recommendation; entity and relationship retrieval; table question answering; automatic completion, imputation, and transformation; and data-lake organization and navigation.

Typical methods combine schema and column labels, keyword and semantic similarity search, word/entity embeddings, table and graph representations, knowledge bases, and entity identifiers. Structural techniques include generalized XPath, recursive tree matching, automatic web wrappers, HTML-table extraction, joins, sketches, locality-sensitive hashing, and fusion-based retrieval. Systems also support interactive exploration, aggregate-answer summarization, spreadsheet assistance, and context-aware or explainable recommendation.

Recent directions emphasize moving beyond simple keyword retrieval toward fine-grained table understanding, entity-aware representations, open-domain question answering, and automatic table generation and population. The papers also show increasing attention to scalable discovery across data lakes and the deep web, robust extraction under structural variation, verifiable program-by-example transformations, and intelligent assistance for users navigating, completing, querying, and integrating web data.

titles<=300|657f469acdce9ed65db54340e4f6.text:
### Path-Based Centrality and Randomized Graph Geometry

This community studies graph structure through path-based measures of node importance, distinctiveness, and distance. A central theme is the interpolation between random-walk behavior and shortest-path structure, enabling analyses that balance exploratory diffusion with efficient connectivity. Several papers develop centrality and criticality measures from collections of paths, including a bag-of-paths node criticality measure, distinctiveness centrality for social networks, and two betweenness variants based on randomized shortest paths.

Typical methods define path functionals or probability distributions over paths, then use them to quantify node participation, network brokerage, or structural uniqueness. Randomized shortest paths provide a recurring framework for softening strict shortest-path assumptions while retaining path efficiency. The community also extends these ideas beyond centrality: randomized optimal transport on graphs introduces a broader framework for comparing graph-supported distributions and deriving new distance measures.

Overall, the research trends from classical shortest-path and random-walk metrics toward unified, tunable formulations based on ensembles of paths, with increasing emphasis on transport-based graph geometry and flexible distance definitions.

titles<=300|a01a5f424dc83acec893cc5e9d6a.text:
### Large-Scale Social and Web Network Analysis

This community examines the structure, dynamics, and measurement of online and web-based networks. Its themes include the distribution and dependence of extreme outcomes in network sampling, macroscopic characterization of the Twitter social graph, and practical strategies for networking in online social networks. A complementary focus is data quality and temporal change, represented by *Liverank*, which addresses how to refresh aging datasets.

Typical methods combine large-scale empirical graph analysis with statistical modeling. Studies characterize degree and edge distributions, analyze network structure at the scale of major social platforms, and investigate sampling processes—particularly their extremes and dependencies. Model-based work uses the Buckley–Osthus model and evaluates it empirically against web-host graph observations.

Recent trends emphasize moving beyond static or small-scale network views: analyzing complete large platforms, validating generative models with observed web data, understanding sampling biases and extreme behavior, and maintaining datasets as networks evolve. Overall, the papers connect theoretical network models with practical measurement, platform-scale analysis, and up-to-date data infrastructure.

titles<=300|aca6841c4a462777d4bcbebe6983.text:
## Influence Maximization and Diffusion in Social Networks

This community centers on maximizing, controlling, and measuring information spread in social and interaction networks. Major themes include viral marketing, advertising and coupon allocation, opinion and welfare maximization, misinformation and rumor blocking, competitive or complementary products, immunization, and influence minimization. Papers also study temporal, continuous-time, non-progressive, cumulative, multiplex, signed, heterogeneous, and evolving diffusion models.

Typical methods exploit monotonicity and submodularity through greedy, adaptive-greedy, approximation, and matroid- or budget-constrained optimization. Scalable influence estimation and seed selection use reverse sampling, randomized and coordinated sampling, random walks, centrality, community structure, hop-based heuristics, GPU computation, and distributed algorithms. Other approaches apply robust optimization, reliability and evidence theory, optimal control, causal analysis, representation learning, online learning, bandits, and reinforcement learning.

Recent directions emphasize adaptive decisions under partial or myopic feedback, online and model-free optimization, nonstationary and dynamic networks, sequential and multiphase seeding, propagation-time awareness, and strategic competition. The literature increasingly addresses billion-scale efficiency, exact or near-optimal computation, uncertainty and robustness, privacy-preserving diffusion, fairness across network positions, diversity of seeds and exposure, and heterogeneous user behavior.

titles<=300|de0de050edcfda24bc710eaa886e.text:
## Networked Social Media Mining for Health and Recommendation

This community centers on extracting knowledge from large-scale, heterogeneous digital traces. Major themes include social-media analysis of attitudes toward China, e-cigarette markets, illicit drug use and dealing, drug interactions, and public-health imagery. A related strand studies electronic health records, revealing demographic biases in the administration of known drug–drug interactions.

Network and information-retrieval methods are prominent: distance-closure and semi-metric network models support recommendation, document analysis, and ranking comparison; proximity networks and linear models uncover protein interactions in text. Other approaches include multimodal analysis of images and timelines, hashtag-centered immersive search, archive search and mining, Pinterest-to-Twitter recommendation, and collective document classification using guided self-organization inspired by T-cell regulation. Biologically motivated distributed designs are also applied to adaptive knowledge management.

Recent work trends toward fine-grained, cross-platform, and multimodal mining—especially Instagram, Reddit, and Twitter—for monitoring health risks, substance use, consumer markets, and public opinion. The community increasingly combines network structure with textual, visual, and temporal signals, while emphasizing comparative analysis across regions and populations and identifying bias in data-driven health practices.

titles<=300|47cef4368995d6929eadba4190ce.text:
## Network Diffusion, Epidemics, and Source Inference

This community studies spreading processes—SIS, SIR, SIRS, rumors, computer viruses, information, and socially contagious attributes—on complex, temporal, adaptive, multilayer, and socio-technical networks. Major themes include epidemic thresholds and transient dynamics; containment through curing, vaccination, awareness, edge removal, protection, and resource allocation; network dismantling and robustness against attacks; and diffusion-source localization.

Typical methods combine random-matrix, spectral, Laplacian, and centrality analyses with message passing, percolation mappings, moment closure, exact Markov models, phase-type transmissions, and weighted-shortest-path simulations. Optimization is addressed through convex frameworks, approximation algorithms, greedy strategies, dynamic policies, genetic algorithms, and budget analyses. Statistical inference and learning methods recover sources, propagation paths, graph structure, or mixtures from cascades, sparse observations, timestamps, queries, or noisy data.

Recent work emphasizes temporal and adaptive contacts, external agents and awareness, uncertainty and bounded susceptibility, multiple or mixed epidemics, and robust source estimation under incomplete information. Privacy and adversarial settings include rumor obfuscation, untruthful answers, and hiding infection sources. Additional trends connect epidemic modeling with cyber-physical self-healing, sensor and observer placement, real-world diffusion networks, and topology inference from limited cascade data.

titles<=300|30358994b7989b8085a5ceda4920.text:
## Scientometrics, Research Assessment, and Academic Inequality

This community focuses on measuring and governing research performance, especially in Italy and other national higher-education systems. Major themes include university and researcher productivity, rankings, research funding, national assessment exercises (particularly Italy’s VQR and scientific habilitation), academic recruitment and careers, and university–industry technology transfer. A substantial strand examines gender, age, seniority, academic rank, migration, nepotism, and regional inequalities, including the North–South divide.

Typical methods are bibliometric indicators (citations, h- and g-indexes, highly cited papers, field-standardized impact, publication counts), fractional and order-sensitive authorship measures, network analysis of collaborations and editorial boards, statistical and stochastic models, DEA and other efficiency analyses, clustering, sensitivity analyses, funnel plots, and author-name disambiguation. Many studies compare bibliometrics with peer review and evaluate ranking robustness under alternative citation windows, scaling factors, and counting rules.

Recent directions emphasize uncertainty and distortion in performance evaluation, citation gaming and opportunistic behavior, the effects of assessment on research practices, interdisciplinarity and diversification, international collaboration, and the role of star scientists. Open scholarly infrastructure and data—including OpenCitations, COCI, CROCI, Google Scholar, and open researcher-evaluation experiments—also become increasingly prominent.

titles<=300|9fddc72421f86e05dd8191160a80.text:
## Geospatial Social Media Analytics for Urban and Crisis Intelligence

This community centers on extracting geographic, temporal, behavioral, and social signals from user-generated data. Major themes include Twitter geolocation and home-location inference; human mobility, migration, commuting, and urban functional regions; spatial interaction and place networks; business-site and route recommendation; and the use of social media for disaster response, emergency awareness, and public health. Additional topics address food and location-based recommendations, urban sentiment and wellbeing, demographic and latent-attribute inference, political communication, social influence, and media polarization.

Typical methods combine convolutional, hierarchical, and graph neural networks with grid-based classification, text and hashtag analysis, ontology and knowledge-based extraction, tensor factorization, topic modeling, embeddings, probabilistic inference, and ensemble learning. Network analysis, trajectory mining and compression, density-based spatiotextual clustering, relational-event and dynamic-network models, optimization, and scalable distributed processing are also prominent. Researchers frequently fuse Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, Flickr, Yelp, check-ins, mobile-phone records, transactions, satellite imagery, and weather data.

Recent work trends toward high-resolution and real-time inference, multimodal crisis analytics, uncertainty and annotation-bias modeling, privacy-aware geolocation, knowledge-enriched recommendation, and deep learning for large-scale mobility and event forecasting.

titles<=300|bfa7f879d4a43301aeaa7420130f.text:
### Structural Balance and Frustration in Signed Networks

This community studies how positive and negative relationships organize signed networks and how closely those networks approach structural balance. A central theme is measuring imbalance through the **frustration index** (also called the **line index of balance**) and through broader notions of partial balance. The papers examine both theoretical measures and applications to signed social networks, including voting relationships in the European Parliament.

Typical methods are computational and combinatorial. Researchers formulate balance and frustration as graph-partitioning problems, use binary and integer programming to obtain exact solutions, and develop modelling and computational procedures for evaluating these measures. Another methodological perspective evaluates balance through the network’s simple cycles, while partitioning provides a way to interpret the role of negative links.

Recent work trends toward exact optimization and computationally tractable measurement, complementing earlier or broader applications of structural balance. Overall, the community connects formal balance indices with empirical social-network analysis and political data, emphasizing how negative ties influence community structure and the detection of imbalance.

titles<=300|32209690aafd1a4eac72e3b1065a.text:
## Dynamic Topic Modeling and Social Sensing

This community centers on extracting evolving knowledge from large, time-stamped text and social-media streams. A major theme is topic modeling: latent Dirichlet allocation and extensions address dynamics, hierarchy, authorship, arbitrary features, limited attention, coupled modalities, and continuous time. These models support timeline construction, scientific-literature mapping, topic bundling, recommendation, and semantic annotation.

A second theme is event and trend intelligence. Researchers detect, retrieve, summarize, and forecast breaking news, scheduled events, sub-events, popularity, and geographically localized phenomena using Twitter, images, knowledge graphs, and interaction networks. Social sensing is widely applied to disasters, sentiment, public opinion, and infectious-disease surveillance, including influenza, dengue, Ebola, and autism-related analysis.

Typical methods combine Bayesian generative models, tensor/matrix factorization, graph and latent-space modeling, incremental machine learning, neural embeddings, deep learning, fuzzy logic, ontologies, and statistical forecasting. Evaluation includes ranking, validation, sensitivity analysis, and user-in-the-loop review.

Recent directions emphasize scalable and real-time inference, continuous-time and temporally evolving communities, cross-source integration of news and social data, semantic filtering, and actionable decision support. Parallel work improves information retrieval, query expansion, summarization, hypothesis generation, and interpretable bibliometric analysis.

titles<=300|e1dbcdbd0a8081f49438326fc03a.text:
## Network Representation Learning and Analysis in Dynamic Social Graphs

This community focuses on learning, measuring, and exploiting structure in large, heterogeneous, and evolving networks. Major themes include node, edge, and whole-network representation learning; link prediction and relationship profiling; community detection, role identification, and centrality; graph similarity and alignment; and applications to recommendation, fraud and anomaly detection, cybersecurity, finance, scholarly data, and social media.

Typical methods span random walks (DeepWalk, node2vec, struc2vec, RiWalk), matrix factorization and spectral techniques, latent-space and stochastic block models, graph grammars, motif and graphlet analysis, and sampling-based estimation. Increasingly, graph convolutional, attention, recurrent, variational, and adversarial neural networks support heterogeneous, attributed, multimodal, and knowledge-graph representation learning. Researchers also study scalable counting, distributed processing, graph coarsening, sparsification, and external-memory algorithms.

Recent trends emphasize temporal and event-based modeling, including dynamic embeddings, change-point detection, temporal motifs, link streams, and models incorporating recent changes or temporal smoothness. Other growing directions include robustness and attacks on graph embeddings, privacy, bias and missing data, explainable anomaly detection, higher-order and signed/multiplex networks, and unified frameworks combining community structure with representation learning.

titles<=300|3ab0911e113f6cdd0a10c2d89d70.text:
### Social Media Mining, Search, and Community Analysis

This community studies how social-media data can reveal identities, interests, attitudes, expertise, and harmful activity. Major themes include identifying gang members on Twitter, analyzing attitudes toward China at state and individual levels, characterizing communities through social identity and cohesion, and tracking illicit drug dealing and abuse on Instagram. Other work addresses public-health image analysis, user expertise through taglines, and cross-platform recommendation, such as Pinterest boards for Twitter users.

Typical methods combine large-scale social-media mining with semantic, network, and content analysis. Word embeddings enhance profile identification, while multimodal analysis integrates images and text for drug and health research. Hashtag-centered immersive search and digital-archive mining systems emphasize interactive information discovery. Several studies also develop or assess retrieval quality, including methods for comparing search-engine rankings.

Overall, the collection moves from detecting users and communities toward richer, fine-grained interpretation of multimodal content and social context. It also highlights a growing emphasis on user-centered search, recommendation, and cross-platform analysis.

titles<=300|6c8eb275dba147e2f5eb066e06e7.text:
## Scholarly Information, Reuse, and Recommendation

This community focuses on computational infrastructure for scholarly communication. Major themes include extracting and interlinking metadata, entities, citations, and author-contribution information; assessing semantic publishing quality; and building knowledge graphs such as the ACL Anthology miner. A second strong theme is research-paper recommendation, including repository and digital-library systems, mind-map-based user modeling, recommendation APIs, related-article datasets, and operational “recommendations as a service” platforms.

Typical methods combine OCR and information-extraction pipelines with citation and reference parsing, rule-based and machine-learning models, retraining comparisons, and meta-learning for parser selection. Large-scale processing relies on Apache Hadoop, while graph mining, bibliographic matching, and massive text corpora support analysis. Text reuse, boilerplate removal, plagiarism, duplicate or contradictory information, and citation-sentence reuse are studied through corpus-scale matching and similarity analysis.

Recent directions emphasize real-world recommender deployment, scalable datasets, and more nuanced evaluation. These include choice overload, position bias, temporal effects, expert-versus-search rankings, and partially randomized result ordering. Overall, the work moves from isolated extraction and ranking techniques toward integrated, user-aware, bias-conscious scholarly discovery systems.

titles<=300|31fa06d23f0824b993a3d84f04d0.text:
## Scalable, Fair, and Socially Enriched Data Management

This community studies scalable systems for searching, querying, indexing, and analyzing massive, heterogeneous data. Major themes include scientific and spatial databases (astronomy, pathology, geographic and array data), hidden-web and distributed databases, graph and social-network analytics, and OLAP-style aggregation. A parallel focus concerns social tagging, collaborative search, expertise location, recommender systems, and user behavior in microblogging and folksonomy networks.

Typical methods include top-*k*, skyline, preference, similarity, and probabilistic queries; crawling and query reranking; clustering, frequent-subgraph mining, ontology matching, and density-based analysis; and relational, graph, XML, and multidimensional data models. Substantial systems work targets compressed bitmap and inverted indexes, integer encoding, hashing, spatial structures, approximate nearest-neighbor search, and efficient set intersection. SIMD/vectorization, GPUs, in-memory execution, distributed dataflows, caching, and adaptive processing are recurring acceleration techniques.

Recent work increasingly addresses fairness, diversity, disparate exposure, demographic satisfaction, and privacy in ranking and recommendation. Other emerging directions include antidote data, image-based fairness representations, collaborative information seeking, real-time and low-latency scientific analysis, exascale metadata management, trillion-cell analytics, and graph-based approximate search. Overall, the field connects database performance engineering with responsible, socially aware information access.

titles<=300|68b06b875f604c9c5f32b7895de8.text:
## Complex Networks for Knowledge, Collaboration, and Software

This community studies social, information, scientific, and software systems as evolving complex networks. Major themes include community structure and group detection; interdisciplinarity and knowledge organization; citation, collaboration, and web-link evolution; software architecture; and social interaction in Wikipedia and online communities. Several works examine conflict, disagreement, norms, status, collective memory, organizational routines, and power in networked groups, including healthcare and nonprofit collaboration.

Typical methods include network construction and statistical comparison, centrality and preferential-attachment analysis, community-detection algorithms, network sampling and simplification, citation and link-structure analysis, and longitudinal, multilevel, and cross-time modeling. Researchers also use sequence analysis, finite-state-machine models of interaction, language clustering, entity-based impact metrics, and frameworks for mapping knowledge structures.

Recent directions emphasize dynamics rather than static topology: evolving collaboration and citation networks, changing Wikipedia norms and editing behavior, temporal disagreement, and the dynamicity of social networks. The work increasingly connects structural network measures with interdisciplinarity, impact, collective behavior, and real-world organizational processes, while addressing multilingual data, database consistency, and robust methodological comparison.

titles<=300|2140b29746789b2fd7d70a6ecfee.text:
### Cross-Modal Hashing and Multimodal Retrieval

This community focuses on efficient cross-modal information retrieval, especially learning compact binary representations that align heterogeneous data such as images and text. A central theme is preserving cross-modal correlations while enabling fast indexing and retrieval over hashing-based datasets.

Typical methods include discrete latent factor models, supervised matrix factorization, and composite correlation quantization. These approaches learn shared latent structures, unified hash codes, or quantized representations, often incorporating supervision and modality correlations to improve semantic consistency. Research also addresses the systems side of retrieval through effective and efficient indexing strategies for cross-modal hashing databases.

Recent work trends toward jointly optimizing hashing functions and unified hash codes, rather than treating representation learning and code generation separately. Another emerging direction is the use of graph convolutional networks for modeling text, suggesting greater attention to structured semantic information within individual modalities and its role in cross-modal alignment. Overall, the papers reflect a progression from factorization- and matrix-based hashing toward more integrated, quantization-aware, and graph-based methods aimed at accurate and scalable multimodal search.

titles<=300|c17649e7a4397eb6eb965c92e5aa.text:
### Natural-Language Interfaces and Query Understanding

This community focuses on making structured databases accessible through natural-language interaction. Core themes include bridging the semantic gap between user language and SQL through query-log analysis, supporting knowledge-rich queries over biological databases, and developing end-to-end neural interfaces. Several works address how users discover and express query intent: example-driven abductive reasoning, semantic similarity, and dual specification for expressive SQL queries.

The papers also examine alternative interaction and presentation mechanisms, including preview-table generation for entity graphs and queried units (“QUnits”) for database search. A comparative survey consolidates recent approaches and situates the field’s broader design space. Complementing system-building work, the study of reverse-engineering complexity for conjunctive queries provides theoretical grounding for reconstructing queries from observed behavior or specifications.

Overall, the research moves from manually engineered semantic mappings and log-based techniques toward neural, example-driven, and richer specification-based interfaces. At the same time, it increasingly combines natural-language understanding with interactive examples, structured knowledge, graph-oriented previews, and formal analysis of query reconstruction and complexity.

titles<=300|e175091ed836bfd57905165393b6.text:
## Data Integration, Uncertainty, and Human-Assisted Database Intelligence

This community centers on making heterogeneous, incomplete, inconsistent, and uncertain data usable for reliable querying and analysis. Major themes include probabilistic databases; data fusion and truth discovery; entity resolution and matching dependencies; integrity constraints, repairs, and consistent query answering; provenance, causality, diagnosis, and explanations; ontology-mediated access and schema mappings; and crowdsourcing for cleaning, labeling, spatial tasks, and collective decisions.

Typical methods combine database theory—Datalog, the chase, conjunctive-query analysis, dependency axiomatizations, repairs, view updates, and complexity dichotomies—with probabilistic inference, Bayesian and Markov models, knowledge compilation, provenance circuits, and approximate or anytime algorithms. Systems work frequently targets scalability through parallel databases, RDBMS-backed inference, graph partitioning, probabilistic signatures, active learning, and human–machine cooperation.

Recent directions emphasize practical, holistic data quality: probabilistic and deep-learning-based cleaning, transfer learning for entity resolution, global-constraint matching, selective anomaly detection, and systems such as Holoclean, Bayeswipe, and ErBlox. Other emerging trends include cloud-aware workflow reproducibility, fine-grained completeness and trust assessment, knowledge-base and linked-data integration, real-time and mobile crowdsourcing, and causal or provenance-based explanations for query behavior and data reliability.

titles<=300|85cdca8ea1ed1f0c693e01b72b0a.text:
### Network-Based Discovery Across Text, Health, and Recommender Systems

This community applies network analysis to uncover indirect relationships and hidden structure in complex data. A central theme is **semi-metric behavior**—relationships that are more efficiently expressed through intermediary nodes than direct links—studied in complex networks, document networks, and recommender systems. These works use distance closures and network-based recommendation to identify meaningful associations beyond explicit similarity.

A second theme is **text-centered knowledge extraction**. Methods include word-proximity networks, novel linear models, and guided self-organization inspired by T-cell cross-regulation dynamics for collective classification of documents. Biologically motivated distributed designs further connect adaptive knowledge management with decentralized learning and organization.

Applications increasingly target **biomedical and public-health intelligence**. Network analysis of Instagram timelines is used to monitor potential drug interactions and adverse reactions, while analysis of electronic health records examines demographic biases in administering known drug–drug interactions. Overall, the papers trend from foundational network measures and biologically inspired adaptive systems toward practical, large-scale recommendation, information extraction, pharmacovigilance, and fairness analysis.

titles<=300|c2b0007d10966ece90ecb6124693.text:
### Network Science, Wikipedia Mining, and Social-System Dynamics

This community centers on complex-network analysis, especially PageRank, Google and reduced Google matrices, centrality, spectral properties, graphons, and network evolution. A major application domain is Wikipedia: studies rank articles, universities, people, and cultures; uncover geopolitical, historical, linguistic, and cross-cultural links; examine gender bias, editing behavior, norms, collaboration, and collective memory; and build Wikidata/DBpedia-based scientometric resources.

Other themes include social-media diffusion and political communication, breaking-news detection, online disagreement and petitions, cultural boundaries, healthcare and software collaboration networks, citation databases, hiring and prestige networks, urban street systems, Bitcoin, and scientific collaboration. Gender inequality and representation recur across Wikipedia, academia, fiction, and online platforms.

Typical methods include Google-matrix and reduced-Google-matrix spectral analysis, PageRank variants and personalized/seeded ranking, centrality comparison and stability analysis, community detection and clustering, graphons, network sampling and simplification, temporal and multilayer analysis, sequence analysis, statistical/text summarization, sentiment and lexical features, and large-scale data mining from Wikipedia and social media.

Recent directions emphasize dynamic and longitudinal networks, cross-cultural and multilingual analysis, uncertainty-aware graph methods, scalable urban-network tooling, richer entity and knowledge-graph metrics, and computational studies of collective behavior, inequality, and information diffusion.

titles<=300|3bd17ede605bd58b83d2c69ac327.text:
## Web-Based Knowledge, Search, and Scholarly Metrics

This community connects information retrieval, web knowledge organization, and research evaluation. Major themes include comparisons of Google Scholar, Web of Science, and Scopus; citation coverage, h-index and journal rankings; open-access measurement; and scholarly assessment. A parallel stream develops Wikipedia- and Wiktionary-based resources, including relational/XML databases, multilingual ontology matching, thesauri, categories, tag hierarchies, and entity ranking.

Typical methods are large-scale empirical comparisons, citation and webometric analyses, search-engine evaluation with representative queries, user studies of simple and complex tasks, and graph-based ranking using PageRank, HITS, influence networks, and community detection. Other approaches include query expansion, faceted classification, native XML retrieval, entity linking and disambiguation, recommendation, learning-to-rank, and personalized or federated search.

Recent work emphasizes personalized talent and expertise search in professional networks, multilingual and cross-platform entity ranking, deep ranking models, and mining large social-network datasets. Increasing attention is also given to the limitations and manipulation of scholarly indicators, Google Scholar’s coverage and changing status, Goodhart’s law, open-access mandates, and fair or quality-aware ranking of web and Wikipedia content.

titles<=300|40ab729c9f715cf087949081ffec.text:
## Opinion, Influence, and Diffusion in Dynamic Social Networks

This community studies how beliefs, opinions, social power, and information evolve over networked interactions.
