This community focuses on improving database efficiency, scalability, and accessibility across specialized and general-purpose workloads. Key themes include efficient indexing and query processing, analytical storage, distributed data management, and natural-language access to databases.

Typical methods include exploiting data structure and domain properties: geometric properties are used to efficiently identify shareable vehicles, while inverted-index compression reduces storage and retrieval costs. A computational model for analytic column stores emphasizes principled understanding of column-oriented analytical execution. AstroServ applies distributed database techniques to serve large-scale astronomical data throughout its full life cycle. Survey work on natural-language database interfaces compares approaches for making database querying more accessible to users.

Recent trends point toward systems designed for growing data volumes and increasingly diverse users. Research combines low-level optimization—such as compression, indexing, and column-store modeling—with system-level concerns including distributed service, end-to-end data lifecycle support, and natural-language interaction. Overall, the papers reflect a movement from isolated database components toward scalable, specialized, and more usable data-management systems.

titles<=300|3cb9c3537d05cab977570eec162d.text:
## Community Report: Semantic Keyphrase Extraction and Privacy-Aware Summarization

This community focuses on extracting concise, informative representations from text and using them for indexing, ranking, categorization, and summarization. Keyphrase research spans automatic term extraction, semantic relatedness, semantic connectivity, semantic roles, medical-document processing, and neural-network approaches. Several works investigate graph-based methods, including personalized PageRank, multipartite graphs, folksonomy graphs, and adaptations of Folkrank for tag recommendation.

Summarization is another major theme, covering single- and multi-document settings, hierarchical aggregation, important-passage retrieval, and privacy-preserving summarization and retrieval. Related work addresses automatic title construction, dependency-tree title generation, and keyphrase clouds for broadcast news.

Typical methods combine linguistic structure and statistical ranking with graph propagation, word embeddings, denoising, and unsupervised or hybrid extraction. Evaluation and modeling of relevance–diversity trade-offs also appear, as does analysis of unstructured data for conceptual representation.

Recent directions represented in the community include neural and embedding-based extraction, richer semantic signals, scalable multi-document and news applications, and privacy preservation. These developments extend traditional keyphrase and summarization systems toward more context-aware, diverse, and deployment-oriented information access.

titles<=300|106496418f145f7f2d6595929817.text:
### Structural Balance and Frustration in Signed Networks

This community studies structural balance in signed networks, with particular attention to measuring imbalance and quantifying the minimum conflict required to achieve balance. Core topics include partial balance, the frustration index, and the line index of balance, alongside broader structural analysis and applications to signed social networks.

Typical methods are computational and optimization-based. Several works formulate frustration or balance measures through binary or integer programming, including exact algorithms and integer-programming optimization. Other approaches evaluate balance through simple cycles, while modelling and computational studies examine the behavior and computation of these measures. The literature also connects theoretical balance concepts with practical analysis of social networks.

A notable trend is the movement from general balance theory toward precise, computable indices and scalable analytical procedures. Exact optimization, cycle-based evaluation, and modelling studies complement foundational and application-oriented work. Overall, the community combines mathematical characterization, algorithmic computation, and empirical application to understand how positive and negative relationships organize network structure.

titles<=300|7b5dd9a3f13b8b4af5febf6e1ad5.text:
## Dynamic Network Representation and Graph Mining

This community focuses on analyzing, modeling, and learning from large, heterogeneous, attributed, signed, and temporal networks. Major themes include node and network representation learning; link prediction; community detection and role discovery; graph similarity, alignment, and classification; anomaly, fraud, spam, and money-laundering detection; and recommendation and social-network analysis. Knowledge graphs, citation networks, online social networks, financial transactions, and information networks are recurring application domains.

Typical methods combine random walks, matrix factorization, graph kernels, spectral and curvature-based measures, probabilistic graph models, stochastic blockmodels, graph grammars, and sampling algorithms. More recent work emphasizes graph neural networks, graph attention, multimodal and content-aware embeddings, meta-paths, temporal motifs, dynamic embeddings, and inductive learning. Scalable computation is central, with MapReduce, GPU and distributed algorithms for triangle, motif, graphlet, centrality, and similarity estimation.

Recent trends include modeling continuous-time and evolving networks, preserving both local and global or structural information, representing multiple social contexts and roles, robust and adversarial graph learning, privacy and sampling bias, and principled evaluation of embeddings and link-prediction systems.

titles<=300|5d831f07801c10b224962b70f760.text:
### Cross-Modal Hashing for Efficient Semantic Retrieval

This community focuses on cross-modal and cross-media retrieval, especially learning compact binary representations for large-scale image–text and multimodal search. Core themes include shared semantic spaces, unified hash codes across modalities, discriminative representation learning, and efficient indexing and ranking.

Methods span shallow and deep approaches. Matrix factorization and latent-factor models learn shared modality structure, while quantization, decorrelation, and cluster-aware losses improve code quality and retrieval efficiency. Supervised methods use labels, correlations, or triplet objectives; other work explores unsupervised learning through coupled CycleGAN networks. Deep architectures jointly learn hashing functions and unified codes, with fusion networks and graph convolutional networks modeling multimodal or textual structure. Correlation alignment is also used to bridge modality distributions, including for cross-modal event retrieval.

Recent directions emphasize scalable and adaptive retrieval: query-adaptive code ranking, efficient indexing, and composite correlation quantization. The field is also moving toward richer semantic modeling, combining deep representations, graph-based text modeling, modality fusion, and distribution alignment rather than relying solely on fixed binary-code objectives.

titles<=300|203d5cbbf4d836ca4619a7844d23.text:
### Neural Graph and Capsule Methods for Structured Text Understanding

This community focuses on extracting and organizing semantic relations from text, with applications to knowledge graphs, large-scale multilabel classification, and search recommendation. A central theme is addressing long-tail relations and complex label structures through graph-aware representations: knowledge graph embeddings and graph convolutional networks support long-tail relation extraction, while hierarchical taxonomy modeling improves multilabel prediction.

Typical methods combine neural encoders with explicit relational structure. Attention mechanisms identify informative contextual features, and capsule networks with dynamic routing model relation-specific patterns. Ensemble learning and adaptive boosting are used to improve the robustness of neural relation extraction. These techniques extend beyond extraction itself: context-aware deep models apply semantic understanding to entity recommendation in search systems.

Overall, the work trends toward integrating attention, graph convolution, capsule architectures, and hierarchical taxonomies rather than relying on conventional flat classifiers. The emphasis is on scalability, handling imbalanced or long-tail relations, exploiting contextual information, and improving generalization through ensembles and structured representations.

titles<=300|0c946e3f1bb1a467a0fdd76a779d.text:
### Knowledge Organization Systems for the Semantic Web

This community studies how information objects, concepts, and relationships should be represented in machine-processable knowledge organization systems (KOS). Major themes include ontological approaches to identifying information carriers, the design choices underlying SKOS, and the relationship between SKOS concepts and natural-language concepts. Several papers examine RDF literals, attributes, catalog structures, and the implications for information visualization.

A second focus is the transformation of library, archive, and museum metadata into linked data. This includes modeling repositories of theses and dissertations for the Web of Data, examining the practical use of linked data, and assessing the conversion of established resources such as LCSH into SKOS.

Typical methods are conceptual and ontological analysis, literature review, comparative examination of concepts and relations, practical modeling studies, and empirical investigation of SKOS vocabulary quality. The literature also considers what scholarly information should be preserved and identifies gaps in preservation practices.

Recent directions emphasize semantic-Web interoperability, greater machine processability, reuse of legacy vocabularies, improved quality detection in SKOS, and rethinking how catalogs and knowledge structures are represented and visualized.

titles<=300|a59a712580c9164df24e3cb133a4.text:
### Scholarly Discovery, Recommendation, and Fair Evaluation

This community focuses on improving scholarly information access through recommender systems, search ranking, and semantic infrastructures. Major themes include related-article and research-paper recommendation, repository and digital-library recommenders, user modeling, preference elicitation, and recommender deployment in academic settings. Several works address scientific knowledge organization through author-contribution extraction, metadata extraction, citation matching, duplicate and contradictory information detection, semantic interlinking, and knowledge-graph construction (including ACL and NLP literature).

Typical methods combine information extraction, keyphrases, terms, and document embeddings; bibliographic and citation parsing; graph mining; and large-scale distributed processing with Apache Hadoop. Recommender research evaluates ranking functions, position bias, choice overload, expert agreement, temporal effects, and practical engagement metrics. User studies, online evaluations, and large datasets—including a 94-million-record related-article dataset—support these assessments.

A strong recent direction is toward more reliable and responsible evaluation: fairness and differential satisfaction across demographics, attention allocation, partially randomized rankings, counterfactual learning-to-rank, active sampling, and unbiased comparative evaluation. Meta-learning is increasingly used for per-instance algorithm selection and parser recommendation. Overall, the field is moving from handcrafted or isolated systems toward scalable, adaptive, semantically enriched, and explicitly fair scholarly discovery.

titles<=300|03bbba726d3eb101ee5b6f43999d.text:
### Deep Multimodal Learning for Music Understanding

This community studies semantic understanding and retrieval of music through complementary modalities, especially lyrics, audio, and neural measures. A central theme is genre classification from lyrics, with hierarchical and self-attentive architectures used to identify informative textual features. These classifiers also support content-based and transparent music recommendation.

Another major direction is cross-modal representation learning: joint embeddings and deep correlation learning connect audio and lyrics to enable music retrieval across modalities. The methods emphasize deep neural networks, attention mechanisms, shared or aligned representations, and content-driven recommendation rather than relying solely on metadata.

Recent work moves beyond explicit audio–text relationships toward deeper modeling of music semantics. In particular, EEG regularizers introduce neural signals as an additional constraint for learning representations that may better reflect human perceptual or cognitive responses. Overall, the research progresses from modality-specific lyric classification toward multimodal alignment, interpretable recommendation, and cognitively informed semantic representations.

titles<=300|fa0ef493f5d7fc398cb73d8d6ea3.text:
## Dynamic Graph Analytics and Utility-Aware Pattern Mining

This community combines scalable graph algorithms with temporal, multilayer, and sequence analytics. A major theme is efficient reachability and distance querying in large or dynamic graphs, including shortest paths, point-to-point distances, latencies, and small-world queries. Typical methods use landmark and label indexing, hop doubling, distance sketches, pruning, hub acceleration, reachability oracles, and distributed or vertex-centric computation.

A second theme concerns temporal network modeling and analysis. Stream and link-stream formalisms, time-varying graphs, temporal indicators, centrality, path queries, and algebraic or semiring-based approaches support analysis of evolving interactions. Multilayer models are applied to movie scripts, social networks, and dynamic centralities.

The community also develops sequence and episode mining methods, emphasizing utility rather than frequency. Work addresses closed and simultaneous episodes, subsequence constraints, individualized or item-specific thresholds, uncertain data, privacy, and multidimensional or complex sequences. Parallel, MapReduce, and scalable analytics are recurring implementation strategies.

Applications include opinion spreading, social influence, trust-aware recommendation, movie prediction, mailing lists, hospitals, knowledge mobilization, and scientific networks. Recent emphasis trends toward streaming and multilayer data, dynamic query processing, window analytics, uncertainty and privacy, and more personalized utility-driven discovery.

titles<=300|757f28f6442719d442ebe1b33224.text:
### Spatial, Networked, and Reflexive Mapping of Science

This community studies how scholarly knowledge and scientific communities can be represented, interpreted, and evaluated. Its main themes include spatialised bibliometrics, mapping subsets of scholarly information, exploring interdisciplinary landscapes, and assembling networks of communities at different sizes and levels of specificity. The papers also extend these approaches to urban theory, suggesting that bibliometric and network perspectives can support reflection on broader theoretical fields.

Typical methods are spatialised indicators, bibliometric mapping, network construction, and analysis of scientific communities and their relationships. Attention is given not only to identifying structures in scholarly production, but also to how those structures should be interpreted.

A recent trend is toward more contextual and reflexive forms of science mapping. Rather than relying solely on aggregate measures, the work emphasizes spatial dimensions, varying analytical scales, interdisciplinarity, and the use of indicators to empower open science. Overall, the community moves from descriptive mapping toward networked, spatially aware, and critically informed tools for understanding scientific communication.

titles<=300|d0b44986a4a06a5fc91a20f61d5b.text:
## Temporal Graphs, Scalable Queries, and Utility-Aware Network Mining

This community centers on algorithms and applications for large, dynamic, and temporally structured networks. A major theme is efficient reachability, shortest-path, distance, and latency querying, including labeling schemes, landmark indices, distance sketches, oracles, hub acceleration, pruning, and distributed or vertex-centric computation.  

Temporal-network research develops link streams, stream graphs, multilayer and weighted/directed models, time-varying graphs, aggregation methods, temporal indicators, centralities, and algebraic or semiring-based analysis. These models support recommendations, trust analysis, IP-traffic outlier detection, hospital-contact studies, mailing-list dynamics, and cryptocurrency interactions.  

A second substantial theme is utility-oriented sequential and episode mining. Work addresses closed and constrained episodes, high-utility and occupancy patterns, individualized or varied thresholds, correlated and uncertain data, privacy, multidimensional sequences, and parallel or projection-based mining.  

Other studies analyze narrative and social structures, extracting character networks from books, films, television, and games, and applying them to genre classification, plot smoothing, cast-size modeling, sentiment-based recommendation, and predicting fictional deaths. Opinion spreading, dynamic monopolies, scientific selection, and information emergence extend the community toward diffusion and evolutionary network processes.  

Recent directions emphasize temporal and multilayer representations, scalable distributed analytics, query optimization, and richer utility-aware mining beyond simple frequency.
